Virtual Reality in forensic and legal Psychology: Emerging Methods and Applications
Co-chair(s) Prof. Dr. Martin Rettenberger (Kriminologische Zentralstelle (KrimZ))
Chair(s) Dr. Barbara Bergmann (Universität Bonn)
Room: Workshop 0
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Fachgruppensymposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

This symposium brings together five contributions that demonstrate how virtual reality (VR) can advance both research and applied practice in forensic and legal psychology by combining experimental control with ecological validity. Jean-Louis van Gelder presents the MAXLab_ABISS scenario set, a collection of immersive 360° VR environments designed to study aggressive intentions and bystander decision-making. Judith Iffland applies one of the MAXLAb_ABISS scenarios to validate Criteria-Based Content Analysis and mnemonic consistency approaches in a female sample. Renate Volbert and colleagues introduce ViContact 2.0, a multimethod VR-based training system aimed at improving professional child interviewing in cases of suspected sexual abuse. The final talks by Ulrike Stühler and Bastian Nau then extend the focus onto eyewitness memory and testimony within different VR-paradigms.

Using virtual reality to study aggressive and bystander decision-making: The MAXLab_ABISS scenario set
Prof. Dr. Jean-Louis van Gelder | Max Planck Institute for the Study of Crime, Security and Law
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Jean-Louis van Gelder | Max Planck Institute for the Study of Crime, Security and Law

Studying violent behavior and responses to aggression poses a variety of challenges for researchers. Field studies, for example, often face threats to internal validity. Laboratory studies and written vignettes, in contrast, tend to suffer from low ecological validity. Ultimately, the lab offers only a faint reflection of the chaotic and emotionally “hot” circumstances under which violence and aggression typically occur. An alternative approach that combines the controlled conditions of the laboratory with a relatively high degree of ecological validity is virtual reality (VR), which enables the use of context-rich environments fully under researcher control. In this talk, I will present the MAXLab_ABISS scenario set, a free resource that leverages immersive 360° VR scenarios to study aggressive intentions and bystander decision-making. I provide an overview of the scenario set, explain its diverse potential applications, and present recent empirical findings. While acknowledging the inherent limitations of the 360° VR methodology, the findings underscore the promise of VR as a tool for bridging laboratory research on violence and aggression with real-world experiences.

Validating Statement Validity Methods using an immersive VR sexual harassment scenario in adult female samples
Dr. Judith Iffland | MSH Medical School Hamburg
Show details
Author:
Dr. Judith Iffland | MSH Medical School Hamburg

Verbal content analyses to differentiate truthful and fabricated statements, such as the Criteria-Based Content Analysis (CBCA), are used in lie detection research as well as in current practice to assess the credibility of statements in criminal court proceedings. Meta-analyses demonstrate the validity of verbal content analyses above chance, especially in field studies, but the traditional research paradigms usually lack either ecological or internal validity. Furthermore, ethical limitations of creating situations resembling sexual victimization in the laboratory have been discussed. In the lecture, the use of the MPI “MAXLab_ABISS” immersive virtual reality sexual harassment scenario in the current DFG project “Empirical Evidence of Statement Validity Methods: Analyzing Mnemonic Consistency and Criteria-Based Content Analysis Using Virtual Reality” is presented involving the validation of the CBCA and Arntzen’s theory of differential mnemonic consistency. Results from the pilot study are being presented as well as the applicability of the “MAXLab_ABISS” software in a female sample.

ViContact 2.0: A Multimethod VR-Based Training System to Improve Professional Child Interviewing in Cases of Suspected Sexual Abuse
Prof. Dr. Renate Volbert | Psychologische Hochschule Berlin
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Renate Volbert | Psychologische Hochschule Berlin
Elsa Gewehr | Macromedia University of Applied Sciences Berlin
Anett Tamm | Psychologische Hochschule Berlin
Herrmann Barbe | Universitätsmedizin Göttingen
Niels Krause | Psychologische Hochschule Berlin
Frieda Mensing | Europa Universität Flensburg
Marie Merschhemke | Europa Universität Flensburg
Jürgen Müller | Universitätsmedizin Göttingen
Simone Pülschen | Europa Universität Flensburg
Bruno Siegel | Universitätsmedizin Göttingen
Peter Fromberger | Universitätsmedizin Göttingen

ViContact 2.0 is a multimethod interactive training system designed to support professionals in conducting conversations with children in cases of suspected sexual abuse. The training program integrates e-learning modules, an in-person seminar, practice interviews with virtual children in a virtual reality (VR) environment, automated feedback, and supervision of real cases from participants’ professional practice. A previous version of the training system demonstrated significant improvements in interviewing skills and self-efficacy in a randomized controlled trial. In a revised version, the level of automation was increased through expanded e-learning components, and a new module on documentation of conversations was added. The effectiveness of the revised training was evaluated with child protection professionals in a pilot study with a small sample (N = 20). The results again showed a significant improvement in interviewing skills. These findings indicate the potential of multimodal, technology-supported training approaches to sustainably enhance professional competencies in child protection contexts.

Eyewitnesses Under the Influence of Alcohol and Anxiety: A Virtual Reality Study of Memory and False Memories
Bastian Nau | University Duisburg-Essen / LVR-Universitätsklinik Essen
Show details
Author:
Bastian Nau | University Duisburg-Essen / LVR-Universitätsklinik Essen

Interviewing eyewitnesses is an essential part of successful police work. However, many witnesses observe crimes while under the influence of alcohol. Additionally, such experiences often cause high levels of stress or anxiety. The mechanisms and the extent to which memory is affected by these conditions remain unclear. Could anxiety and alcohol even lead to an increased susceptibility to false memories? This project employs virtual reality (VR) to investigate the influence of alcohol on memory in an immersive and realistic manner. In two sub-studies, participants first consume alcohol, then observe an assault in a bar and experience a height-based fear paradigm in a VR setting. They are then questioned in interviews, which also include suggestive questions. A Deese-Roediger-McDermott paradigm is used to further examine susceptibility to false memories. Another interview, conducted the following morning, allows comparisons to be made between memory performance during acute intoxication and in a sober state. Additionally, the results are compared with those of a sober control group. Hopefully, the results of this project will contribute to the development of scientifically sound guidelines for dealing with intoxicated or potentially anxious eyewitnesses in forensic practice, which could have long-term benefits for interview quality and reliability.

Eyewitness Accuracy after a Virtual Reality Theft Scene: Comparing 2D and 3D Lineups
Dr. Ulrike Stühler | Marburg University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Ulrike Stühler | Marburg University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Kristina Suchotzki | Marburg University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Stefan R. Schweinberger | Friedrich-Schiller Universität Jena

Eyewitness identification is a key form of evidence, yet errors can have serious consequences. The use of three-dimensional (3D) images in lineup procedures has been increasingly discussed as a potential methodological improvement. However, much of the existing evidence relies on paradigms with limited ecological validity. The present study examined whether 3D lineups improve identification performance following a VR-based event presentation and a longer retention interval. In a laboratory experiment, N = 116 participants viewed a 360° VR video depicting a wallet theft involving two perpetrators. Two days later, participants completed sequential lineups for both perpetrators, presented either as standard two-dimensional (2D) photos or as non-interactive 3D video lineups. Identification accuracy did not differ between 3D and 2D lineup formats for either perpetrator. The expected benefits of 3D lineups did not occur under the conditions tested. These findings suggest that adding depth cues or multiple viewpoints in a non-interactive format may be insufficient to improve eyewitness identification. Previously reported advantages may depend on witnesses’ ability to actively control the viewing perspective or on more realistic facial texture information. A follow-up study comparing 2D, 3D non-interactive and 3D interactive lineups is therefore currently underway. Its results will be presented and discussed alongside the present findings.

Active living and well-being in urban areas
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Matthias Weigelt (Paderborn University)
Co-chair(s) Prof. Dr. Jan Keller (Heidelberg University)
Room: Workshop +1
Topic: Psychology of Sustainable Behavior
Form of presentation: Fachgruppensymposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Rapid urbanization and challenges due to global warming are transforming daily activity patterns and health behaviors, with consequences for physical, psychological, and social well-being. Combining perspectives from two DGPs sub-divisions, health psychology and sport psychology, this symposium focuses on active living and well-being by examining individuals from different urban settings by using Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) methods. Four contributions will examine interrelations between psychological determinants, factors from the built or natural environment, physical activity or mobility behaviors and facets of mental health or well-being. Empirical findings from these contributions will be integrated to better understand how individual factors interact with urban environments and implications from all talks can be used for refinement of behavioral interventions.
The symposium aims to stimulate interdisciplinary exchange, identify shared theoretical frameworks and methodological approaches, and discuss implications for research, practice, and urban health promotion. Ultimately, it seeks to advance psychological knowledge that supports active living and well-being in urban populations.
First, Markus Reichert will summarize evidence from EMA studies on interrelations between urban nature factors, physical activity, and well-being. Second, Martina Kanning will present how green and social contexts shape affective experiences using a within-subject design. Shifting to the topic of increasingly occurring heat waves in Germany, Jan Keller will investigate how individuals adjust their daily mobility behaviors during and after a heat wave in Berlin. Fourth, using data from the same EMA study, Mira Tschorn will present how heat stressors might influence affective well-being as well as feelings of worry about people and the environment. Finally, Nelli Hankonen will lead the discussion on the four presentations in order to shape future avenues for research on active living and well-being in urban areas.

Urban nature, physical activity, and human mental health: Insights from daily life studies
Prof. Dr. Markus Reichert
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Markus Reichert

Nature environments benefit mental health, with recent studies showing nature exposure to decrease the risk for mental illness, to improve psychological well-being, and to foster social interactions. Similarly, physical activity has been evidenced to entail various mental health benefits. However, the interaction of nature environments and physical activity has rarely been studied to date. Given the rapid urbanization in the 21st century, research on the interplay of urban nature and physical activity within city landscapes appears crucial for fostering human health. To study these interactions, a combination of methods often called Ambulatory Assessment or Ecological Momentary Assessment predestinates itself. Smartphones allow to continuously track participants' locations which can be intersected with urban landscape information, acceleration sensors attached to participants' hip or thigh enable a device-based measurement of physical activity, and electronic smartphone-diaries allow to repeatedly capture participants' psychological states during their daily routines. The resulting intensive longitudinal data cannot only reveal insights into within-person mechanisms but the digital phenotypes can also be linked to in-depth laboratory characterization, e.g., via brain imaging. We will present a summary of a range of recent findings from daily life studies and show how city versus rural landscapes are associated with physical activity participation and how nature environments shape this relation. Then, we link these accounts to mental health, expanding on how momentary inner-city greenspace exposure modulates affective well-being and relates to neurobiological correlates of mental health risk and resilience. Finally, we provide first insights from intensive longitudinal data to discuss which features of the urban nature environment can be especially beneficial to foster physical activity participation in city dwellers towards mental health prevention and intervention.

Urban health benefits of walking: How green and social contexts shape momentary affective experiences
Prof. Dr. Martina Kanning
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Martina Kanning

Health-enhancing urban environments include mostly walkable areas, because walking is associated with positive effects on physical and mental health. However, the role of physical and social contexts during everyday walking remains insufficiently understood. This study examined momentary person–place interactions between environmental characteristics (greenness, social interaction) and affective states during outdoor walking. Using a within-subject design, walking-triggered e-diaries were administered via smartphones connected to a accelerometer (move3). E-diaries were triggered after 100 m of outdoor walking between 6 am and 10 pm across nine consecutive days. Momentary affective states (valence, calmness, energetic arousal) and social interaction (walking alone; seeing others; short interaction; walking with a known person) were assessed. Greenness was quantified retrospectively using GPS and GIS data. Multilevel models were computed in R for 46 participants (Mage = 41.2 ± 13.2; 52% female). Higher levels of greenness were associated with increased energetic arousal and calmness (ps < .05). Compared with walking alone, participants reported higher energetic arousal when briefly interacting with others (p = .02) and greater calmness when walking with a known person (p = .01). No significant associations were observed for valence. The findings highlight the importance of physical and social contexts in shaping affective experiences during everyday walking. Urban design strategies that increase access to green spaces and opportunities for social encounters may enhance the mental health benefits of walking. Walking-triggered, GPS-based experience sampling appears particularly suitable for capturing such dynamic contextual influences. Future research should investigate temporal and reciprocal effects to further elucidate these mechanisms.

Adjustment of mobility behaviors during a heat wave in Berlin
Prof. Dr. Jan Keller
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Jan Keller
Siiri Tunn
Karsten Valerius
Vivian Frick
Dr. Mira Tschorn

Background:
With heat waves becoming more frequent, rural and urban areas deal with challenges regarding public health and climate change adaptation. One challenge refers to people adjusting their mobility behaviors (e.g., walking, cycling) due to threatening temperatures, which serves a health-protective function, but corresponds with reduced physical activity. This study aims to examine heat wave-related effects for a set of mobility behaviors.
Methods:
In a Citizen Science study with an Ecological Momentary Assessment phase during a heat wave, seven end-of-day questionnaires were sent to Berlin citizens in August 2025. Three days were part of a heat wave (maximum temperature: 31.8-33.8℃), followed by 4 days with a maximum temperature of 23.0-27.1℃. From 207 citizens (Mage=49 years, 18 to 87; 59% female) of the overarching study, 149 citizens were in Berlin during the heat wave and responded to questionnaires. They self-reported daily mobility plan adjustment (due to weather conditions) as well as daily minutes of foot/wheelchair mobility, cycling, car use, and public transport use. Multilevel models were fit using heat day (vs. not) as a daily predictor.
Results:
During heat days (vs. not), mobility plan adjustment was more likely and a reduction of foot/wheelchair mobility (heat days: 44 min/day; other days: 58 min/day) was observed. No differences were found for cycling, car use, and public transport use.
Conclusions:
Fitting public recommendations to avoid physical exhaustion, citizens showed lower levels of foot/wheelchair mobility during heat days. To guarantee societal participation during heat waves, heat-protective measures (e.g., green spaces, water sources) are needed.

Heat stress, worry, and affective well-being: Evidence from a Berlin-based citizen science study
Dr. Mira Tschorn
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Mira Tschorn
Siiri Tunn
Karsten Valerius
Vivian Frick
Jan Keller

Background:
Increasing heat waves due to climate change pose growing challenges for mental health, particularly in urban environments. Beyond physiological strain, heat exposure can act as a psychological stressor by increasing perceived threat, restricting daily activities, and eliciting worries about one’s own health, vulnerable others, animals, or the environment. However, empirical evidence on how acute heat stress affects affective well-being in everyday life remains limited.
Methods:
This study used data from a participatory Citizen Science project conducted in Berlin in August 2025. Over seven consecutive days, participants completed brief end-of-day smartphone-based assessments. The study period included three heat wave days with maximum temperatures between 31.8 and 33.8 °C, followed by four cooler days (23.0–27.1 °C). Analyses were restricted to citizens who were in Berlin during the heat wave (N = 149). Daily measures assessed positive and negative affect as well as heat-related worries concerning personal health, children, relatives, (companion) animals, plants, and urban green spaces. Multilevel models were applied to examine associations between heat days, daily worries, and affective well-being.
Results:
Affective well-being was significantly worse on heat days compared to non-heat days. Additionally, higher levels of daily heat-related worries were associated with stronger negative affect.
Conclusions:
The findings indicate that heat waves are associated with immediate changes in affective well-being in everyday urban life and identify heat-related worry as an important correlate of mental well-being under heat exposure. Considering psychological responses to heat may inform the development of prevention and intervention strategies that aim to support mental health and living in increasingly heat-exposed cities.

Integrative discussion
Prof. Dr. Nelli Hankonen
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Nelli Hankonen

Following the four presentations, Nelli Hankonen will serve as a discussant, highlighting key findings, shared themes, and methodological insights. This integrative discussion will aim to identify gaps in current knowledge and foster interdisciplinary dialogue. It will further help to shape future research directions and inform strategies to promote active living and well-being in urban areas.

Form of presentation: Research Talk

Linking Digital Media Use and Mental Health: A Multiverse Analysis of Survey and Web-Tracking Data
Prof. Dr. Tobias Koch | Friedrich-Schiller Universität Jena, Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Tobias Koch | Friedrich-Schiller Universität Jena, Institut für Psychologie | Germany

There is growing interest in linking digital media use (DMU) with mental health (MH) outcomes. Yet empirical conclusions often differ as a function of how both constructs are conceptualized, operationalized, and analyzed. In this study, we applied a multiverse approach in a sample of 678 individuals who completed a comprehensive survey covering a broad spectrum of mental health indicators, ranging from psychopathology and distress to diverse facets of well-being. In parallel, participants provided digital trace data in the form of web-tracking records, enabling the integration of self-reported MH with behaviorally measured DMU. Across analytic specifications, results indicated only a small degree of overlap between web-tracked digital media use and mental health dimensions. We discuss implications for theory and measurement, and outline directions for future research.

From Swipe to Sleep: An Experience Sampling Study Using Smartphone Sensing to Examine Evening Smartphone Usage and Sleep Outcomes
Fenne große Deters | Philipps-Universität Marburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Fenne große Deters | Philipps-Universität Marburg | Germany
Thomas Reiter | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München | Germany
Ramona Schoedel | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule | Germany

Inadequate sleep is a widespread issue with serious consequences for health and well-being. Smartphone usage is often blamed, with frequent recommendations to avoid evening use to improve sleep. Surprisingly, there is a lack of rigorous studies to substantiate these claims or inform targeted interventions. Using objectively measured smartphone usage and experience sampling data from N = 401 adults, we investigated within-person effects of evening smartphone usage on the self-reported sleep outcomes duration, latency, quality, shuteye time, and wake-up time. Notably, we assessed smartphone usage across four different time windows (30, 60, 120, and 180 minutes before shuteye time), rather than focusing on a single period. Our findings align with prior research employing intensive longitudinal methods, which also failed to identify harmful effects of evening smartphone usage on sleep. In fact, we observed a small but consistent association between longer evening smartphone usage and both earlier shuteye times and longer sleep duration. These results challenge the notion that evening smartphone usage is inherently detrimental to sleep and should be avoided.

Das Bezugssystem von Phubbing: Vulnerabler Narzissmus, ängstliche Bindung und FoMO und Social Media Addiction
Dr. Elke Rohmann | Ruhr Universitaet Bochum | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Elke Rohmann | Ruhr Universitaet Bochum | Germany
Prof. Dr. Phillip Ozimek | Vinzenz Pallotti University
Prof. Dr. Hans-Werner Bierhoff | Ruhr Universität Bochum (RUB)

Ob bei einem Treffen mit Freund*innen, einem Gespräch mit Kolleg*innen oder bei Zusammenkünften in der Familie, häufig blicken Personen während der Interaktion auf ihr Handy. Dadurch können sich die anderen teilnehmenden Personen brüskiert fühlen, da sie weniger beachtet werden. Die Verwendung des Handys im sozialen Kontext wird Phubbing genannt. Phubbing = Neologismus, aus den Begriffen “phone” and “snubbing”. Phubbing bedeutet eine Brüskierung in der Gesellschaft mit einer anderen Person, indem diese Person währenddessen ihr Handy nutzt. Bisherige Studien zeigen, dass Phubbing mit vulnerablem Narzissmus sowie mit ängstlicher partnerbezogener Bindung, Fear of Missing out (FoMO) und der problematischen Verwendung sozialer Medien verbunden ist. Zudem zeigen Studien, dass vulnerabler Narzissmus mit FoMO zusammenhängt. Ziel unserer Studie war die dem Phubbing zugrunde liegenden relevanten Mechanismen zu verstehen bzw. zu identifizieren. Hierzu haben wir untersucht, inwieweit der Zusammenhang zwischen vulnerablem Narzissmus und Phubbing durch die unsichere ängstliche partnerbezogene Bindung und Fear of Missing out (FoMo) vermittelt wird. Die Ergebnisse der Studie 1, die auf N = 453 Personen basieren, die eine Partnerschaft führten, zeigen signifikante Zusammenhänge zwischen Phubbing, vulnerablem Narzissmus, ängstlicher Bindung an den Partner und FoMO sowie den erwarteten indirekten Zusammenhang zwischen vulnerablen Narzissmus und Phubbing vermittelt über die ängstliche partnerbezogene Bindung und FoMO. Studie 2 (N = 271) repliziert und erweitert das Ergebnismuster. Denn der Zusammenhang zwischen vulnerablen Narzissmus und Phubbing wird vollständig über die ängstliche Bindung, FoMO und Social Media Addiction vermittelt. Die Ergebnisse können dazu dienen, die Persönlichkeitsstruktur und die psychologischen Mechanismen, die beim Phubbing eine Rolle spielen, zu verstehen.

Kampf um den Blick: Visuelle Aufmerksamkeitsprozesse bei Instagram-Benachrichtigungen in Abhängigkeit von problematischer Nutzung
Dr. Lea-Christin Wickord | Universität Koblenz | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Lea-Christin Wickord | Universität Koblenz | Germany
Lara M. Rüthers | Universität Koblenz
Melissa Gärtner | Universität Koblenz
Carlotta Schäper | Universität Koblenz

Soziale Medien sind durch aufmerksamkeitsbindende Reize wie Benachrichtigungen charakterisiert, die potenziell verstärkende Wirkmechanismen entfalten. Theoretische Modelle problematischer Social-Media-Nutzung betonen dabei weniger die reine Nutzungsdauer als vielmehr suchtähnliche Tendenzen wie Kontrollverlust, Vermeidungsverhalten oder die Angst, etwas zu verpassen. Vor diesem Hintergrund untersuchte die vorliegende explorative Studie, inwiefern individuelles Instagram-Nutzungsverhalten mit der visuellen Aufmerksamkeit gegenüber benachrichtigungsbezogenen Reizen zusammenhängt.

In einer mobilen Eye-Tracking-Erhebung wurden N = 96 Personen (MAlter = 25,84 Jahre, SD = 11,13; 68 weiblich, 27 männlich, 1 divers) mittels Tobii Pro Nano (60 Hz) untersucht. Nach Kalibrierung beantworteten die Teilnehmenden soziodemografische Fragen sowie die Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale (BSMAS). Anschließend wurden drei Instagram-Screenshots (u. a. Sperrbildschirm mit Pop-up-Benachrichtigung sowie Feed mit Benachrichtigungssymbol) jeweils für drei Sekunden präsentiert. Als abhängige Variablen wurden Dwell-Time und Fixation Count auf die jeweiligen Benachrichtigungsbereiche erfasst. Zusätzlich wurde die durchschnittliche tägliche Instagram-Nutzungsdauer als Prädiktor berücksichtigt.

Multiple lineare Regressionsanalysen zeigten, dass die Social-Media-Suchttendenz signifikant mit einer erhöhten Anzahl an Fixationen sowie einer längeren Verweildauer auf Benachrichtigungsreizen zusammenhing, während für die reine Nutzungsdauer keine systematischen Effekte nachgewiesen werden konnten.

Die Befunde legen nahe, dass nicht die Quantität der Nutzung, sondern qualitative Merkmale problematischen Nutzungsverhaltens mit einer gesteigerten visuellen Empfänglichkeit für aufmerksamkeitsbindende Reize assoziiert sind. Dies unterstreicht die Relevanz differenzierter Indikatoren problematischer Social-Media-Nutzung jenseits bloßer Zeitmaße.

Can digital meditation programs improve sleep? Effects of digital mindfulness-based interventions on adults’ sleep quality in randomized controlled trials: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Dr. Lorenz Grolig | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Lorenz Grolig | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany
Hanna Brückner | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany
Lina Kalon | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Dirk Lehr | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany

Background: About 10% of adults suffer from insomnia. The first line treatment (cognitive behavioral therapy; CBT-I) effectively reduces insomnia severity in 50–70% of patients. For some patients, sleep restriction therapy – the most effective method of CBT-I – is not feasible, or not recommended due to comorbid conditions. Therefore, new treatments are needed to improve access to treatment. Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) could reduce hyperarousal, which is hypothesized to be a key cause of insomnia. This meta-analysis is the first to evaluate the potential of digital MBIs (dMBIs) to improve sleep quality.

Research question: How effective are dMBIs in improving sleep quality compared to different control groups?

Methods: In a systematic search according to PRISMA guidelines (PubMed, PsycINFO, Web of Science), randomized controlled trials with adults were included. Primary outcome: Subjective sleep quality (Insomnia Severity Index and similar questionnaires) post-intervention. Registration: PROSPERO (CRD42024601967).

Results: 142 full texts were reviewed, 42 studies were included. There was a small effect of dMBIs on sleep quality in comparison to no treatment controls at post-test (g = -0.34 [-0.46; -0.22]) and at 3-6 months follow-up (g = -0.33 [-0.54; -0.11]). At post-test, effects of dMBIs were not superior to active controls (e.g., attention control; sleep hygiene).

Conclusions: DMBIs could improve access to effective insomnia treatment for patients. Further high-quality trials with active comparison groups and follow-up assessments are needed for an evaluation of long-term effects. We discuss the clinical significance, methodological problems, and how access to insomnia treatment in mental health care can be improved.

Position Paper: Cultural Basis Democracy / Power Balance Relationships
Room: FR
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Position Paper
Duration: 90 Minutes

Power Balance, Trust, and Freedom as Cultural Basis for Explaining Democracy, Prosperity, Human Wellbeing, and Conservation
Prof. Dr. Wolfgang Scholl | Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Wolfgang Scholl | Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin | Germany

Many culture studies are based on correlational evidence from single factors. For predicting the extent of real democracy and economic performance, the economic analyses of Acemoglu and Robinson (2012, 2020) and the anthropological analyses of Henrich (2021) helped to construct a culture measure called Power Balance, Trust, and Freedom (PBTF). This measure contains Hofstede’s Power Distance (reversed) and Individualism indices, Inglehart’s Trust measure, Ingroup collectivism from House et al., and Van de Vliert`s In-Group Favoritism (both reversed). The conceptual connections of these five factors in PBTF is empirically confirmed in a 2nd order factor analysis with 15 culture factors. PBTF has high reliability (0.93) and high validity because in societies with balanced power distribution, people have more individual freedom, fear less harm, can be more open toward others because of less in-group loyalties, and can be more trustful in others.
PBTF predicts with path-analytical models of 85 nations Rule of Law as measure of Democracy versus Autocracy, National Posperity measured by Gross Domestic Product per capita (GDP), and Human Wellbeing measured by UN’s Inequality adjusted Human Development Index (IHDI). Moreover, the climate and environmental problems as measured by UN’s Planetary Pressures (PP) index are negatively affected by GDP and IHDI, the fruits of a democratic culture. Yet, PBTF predicts PP negatively, too, i.e. the efforts for conservation. About 2/3 of each of the 4 endogenous variables are explained in the models. The path models quantify a complex nomological web which encompasses 12 of the 17 UN’s Sustainable Development Goals.

08:45 am
Power in Romantic Relationships: Theoretical Perspectives, Correlates, and Methodological Challenges
Dr. Robert Körner | University of Bamberg | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Robert Körner | University of Bamberg | Germany

Power is central to understanding how people experience and navigate their relationships. Every couple member has the power to fulfill their partner’s needs and wishes—and the power to harm their well-being. People who feel able to influence their partner to achieve desired outcomes (= power) can confidently pursue their needs and goals. Yet our understanding of power in relationships has been limited until recently because relationship science focused on intrapersonal associations, heterosexual couples, and measures and analytical approaches that did not account for the dyadic nature of power. Guided by key power theories I will present correlates I identified in our research—spanning dyadic studies, daily diaries, and lab-based interactions—on power in intimate relationships (satisfaction, forgiveness, jealousy, aggression, sexuality, attachment). The focus will be on subjective power, but also other forms (desired power, power imbalances, positional power) will be addressed. Findings on power among LGBTQ couples and in friendships will be included. The moderating role of gender and traits (self-esteem, psychopathy) will be clarified. Finally, research on the interpersonal perception of power will be presented: Partners typically underestimate their power—and this underestimation is stronger for people higher in self-protection and power motives. In the talk, methodological questions on power research (e.g., fit between measures and theory, conflation of actor and partner power, curvilinear relationships) will be highlighted. Overall, based on own research I will offer a thorough overview about the current knowledge base on power in romantic couples, methodological challenges and future research directions in this domain.

Who are you to judge? Trustworthiness and acceptance of generative AI in judicial decision-making

Show details
Authors:
Dr. Marvin Walczok | Ludwig Maximilian Universität München (LMU) | Germany
Prof. Dr. Friederike Funk

Generative Artificial Intelligence (genAI) could revolutionize the legal system by assisting or replacing judges in judicial decision-making. Findings indicate that laypeople trust and accept human judges more than automated judicial decision-making. But research has neglected the perception of hybrid decision-making – human judges with genAI support – which would be the most realistic scenario under the European Union’s AI Act. Building on the organizational trust model, machine heuristic, Capability-Personalization Framework, and findings on algorithmic decision-making, we investigated the effect of the type of decision-maker on perceived trustworthiness (ability, benevolence, and integrity) of the decision-maker and acceptance of judgments. We hypothesized higher ability, benevolence, and acceptance, and lower integrity for human and hybrid judicial decision-making than for genAI. In two online experiments with German laypeople, we presented hypothetical crime cases, court proceedings, and judgments. We manipulated the type of decision-maker as between-factor with four levels: (1) human judge, (2) hybrid with high human involvement, (3) hybrid with low human involvement, (4) genAI. Results from Experiment 1 (N1 = 323) demonstrated linear decreases in ability, benevolence, integrity, and acceptance with decreasing human involvement. Experiment 2 (N2 = 674) showed similar ratings in trustworthiness and acceptance for human and hybrid conditions which were significantly higher than in genAI. These findings provide mixed evidence on the perception of hybrid judicial decision-making but support preferences for human judges. Overall, they warn of potential losses of trustworthiness and acceptance in judicial decision-making if genAI were used in judicial decision-making, even if only to support human judges.

The double blind spot in human–AI decision making: The role of AI literacy, gender, and stereotypical expectations in reliance on algorithmic advice
Dr. Vera Ruthsatz | University of Koblenz | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Vera Ruthsatz | University of Koblenz | Germany
Dr. Irina Heimbach | Weizenbaum Institut | Germany
Prof. Dr. Oliver Müller | Paderborn University | Germany

While AI fairness has been extensively studied technically, little is known about how people interact with biased outputs in real decision-making contexts. Drawing on Judge-Advisor System frameworks, we investigate whether AI literacy (AIL) and the bias blind spot (BBS)– particularly the tendency to underestimate one’s own biases in human–machine interactions – are related to advice utilization from biased and unbiased algorithms.
This approach moves beyond subjective perceptions to examine actual decision-making behaviour in a controlled laboratory experiment. Psychology students acted as proxies for future HR managers, selecting candidates for promotion using a specially designed algorithm. Algorithmic bias was manipulated (favoring men, favoring women, or unbiased), and participants’ AIL, BBS, gender and perceived algorithm’s performance were assessed. Advice utilization measured the extent participants adjusted their judgments.
Preliminary results from N = 112 participants indicate that algorithmic bias is rarely detected, though AI-supported decisions outperformed unaided judgments across conditions. Higher AIL was associated with reduced reliance on biased advice, suggesting a more critical evaluation of algorithmic outputs. Interestingly, participants with higher BBS scores were more likely to counteract biased recommendations. Gender effects also emerged, with male participants relying more on AI advice for female profiles.
These findings suggest that a psychological double blind spot operates, in which participants remain unaware of both algorithmic bias and their own cognitive biases, while stereotypical expectations seem to override objective algorithmic information. Reliance can still be adjusted based on AIL, highlighting the importance of human-in-the-loop decision-making, targeted training, and fair AI system design.

Dual Pathways to Thriving and Strain in Generative AI–Enabled Work: Task–Technology Fit and Organizational AI Support Shape Need Satisfaction and Thwarting
Dr. Alexander Götmann | Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts | Switzerland
Show details
Author:
Dr. Alexander Götmann | Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts | Switzerland

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming routine in knowledge work, yet its motivational consequences remain poorly understood. Integrating Job Demands–Resources Theory with Self-Determination Theory, we propose a dual-route model in which GenAI-related resources foster thriving through need satisfaction, whereas AI-specific hindrance demands undermine well-being through need thwarting. We tested preregistered hypotheses in a three-wave panel of knowledge workers who used GenAI at least weekly (N = 741 at T1; N = 526 at T3; 3-week lags). Predictors (T1) included task–technology fit, organizational AI support, AI self-efficacy, and AI technostress. Mediators were need satisfaction and need thwarting (T2). Outcomes were thriving (vitality, learning) and strain (exhaustion, anxiety), assessed at T2 and T3 to enable adjacent-lag autoregressive controls. Longitudinal latent-variable models with bootstrapped indirect effects revealed that task–technology fit (β = 24) and organizational AI support (β = .28) predicted higher need satisfaction, which in turn predicted increases in vitality (β = .22) and learning (β = .15). AI self-efficacy did not predict need satisfaction among these regular users. AI technostress predicted higher need thwarting (β = .25), but need thwarting did not predict residual change in strain over the three-week interval. These findings position contextual resources, task-technology fit and organizational AI support rather than individual confidence as the primary levers for need-satisfying GenAI work.

Hannah Grosswieser | Johannes Kepler Universität Linz | Austria

As AI chatbots are increasingly consulted for advice in ambiguous, creative, and moral questions rather than only in objective tasks, it becomes essential to better understand what drives user conformity with this AI advice. Drawing on theories of machine heuristics and anthropomorphism, this experimental study examined whether users revised their initial judgments after receiving recommendations from ChatGPT across different tasks (dot counting, art interpretation, moral dilemma). In an online experiment, 201 UK and US adults completed a set of numerical dot-counting trials, art-interpretation trials, and a moral-dilemma decision. For each trial, participants received a recommendation from ChatGPT – varied in its degree of human-likeness – and could then revise their initial answer. Conformity was measured as the extent to which participants adjusted their responses toward the AI’s advice. Across all task domains, participants’ judgements were significantly influenced by the AI advice with the highest conformity scores in the numerical dot-counting task. Contrary to expectations, manipulating the chatbot’s verbal human-likeness did not systematically alter perceived human-likeness or conformity with the AI. However, participants’ own perceptions of the AI’s human-likeness and, especially its task-specific competence, emerged as robust predictors of conformity. In the moral dilemma, these perceptions of human-likeness and competence were also closely linked. The study applies theories of automation and anthropomorphism to examine conformity to an AI chatbot across objective and subjective tasks, demonstrating that AI influence varies by task domain and depends on users’ perceptions of human-likeness and competence.

Form of presentation: Research Talk

Epistemic orientation shapes the ability to discern true from false news
Dr. Christoph Abels | Universität Potsdam | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Christoph Abels | Universität Potsdam | Germany
Prof. Dr. Stephan Lewandowsky | University of Bristol

The concept of truth is increasingly contested, giving rise to what is often described as a “post-truth” era. Within this context, individuals differ systematically in their epistemic beliefs, particularly regarding whether truth is understood as something that can be established through evidence and scientific reasoning (evidence-based) or as something that can be accessed through feelings and intuition (intuition-based).

The present research examines how these differing epistemic orientations affect people’s ability to discern true from false news headlines. Across three preregistered studies (total N = 1,280), we investigated the effects of epistemic orientation, headline framing, and inoculation interventions on truth discernment. Headlines were sourced from The Washington Post and The Wall Street Journal and rephrased by the large language model Claude to reflect either an evidence-based or intuition-based framing; additionally, factually false counterparts were generated. The design crossed participant orientation (evidence vs. intuition), inoculation condition (evidence vs. intuition vs. control), headline veracity (true vs. false), and headline framing (evidence vs. intuition). In Study 3 (N = 680), the inoculation was combined with an accuracy prompt.

Across all studies, epistemic orientation consistently predicted discernment accuracy: participants with an evidence-based orientation were better able to distinguish true from false headlines across framing and treatment conditions. Moreover, intuition-framed headlines were judged as less likely to be true - even when factually accurate. Generic inoculation was ineffective, however, creating. new boundary condition. These findings underscore the importance of epistemic beliefs for understanding susceptibility to misinformation and inform interventions aimed at strengthening epistemic resilience.

Show details

Prof. Dr. Markus Appel | Julius-Maximilians Universität Würzburg | Germany

Concerns about misinformation and science rejection are paramount. The proliferation of misinformation, polarization, and rejection of science has coincided with a shift in the standards parts of the population use to evaluate information (Carella et al., 2025; Lasser et al., 2023; Lewandowsky et al., 2024). In the U.S., politicians and the public alike seem to place increasingly little importance on facts and evidence and instead rely on an intuitive sense of authenticity in speaking one’s beliefs – regardless of the belief’s actual veracity (Ayorhehun et al., 2025; Garrett & Weeks, 2017): A phenomenon Lewandowsky and Garcia (2026) have recently identified as an epistemic drift.

In two online-experiments (N = 1002), we found a scalable and replicable way to mitigate epistemic drift. Specifically, we tested a scalable intervention – epistemic discussions with an AI conversational partner – designed to make implicit standards of justification explicit and open to reflection. Through epistemic discussions with an LLM based on GPT-4o-mini, need for evidence was significantly increased one week after the first measurement (η² = .02), and faith in intuition was significantly reduced (η² = .03). This had causal consequences for argument evaluation as measured by a discernment task between low- and high-quality arguments (Marin et al., 2024; Svedholm-Häkkinen et al., 2024). Epistemic discussions furthermore prompted participants to consult more sources on polarized issues in a newly developed Google search paradigm, and reduced science-related populism (Mede et al., 2021). All effects were mediated by causal shifts in epistemic beliefs.

Individual differences in the truth effect can be reliably measured and are temporally stable
Selina Zajdler | University of Mannheim | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Selina Zajdler | University of Mannheim | Germany
Prof. Dr. Lena Nadarevic | Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule
Markus Wache | University of Mannheim
Dr. Martin Schnuerch | University of Mannheim

The truth effect describes the influence of repetition on judgments of truth, whereby previously encountered statements are judged as more valid than novel statements. This effect is highly robust at the group level, yet research on individual differences and their covariation with other psychological constructs, such as personality traits, has yielded inconsistent results. These inconsistencies may have methodological origins. Namely, before such relationships with traits can be meaningfully interpreted, it is essential to determine whether the truth effect constitutes a temporally stable characteristic within individuals. Moreover, assessing such temporal stability – and, more generally, relationships with other variables – requires that the truth effect can be measured reliably at the individual level, as correlations are attenuated under low reliability. We show that, when adhering to experimental design recommendations identified in previous work, such as sufficiently large trial sizes, individual truth effects can be reliably measured in a single session using difference scores. In a typical test-retest design, we then find a strong association between individual truth effects across two sessions spaced one week apart, providing evidence for a stable component of the truth effect. Thus, we demonstrate that the truth effect can be reliably measured in a single session, given enough trials, and that it contains a temporally stable component. This lays the foundation for further research on individual differences in the truth effect and how they relate to other dispositional variables.

Prof. Dr. Lena Nadarevic | Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Lena Nadarevic | Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule | Germany

Several factors affect memory for truth and falsity, such as statement plausibility or the informational value of „true“ or „false“ feedback. Yet, it is unclear how aware people are of these influences. One way to gain insights into participants’ metacognitive processes is by asking them directly how likely they are to remember a specific statement (referred to as judgment of learning, or JOL) or the statement’s veracity (referred to as judgment of veracity, or JOV). However, these metacognitive judgments have the potential to cause reactivity, that is, they may alter memory performance. As no research has yet examined whether metamemory judgments affect memory for truth and falsity, two experiments were conducted to address this research gap. In the control groups, participants studied individual statements together with veracity feedback, while in the experimental groups, participants additionally provided JOLs and JOVs (Experiment 1) or JOVs only (Experiment 2). The results of Experiment 1 showed that metamemory judgments improved statement memory but did not affect memory for truth and falsity. Furthermore, in Experiment 2, JOVs alone did not produce any reactivity effects. These findings suggest that researchers need not worry about reactivity when incorporating JOVs in studies on metamemory for truth and falsity. However, both experiments reveal a metamemory illusion that warrants further investigation in future research.

Der Einfluss von Motivation auf kognitive und emotionale Prozesse während des Lügens
Tabea Wächtershäuser | Philipps Universität Marburg, Germany | Germany
Show details
Author:
Tabea Wächtershäuser | Philipps Universität Marburg, Germany | Germany

Lügen ist ein kognitiv und emotional anstrengender Prozess und geht in der Praxis häufig mit der Motivation einher, nicht entdeckt zu werden. Bisherige Studie berichten widersprüchliche Effekte der Motivation auf die Lügenleistung. Während metaanalytische Befunde darauf hindeuten, dass positive Anreizsetzung mit geringeren Reaktionszeitunterschieden zwischen Wahrheit und Lüge einhergeht, zeigt sich in Studien mit experimenteller Manipulation negativer Anreizsetzung eine Erhöhung entsprechender Unterschiede in psychophysiologischen Messerwerten. Ziel der vorliegenden Studie war es daher, den Einfluss unterschiedlicher Motivationsformen innerhalb eines experimentellen Paradigmas systematisch zu vergleichen.
Hierzu wurde eine adaptierte Version des Sheffield Lie Tests eingesetzt, in dem Versuchspersonen (n=99) identische Fragen entweder wahrheitsgemäß oder mit einer Lüge beantworten sollten. Die Teilnehmenden wurden zufällig einer von drei Motivationsbedingungen (Verlust-, Gewinn-, oder Kontrollbedingung) zugewiesen, in denen der finanzielle Anreiz im Rahmen einer Diebstahlaufgabe variiert wurde. In einem anschließenden computerbasierten Experiment wurden Reaktionszeiten sowie selbstberichtete kognitive und emotionale Beanspruchung während des Lügens im Vergleich zur Wahrheit erfasst.
In Übereinstimmung mit den Hypothesen zeigten sich längere Reaktionszeiten sowie eine erhöhte kognitive und emotionale Beanspruchung während der Lüge im Vergleich zur Wahrheit. Entgegen der Erwartungen ergaben sich jedoch weder signifikante Haupteffekte der Motivation noch Interaktionseffekte zwischen Motivation und Instruktion.
Da die Teilnehmenden über alle Bedingungen hinweg ein hohes Motivationsniveau angaben, könnten Deckeneffekt in dieser Studie (aufgrund des spannenden Rollenspiels) eine mögliche Erklärung bieten. Zukünftige Studien sollen die Befunde unter stärker differenzierten Motivationsbedingungen replizieren und prüfen, ob die Ergebnisse auch auf andere Motivationsarten, etwa verbale oder soziale Motivation, übertragbar sind.

Applying Next-Generation Methods for Advancement in Personality Research and Psychometrics
Chair(s) Julian G. Scherhag (Trier University)
Room: FI
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

The rise of high-resolution data and potent computational methods offers an opportunity for advancement in personality research and psychometrics. This symposium explores how advanced methodologies, including Large Language Models (LLMs), Machine Learning (ML) and Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling (DSEM), can be leveraged to gain new insights into established models and constructs. Beyond showcasing these applications, we critically discuss key methodological challenges, focussing on stability, replicability, and practical utility of these methods.

First, Lazarević et al. demonstrate the power of LLMs to perform a historical conceptual analysis of psychosis-proneness. By summarizing and comparing historical texts from antiquity to the pre-modern era, they discuss how these historical concepts map onto our contemporary theoretical understanding. Shifting from history to real-time dynamics, Barthelmäs & Keller present evidence from two general population Experience Sampling studies to examine how basic personality traits (HEXACO) extended with psychosis-proneness influence the daily fluctuation of psychotic-like states, physical exhaustion, and affective dynamics. The discussion then moves toward the critical evaluation of data-driven versus theory-driven modeling. Scherhag & Bosnjak investigate whether high-dimensional personality data (Facet MAP) truly benefit from supervised ML algorithms and if these approaches offer incremental theoretical insights beyond traditional theory-driven models. Complementing this, Ammann & Stachl assess the robustness of personality prediction models trained with smartphone-sensing data, focusing on their generalizability to new samples and their temporal stability. Finally, Trautwein & Schroeders address a key psychometric challenge by comparing two promising approaches (Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) vs. Ant Colony Optimization (ACO)) for parallel short test construction.

Psychosis-Proneness Across History: A Conceptual Analysis and Synthesis Using Large Language Models.
Prof. Dr. Michael Bosnjak | Trier University & University of Ljubljana | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Ljiljana B. Lazarević | Institute of Psychology, University of Belgrade | Serbia
Prof. Dr. Michael Bosnjak | Trier University & University of Ljubljana | Germany
Julian G. Scherhag | Trier University | Germany
Prof. Goran Knežević | University of Belgrade | Serbia

This presentation will explore the historical development in understanding psychotic-like experiences and behaviors (PLEBs), conceptualized today by contemporary dimensional models, such as the HEXACOD model. If psychosis-proneness reflects a fundamental disposition, its manifestations should be evident across history.

We elaborate on how interpretations of PLEBs have consistently drawn attention but varied across time, moving from: 1) Antiquity (e.g., divine madness or humoral imbalance); 2) the Medieval period (religious interpretations like demonic possession); 3) the Renaissance and Enlightenment (rationalist classification and medicalization); to 4) Modernity (19th-21st century).

Modernity introduced diverse perspectives—including neurobiological, psychoanalytic, and trauma-informed—which eventually led to dimensional-trait models. Meehl's schizotypy and Eysenck's psychoticism prefigured contemporary frameworks like Disintegration, which synthesizes these views by recognizing proneness to PLEBs as a stable personality disposition with potential for both dysfunction and adaptation. The presentation will also address the various approaches used to identify and process historical texts through the application of AI tools.

Psychotic-Like Experiences at the State- and Trait-Level: Micro-Longitudinal Evidence from Experience Sampling
Dr. Michael Barthelmäs | Ulm University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Michael Barthelmäs | Ulm University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Johannes Keller | Ulm University | Germany

The Disintegration trait captures individual differences in the propensity for psychotic-like experiences and behaviors and explains variance beyond the HEXACO traits in criteria such as conspiracy beliefs. Prior work indicates that Disintegration is normally distributed in the general population. Less clear is the extent to which momentary psychotic-like experiences (MPLEs) fluctuate within persons and how these fluctuations relate to fatigue, sleep quality, and affective states. To address these questions, we conducted two experience-sampling method studies (Study 1: N = 178; 2,988 episodes across 5 days; Study 2: N = 284; 5,161 episodes across 7 days). Both studies revealed between-person differences and within-person variability in MPLEs. Trait Disintegration emerged as the strongest predictor of MPLEs. Poor sleep quality predicted higher MPLEs on the following day at both the within- and between-person levels, and momentary fatigue was positively associated with concurrent MPLEs at both levels. The inverse association between momentary positive and negative affect was stronger at occasions characterized by elevated MPLEs and among individuals scoring higher on Disintegration. This pattern is consistent with a more polarized (“black-or-white”) affective experience under higher Disintegration/MPLEs. Dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM) further suggested temporal asymmetry: lagged MPLEs predicted subsequent decreases in positive affect and increases in negative affect, whereas lagged affect showed little association with subsequent MPLEs. Taken together, these micro-longitudinal findings indicate that psychotic-like experiences in the general population manifest at both trait and state levels and vary meaningfully within individuals over time, and that physical exhaustion seems to intensify subsequent momentary psychotic-like experiences.

Do we Need Machine Learning for High-Dimensional Personality Data or is Theory Enough? Evidence from the German Facet MAP.
Julian G. Scherhag | Trier University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Julian G. Scherhag | Trier University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Michael Bosnjak | Trier University & University of Ljubljana | Germany

The Facet-level Multidimensional Assessment of Personality (Facet MAP) introduces 70 unidimensional, non-redundant personality facets designed to capture unique variance often lost in broader trait models. While facets generally outperform broad traits in predicting life outcomes, traditional assessments frequently suffer from item overlap and multicollinearity, especially in higher-dimensional data. The Facet MAP addresses these limitations, offering a refined tool for predictive personality science. This study evaluates the German translation of the Facet MAP across various political and mental health outcomes. Using a comparative framework, we treat theory-driven models as the benchmark against which data-driven supervised machine learning (ML) approaches, including LASSO, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machines, are compared. This comparison reveals whether data-driven models can uncover novel theoretical insights through previously neglected facets, and conversely, how theory serves as a vital validation for interpretable ML. Ultimately, we discuss the necessity of sophisticated ML algorithms when analysing high-dimensional personality data.

Parallel Short-Form Construction: A Comparison of Mixed-Integer Linear Programming and Ant Colony Optimization
Tim Trautwein | University of Kassel | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Tim Trautwein | University of Kassel | Germany
Prof. Dr. Ulrich Schroeders | University of Kassel | Germany

The development of parallel short test forms is essential for score comparability across measurement occasions, booklet designs, and examinee groups. Parallelism often concerns similar content coverage, mean item difficulty, and measurement precision across test forms. Accordingly, assembling such forms constitutes a complex combinatorial optimization problem, for which mainly two methods can be used: (a) Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP), which relies on fixed, pre-calibrated item parameters and hard constraints; and (b) metaheuristics such as Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), which employ stochastic search, soft constraints, and iterative parameter re-estimation. In the first step, we quantify parameter uncertainty in the generated values of unidimensional short forms by using Monte Carlo simulation (sampling variance). In more detail, we systematically vary the following factors: (1) calibration sample size (N = 200, 500, 1,000, 10,000), (2) test length (10%, 20%, 30% of the item pool), (3) model complexity (1PL, 2PL, 3PL), and (4) trait distribution (normal, left-leaning). In the second step, we exemplify the consequences of this uncertainty in the construction of parallel short forms using either MILP or ACO under specific constraints (e.g., content coverage, difficulty distribution). Preliminary results indicate small differences under the 1PL model, where parameter estimates remain highly correlated with generating values even in small samples. Differences increase with model complexity and smaller calibration samples. We discuss the trade-off between MILP’s mathematical optimality—which may capitalize on chance when calibration error is ignored—and ACO’s flexibility, which can reduce sensitivity to miscalibration but risks overfitting without validation.

From unequal burdens to collective action: The psychology of climate justice
Chair(s) Lisa Marie Hempel (Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine, Hamburg)
Room: GR
Topic: Psychology of Sustainable Behavior
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Climate change raises profound questions of justice, as responsibilities for causing climate change, exposure to its impacts, and capacities to respond are unequally distributed across countries, social groups, and generations. Beyond their normative relevance, these inequalities are psychologically consequential: justice-related beliefs and sensitivities shape how people evaluate climate policies, negotiate responsibility, and engage in collective and political action.
This symposium advances a psychological perspective on climate justice across mitigation and adaptation contexts. At its conceptual and methodological core, it introduces a validated measure that captures individual differences in sensitivity to climate injustice (Hempel). The symposium further focuses on climate financing as a key mechanism for addressing climate injustice (Köchling), investigating public preferences for responsibility allocation, funding design, and recipient groups (Bosshard), and examines fairness perceptions in local adaptation policies (Kollmann). Extending beyond policy evaluations, it also examines how climate litigation as a form of political participation can advance climate justice and climate action (Maur).
Based on methodologically diverse approaches, the symposium combines measurement development, representative surveys, and experimental designs to trace how justice considerations operate across global, national, and local levels. Across these contexts, the contributions address multiple forms of climate justice, including distributive, intergenerational, and recognition-based justice. Importantly, the symposium also discusses potential tensions, showing how increased climate justice sensitivity and justice claims may foster intergroup conflict or political resistance.
The symposium concludes with an integrative discussion (Reese), which synthesizes the contributions and positions climate justice as a central psychological lens for linking inequality and climate action.

Climate change poses geophysical challenges that exacerbate social inequalities by disproportionately burdening already disadvantaged groups. Despite the central role of justice considerations in shaping climate action, psychological instruments capturing public perception and understanding of climate justice are lacking. Drawing on a newly developed climate justice taxonomy and operationalizing two central dimensions (unequal contributions and unequal suffering), we introduce and validate the Sensitivity to Climate Injustice (SCI) scale, a theory-driven self-report measure assessing individual differences in sensitivity to climate injustices across groups differentially affected by climate change. Across four studies with German-speaking samples from the general population (N1 = 1084, N2 = 1998, N3 = 1092, N4 = 1119), we developed and validated a robust measurement model based on eight items. This model comprises two correlated factors: unequal contributions to climate change (factor Cause) and unequal suffering from climate change (factor Suffer), and demonstrates metric invariance across various contexts. Validity analyses positioned the SCI within a nomological network, revealing theoretically consistent associations with justice sensitivity, climate change knowledge, basic human values, and prosocial orientations. Criterion validity analyses showed that the two factors differentially predicted readiness for climate action—including individual behaviour, policy acceptance, and political participation. The SCI predicted real world political participation behaviours in a longitudinal design, providing rare behavioural validation beyond self-reported measures. By providing a reliable, valid, and parsimonious measure, the SCI scale fills an important gap in environmental psychology and enables systematic research on how sensitivity to climate injustice shapes climate action.

A key question in international climate negotiations concerns the fair distribution of responsibilities and costs for climate mitigation and adaptation. Several principles for allocating responsibility are discussed, including current and historical national emissions as well as national wealth. These principles often lead to diverging conclusions about fair country contributions. This study examines which allocation principles are preferred by the public and what levels of contribution are expected from Germany and the United States.
We collected two representative samples in Germany (N=1,050) and the United States (N=1,010). Participants indicated their agreement with different principles for allocating climate finance and specified preferred contribution weights for each principle. Furthermore, participants rated how much selected countries should contribute to global climate finance.
In both countries, despite differences in overall agreement levels, participants expressed stronger support for allocation based on current national emissions and current national wealth (min: 74%) than for allocation based on historical emissions (min: 62%). When asked to specify concrete contribution weights, current emissions were clearly prioritized, accounting on average to approximately 50% of the allocation basis. Across both samples, participants allocated around one third of total climate finance responsibility to the US and up to one fifth to Germany.
Understanding public preferences regarding climate finance is crucial, as climate policies that conflict with dominant fairness perceptions may risk political resistance and reduced public support. Cross-national comparison of fairness perceptions further provide an important basis for identifying potential areas of common ground in international debates on climate justice.

Enhancing public support for global climate funding: Evidence from the Netherlands
Anna Bosshard | Universiteit van Amsterdam | Netherlands
Show details
Authors:

Countries in the Global South have contributed the least to global carbon emissions yet face the most severe consequences of climate change. Despite the critical need for large-scale, grant-based funding from wealthy countries, current institutional funding is insufficient and often comes in the form of loans, exacerbating financial debt. Because citizens are critical agents of change in policymaking, this study investigates how to enhance public support for international climate funding. We employed a choice-based conjoint survey experiment among a quota sample of 1,034 Dutch residents and systematically assessed the impact of three policy attributes on support for global climate funding: its goals (mitigation vs. adaptation vs. loss and damage), source (wealth tax vs. fossil fuel tax vs. existing national budget), and recipients (important trade partners vs. former colonies vs. countries most vulnerable to climate impacts). In contrast to previous work emphasizing the importance of perceived co-benefits (i.e., reducing global carbon emissions), mitigation payments did not increase policy support relative to adaptation payments. However, loss and damage compensation reduced support relative to mitigation and adaptation payments. Second, participants were more likely to support funding based on climate vulnerability than based on colonial or economic ties. Third, relative to using the existing national budget, wealth taxation increased support across political ideologies, while fossil fuel taxation was popular only among left-leaning participants. Overall, the findings suggest that equitable burden sharing in policy design and emphasizing disproportionate vulnerabilities could enhance support for global climate funding.

Show details
Authors:
Dr. Josianne Kollmann | Eawag: Swiss Federal Institute of Aquatic Science and Technology | Switzerland
Sasha Harris-Lovett | University of California | United States
Prof. Dr. Kara L. Nelson | University of California | United States
Dr. Nadja Contzen | Eawag: Swiss Federal Institute of Aquatic Science and Technology | Switzerland

With increasing water scarcity worldwide, policies regulating wastewater reuse are becoming increasingly important. In San Francisco, on-site wastewater treatment and reuse is mandatory for large residential buildings, while other buildings continue using centralised systems without reuse. This disparity may affect perceived fairness and policy acceptance. Yet, research indicates that not all groups of society are equally considered in peoples’ fairness and acceptance ratings of policies, but it has not yet been investigated which groups are considered in the context of wastewater reuse. To examine this question, we conducted an online survey with residents of San Francisco who were not covered by the policy (N=176). We assessed policy acceptance, perceived fairness, and perceptions of a range of policy implications for five societal groups and one entity: residents and owners of buildings with mandated on-site systems, San Francisco's population, low-income residents, future generations, and the environment. Regression analyses showed that both positive and negative policy implications explained perceived fairness. Policy acceptance was explained by perceived fairness for future generations, San Francisco's population, and building owners, but not other groups or entities. Results suggest that collective fairness considerations and impacts on most-affected groups are key to policy acceptance, indicating policymakers should consider implications across different societal groups when designing water reuse policies.

Using climate litigation to advance climate justice: Insights into citizens’ participation in a constitutional complaint
Kira Maur | Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine, Hamburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Kira Maur | Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine, Hamburg | Germany
Lisa Marie Hempel | Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine, Hamburg | Germany
Mattis Geiger | Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine, Hamburg | Germany
Kevin E. Tiede | University of Erfurt | Germany
Prof. Dr. Cornelia Betsch | University of Erfurt | Germany

Effective climate change mitigation requires not only rapid decarbonisation but also mechanisms enabling citizens to hold governments accountable for insufficient climate action. Climate litigation, referring to legal actions that use courts to hold governments or corporations accountable for their contributions to climate change, has emerged as a powerful instrument of climate justice by allowing individuals to challenge policies that disproportionately shift climate risks and burdens to vulnerable populations and future generations. Despite its growing relevance, little is known about the individual-level factors shaping people’s participation in climate litigation. We address this gap with a preregistered longitudinal experiment (N = 1,998) conducted during Germany’s 2024 constitutional climate complaint against the German government (“Zukunftsklage”), which allowed every German resident to join as a claimant by ordering and submitting paperwork to the law firm. We assessed intention to participate and verified actual participation in the complaint. Prior, we experimentally manipulated theoretically and empirically derived determinants of participation to identify psychological levers. Overall, 24.5% intended to participate, 9.4% ordered the paperwork and 2.8% ultimately joined as official claimants. Neither informational nor social-norm cues increased participation. In contrast, making particularly affected groups salient combined with a self-affectedness exercise prompting reflection on how delayed, strict climate policies would affect one’s own future significantly increased participation. Our findings highlight psychological processes of climate litigation as a democratic instrument shaping climate governance and policy feedback loops that affect political feasibility of rapid decarbonisation and thus enhancing climate justice.

Strengths and Weaknesses of Evidence Syntheses on AI in Education
Chair(s) Dr. Valentin Emslander (University of Giessen)
Co-chair(s) Prof. Dr. Lisa Bardach (University of Giessen)
Room: SI
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and large language models have entered classrooms with promises of transformative learning gains, but the empirical foundation supporting these claims remains fragmented. Existing evidence syntheses differ widely in reported effects, methodological rigor, and, crucially, in the relevance of the outcomes they synthesize, raising doubts about the reliability of current policy recommendations (Bond et al., 2024; Buntins et al., 2024; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2025). In addressing issues related to the quality and rigor of evidence synthesis, this symposium brings together four complementary contributions:

Contribution 1 argues that many recent meta‑analyses overstate AI’s impact because they rely on unclearly defined, over‑aligned outcomes with non-standardized measures. Recoding two published meta-analyses indicates that standardized tests and real-life educational outcomes are rarely used, prompting concrete recommendations for outcome selection and moderation.
Contribution 2 reports a preregistered meta‑meta‑analysis of 45 prior meta‑analyses that yields a moderate-to-large pooled effect but exhibits extreme heterogeneity, recent‑study inflation, and systematic methodological deficits, underscoring the need for stricter reporting standards and high‑quality randomized trials.
Contribution 3 conducts a systematic audit of five meta-analyses on ChatGPT. The audit reveals major gaps in transparency, open‑science practice, and construct validity. Most primary studies focus on short‑term performance rather than genuine learning, suggesting that current meta‑analytic conclusions convey a false sense of certainty.
Contribution 4 presents an expanded study‑level meta‑meta‑analysis of 1 840 effect sizes from 67 meta‑analyses. Severe publication bias and heterogeneity reduce the bias‑adjusted effect to a small magnitude with wide prediction intervals, and no robust moderators emerge, calling into question broad claims of AI‑driven learning gains.
Together, these contributions map the current landscape, diagnose its systematic weaknesses, and outline steps toward more rigorous, transparent, and meaningful research on AI in education.

Literature
