A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: A call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 21(1). https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00436-z

Buntins, K., Bedenlier, S., Marín, V., Händel, M., & Bond, M. (2023). Methodological Approaches to Evidence Synthesis in Educational Technology. MedienPädagogik: Zeitschrift Für Theorie Und Praxis Der Medienbildung, 54, 167–191. https://doi.org/10.21240/mpaed/54/2023.12.20.X

Zawacki‐Richter, O., Cefa, B., & Bai, J. Y. H. (2025). Towards reproducible systematic reviews in Open, Distance, and Digital Education—An umbrella mapping review. Review of Education, 13(1), e70031. https://doi.org/10.1002/rev3.70031

Research Syntheses on AI in Education Offer Limited Educational Insights
Prof. Dr. Lisa Bardach | University of Giessen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Lisa Bardach | University of Giessen | Germany
Dr. Valentin Emslander | University of Giessen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Enkelejda Kasneci | Technical University of Munich | Germany
Prof. Dr. Alexander Eitel | University of Giessen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Marlit Lindner | Europe-University Flensburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Drew H. Bailey | University of California Irvine | United States

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in education. As research in this area grows rapidly, so does the number of meta-analyses. In this commentary, we argue that claims in recent meta-analyses are sometimes overstated and risk misrepresenting the strength of evidence. This issue is not limited to the meta-analyses themselves but indicates broader problems in the field. We focus on a key issue that, in our view, significantly limits the current understanding of the effects of AI in education: the choice of outcome measures. Drawing on educational intervention research, we examine five often-overlooked aspects of performance outcomes in AI in education: (a) standardized versus self-developed tests, (b) broad versus narrow outcome measures, (c) over-alignment between intervention and assessment, (d) lack of real-life educational outcomes, and (e) AI-specific challenges, such as hybrid human-AI performance measurement. To illustrate the scope of these concerns, we coded outcome measures from studies included in two recent meta-analyses: the most comprehensive to date on chatbots and on learning with ChatGPT, respectively. We found, for example, that only 12% of studies used standardized achievement tests, and 10% assessed real-life educational outcomes (e.g., course grades.) These design features limit the applied relevance of the field and reduce the usefulness of research syntheses for informing educational theory and practice. We suggest that insights from educational intervention research can help address these measurement issues. Our commentary offers actionable recommendations, including moderating meta-analyses by outcome type and prioritizing distal outcomes, to strengthen the empirical foundation of AI in education research.

A Meta-Meta-Analysis on AI in Education
Dr. Valentin Emslander | University of Giessen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Valentin Emslander | University of Giessen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Marlit Lindner | Europe-University Flensburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Alexander Eitel | University of Giessen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Enkelejda Kasneci | Technical University of Munich | Germany
Prof. Dr. Lisa Bardach | Germany

The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in classrooms has attracted considerable attention from researchers, educators, and policymakers. AI applications range from automated essay‑scoring and language‑learning chatbots to large generative language models such as ChatGPT, yet many are deployed without rigorous efficacy testing. Despite this field being relatively young, several meta-analyses have been conducted, exploring various AI interventions and experiments in education. However, these meta-analyses have differed substantially in their reported effects, identified moderators, and methodological quality, leaving the field fragmented and inconclusive. To resolve these contradictions, we conducted a preregistered meta‑meta‑analysis that aggregates the evidence across existing meta‑analyses (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/K5JG4). We aimed to (a) estimate the overall magnitude of AI‑driven learning effects, (b) identify which contextual moderators systematically inflate or deflate those effects, and (c) evaluate the methodological quality of the underlying meta‑analyses. We synthesized 45 meta-analyses, totaling 129 meta-analytic effect sizes, based on approximately 197,000 learners from prekindergarten through university level. The three-level meta-meta-analyses yielded a medium-sized average effect for AI in education across all outcomes and AI types, with substantial heterogeneity within and between meta-analyses. Effects were significantly larger in recent meta-analyses, with university samples and broader learning outcomes, and we detected publication bias. Methodological quality did not explain variance in effect sizes, but showed a systematic quality deficit. Future research must adopt stricter reporting standards, prioritize high‑quality randomized trials, and interrogate the ethical and equity implications of AI‑driven education.

A Critical Epistemological Audit of Early Evidence Syntheses in Generative AI Educational Research
Nina Peltzer | University of Munich (LMU) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Tim Fütterer | University of Tübingen | Germany
Nina Peltzer | University of Munich (LMU) | Germany

Prof. Dr. Detmar Meurers | Leibniz-Institut für Wissensmedien | Germany
Dr. Tamara Tate | University of California | United States
Prof. Dr. Mark Warschauer | University of California | United States
Prof. Dr. John Hattie | University of Melbourne | Australia
Prof. Dr. Michael Sailer | University of Augsburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Lisa Bardach | University of Giessen | Germany
Dr. Valentin Emslander | University of Giessen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Jochen Kuhn | University of Munich (LMU) | Germany

The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), following the release of ChatGPT in late 2022, has triggered a swift empirical response, including early meta-analyses aimed at assessing ChatGPT's effects on student learning outcomes. However, given the novelty and volatility of this research field, concerns have emerged regarding the maturity and quality of the underlying evidence base. This study presents a systematic epistemological audit of published meta-analyses on ChatGPT in education, aiming to exemplify whether these syntheses rest on a sufficiently robust empirical foundation. Following PRISMA guidelines and a preregistered protocol, we identified five eligible meta-analyses comprising 92 primary studies. Using a comprehensive coding scheme, we evaluated methodological rigor, transparency, and open science practices at both the meta-analytic and primary-study level. Results indicate substantial methodological limitations. Although all meta-analyses reported systematic searches and basic statistical diagnostics, none employed independent double screening or coding, preregistration, or full data and code sharing. The primary studies showed moderate overall quality, with pronounced weaknesses in open science practices and key design and reporting standards. Most primary studies focused on short-term performance outcomes rather than learning outcomes, raising concerns about construct conflation and the interpretability of aggregated effects. Overall, our findings suggest that current meta-analytic conclusions on the educational effectiveness of ChatGPT may convey a misleading sense of certainty. At the conference, we will extend this audit by examining the learning activities and support strategies targeted in the primary studies and by comparing effect size distributions between studies focusing on learning versus performance outcomes.

Effect of Artificial Intelligence on Learning: A Meta-Meta-Analysis
František Bartoš | University of Amsterdam | Netherlands
Show details
Author:
František Bartoš | University of Amsterdam | Netherlands

Artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) are believed to revolutionize education. This claim is supported by empirical evidence from dozens of meta-analyses that report large and statistically significant average effects of AI/LLMs on learning outcomes. Here we challenge the empirical base by a study-level meta-meta-analysis of 1,840 effect size estimates from 67 meta-analyses. The results show strong evidence of severe publication bias and extreme between-study heterogeneity. Publication-bias adjusted analyses reveal model-averaged effects approximately one-third the magnitude of unadjusted estimates (standardized mean difference, SMD = 0.196, 95% credible interval from 0.000 to 0.323), along with wide prediction intervals spanning both large negative and positive effects (-1.521 to 1.908). Subgroup analyses fail to identify specific moderators, such as outcome type, education field, education level, or AI/LLMs role, that yield consistent benefits. Neither we find substantial differences when analyzing studies published through 2022 and after 2022 separately. Overall, broad claims of generalized learning gains resulting from AI and LLMs appear premature; the current evidence is insufficient to support robust policy or practice recommendations.

Meetings gestalten: digital, hybrid, immersiv und interorganisational
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Simone Kauffeld (Technische Universität Braunschweig, Institut für Psychologie)
Room: CZ
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Meetings haben sich zu zentralen Orten der Zusammenarbeit, Führung und Beteiligung in modernen Arbeitskontexten entwickelt. Gestalterische Herausforderungen stellen sich durch neue technologische Möglichkeiten. Nesher Shoshan & Cloos eröffnen das Symposium mit einer feldnahen Experience-Sampling-Studie zu virtuellen Meetings und untersuchen, wie Kameraautonomie das aktive Beteiligungsverhalten beeinflusst. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass das Schließen der Kamera mit geringerer aktiver Teilnahme einhergeht – selbst bei hoch engagierten Mitarbeitenden – und verdeutlichen die Relevanz klarer Gestaltungsregeln. Stegmann et al. erweitern diese Perspektive um v.a. interorganisationale Meetings im Baubereich. Auf Basis qualitativer Interviews und einer Critical-Incident-Analyse werden zentrale Erfolgsfaktoren für vertrauensbasierte, effektive Zusammenarbeit über Organisationsgrenzen hinweg identifiziert. Bruhn et al. richten den Fokus auf Führung und Gesundheit in digitalen Meetings. In einer experimentellen Between-Subjects-Studie wird geprüft, ob immersive Virtual Reality gegenüber Videokonferenzen und Face-to-Face-Settings Offenheit, Vertrauen und gesundheitsorientierte Führung begünstigt. Die Ergebnisse deuten auf ein besonderes Potenzial von VR für soziale Präsenz und Teamvertrauen hin. Ritter et al. analysieren mikrodynamische Führungsprozesse in virtuellen Meetings mithilfe eines interaktionsbasierten Codierschemas. Die Daten zeigen, dass Führung situativ und verteilt entsteht und nicht primär an formale Rollen gebunden ist. Bödding & Maier untersuchen in einer präregistrierten experimentellen Studie, wie Augmented Reality Präsenz, kognitive Aktivierung und Interaktion in arbeitsbezogenen Kontexten fördern kann. Weber & Kauffeld schließen das Symposium mit einer netzwerkanalytischen Längsschnittstudie zu Beteiligungsmustern in hybriden Meetings ab. Die Analysen zeigen, dass sich Interaktionsstrukturen mit zunehmender Meetingerfahrung angleichen und remote Teilnehmende stabile zentrale Rollen einnehmen. Insgesamt integriert das Symposium verschiedene theoretische Perspektiven und experimentelle, qualitative, netzwerkanalytische und feldbasierte Methoden, um Meetings als zentrale psychologische Handlungskontexte der Zusammenarbeit zu beleuchten.

Do engaged employees still participate in virtual meetings when their camera is closed?
Prof. Dr. Hadar Nesher Shoshan | Institut für Psychologie
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Hadar Nesher Shoshan | Institut für Psychologie
Helene Carla Cloos | Institut für Psychologie

Virtual meetings have become a highly relevant tool in the post-pandemic work world. A question is whether participants in virtual meetings should be allowed to close their cameras (have “camera autonomy”) or whether opening the camera should be mandatory. To this end, in this study, we investigated if people still actively participate in virtual meetings when their camera is closed, and whether there are individual differences in this behavior, such that employees with high work engagement keep active participation even if allowed to close their camera. In an experience sampling study,125 employees reported on their video meetings (n video meetings = 670) three times a day over 10 days (n days = 467). They answered questions about their free choice whether to close their camera (“camera autonomy”), the amount of time using the camera in the meeting, their active participation in the meeting, and their general work engagement. Results of three-level analysis showed that when closing their camera, employees reduced their active participation in the meeting, even if they were high in work engagement. Camera autonomy was related to less use of the camera, and there was also an indirect effect between camera autonomy and active participation through camera use. Our results show that people prefer not to use their cameras when they are allowed to. However, closing the camera comes with a price of less active participation in the meeting, even for engaged employees. Thus, organizations should carefully consider their regulations regarding camera use in video meetings.

Interorganisationale Meetings im Bau: Erfolgreiche Zusammenarbeit durch Vertrauen und Klarheit
Elija Stegmann | Technische Universität Braunschweig / Institut für Arbeits-, Organisations- und Sozialpsychologie | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Elija Stegmann | Technische Universität Braunschweig / Institut für Arbeits-, Organisations- und Sozialpsychologie | Germany
Dr. Sandra Rothenbusch | Technische Universität Braunschweig / Institut für Arbeits-, Organisations- und Sozialpsychologie
Prof. Dr. Simone Kauffeld | Technische Universität Braunschweig / Institut für Arbeits-, Organisations- und Sozialpsychologie

Eine erfolgreiche Zusammenarbeit in interorganisationalen Teams hängt entscheidend von effektiver, adressatengerechter Kommunikation und Vertrauen ab (u.a. Chong et al., 2013; Dregger, 2021). Im Baubereich treten diese Bedingungen häufig nicht optimal auf: Mangelnde Abstimmung und starkes Misstrauen zwischen den Akteur*innen erschweren die Kooperation (Kwofie et al., 2019; Ibrahim et al., 2015; Jaffar et al., 2011). Wie effektive Meetings in diesem Kontext konkret gestaltet werden können, ist bisher wenig erforscht.
Zur Entwicklung praxisnaher Lösungsansätze wurden 31 Personen aus dem Baubereich zu interorganisationalen Besprechungen interviewt. Sie berichteten über besonders erfolgreiche und misslungene Meetings und beschrieben Aussagen, Handlungen oder Tools, die zum Erfolg oder Misserfolg beitrugen (Flanagan, 1954).
Die Ergebnisse verdeutlichen, dass bereits im Vorfeld klare Zielsetzungen, eine sorgfältige Auswahl der Teilnehmenden sowie Dauer und Format entscheidend für einen strukturierten und störungsfreien Ablauf sind. Erfolgreiche Meetings fördern einen offenen Informationsaustausch, vermeiden taktisches Zurückhalten von Informationen und legen den Fokus auf gegenseitige Vorteile. Unterstützendes Verhalten ermöglicht allen Teilnehmenden, sich aktiv einzubringen.
Die Befunde unterstreichen die zentrale Rolle von Vertrauen und Rollenklarheit und liefern konkrete Ansatzpunkte, wie interorganisationale Meetings im Bau effektiv gestaltet werden können. Sie bieten sowohl praktische Hinweise für die Meeting-Gestaltung als auch theoretische Implikationen für Forschung zu Teaminteraktion, Kooperation und Kommunikation über Organisationsgrenzen hinweg.

Die paradoxe Rolle virtueller Realität in der Gesundheitsorientierten Führung
Dr. Katharina Bruhn | Helmut Schmidt University
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Katharina Bruhn | Helmut Schmidt University
Franziska Münstermann
Yannick Frontzkowski
Philip Gubernator
Prof. Dr. Jörg Felfe

Digitale Arbeitskontexte haben Teaminteraktionen grundlegend verändert und stellen Führungskräfte vor die Herausforderung, neben der Koordination der Zusammenarbeit auch die Gesundheit und das Wohlbefinden ihrer Mitarbeitenden zu fördern. Gleichzeitig erschwert die physische Distanz digitaler Kommunikation eine Gesundheitsorientierte Führung, da sie die Wahrnehmung relevanter Signale sowie den Aufbau psychologisch sicherer und unterstützender Arbeitsumgebungen beeinträchtigen kann. Diese Aspekte sind jedoch zentral für die frühzeitige Erkennung von Frühwarnsignalen, rechtzeitige Interventionen und die persönliche Öffnungsbereitschaft im Team. Während frühere Forschung entsprechende Herausforderungen insbesondere für Videokonferenzen und Telefonate dokumentiert hat, ist bislang offen, ob immersive virtuelle Realität (VR) diese Einschränkungen überwinden kann. Auf Grundlage der Media-Richness-Theorie lässt sich vermuten, dass VR durch unmittelbares Feedback, reichhaltigere nonverbale Kommunikation und eine erhöhte soziale Präsenz günstigere Bedingungen für eine Gesundheitsorientierte Führung schafft. Zur Prüfung dieser Annahme wurde eine experimentelle Between-Subjects-Studie (N = 169) durchgeführt, in der drei Kommunikationssettings (Face-to-Face, Videokonferenz, VR) verglichen wurden. Die Teilnehmenden arbeiteten in zufällig zugewiesenen Triaden an einer strukturierten Team-Entscheidungsaufgabe und berichteten anschließend über ihre Wahrnehmung von Warnsignalen sowie über ihre persönliche Öffnungsbereitschaft. Hinsichtlich der Wahrnehmung von Warnsignalen zeigten sich keine signifikanten Unterschiede zwischen den Bedingungen, wenngleich deskriptive Trends zugunsten von VR gegenüber der Videokonferenz erkennbar waren. Die Öffnungsbereitschaft war in der VR-Bedingung jedoch signifikant höher als in der Videokonferenz und, entgegen der Annahme, auch höher als im Face-to-Face-Setting. Insgesamt deuten die Befunde auf ein Potenzial immersiver Technologien zur Förderung

Leader by title or interaction? A Micro-Temporal Analysis of Leadership Emergence in Virtual Teams
Dr. Marie Ritter | Technische Universität Braunschweig / Institut für für Arbeits-, Organisations- und Sozialpsychologie | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Marie Ritter | Technische Universität Braunschweig / Institut für für Arbeits-, Organisations- und Sozialpsychologie | Germany
Prof. Dr. Simone Kauffeld | Technische Universität Braunschweig / Institut für für Arbeits-, Organisations- und Sozialpsychologie | Germany
Darien Tartler | Technische Universität Braunschweig / Institut für für Arbeits-, Organisations- und Sozialpsychologie | Germany
Nico Wegner | Technische Universität Braunschweig / Institut für für Arbeits-, Organisations- und Sozialpsychologie | Germany

Virtual workplace meetings have become a central coordination mechanism in contemporary organizations, yet the micro-level interaction processes through which leadership emerges in these settings remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on leadership identity construction theory, we conceptualize emergent leadership as a dynamic claiming–granting process in which team members assert leadership (claims) and others respond by endorsing or accepting this influence (grants). While prior experimental research highlights the relevance of claim→grant sequences, evidence on the interaction between formal and emergent leadership from real-world organizational contexts—particularly in established teams operating virtually—remains limited.
We analyzed 55 virtual meetings from a large German engineering organization. Meetings were coded using an interaction-based coding scheme. Results supported the presence of both claim→grant and grant→claim sequences in virtual meetings. Contrary to expectations, leadership claims by formal leaders were not more likely to be granted than claims by other team members. Moreover, successful leadership interactions (claim→grant and grant→claim) were not associated with meeting satisfaction. Instead, competitive sequences (claim→claim) were negatively related to meeting satisfaction, whereas submissive sequences (grant→grant) were unexpectedly associated with higher meeting satisfaction.
Overall, the findings suggest that leadership dynamics in virtual meetings are more nuanced than anticipated: emergent influence is not necessarily anchored in the formal leader role but may be enacted by multiple team members and potentially distributed across the team. By adopting a micro-level interaction perspective, this study offers novel insight into everyday leadership processes in virtual work meetings and advances both theory and practice in leadership and meeting research.

Do Virtual Meetings Make Us too Tired to Take a Break? Understanding Videoconference Fatigue and Recovery in Daily Work Life
Dr. Agnieszka Paruzel
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Agnieszka Paruzel
Lisa Bemmann
Justin Hachenberger
Sakari Lemola
Prof. Dr. Günter W. Maier

The increasing prevalence of virtual meetings has raised concerns about videoconference fatigue and its consequences for employee well-being. Fatigue has become a major challenge in digital work, highlighting the critical role of recovery ̶ yet little is known about effective within-day strategies and how they work. Grounded in Conservation of Resources Theory, this preregistered study examined daily recovery processes in virtual work environments by integrating videoconference fatigue, recovery strategies, and organizational context factors. We hypothesized that meeting duration and frequency would predict videoconference fatigue, that this fatigue would be linked to microbreak behavior through the desire to detach, that microbreak climate would moderate this relationship, and that microbreaks would mediate the association between fatigue and evening strain. Using a five-day daily diary design, 74 employees reported their experiences across 271 daily  observations. Multilevel analyses revealed that meeting frequency - but not duration - was positively related to videoconference fatigue. Fatigue increased the desire to detach, yet this motivation did not lead to more microbreaks. The link between desire to detach and microbreak-taking depended on microbreak climate: In supportive environments, employees were more likely to act on their recovery motivation. Overall, the findings emphasize the importance of motivational and contextual mechanisms for managing videoconference fatigue in daily work life.

Dabei sein ist alles? Eine netzwerkanalytische Betrachtung der Teilnehmerbeteiligung in digitalen Meetings
Maischa Weber | Technische Universität Braunschweig / Institut für Arbeits-, Organisations- und Sozialpsychologie | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Maischa Weber | Technische Universität Braunschweig / Institut für Arbeits-, Organisations- und Sozialpsychologie | Germany
Prof. Dr. Simone Kauffeld | Technische Universität Braunschweig / Institut für Arbeits-, Organisations- und Sozialpsychologie | Germany

In zunehmend räumlich verteilten Arbeitskontexten sind digitale Meetings zentral für Informationsaustausch, Entscheidungsfindung und soziale Teilhabe (Kauffeld & Sauer, 2021). Dabei ist eine aktive Beteiligung aller Teilnehmenden essentiell und gleichzeitig eine Herausforderung im digitalen Raum (El Zouhbi et al., 2025; Yarmand et al., 2024). Ausgehend von Teams als dynamischen Systemen (Mathieu et al., 2019) sind wir den Fragen nachgegangen, wie sich die Meetingbeteiligung in Form von Sprechbeiträgen („Turns“) mit zunehmender, digitaler Meetingerfahrung entwickelt und inwiefern sie in hybriden Formaten von dem individuellen Teilnahmemodus (digital /Präsenz) abhängt. Dazu wurden über ein Jahr wöchentl. Regelmeetings eines Teams aufgezeichnet, die Turns der Teilnehmenden kodiert und netzwerkanalytisch ausgewertet. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass im Netzwerk zentrale Personen mit zunehmender Meetingdurchführung dezentraler wurden und weniger eingebundene Personen sich zunehmend mehr beteiligten. Darüber hinaus konnte bestätigt werden, dass die Teilnahmeform in hybriden Meetings mit der individuellen Netzwerkzentralität zusammenhängt: Interessanterweise hatten entgegen unserer Annahmen, Remoteteilnehmende insgesamt mehr Turns und waren damit innerhalb eines Meetingnetzwerks zentraler als Teilnehmende vor Ort. Dieser Effekt bleibt zudem zeitl. stabil. Während frühere Studien den physischen Raum in hybriden Meetings als dominanten Primärraum (Karis et al., 2016; Saatçi et al., 2020) beschreiben, verdeutlicht das vorliegende Fallbeispiel, dass sich Beteiligungsmuster mit wachsender Meetingerfahrung angleichen und auch eine Remoteteilnahme eine zentrale Position einnehmen kann. Entsprechend sollten Teilnahmeformen stärker in Abhängigkeit vom tatsächlich wirksamen Primärraum berücksichtigt werden, um gleichmäßige Inklusion zu fördern. Das Fallbeispiel bildet den Ausgangspunkt für weitere Untersuchungen zur integrativen Gestaltung hybrider Meetings in verteilten Arbeitsteams.

Room: DK
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Coupled symposium
Duration: 195 Minutes

Machine learning methods are increasingly used in psychological research to analyze complex data and improve predictive accuracy. However, their rapid adoption raises fundamental questions about interpretation, measurement, inference, and theoretical integration. This two-part symposium brings together recent methodological advances and substantive applications using machine learning in psychological research, beyond prediction alone.
The first part focuses on methodological and conceptual foundations. It starts with a review of how machine learning is currently used and interpreted in psychological research. Contributions then address how machine learning results can be integrated with hypothesis testing and preregistration, how measurement error in psychological constructs affects prediction, how multilevel data structures challenge tree-based methods, and why commonly used model fit cutoffs may be misleading.
The second part showcases applications to core psychological questions, including climate adaptation and collective action, well-being captured via smartphones and Danish register data, and individual differences in behavioral predictability across life domains. In addition, a proof-of-concept study demonstrates how large language models can support research synthesis workflows.
Together, the symposium illustrates how machine learning can be used responsibly in psychological research, emphasizing statistical integrations, interpretability, and theoretical relevance.

How is Machine Learning Used and Interpreted in Psychological Research?
Jan Radek | Faculty of Psychology, University of Basel | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Jan Radek | Faculty of Psychology, University of Basel | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Carolin Strobl | Institute of Psychology, University of Zurich | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Rosa Lavelle-Hill | Digital Humanities Lab and Department of Social Sciences, University of Basel | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Mirka Henninger | Digital Humanities Lab and Department of Social Sciences, University of Basel

The use of machine learning is experiencing an upswing in many areas of psychology and related disciplines. However, there is limited knowledge of how and for what purposes researchers employ machine learning to analyze psychological data. To investigate the extent and form in which machine learning is applied in psychological research, we developed a structured description framework that consists of four major steps: Data assessment and preprocessing (1), fitting the models (2), identifying informative variables (3) and interpreting their relationship with the outcome (4). Using this framework, we systematically examined the current state of the field by reviewing psychological and psychiatric research articles published in 2022 and between June 2024 and May 2025. All selected articles present an empirical study and employ one or more supervised machine learning models for data analysis. We observed that most psychological researchers (1) utilized low-dimensional data typical for the field, (2) performed a variety of model fitting approaches using cross-validation and train-test splits, (3) identified informative variables, but (4) rarely interpreted the relationship between these variables and the model’s outcome. Furthermore, we discuss the generally heterogeneous picture of machine learning reporting in our discipline and emphasize the need for standardized reporting guidelines.

Are my Machine Learning Results Statistically Significant? A Guide for Integrating Hypothesis Testing and Pre-registration
Prof. Dr. Rosa Lavelle-Hill | Digital Humanities Lab and Department of Social Sciences, University of Basel | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Rosa Lavelle-Hill | Digital Humanities Lab and Department of Social Sciences, University of Basel | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Kou Murayama | Hector Research Institute of Education Sciences and Psychology, University of Tubingen | Germany

Machine learning methods are increasingly used in psychology for their ability to model complex, high-dimensional data and generate accurate predictions. However, their growing adoption has also raised concerns about how to evaluate statistical significance, theoretical relevance, and the generalizability of predictive findings. In contrast to traditional statistical modeling, supervised machine learning is rarely embedded within a formal framework of hypothesis testing or pre-registration, limiting its interpretability and inferential value for theory-driven research. This article provides a comprehensive guide to integrating hypothesis testing with supervised machine learning, with a particular focus on applications in psychological science. We first review existing statistical methods for testing the significance of predictive performance, comparing models, and feature importance results. We then propose a framework of different use cases for using statistical testing in machine learning: to test i) whether a model predicts better than theoretically relevant baselines, ii) whether competing theories differ in predictive power, iii) whether findings generalize across different datasets or subsets, and iv) to evaluate whether individual predictors or sets of predictors contribute significantly to the prediction. Further, we discuss how these approaches can be incorporated into pre-registrations and registered reports to reduce researcher degrees of freedom and procedural overfitting. Finally, we highlight key limitations of significance testing in large-scale predictive contexts and emphasize the importance of effect sizes, uncertainty quantification, and transparent reporting. Together, this paper aims to bridge predictive and inferential traditions, offering practical guidance for researchers seeking to draw theoretically meaningful conclusions from machine learning analyses.

Garbage In, Garbage Out: Does Psychometric Modeling Improve Machine Learning Prediction in Empirical Data?
Dr. Larissa Sust | Department of Psychology, Ludwig Maximilian University Munich | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Larissa Sust | Department of Psychology, Ludwig Maximilian University Munich | Germany
Prof. Dr. David Goretzko | Institute of Psychology, Goethe University Frankfurt | Germany
Dr. Philipp Sterner | Centre for International Student Assessment, Technical University of Munich | Germany
Dr. Jan Digutsch | Faculty of Psychology, Ruhr University Bochum | Germany

An increasingly prominent goal in psychological research is to leverage machine learning (ML) to predict psychological constructs from ecologically valid digital behavioral data (e.g., Facebook likes, spending records). Yet, the target variables in these models are typically derived from self-report questionnaires, whose item responses contain measurement error and thus serve as imperfect indicators of the latent psychological constructs. When aggregate item scores are used in ML, these psychometric limitations are directly propagated into the prediction model. Simulation studies suggest that such measurement error can attenuate predictive performance and mask potential benefits of complex, nonlinear algorithms. However, it remains largely unclear how these effects manifest in real-world psychological data.
In this talk, we use data from a large-scale mobile-sensing study (N = 800) to examine how measurement error in psychological target variables affects ML-based prediction. Passively sensed smartphone behaviors serve as largely error-free predictors of several widely studied constructs, including the Big Five personality traits, trait affect, life satisfaction, and motive-specific contingencies, all assessed with Likert-style questionnaires. We systematically compare the predictive performance of models trained on item-sum scores with models predicting latent factor scores derived from confirmatory factor analysis. We evaluate both linear and nonlinear ML algorithms and test whether modeling constructs at the latent level yields performance gains over sum-score–based targets. By holding predictors constant and varying only the target variable’s representation, our work isolates the role of measurement error in ML and fuels discussion of how to integrate psychometric modeling more explicitly into predictive workflows.

Tree-based Machine Learning Methods for Multilevel Data: The Impact of Predictor Levels and Clustering on Prediction and Inference
Linus Hany | Faculty of Psychology, University of Basel | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Linus Hany | Faculty of Psychology, University of Basel | Switzerland
Dr. Marjolein Fokkema | University of Leiden | Netherlands
Constantin Wiegand | Faculty of Psychology, University of Basel | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Mirka Henninger | Faculty of Psychology, University of Basel | Switzerland

Machine learning methods, such as decision trees and random forests, allow researchers to investigate complex non-linear and interaction effects. Therefore, these methods have become valuable tools for exploring complex psychological processes. In recent years, first attempts have been made to extend decision tree methods (multilevel trees) for their application to multilevel data, e.g., with level-1 (e.g., students) and level-2 (e.g., classes) units. While these adaptations often include adding random effects to the models, they typically do not address the influence of the levels at which the predictor variables operate. We investigate how predictor level (level-1 vs. level-2) and clustering (Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC), number of clusters, cluster size) affect inference and prediction in six tree methods: rpart, ctree, REEMtree, REEMctree, MERT, and lmertree. Using simulation studies, we evaluate variable selection, predictive performance (PMSE, r2), and partial dependence. Our results show that inference as well as prediction in multilevel tree methods are seriously affected by the level of the predictor variables and clustering in the data. In particular, the risk of falsely selecting non-informative level-2 predictors is increased when the ICC is substantial. Ignoring the multilevel structure of the data might lead to erroneous research conclusions despite the multilevel extensions of the tree methods. We conclude by discussing potential remedies for empirical researchers.

Why We Should not Blindly Trust Fixed Cutoffs for Model Fit Indices―Insights from Interpretable Machine Learning
Dr. Melanie Viola Partsch | Utrecht University | Netherlands
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Melanie Viola Partsch | Utrecht University | Netherlands
Prof. Dr. Mirka Henninger | Faculty of Psychology, University of Basel | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Carmen Ximénez | Autonomous University of Madrid | Spain
Prof. Dr. David Goretzko | Institute of Psychology, Goethe University Frankfurt | Germany

To evaluate the global fit of their measurement and structural equation models, researchers commonly rely on model fit indices, such as the CFI, RMSEA, or SRMR, in combination with fixed cutoff rules. However, such cutoff rules were originally derived from relatively simple simulation studies and often do not generalize well to researchers’ real-world use cases. This is because the size of the model fit indices does not only depend on a model’s fit to the data but also on various other model and data characteristics, so-called “nuisance parameters”. In this talk, I will present a machine learning (ML) approach to examine and demonstrate these interaction effects among model fit indices, nuisance parameters, and model (mis-)fit. In our study, we used an ML model that was trained to classify the misspecification of a measurement model based on different model fit indices and various nuisance parameters. Analyzing this ML model with two different Interpretable ML methods—Feature Interaction and two-dimensional Accumulated Local Effects—provided insights into how the model fit indices and nuisance parameters interacted in shaping the ML model’s classification decisions. We will discuss both the practical implications of these insights and the limitations of Interpretable ML methods in examining the intricate interplay of model misspecifications, fit indices, and nuisance parameters.

Predicting Climate Adaptation Intention and Collective Climate Action: A Supervised Machine Learning Approach
Elisabeth Glunz | Digital Humanities Lab, University of Basel | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Elisabeth Glunz | Digital Humanities Lab, University of Basel | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Rosa Lavelle-Hill | Digital Humanities Lab, University of Basel | Switzerland
Dr. Daniela Stelzmann | Department of Economic Sciences and Media, Technische Universität Ilmenau | Germany
Prof. Dr. Lars Gerhold | Faculty of Psychology, Technische Universität Braunschweig | Germany

Individual engagement in adaptation to climate hazards (e.g., create an emergency plan) and collective climate action (e.g., participate in a protest) arises from the interplay of numerous variables. This study employed a supervised machine learning (ML) approach to address two questions: first, how accurately ML models – incorporating a theory-transcendent set of variables ranging from trust in relevant actors to climate emotions, predict climate adaptation intention and collective climate action compared to linear models based on established theories; and second, which variables are most important for these predictions. Data were collected in 2024 from 4,246 participants in the UK, Italy, Germany, and the USA using online representative quota sampling. We applied models of varying complexity, including three ML algorithms, to predict engagement in climate adaptation and collective climate action. The ML algorithms which model 94 variables substantially improved predictive performance beyond linear regressions grounded in established theories. Climate emotions (particularly enthusiasm, guilt, and isolation), general coping styles and age were key predictors of both climate adaptation intention and collective climate action. Additionally, media exposure to climate change and extreme weather, along with social support for these issues, emerged as important predictors. These findings underscore the complexity of predicting individual engagement in climate adaptation and mitigation efforts due to the large number of interacting variables. We discuss potential leverage points to be tested in future studies, such as climate emotions and the social amplification of climate change impacts through media and interpersonal channels.

Satisfaction with Life Manifests in Physical Activity Patterns Captured with Smartphones
Max Bergmann | University of St. Gallen | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Max Bergmann | University of St. Gallen | Switzerland
Sarah Mueller | Leibniz Institute for Psychology | Germany
Prof. Dr. Ramona Schoedel | Ludwig Maximilian University Munich | Germany
Prof. Dr. Gabriella Harari | Stanford University | United States
Dr. Mirjam Stieger | Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts
Prof. Dr. Samuel Gosling | University of Texas | United States
Dr. Mathias Allemand | University of Zürich | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Clemens Stachl | University of St. Gallen | Switzerland

Satisfaction with life (SWL) plays a vital role in human prosperity, making it a key focus for practitioners and researchers alike. Research has shown that between-person differences in SWL relate to self-reported patterns in physical activity including activity and inactivity during daytimes and overnight. However, these relationships rarely replicate in objective measures of activity, leaving real-life manifestations of SWL obscure. Here, we use an interpretable machine learning approach to examine how smartphone-captured patterns of everyday activity (1,232 behavioural features) relate to SWL in an international dataset (N = 2,272) combining four independently collected samples. The cross-validated results demonstrate that especially extremeness and variation in everyday activity patterns predict SWL (𝑟𝑀𝑑 = .18, 𝑟𝐼𝑄𝑅 = [.14, .21]) and that predictiveness varies especially with individuals’ personality. These findings enhance our understanding of real-life manifestations of SWL in everyday activity patterns, highlighting the potential of smartphone-based methods for well-being research and interventions.

Satisfaction, Meaning, and Richness – Using Machine Learning to Uncover the Secrets of a Good Life
Marten Appel | Copenhagen Center for Social Data Science, University of Copenhagen | Denmark
Show details
Authors:
Marten Appel | Copenhagen Center for Social Data Science, University of Copenhagen | Denmark
Prof. Dr. Ingo Zettler | Copenhagen Center for Social Data Science and Department of Psychology, University of Copenhagen | Denmark
Prof. Dr. Lau Lilleholt | Copenhagen Center for Social Data Science and Department of Psychology, University of Copenhagen | Denmark
Prof. Dr. Rosa Lavelle-Hill | Digital Humanities Lab, University of Basel | Switzerland

Building on Oishi and Westgate's (2022) three-dimensional framework of a good life, distinguishing between happiness, meaning, and psychological richness, this preregistered study examines the replicability of the suggested structure in a Danish context using 5,464 respondents. In addition to replication, we link respondents panel survey data to Danish register data to do two further analyses: Hypothesis testing of known relationships and, via the use of interpretable machine learning, investigating the most important predictors of each dimension.
Confirmatory factor analysis supports the three-factor model despite fit indices not fulfilling preregistered thresholds. A follow-up exploratory factor analysis confirmed the structure while identifying possible problematic items. Moreover, when examining hypothesized relationships between dimensions and theoretical variables, such as income and extraversion, findings show that most relationships replicate in the expected directions.
Interpretable machine learning is used to predict the dimensions with 193 covariates (36 from survey, 157 from registers), allowing for interactions and non-linearities. The final ensemble model achieved an out-of-sample R² of 0.42 for happiness, 0.27 for meaning, and 0.41 for richness, substantially outperforming literature-based benchmarks (0.31; 0.22; 0.35). Preliminary analysis also reveals that across dimensions the most important predictor remains extraversion, but meaningful differences in other predictors do occur, with examples being marriage for happiness and risk propensity for richness.
Taken together, the study supports a three-dimensional framework in a Danish context, quantifies known relationships across dimensions, and reveals important differential predictability and predictors through systematic exploration of many commonly unavailable covariates.

Is Individual Predictability Trait-Like?
Dr. Johanna Einsiedler | Digital Humanities Lab, University of Basel | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Johanna Einsiedler | Digital Humanities Lab, University of Basel | Switzerland
Marten Appel | Copenhagen Center for Social Data Science | Switzerland
Maximilian Bergmann | University of St. Gallen | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Lau Lilleholt | Copenhagen Center for Social Data Science and Department of Psychology, University of Copenhagen | Denmark
Prof. Dr. Ingo Zettler | Copenhagen Center for Social Data Science and Department of Psychology, University of Copenhagen | Denmark

Human behavior is shaped by a multitude of interacting factors, yet individuals differ substantially in how predictable their life outcomes are. While prior research has largely focused on predicting outcomes, relatively little is known about whether behavioral predictability constitutes a stable, trait-like individual difference. In this study, we employ a large-scale supervised machine learning approach to investigate heterogeneity, consistency, and stability in individual behavioral predictability. Using linked Danish population register data and longitudinal survey data from the Danish Personality and Social Behavior Panel, we predict five major life outcome domains—education, income, profession, health, and family status. We apply an ensemble of supervised learning models of varying complexity to estimate individual-level predictive uncertainty, which we interpret as an indicator of behavioral predictability. We address four core questions: (1) whether behavioral predictability meaningfully varies across individuals and sociodemographic groups; (2) whether individuals’ predictability is consistent across different life domains; (3) whether predictability is stable across time horizons and outcome years; and (4) whether predictability is systematically related to established personality traits. Our modeling framework integrates uncertainty-aware prediction, calibrated ensemble learning, and explainable machine learning techniques. By shifting the focus from average model accuracy to individual-level uncertainty, this study advances a psychological perspective on predictability and provides empirical evidence on whether predictability can be understood as a trait-like characteristic. The findings have implications for fairness, ethics, and accountability in algorithmic decision-making, as well as for theories of personality and life-course development.

Using Large-language Models for Abstract Screening in Research Synthesis: A Proof-of-concept and Recommendations
Prof. Dr. Mirka Henninger | Faculty of Psychology, University of Basel | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Mirka Henninger | Faculty of Psychology, University of Basel | Switzerland
Jan Radek | Faculty of Psychology, University of Basel | Switzerland
Dr. Jean-Paul Snijder-Steinhilber | RWTH Aachen University | Germany

Conducting research synthesis projects, such as systematic reviews or meta-analyses, requires identifying all relevant studies, screening titles and abstracts, and extracting information from full-text articles. This screening and data extraction process is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and prone to errors, demanding substantial training and expertise from reviewers.
In this project, we explore how large language models (LLMs) can be used to automate and streamline the abstract screening process in research synthesis. We begin with an overview of key LLM characteristics, then present a practical procedure for integrating LLMs into abstract screening workflows. We illustrate this procedure using data from an ongoing research synthesis project, demonstrating how the process can be automated, how prompts and hyperparameters can be adapted, and how outputs vary across different settings.
Because LLMs are developed and updated at high speed, our goal is not to provide a definitive protocol but to share insights and experiences from our application, offering a foundation for future discussions, methodological innovations, and workflow optimizations in research synthesis.

Research Talks: Childhood and Parenting
Room: BE
Topic:
Form of presentation: Research Talk
Duration: 90 Minutes
Parenting in the Age of AI: An Exploratory and Confirmatory Analysis of Parental Mediation Drivers
Natalia Szymczyk | Duisburg Essen University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Natalia Szymczyk | Duisburg Essen University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Nicole Krämer | Duisburg Essen University

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in children’s everyday environments, reshaping family life through algorithmic systems. These developments introduce challenges distinct from legacy media, such as emotional dependency or algorithmic bias. While research has extensively examined parental mediation – how parents guide and regulate children's media use – for television and the internet, large-scale evidence on AI mediation for young children (aged 5–10) remains scarce.
To close this gap, this study analyzes data from a cross-national sample of N = 995 parents across Germany, USA, and UK. A twofold methodological framework is applied: an exploratory person-centered approach using cluster analysis identifies distinct “AI parenting profiles” based on psychological drivers (subjective AI literacy, parental self-efficacy, perceived AI risks, and trust in AI), followed by a confirmatory variable-centered approach using hierarchical regression analyses to test how these drivers predict enabling versus restrictive parental mediation strategies.
Results identify three distinct AI parenting profiles characterized by varying configurations of these psychological drivers: “Concerned Confidents,” “Relaxed Optimists,” and “Skeptical Critics.” Furthermore, regression analyses reveal that AI literacy and trust are the strongest predictors for both mediation strategies, yet in opposite directions: While high levels of AI literacy and trust drive enabling mediation, low levels of both factors are the primary determinants of restrictive mediation.
Overall, the study advances parental mediation research by integrating AI-specific psychological drivers into a cross-national, dual-analytic framework, thereby clarifying how parents’ orientations toward AI systematically shape mediation practices in families with young children.

Understanding early regulatory disorders: An online study for parents of 0-3 year olds.
Dr. Katharina Laux | Johannes Gutenberg - Universität Mainz | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Katharina Laux | Johannes Gutenberg - Universität Mainz | Germany
Prof. Dr. Stefanie Jungmann | Johannes Gutenberg - Universität Mainz | Germany

Early regulatory disorders, including excessive crying, sleeping, and feeding difficulties, affect approximately 5–20% of infants and toddlers and pose significant challenges for early parent–child regulation processes. From a theoretical perspective, parental stress and parental self-efficacy are considered key determinants of adaptive caregiving and may be particularly relevant in the context of early regulatory disorders. However, empirical evidence on their interplay remains limited.
The present study aimed to investigate the association between parental stress and parental self-efficacy in parents of children aged 0–3 years, comparing families with children with and without early regulatory disorders.
Data were collected via an online survey (12/2025-01/2026) in a German population sample (N = 343; 30.6% parents of children with a regulatory disorder). Standardized measures of parental stress (PSS-10, PHQ-4) and parental self-efficacy (SWE) were administered. Group differences were analyzed using multivariate analysis of variance, and moderation effects were tested using linear regression models.
Results indicated that parents of children with regulatory disorders reported significantly higher stress levels and lower self-efficacy compared to parents of children without such disorders (F(3,339)=12.84, p < .002, Wilks Λ=.90, partial ŋ2=.102). Contrary to theoretical assumptions, regulatory disorder status did not moderate the relationship between parental self-efficacy and parental stress (b=0.021, t(339)=0.163, p=.871, ΔR2=.000).
These findings have direct implications for clinical practice and early intervention. They highlight the importance of systematically assessing parental stress in families presenting with early regulatory disorders and of implementing interventions that strengthen parental self-efficacy and coping strategies.

Acts & Facts of Life in Childhood - a Biographical Approach to Understand Children’s Personality
Annika Wilke | Ulm University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Annika Wilke | Ulm University | Germany
Elisa Altgassen | Ulm University
Benjamin Goecke | Hector Research Institute of Education Sciences and Psychology, University of Tübingen
Oliver Wilhelm | Ulm University

Psychological assessment of children often focuses on either educational competencies, such as command of elementary mathematics, or mental health problems, such as symptoms of generalized anxiety. Yet relevant characteristics may also reflect in what they actually do and pursue in their everyday lives. These behavioral acts and biographical facts of children’s lives could meaningfully complement cognitive tests and personality questionnaires because they may capture activities, routines, and abilities that go beyond what can be measured in traditional assessment approaches. However, such indicators are rarely studied. To close this gap, we introduce a comprehensive parent-reported inventory for acts and facts about children. Importantly, the inventory focuses on concrete and in principle verifiable indicators.
We report longitudinal data from the first cohort of the PINGUIN study conducted in primary schools in Southern Germany. At the first measurement point (n_t1 = 387 parent reports), we administered the newly developed instrument (112 items) together with additional questionnaire-based measures and ability tests. We examined the factor structure of the inventory using k-medoids clustering and an interactive "human in the loop" procedure. The second measurement point, collected 10 months later (n_t2 = 196 parent reports), investigated replicability of the structure and patterns of developmental stability. Furthermore, we report on the convergent and discriminant validity with achievement, ability, and personality data as well as relations with socioeconomic background and other context variables. We discuss the potential of biographical questionnaires to serve as more multivariate convergent outcomes of traditional measures and to complement established traits and abilities.

Kindchenschema and Care: What Cute Babies and Fluffy Kittens Can (and Cannot) Tell us About the Parental Care Motivational System
Dr. Tobias Heikamp | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Tobias Heikamp | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Ingrid Josephs | FernUniversität in Hagen

Kindchenschema features (e.g., a round face with large eyes) are typically perceived as cute and assumed to evoke a motivation to protect and care (Parental Care Motivational System, PCMS; Schaller, 2018). Here, we examined two potential mechanisms linking perceived cuteness to caregiving intentions: the cognitive appraisal of vulnerability and the affective experience of tenderness. We also investigated whether these relations generalize across human and animal babies.
In Online Study 1, 725 participants (Age=32.8 [SD=12.4], 81.7% female, 29.0% parents) viewed babies with more- or less-pronounced Kindchenschema features (more- versus less-cute condition) and reported their immediate reactions. Factor analysis identified core tenderness terms ("Zartheit-Warmherzigkeit-Sanftmütigkeit"). Cuter babies were perceived as more vulnerable, which predicted stronger feelings of tenderness. Notably, tenderness was uniquely associated with caregiving intentions, suggesting that affective responses play a central role in translating cuteness into care.
In Online Study 2 (N=524; Age=35.9 [SD=14.1], 72.7% female, 38.2% parents), we compared reactions to human and animal babies (kittens) and assessed dispositional care tendencies to capture individual differences in the propensity to activate the PCMS. Perceived vulnerability was linked to caregiving intentions via feelings of tenderness toward human and animal babies alike. Although human and animal babies elicited similar levels of tenderness, intentions to care for animal babies were stronger. Furthermore, stronger caregiving intentions toward human babies than toward animal babies were associated with dispositional care.
Together, the findings underscore tenderness as a key mechanism of the PCMS and shed light on motivational processes that sustain care beyond the initial appeal of cuteness.

Leadership Gone Wrong: Dynamics and Impacts of Destructive Behavior in Physical and Digital Work Environments
Chair(s) Dr. Melanie Vilser (University of the Bundeswehr Munich)
Dr. Iris K. Gauglitz (NEOMA Business School )
Room: EE
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Coupled symposium
Duration: 195 Minutes

In this symposium, we bring together a set of talks that illuminate the many forms destructive leadership can take and the wide-ranging effects it has on individuals, teams, and organizations. At the same time, we turn our attention to a rapidly evolving domain: how destructive leadership unfolds in different contexts.

Togehter the talks in the symposium will focus on several key questions: In what ways do relational dynamics, team histories, and digital communication patterns amplifiy of buffer the harmful effects of destructive behavior? How do differnet destructive leadership styles mainfest across varying contexts, from face-to-face enviroments to remote and hybrid teams? And how can we build assesment approaches that more accurately captarure these nunces?

By integrating insights from multiple perspectives, this symposium offers a grounded and psychologically informed understanding of destructive leadership - one that refelcts the relaties of modern work and supports more precise identification, prevention, and intervention.

Social Class Shapes Employee Responses to Abusive Leader Behavior
Dr. Martin Fladerer | Technical University of Munich | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Martin Fladerer | Technical University of Munich | Germany
Lena Zeller | Technical University of Munich | Germany
Karolina W. Nieberle | Durham University | United Kingdom

Background: Research suggests that about 10% of employees experience abusive leader behaviors at work, but the dark figure is likely much higher. To stop this behavior, it is essential to understand why employees choose to remain silent or speak up. One explaining factor can be their emotional response to abusive supervision, which itself is shaped by one’s upbringing (i.e., social class background). Guided by Emotion Process Theory, we investigate the role of social class background in modulating the indirect effect of abusive supervision on employees’ behavioral response via their experienced emotions.

Method: In a recall experiment (N = 189), participants were instructed to remember an interaction with their supervisor that was either neutral or abusive (based on Tepper's definition). Afterwards, participants reported on their emotional (i.e., anger and anxiety) and behavioral (i.e., silence and voice) responses. Objective social class background was determined based on the parents’ highest occupational prestige and educational background.

Results: Abusive supervision was positively related to silence via anxiety and voice via anger, supporting the mediating role of emotions. Social class background did not moderate the anxiety-silence-pathway, suggesting that anxiety-driven silence is a universal coping mechanism. However, social class background moderated the anger-voice-pathway: higher SCB employees were more likely to channel their emotions into voice.

Discussion: Our findings contribute to the literature on abusive supervision by demonstrating the role of social class background in shaping employees’ responses and highlighting the differential impacts of activating versus inhibiting emotions.

The Reciprocal Relationship between Employee Mental Illness and Destructive Leadership
Dr. Kai Klasmeier | Bundesagentur für Arbeitsschutz und Arbeitsmedizin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Kai Klasmeier | Bundesagentur für Arbeitsschutz und Arbeitsmedizin | Germany
Birgit Schyns | NEOMA Business School | France
Prof. Susanne Braun | Durham University Business School | United Kingdom

Background: Despite the high prevalence of mental illness, organizations fail to provide adequate support for employees experiencing it. Oftentimes, leaders are expected to take care of employees with mental illness to leverage their psychological functioning. However, destructive leader behavior has been found to intersect with symptoms of mental illness, yet the directionality of effects remains unclear. Recent theories propose that leaders exhibit destructive behavior towards them, as this group is at a higher risk of being abused, and that leaders feel challenged to lead them. Thus, our research aims to better understand the reciprocal relationships between destructive leader behavior and employee mental illness over time.

Method: We applied CLPM on the panel subsample of employees (N = 2,637) of the S-MGA dataset, which is a representative longitudinal dataset of the German workforce.

Results: We found that mental illness status at t2 was not affected by previous destructive leader behavior. Conversely, mental illness status at t1 predicted destructive leader behavior at t2. This pattern held even when controlling for employee self-efficacy and trait negative affect.

Discussion: The findings indicated that destructive leader behavior is rather a consequence of employee mental illness than vice versa. Theoretically, this reinforces models that a) consider employees with mental illness as a vulnerable group experiencing marginalization and b) position destructive leadership as a leader’s reaction to employee mental illness status. Practically, the findings suggest that mitigating harmful leadership behaviors may be an effective lever for improving mental health outcomes, beyond traditional employee well-being support.

Complementarity or Collision? How Leader and Follower Narcissism Shape Relationship Quality and Leadership Effectiveness
Marco Held | University of Bamberg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Marco Held | University of Bamberg | Germany
Dr. Iris K. Gauglitz | NEOMA Business School | France
Melissa Schütz | University of Bamberg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Astrid Schütz | University of Bamberg | Germany

Background: Narcissistic leaders can undermine the quality of the leader-follower relationship. According to the dominance complementarity model (DCM; Grijalva & Harms, 2014) followers’ own narcissistic tendencies can exacerbate the negative relationship between leader narcissism and relationship quality. Consequently, we propose that leader and follower narcissism influence relationship quality interactively. Based on the DCM, we further propose that relationship quality mediates the link between leader narcissism and leadership effectiveness, and that this indirect effect is also contingent on follower narcissism.

Method: We collect data from followers across three waves, each four weeks apart. At Time 1, participants report perceived leader narcissism and their own narcissism using the Narcissistic Admiration and Rivalry Questionnaire (Back et al., 2013). At Time 2, participants complete the LMX7 to assess relationship quality (Schyns & Paul, 2002). At Time 3, perceived leadership effectiveness is assessed with three items adapted from de Hoogh et al. (2015).

Results: We will use model 7 of the SPSS PROCESS macro to test moderated mediation. Perceived leader narcissism will serve as independent variable, relationship quality as mediator, leadership effectiveness as dependent variable, and follower narcissism as moderator. Additionally, we will run exploratory analyses for each narcissism subdimension.

Discussion: We extend prior research by examining the interactive effects of leader and follower narcissism and will critically reflect the results in the light of the DCM. Limitations and implications for future research will be discussed.

The Vulnerable Leader: How Isolation and Enmity Undermine Leader Effectiveness Through Passive Leadership Styles
Melissa Schütz | NEOMA Business School | France
Show details
Authors:
Melissa Schütz | NEOMA Business School | France
Dr. Iris K. Gauglitz | NEOMA Business School | France
Marco Held | University of Bamberg | Germany
Prof. Astrid Schütz | University of Bamberg | Germany

Background: Research on leader narcissism has mainly focused on grandiose narcissism, neglecting its vulnerable form (Gauglitz, 2022). This study builds on the Vulnerable Isolation and Enmity Concept (VIEC; Rogoza et al., 2022) to investigate the relationship between two dimensions of leaders’ vulnerable narcissism - isolation and enmity - and leader effectiveness. We hypothesize that leader isolation (H1a) and enmity (H1b) are negatively associated with perceived leader effectiveness, mediated by passive leadership (leader isolation; H2a) and passive abusive supervision (leader enmity; H2b).

Method: A cross-sectional online study with leader-follower dyads is conducted. Leaders report their vulnerable narcissism with the Vulnerable Isolation and Enmity Questionnaire (Rogoza et al., 2022), passive leadership with the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire (Bass & Avolio, 1995), and passive abusive supervision (Mitchell & Ambrose, 2007). Followers rate their leaders’ effectiveness with three items adapted from de Hoogh et al. (2015).

Results: Data are being collected. To test H1a/b, we will employ multiple linear regression with vulnerable narcissism dimensions as predictors and perceived leadership effectiveness as outcome. To test H2, we will conduct mediation analyses with leader isolation or enmity as predictors, perceived leader effectiveness as outcome, and the respective leadership style as mediator.

Discussion:This study extends the literature by focusing on the less-researched dimension of vulnerable narcissism in leadership and leadership styles as mediating mechanisms. We will discuss limitations and implications for future research.

Jan Schilling | HSBI University of Applied Sciences and Arts | Germany

Background: Estimates say 25 to 40 percent of all doctoral students in Germany are quitting prematurely. International research points out that a negative relationship between the students and academic supervisors seems to be the major reason for such a decision. To get a clearer picture for the German context, it seems necessary to get an in-depth understanding of the personal experiences of the victims of power abuse.

Method: As part of a survey with a newly developed instrument on power abuse in academia (conducted between January and May 2025), participants (Ntotal = 326) had the chance to comment on their personal experiences of power abuse in an open-ended question (N = 160). These answers were structured and categorized using qualitative content analysis by Mayring.

Results: The content of their answers could be structured into three major dimensions: abusive behavior, antecedents, and consequences of power abuse. With regard to power abuse, the victims reported a wide variety of behaviors they experienced ranging from lack of support and resources, isolation, authoritarian and inconsistent supervision to manipulation, intimidation, personal offenses, emotional and sexual abuse. Consequences mainly focused on personal disadvantages but also the experience of overcoming hardship. Antecedents included not only personal characteristics of the academic supervisor, but also organizational factors enabling power abuse like institutional inactivity or even complicity.

Discussion: The results give vivid impressions of the personal experiences of power abuse in academia, its supporting factors and consequences. They will be discussed with regard to theoretical and practical implications.

Background: This study adopts a comprehensive dyadic approach to examine the emergence of exploitative leadership in digital work environments. Grounded in the Toxic Triangle model (Padilla et al., 2007), the study investigates how the interplay of leader and follower personality traits, media richness, digital stress, and psychological distance contributes to the occurrence and perception of exploitative leadership in digital work environments.

Method: A two-wave quantitative survey design is employed, collecting data from 220 leader–follower dyads six weeks apart using standardised online questionnaires. Hypotheses will be tested through a Structural Equation Model incorporating actor and partner effects in line with the Actor–Partner Interdependence Model (APIM).

Results: Data collection is ongoing; final analyses and results are not yet available.

Discussion: The research aims to offer insights into how dyadic interactions in a digital work environment influence exploitative leadership, providing practical applications for leadership development and the management of digital collaboration. In doing so, the study enhances understanding of exploitative leadership within digital collaboration and supplies practical knowledge to prevent such behaviours.

Digital Dictators and Ghost Managers: Destructive Leadership Behavior in Virtual Work Environments
Anne Kühn | Tilburg University | Netherlands
Show details
Authors:

Background: Despite the global shift to technology-enabled work, there is limited research on the nature of destructive leadership behavior (DLB) in these virtual work environments. Moreover, the limited knowledge about this topic comes from the perspective of the follower. Therefore, the primary goal of this qualitative interview study was to add insights from the perspective of leaders on their own virtual DLB and develop an initial framework of the nature of DLB in virtual environments. 

Method: We interviewed leaders but also followers in virtual and hybrid environments. Data analysis focused on (a) what kind of behaviors the leaders see as DLB (incl. own behavior), (b) which organizational, personal, and work setting-related factors contribute to or prevent these behaviors, and c) whether there are differences and similarities in the views within dyads.

Results: We identified categories of virtual DLB that are either unique to or distinctively expressed in virtual environments. We also identified company factors, digital tools, and intra- and interpersonal factors that may influence the occurrence of virtual DLB. Leaders and followers differed in their perceptions of DLB.

Discussion: Semi-structured interviews provide good insights into the perspective of leaders. Nonetheless, leaders’ ability to report their own DLB depends on their memory, awareness of own misbehaviors, and self-reflection. As we cannot validate the intentionality of leaders, further research should focus on their motivations to better understand why certain behavior is expressed. This research brings new insights on which DLB emerges uniquely or very differently in virtual setups.

How Context Triggers Destructive Leadership: A Computerized Language-Based Assessment
Arij Briki | Technical University of Munich | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Arij Briki | Technical University of Munich | Germany
Dr. Martin Fladerer | Technical University of Munich | Germany
Prof. Dr. Claudia Peus | Technical University of Munich | Germany

Background: Destructive leadership is increasingly seen as a context-dependent phenomenon rather than a stable individual tendency. This study examines how destructive leadership emerges through leaders’ verbal reactions to scenarios involving susceptible followers, conducive environments, or time pressure. We also test whether stress mediates the effect of these triggers on destructiveness, controlling for Dark Triad traits.

Method: In a pilot study, we developed and validated scenarios with high versus low trigger intensities across three contexts. We then compiled a dictionary of destructive leadership typologies and their corresponding verbal markers. In a subsequent study, participants in leadership positions completed an online experiment, assuming the role of a project manager for a VR-based soft skills training initiative. They provided open-ended responses to different scenarios and rated their perceived stress levels. We derived a destructiveness score and a negative sentiment index for each response through dictionary-based language analysis.

Results: Findings show that destructive leadership is not uniformly expressed across contexts. Susceptible followers consistently elicited higher destructiveness, independent of stress. Conducive environments increased stress yet paradoxically suppressed destructive expressions. Only time pressure showed partial support for a stress-mediated pathway via increased negative sentiment. Negative sentiment rose across all trigger types, with Machiavellianism being the only significant predictor among the Dark Triad traits under the environment condition.

Discussion: Our results highlight the context-dependent nature of destructive leadership, demonstrating that behaviors can emerge through mechanisms of suppression, provocation, or shifts in verbal tone. The assessment also provides a methodological alternative to questionnaires that mitigates subjectivity and bias.

Position Paper: Construct Validity
Room: PL
Topic:
Form of presentation: Position Paper
Duration: 90 Minutes
Jenseits der Intervallannahme -- Ein messtheoretischer Blick auf psychologische Konstrukte
Prof. Dr. Jörg Heine | Universität der Bundeswehr München (UniBW M) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Jörg Heine | Universität der Bundeswehr München (UniBW M) | Germany
Prof. Dr. Christian Tarnai | Universität der Bundeswehr München (UniBW M)

Psychologische Konstrukte werden routinemäßig als intervallskalierte latente Variablen behandelt und mit metrischen, linearen Modellen analysiert. Diese Praxis steht jedoch in einem zunehmenden Spannungsverhältnis zu messtheoretischen Überlegungen (z.B. Uher et al., 2025). Insbesondere wurde kürzlich argumentiert (vgl. Heine & Heene, 2025), dass aus der erfolgreichen Anpassung psychometrischer Modelle aus der Item-Response-Theory (IRT) nicht automatisch auf eine intervallskalierte Struktur psychologischer Eigenschaften selbst geschlossen werden darf. Der Positionsvortrag greift diese Perspektive auf und richtet den Fokus auf die bislang unzureichend geklärte Frage, wie psychologische Vergleichs- und Messoperationen kognitiv und messtheoretisch fundiert sind. Ausgangspunkt ist die Annahme, dass abstrakte psychologische Konzepte primär über konzeptuelle (z.B. räumliche) Metaphern strukturiert werden – z. B. Offenheit als Weite, Intimität als Nähe (vgl. Kövecses, 2010; Lakoff & Johnson, 1980). Solche sprachlichen Metaphern erzeugen qualitative, geordnete Merkmalsräume, die Vergleichbarkeit ermöglichen, ohne notwendigerweise metrische Abstände zu definieren. Es wird argumentiert, dass psychologische Vergleiche eher als merkmalsbasierte Ähnlichkeitsurteile zu verstehen sind, die durch gerichtete und potenziell asymmetrische Kontrastprozesse entstehen, anstatt durch symmetrische Distanzen in einem metrischen, intervallskalierten Raum. Der Vortrag entwickelt ein integriertes theoretisches Modell, das konzeptuelle Metaphern (Kövecses, 2010), Tverskys Kontrastmodell der Ähnlichkeit (Tversky, 1977) und die repräsentationstheoretische Messtheorie (Krantz, Suppes & Luce, 1971) verbindet. Exemplarisch werden zwei mögliche experimentelle Ansätze skizziert, die (a) metaphorisch strukturierte Merkmalsräume empirisch rekonstruieren und (b) prüfen, ob Ähnlichkeitsurteile zwischen Personenprofilen stabile ordinale Ordnungen erzeugen. Ziel ist es, die messtheoretischen Voraussetzungen psychologischer Quantifizierung explizit zu machen und die verbreitete und methodisch bequeme, aber theoretisch problematische Annahme einer generellen Intervallskalierung kritisch zu überprüfen und zu diskutieren.

Why conventional practices in construct validation provide limited evidence of construct validity
Dr. Leon Wendt | Universität Kassel | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Leon Wendt | Universität Kassel | Germany
Steffen Müller | Independant | Germany

The construct validity of psychometric measures is a foundation of credible psychological science, ensuring that measures reflect their intended theoretical constructs rather than unintended ones. Yet many conventional construct validation practices produce weak, uninformative evidence and fall short of the strong, risk-bearing tests emphasized by validity theorists. As a result, the available evidence is often insufficient to support meaningful claims about construct validity. In this position paper, we introduce a framework based on Meehl’s logic of hypothesis testing that can be used to evaluate the evidential value (or quality) of construct validation efforts. We define evidential value as the extent to which conducting a test of construct validity can shift confidence in the proposed construct interpretation of a measure over plausible alternative interpretations. Using this framework, we identify three conventional practices that contribute to low evidential value in construct validation: (a) treating theoretical constructs as conceptual placeholders, (b) relying on generic psychometric methods, and (c) performing post hoc revisions to the nomological network (i.e., employing the Lakatosian defense). This article demonstrates how using these practices allows virtually any psychometric measure to be portrayed as “validated”, while providing only nominal evidence of construct validity. We offer recommendations to help researchers design construct validation studies of high evidential value.
