Perspectives on Self-Regulation: New Approaches in Basic and Applied Research
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Caterina Gawrilow
Chair(s) Gertraud Turu Stadler
Room: PT
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Self-regulation is a core psychological capacity underlying many aspects of everyday life, including learning, health behavior, and mental well-being across the lifespan. This symposium brings together four complementary contributions that advance contemporary perspectives on self-regulation by addressing cognitive, affective, and behavioral processes in basic and applied research contexts. Collectively, the contributions illustrate the multifaceted nature of self-regulation and highlight the necessity of integrating diverse theoretical frameworks with a broad range of empirical methods.
The first contribution examines the impact of menstrual pain on attention and learning processes in university and high school students. By focusing on a frequently neglected yet highly prevalent physiological stressor, this work demonstrates how pain-related self-regulatory demands can interfere with cognitive control and learning outcomes, with important implications for educational and occupational settings.
The second contribution presents a comprehensive meta-analysis of interventions targeting procrastination, a prototypical failure of self-regulation. The results reveal substantial heterogeneity at both post-intervention and follow-up assessments. While no significant moderating effect of intervention type was found overall, in-person interventions showed a markedly larger reduction in procrastination compared to digital or blended formats. Evidence for publication bias underscores the need for cautious interpretation.
The third contribution reports a cluster-randomized controlled trial evaluating an innovative preventive approach for adolescents that integrates psychoeducation with a future-oriented self-regulatory skill: Positive Episodic Future Thinking (Positive EFT). By examining the feasibility and acceptability of a school-based Positive EFT program, this study addresses a critical gap in the development of scalable, preventive interventions targeting motivation and emotional well-being in adolescence.
The fourth contribution focuses on a nicotine prevention conducted with children in primary schools. By targeting self-regulatory skills early in development, this work emphasizes the importance of age-appropriate interventions to promote health-related self-regulation within its social context and to prevent maladaptive habits before they become entrenched.
Together, these contributions illustrate the manifold ways in which self-regulation manifests in real-life contexts across domains and developmental stages. The symposium underscores the value of diverse theoretical and methodological approaches and highlights emerging perspectives that integrate cognitive, emotional, and behavioral dimensions of self-regulation.

Self-Regulation as a Protective Factor in the Context of Dysmenorrhea and Working Memory
Olivia Krokos
Show details
Authors:
Olivia Krokos
Caterina Gawrilow
Kou Murayama
Michiko Sakaki

Menstrual pain (dysmenorrhea) is among the most prevalent pain conditions in women and is associated with impairments in everyday functioning, including cognitive performance and academic attendance. Despite its high prevalence, the cognitive correlates of dysmenorrhea and potential protective factors remain understudied. Self-regulation is central to coping with demands across life domains and is positively associated with cognitive functioning. The present study therefore examined the moderating role of self-regulation in the association between dysmenorrhea-related pain and cognitive performance.
In a pilot study using an intensive longitudinal design, 81 university students (M = 23.2 years, SD = 3.1) were assessed daily in the evening over a period of seven consecutive days. Participants completed a battery of questionnaires and two tasks assessing working memory performance. For female participants, the assessment period was individually aligned with their menstrual cycle, while male participants were temporally matched accordingly.
Results from mixed-effects linear regression analyses revealed a significant moderation effect of trait self-regulation on the association between pain intensity and working memory performance. In addition, significant differences emerged between female participants with a natural menstrual cycle and those using hormonal contraception.
These findings suggest that higher levels of trait self-regulation may buffer the detrimental effects of pain on working memory performance. This points to self-regulation as a potential target for intervention strategies aimed at mitigating pain-related cognitive impairments. Furthermore, the results highlight the importance of considering inter- and intraindividual differences to better understand pain-associated cognitive effects.

A meta-analysis update and extension on procrastination interventions
Tamara Schneider
Show details
Authors:
Tamara Schneider
Wendelin van Eerde
Katrin Klingsieck

This meta-analysis updates and extends van Eerde and Klingsieck’s (2018) review of procrastination interventions by including studies published between September 2016 and December 2025.
Relevant records were identified through systematic searches in PsycINFO, Google Scholar, ERIC, Web of Science, Business Source Premier, and PubMed. Following Harrer et al. (2022), we calculate Hedges’ g as the group difference between experimental and control groups at post- and follow-up measurements, test for heterogeneity and potential risks of bias, and consider additional moderators such as the mode of delivery.
Until now, we have analyzed studies until September 2023. Of the 1,323 records identified, we included 18 control-group studies (k = 27 pre-post-comparisons, N = 2077; k = 11 post-follow-up-comparisons, N = 461). Overall effect size g when comparing experimental to control groups at post-measurement was -1.30, [-1.83; −0.78], p < .0001, being a larger effect size than in 2018. Contrary to the results in 2018, the follow-up measurements showed a significant decline −1.0405 [-1.76; −0.32], p = .0090.
The results reveal significant heterogeneity at post- (I2 = 90%) and follow-up measurement (I2 = 83 %). For intervention type, no significant moderating effect was found; however, in-person interventions showed a larger reduction of procrastination (g = -1.38, [-1.81; −0.94], p < .00; I2=75%) than digital or blended interventions. Eggert test results showed that a publication bias is likely (Z = -3.60 [-5.99; -1.21], p = .0071).
At the conference, all studies until December 2025 will be included, and results will be updated accordingly.

Future Thinking as a Mechanism of Adaptive Self-Regulation: Feasibility of a School-Based Positive EFT Prevention Program
Felix Schreiber
Show details
Authors:
Felix Schreiber
Kou Murayama
Michiko Sakaki
Tobias Renner
Caterina Gawrilow

Adolescence is a sensitive developmental period in which self-regulatory capacities undergo major reorganization, while vulnerability to internalizing mental health problems increases. School-based psychoeducation is an accessible preventive strategy that enhances mental health literacy and stigma-related attitudes, yet effects on emotional symptoms remain limited without actionable self-regulation tools. This highlights the need for interventions targeting core cognitive–affective mechanisms of adaptive regulation.
We present a feasibility cluster-randomized controlled trial evaluating an innovative preventive approach integrating psychoeducation with a future-oriented skill: Positive Episodic Future Thinking (Positive EFT). The ability to vividly simulate specific and emotionally engaging positive future events is increasingly recognized as a mechanism supporting motivation and resilience. Conversely, impairments in positive future simulation are linked to depression and anxiety, while EFT-based trainings in adults show promising effects on well-being. Scalable adolescent adaptations in school contexts remain scarce.
Approximately 60 adolescents aged 12–16 years will be recruited via secondary schools in the Tübingen region and randomized by classroom to either (1) an eight-week intervention combining brief mental health psychoeducation with structured Positive EFT micro-skills (e.g., vivid imagery, affective future connection), or (2) an active psychoeducation-only control condition. Sessions are brief (15 minutes weekly) and include guided home practice.
Primary outcomes assess feasibility and acceptability, while exploratory analyses examine changes in well-being and internalizing symptoms alongside mechanistic targets such as imagery vividness and affective resonance.
By embedding future-oriented cognitive tools into scalable psychoeducational prevention, this project advances theory-driven adolescent mental health promotion by targeting a central mechanism of adaptive self-regulation.

Self-regulation and behavior at the individual and social level - Children's nicotine consumption as a test case
Gertraud Turu Stadler
Show details
Authors:
Gertraud Turu Stadler
Julia Kohn
Lilly Buhr
Patrick Shrout

Research on self-regulation usually focuses on individuals while studies of self-regulation within its social context are still relatively rare. In this talk, we examine children's self-regulation in schools focusing on prevention of nicotine consumption.
Children (N = 1706, age: M = 10.7 years, female: 49.1%) in 42 primary schools reported on self-regulation variables and behavior (nicotine consumption) as part of baseline assessments for a cluster-randomized trial of a nicotine prevention intervention. In multilevel analyses, we analyzed how self-regulation is related to behavior on the school and individual level. We focus on action planning and e-cigarette use to illustrate our results.

Schools in which children reported higher planning to stay smoke free showed a higher percentage of nicotine-free students. On the individual level, children who reported higher planning to stay smoke free showed a higher likelihood of being nicotine free. Interestingly, variation in self-regulation and e-cigarette use was best accounted for by the school level, with higher effect sizes on the school level (r = .49, p < .05) than on the individual level (r = .24, p < .05).

Results suggest that children who are surrounded by highly self-regulated peers are better protected from initiating substance use. We will discuss how integrating social influences into research and theory building could enhance our understanding of self-regulation.

Arbeitsbezogenes Lernen: Kultur, Kontext und KI
Chair(s) Dr. Julian Decius (Universität Bremen)
Prof. Dr. Simone Kauffeld (TU Braunschweig)
Room: MT
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Coupled symposium
Duration: 195 Minutes

Forschungsstand
Arbeitsbezogenes Lernen wird in einer Arbeitswelt mit hoher Veränderungsdynamik zur zentralen Voraussetzung für Beschäftigungsfähigkeit, Innovationskraft und organisationale Anpassungsfähigkeit. Gleichzeitig bleibt die Evidenz oft fragmentiert: Begriffe wie organisationale Lernkultur sind konzeptionell und methodisch uneinheitlich, zentrale Ressourcen wie Zeit fehlen im Alltag, und die Übersetzung von Lernintentionen in tatsächliches Handeln (und wirksame Umsetzung) gelingt häufig nicht. Parallel verändern digitale Technologien – insbesondere generative Künstliche Intelligenz (KI) – sowohl formale Weiterbildungs- und Lernformate als auch Arbeitsaufgaben und damit informelle Lerngelegenheiten. Daraus ergibt sich Forschungsbedarf, wie Lernumwelten gestaltet werden können, damit Lernen (a) möglich wird, (b) tatsächlich stattfindet und (c) unter digitalen Bedingungen verantwortungsvoll unterstützt wird.

Neue Perspektiven/Beitrag
Das Doppelsymposium bündelt zehn Beiträge entlang einer gemeinsamen Leitfrage: Wie lassen sich arbeitsbezogene Lernprozesse unter knappen Ressourcen, organisationalem Wandel und neuer Technologie wirksam und verantwortungsvoll unterstützen?
Teil 1 fokussiert organisationale Voraussetzungen, psychologische Mechanismen und Umsetzungsprozesse: Kortsch & Schmitz ordnen das Feld organisationaler Lernkultur systematisch, identifizieren dominierende Messlogiken und „Emerging Topics“ (u. a. Digitalisierung/KI, Nachhaltigkeit) und legen damit eine begriffliche und methodische Basis. Häußermann et al. beleuchten qualitativ die Idee organisationaler Lernzeit und zeigen sowohl Potenziale (Wertschätzung, Entwicklung) als auch Risiken (Konkurrenz zum Tagesgeschäft) sowie zentrale Nutzungsbedingungen (Lerngelegenheiten, soziale Akzeptanz, Workload). Fröhlich & Kortsch untersuchen in einer dreiwelligen Längsschnittstudie im Onboarding, wie Bedürfnisbefriedigung unterschiedliche Pfade informellen Lernens aktiviert und spätere Leistung erklärt – mit besonderem Fokus auf selbstbasiertem informellem Lernen. Eller et al. analysieren in einem intensiven längsschnittlichen Einzelfall-Design die „Lücke“ zwischen Intention und Implementation bei Change Agents und zielen auf Wirkmechanismen proaktiven Handelns in Veränderungsprojekten. Creon et al. erweitern den Blick über Organisationsgrenzen hinaus und untersuchen stellvertretendes Lernen in interorganisationalen Formaten, inklusive der kritischen Frage, ob wahrgenommene Vorteile „externen“ Wissens eher auf Qualität oder auf Attributionen zurückgehen.
Teil 2 richtet den Fokus auf digitale Lernunterstützung und die Rolle von KI beim Lernen: Decius et al. untersuchen qualitativ, wann Mitarbeitende KI-, menschliche oder hybride Lernunterstützung bevorzugen, und welche Rolle u. a. Vertrauen, Fairness, Aufwand, Aufgabeneigenschaften und organisationale Normen spielen. Neufeld et al. verbinden Fallanalysen mit Work-Design-Theorie, um zu prognostizieren, wie generative KI Arbeitsmerkmale (z. B. Komplexität, Problemlösen) verschiebt und dadurch arbeitsbezogenes Lernen anregen kann. Czora et al. berichten erste Befunde aus einer berufsbegleitenden KI-Fortbildung und zeigen, dass individuelle (z. B. KI-Angst/Selbstwirksamkeit) und organisationale Faktoren gemeinsam mit der tatsächlichen Nutzungsabsicht verknüpft sind. Bödding & Maier prüfen experimentell, ob Augmented Reality (AR) durch theoriegeleitete generative Lernaktivitäten über ein reines „Mehr“ an AR hinaus lernwirksam wird. Abschließend zeigen Kauffeld et al. in ihrer multimethodalen Studie, dass digitale Mikrointerventionen als formale Lerneinheit zum Auslöser für den Spillover in informelles Lernen und Wissensaustausch werden können.

Theoretische/Praktische Implikationen
Theoretisch liefert das Symposium eine integrative Perspektive für die arbeitsbezogenen Lernforschung, die Kultur/Ressourcen, Motivation/Handeln und Technologie/Arbeitsgestaltung vereint, und gleichzeitig methodische Spannungen sichtbar macht (z.B. heterogene Konstrukte, begrenzte Generalisierbarkeit einzelner Designs). Praktisch ergeben sich klare Gestaltungsfragen für Organisationen: Lernkultur mess- und gestaltbar machen, Lernzeit so einbetten, dass sie nicht am Tagesgeschäft scheitert, Onboarding bedürfnisförderlich designen, Implementierung proaktiv unterstützen und KI/AR so einsetzen, dass Wirksamkeit, Akzeptanz und Verantwortung zusammenpassen.

Organisationale Lernkultur: Konzeptionen, Operationalisierungen und Emerging Topics – ein Scoping Review
Prof. Dr. Timo Kortsch | IU - International University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Timo Kortsch | IU - International University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Anja Schmitz | Hochschule Karlsruhe | Germany

Organisationale Lernkultur (OLK) gilt als zentrale organisationale Rahmenbedingung für Lernen in und durch Arbeit, Wissenstransfer und organisationale Anpassungsfähigkeit (Marsick & Watkins, 2003; Škerlavajet al., 2007). Konzeptionelle und definitorische Unschärfen sowie eine Vielzahl an Operationalisierungen erschweren allerdings die kumulative Evidenzbildung (z.B. Örtenblad, 2018).
Vor diesem Hintergrund berichten wir ein Scoping Review, das einen Überblick über die Konzeptlandschaft, Messansätze, Untersuchungskontexte, typische Modellrollen und Emerging Topics der OLK-Forschung gibt. Die Suche in Scopus (n= 371), Web of Science (n = 349) und EBSCO (n = 236) ergab nach Deduplikation 634 eindeutige Treffer; 178 education-bezogene Treffer wurden im Pre-Screening ausgeschlossen. Die verbleibenden 456 Treffer werden aktuell gescreent. Für erste Tendenzen wurde eine Volltext-Stichprobe als Datenquelle geprüft (FT1 =yes: n = 195).
Vorläufig zeigen die Volltexte eine konzeptionelle Zweiteilung: OLK wird teils als Kulturkonstrukt, teils über die Learning-Organization-Tradition gerahmt, allerdings bleiben klare Abgrenzungen häufig aus. Der Dimensions of the Learning Organization Questionnaire dominiert als Messinstrument. Branchenkontexte sind oft nur indirekt berichtet (u. a. Gesundheitswesen, IT/Tech, Finanzdienstleistungen). OLK wird in empirischen Modellen gleichermaßen als Outcome (häufige Antezedenz: Führung), Antezedenz (häufige Outcomes: Performance, Commitment) und Mediator untersucht; es dominieren dabei Querschnittdesigns. Als emerging topics werden häufiger generelle Technologiethemen untersucht als explizite KI/Analytics-oder Nachhaltigkeitsbezüge.
Die ersten Ergebnisse deuten darauf hin, dass die zukünftige Forschung sich der Präzisierung des Konstruktes OLK zuwenden muss. Stärkere Forschungsdesigns (v.a. längsschnittlich) mit klarer Rolle von OLK wären ebenso wünschenswert wie die Untersuchung praxisrelevanter aktueller Fragestellungen, z.B. in Hinblick auf die Transformationsfähigkeit von Unternehmen.

Zeit zum Lernen? Qualitative Erkenntnisse zur hypothetischen Einführung organisationaler Lernzeit
Katja Häußermann | Uni Ulm | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Katja Häußermann | Uni Ulm | Germany
Lea Ghebre | Uni Ulm | Germany
Prof. Dr. Tina Seufert | Uni Ulm | Germany

Arbeitsbezogenes Lernen wird in Zeiten schnellen (technologischen) Wandels immer wichtiger, fehlende Zeit gilt jedoch als große Lernhürde für Arbeitnehmende. Als mögliche Lösung könnten Unternehmen den Arbeitnehmenden organisationale Lernzeit in festgelegtem Umfang zur Verfügung stellen, damit diese sich auf freiwilliger Basis eigenständig, bewusst und informell mit arbeitsbezogenen Themen auseinandersetzen. Organisationale Lernzeiten, wurden bislang jedoch nicht systematisch erforscht. Das Ziel dieser qualitativen explorativen Interviewstudie war es daher zu untersuchen, wie Arbeitnehmende die hypothetische Einführung einer organisationalen Lernzeit von einer Stunde pro Woche in ihrem Unternehmen beurteilen und welche Einflussfaktoren auf deren Nutzung genannt werden. Zehn Arbeitnehmende mit Büroarbeitsplatz im Alter zwischen 25 und 53 Jahren aus verschiedenen Branchen (z.B. Informatik, Ingenieurwesen) wurden anhand halbstrukturierter Leitfadeninterviews im Rahmen eines Gedankenspiels zur Lernzeiteinführung befragt. Die inhaltlich strukturierende qualitative Inhaltsanalyse nach Kuckartz und Rädiker (2022) erfolgte mittels deduktiver Kategorienbildung und induktiven Subkategorien. Die Arbeitnehmende nahmen Lernzeit überwiegend positiv als Möglichkeit zur persönlichen Weiterentwicklung wahr (n = 7) und fühlten sich vom Unternehmen wertgeschätzt (n = 5), jedoch wurde auch die Konkurrenz zum Tagesgeschäft befürchtet (n = 5). Da das Lernens während der organisationaler Lernzeit Parallelen zum bewussten informellen lernen mit explizit geplanten Lernzielen und Zeit aufweist, nutzten wir die Meta-Analyse zu Einflussfaktoren informellen Lernens von Cerasoli et al. (2018) als Strukturgrundlage zur deduktiven Kategorienbildung. Die meistgenannten Einflussfaktoren auf die Lernzeitnutzung – mit starken Übereinstimmungen zur informellen Lernforschung – waren informelle Unterstützung in Form von vorhandenen Lerngelegenheiten und sozialer Akzeptanz/gelebter Praxis sowie die fehlende Ressource Zeit – durch Personalmangel und hohen Workload.

Arbeitsbezogene Bedürfnisbefriedigung, informelles Lernen und Leistung von Neueinsteigern: Eine dreiwellige Mediationsstudie
Dr. Patrik Fröhlich | Uni Wuppertal | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Patrik Fröhlich | Uni Wuppertal | Germany
Prof. Dr. Timo Kortsch | IU - International University | Germany

Der Eintritt in eine neue Organisation ist eine lernintensive Phase, in der Neueinsteiger Wissen erwerben, sich mit sozialen Normen vertraut machen und Routinen entwickeln, oft durch informelles Lernen. Aufbauend auf der Selbstbestimmungstheorie nehmen wir an, dass die Befriedigung arbeitsbezogener Grundbedürfnisse (Autonomie, Kompetenz, Eingebundenheit) informelles Lernen am Arbeitsplatz (IWL) fördert und dadurch zu innovativer Leistung und Extrarollenverhalten (OCB) beiträgt. Wir testen diese Annahmen bei N = 161 Neueinsteigern einer deutschen Universität, die wir zu drei Messzeitpunkten über ein halbes Jahr befragten. Befriedigung arbeitsbezogener Bedürfnisse wurde einen Monat nach Eintritt, IWL (sozial- und selbstorientiert) drei Monate nach Eintritt, und innovative Leistung sowie OCB sechs Monate nach Eintritt gemessen. Pfadanalysen mit MPlus ergaben, dass die Befriedigung des Kompetenzbedürfnisses selbstorientiertes IWL und spätere innovative Leistung direkt positiv vorhersagte. Ebenso sagte die Befriedigung des Bedürfnisses nach Eingebundenheit sozialorientiertes IWL und späteres OCB direkt positiv vorher. Selbstorientiertes IWL sagte sowohl innovative Leistung als auch OCB vorher, nicht aber sozialorientiertes IWL. Ein signifikanter indirekter Effekt fand sich von Befriedigung des Kompetenzbedürfnisses über selbstorientiertes IWL auf die innovative Leistung, ein marginaler indirekter Effekt auf OCB. Die Ergebnisse deuten darauf hin, dass unterschiedliche Facetten der Bedürfnisbefriedigung während der Einarbeitungsphase unterschiedliche Arten des IWL aktivieren und dass selbstorientiertes IWL für die Leistung von Neueinsteigern besonders wichtig sein kann.

Von der Intention zur Implementation: Proaktives Handeln und Zielerreichung bei Change Agents – Eine experimentelle Einzelfallstudie (AB-Design)
Cathrine Eller | TU Braunschweig | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Cathrine Eller | TU Braunschweig | Germany
Stephanie Hirschberger | TU Braunschweig | Germany
Dr. Anja Isabel Morstatt | TU Braunschweig | Germany
Prof. Dr. Simone Kauffeld | TU Braunschweig | Germany

Organisationale Veränderungsprozesse scheitern häufig daran, dass geplante Maßnahmen nicht nachhaltig umgesetzt werden. Integrative Ansätze, die Bottom-up- und Top-down-Prozesse verbinden, gelten als vielversprechend, um Veränderungsprozesse erfolgreicher zu gestalten. Das Qualifizierungsprogramm VeränderungsMacher:in folgt diesem Prinzip, indem Beschäftigte zu VeränderungsMacher:innen ausgebildet werden, die eigenständig Veränderungsprojekte umsetzen, während Führungskräfte unterstützend wirken und Handlungsspielräume gewähren. Ziel der vorliegenden Studie ist es, zentrale Wirkmechanismen dieser Qualifizierung zu untersuchen.
Fragestellung. Auf Within-Person-Ebene wird geprüft, ob wöchentliche Schwankungen im Lösungsfokus und im Rollen-Fit mit einer höheren Intention zur Projektarbeit einhergehen und ob diese Intention wiederum proaktives Projektverhalten sowie die Umsetzung projektbezogener Schritte vermittelt.
Untersuchungsdesign. In einer longitudinalen Einzelfallstudie nehmen 21 Teilnehmende aus zehn Unternehmen an einer modularen Qualifizierung teil und setzen in Tandems bzw. Triaden ein organisationsrelevantes Veränderungsprojekt um. Über den gesamten Erhebungszeitraum werden wiederholt Selbstauskünfte erhoben. Ergänzend werden kontextuelle Einflussfaktoren, die die Umsetzung beeinflussen können, erhoben. Auch Führungskräfte geben Auskunft zur Entwicklung der Teilnehmenden sowie der Kontextfaktoren. Der Erhebungszeitraum ist 27 Wochen lang.
Ergebnisse. Zum Zeitpunkt der Einreichung liegen noch keine Ergebnisse vor, da die Studie läuft. Geplant sind Multilevel-Mediationsanalysen sowie visuelle Analysen zur Untersuchung phasenbezogener Veränderungen. Die vollständigen Daten werden im Juli 2026 erwartet.
Limitationen. Aufgrund der kleinen Stichprobe sind ausschließlich Within-Person-Analysen möglich. Dies ermöglicht jedoch eine differenzierte Abbildung intraindividueller Prozesse über die Zeit. Die Baseline-Phase mit drei Wochen ist vergleichsweise kurz.
Implikationen. Die Studie gibt Einblicke in die Umsetzung organisationaler Veränderungsinitiativen. Dadurch werden Wirkmechanismen integrativer Veränderungsansätze sichtbar. Das Design eröffnet neue Perspektiven für die Evaluation von Interventionsmaßnahmen im arbeits- und organisationspsychologischen Kontext.

Ist das Gras auf der anderen Seite grüner? Stellvertretendes Lernen in interorganisationalen Kontexten
Dr. Laura Creon | SRH University / HRpepper | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Laura Creon | SRH University / HRpepper | Germany
Dr. Julian Decius | Uni Bremen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Carolin Graßmann | IU - International University | Germany
Sarah Pielke | International Psychoanalytic University | Germany

In einer zunehmend durch nationale Abschottung gekennzeichneten Welt besteht die Gefahr, dass auch Organisationen sich zunehmend nach innen wenden. Dies kann interorganisationalen Austausch einschränken und Innovationspotenziale sowie die Zusammenarbeit an interorganisationalen Schnittstellen gefährden. Während interorganisationales Lernen bislang vor allem auf organisationaler Ebene betrachtet wurde (z. B. Absorptive Capacity), ist wenig darüber bekannt, wie es sich als interindividueller Lernprozess vollzieht und welche spezifischen Vorteile es im Vergleich zu intraorganisationalem Lernen generiert.
In unserer Studie nehmen wir eine individuelle Perspektive auf interorganisationales Lernen ein und fokussieren Vicarious Learning (Myers, 2018), d.h. stellvertretendes informelles Lernen von anderen. Wir definieren interorganisationales Lernen als soziale Lernaktivität im Rahmen beruflicher Aktivitäten zwischen Mitgliedern unterschiedlicher Organisationen (vgl. Akinci & Macpherson, 2025). Daraus können nützliche Konsequenzen auf individueller (z. B. neue Problemlösestrategien) und organisationaler Ebene (z. B. Übertragbarkeit auf eigene Prozesse) entstehen.
Explorativ untersuchen wir, wie Erfahrungen von Personen aus anderen Organisationen im Vergleich zu solchen aus der eigenen Organisation bewertet werden (z. B. hinsichtlich Divergenz, Originalität) und ob wahrgenommene Unterschiede auf tatsächlichen Qualitätsunterschieden oder primär auf Attributionen der Lernenden beruhen. Hierzu nutzen wir ein zweistufiges Mixed-Methods-Design mit Teilnehmenden interorganisationaler Lernformate (z. B. Konferenzen): qualitative Interviews (geplantes N = 15, Auswertung mittels thematischer Analyse, Braun & Clarke, 2006) und eine quantitative Befragung (geplantes N = 200). Die Ergebnisse sollen einen theoretischen Beitrag leisten, indem sie zentrale Merkmale, Mechanismen und Konsequenzen interorganisationalen Lernens auf individueller Ebene herausarbeiten und in die Literatur zu arbeitsbezogenem Lernen einordnen. Darüber hinaus sollen sie Learning-&-Development-Verantwortlichen Hinweise liefern, welchen Beitrag interorganisationale Lernformate zur Förderung innovativer Lernprozesse leisten können.

Wer hilft beim Lernen im Job? Entscheidungsfaktoren für KI-, menschliche und hybride Lernunterstützung
Dr. Julian Decius | Uni Bremen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Julian Decius | Uni Bremen | Germany
Hannah Louisa Krüger | Uni Bremen | Germany
Sandra Sokolov | Uni Bremen | Germany
Justin Banfi | Portland State University | United States
Prof. Dr. Jason Randall | Portland State University | United States

Obwohl Mitarbeitende zunehmend KI-Tools wie LLM-basierte Chatbots für ihr arbeitsbezogenes Lernen nutzen, ist wenig darüber bekannt, wie sie zur Lernunterstützung zwischen KI, menschlichen Kolleg*innen oder einer hybriden Kombination wählen. Unsere qualitative Studie untersucht die individuellen, aufgabenbezogenen und situativen Faktoren der Präferenzen und Entscheidungen zu diesen Lernunterstützungsquellen. An der Schnittstelle von Forschung zur Lerntiefe (z. B. Deep vs. Shallow Learning) und Technologieakzeptanz (UTAUT-Modell) betrachten wir, wie Mitarbeitende (nicht-)menschliche Lernressourcen im Arbeitsalltag bewerten.

In unserer präregistrierten Studie führen wir halbstrukturierte Interviews mit 40 deutschen und amerikanischen Erwerbstätigen (20 pro Land) durch. Die Teilnehmenden berichten von konkreten Episoden arbeitsbezogenen Lernens und ihren Entscheidungen für bestimmte Lernunterstützungsquellen. Die Leitfragen decken folgende Aspekte ab: Treiber und Barrieren; Emotionen; erwartete Wirksamkeit und Aufwand; Vertrauen, Fairness und Transparenz; Datenschutz und ethische Bedenken; Aufgabenanforderungen wie Komplexität, Neuartigkeit oder Zeitdruck; Autonomie; sowie organisationale Richtlinien und Normen.

Die Interviews werden audioaufgezeichnet, wörtlich transkribiert und anonymisiert. Wir analysieren die Transkripte in der jeweiligen Originalsprache mittels reflexiver thematischer Analyse, um eine theoretische Taxonomie von Einflussfaktoren und Rahmenbedingungen für die Präferenz von KI, Mensch oder einer hybriden Mischung als Lernunterstützungsquelle zu entwickeln. Anschließend werden im internationalen Forschungsteam Unterschiede und Gemeinsamkeiten der deutschen und amerikanischen Themenmuster verglichen.

Die Datenerhebung läuft derzeit; die Auswertung wird vor der DGPs-Konferenz abgeschlossen sein. Die qualitativen Studienergebnisse sollen erste Hinweise geben, wann eine kombinierte Mensch–KI-Unterstützung bevorzugt wird, und Ansatzpunkte für verantwortungsvolle KI-Gestaltung beim arbeitsbezogenen Lernen liefern. Basierend auf den qualitativen Ergebnissen ist außerdem ein anschließendes Online-Vignettenexperiment geplant, für das die zu identifizierenden Themen die Vignettenmerkmale liefern sollen.

Welchen Einfluss hat der Einsatz generativer KI bei der Arbeit auf das Lernen? Eine Prognose
Katharina Neufeld | Uni Kassel | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Katharina Neufeld | Uni Kassel | Germany
Prof. Dr. Sandra Ohly | Uni Kassel | Germany
Anna Eich | Uni Kassel | Germany
Xenia Kiefer | Uni Kassel | Germany
Christian Kordes | Uni Kassel | Germany
Bastian Mrochen | Uni Kassel | Germany
Emilie Nerlich | Uni Kassel | Germany
Janina Schneider | Uni Kassel | Germany

Seit dem Jahr 2023 ist eine Zunahme der Nutzung generativer KI (genKI) beobachtbar (McKinsey, 2024). Dabei erhalten 67,3% ihren Zugang zu genKI durch den Arbeitgebenden (Neufeld et al., 2025). Teilweise können Aufgaben durch die genKI übernommen werden, sodass sich der Fokus der eigenen Tätigkeit potenziell verschiebt, wenn die genKI beispielsweise Routineaufgaben übernimmt. Dies legt die Vermutung nahe, dass der Einsatz von genKI in der Arbeitswelt in einer Veränderung der individuellen Arbeitsplatzmerkmale (z.B. Komplexität, Problemlösen, Informationsverarbeitung) resultiert. Gemäß dem Work Design Growth Model (WDGM; Parker, 2017) können Arbeitsplatzmerkmale Lernprozesse beeinflussen. Zur Auseinandersetzung mit der Forschungsfrage, wie der Einsatz von genKI bei der Arbeit das Lernen beeinflusst, wurden 6 Fälle von verschiedenen Berufstätigen (z.B. Softwareentwickler, Fliesenleger, Assistenzarzt) untersucht. Basierend auf dem WDGM fand eine Analyse der Fälle in Bezug auf die Arbeitsplatzmerkmale statt. Anschließend konnte eine Prognose abgeleitet werden, inwiefern sich die Arbeitsplatzmerkmale durch den Einsatz von genKI potenziell verändern, was Rückschlüsse in Bezug auf Lernprozesse ermöglicht. Es scheint, dass informelle Lernprozesse hier von Bedeutung sind und beispielsweise die Anforderungen an das Problemlösen und die Komplexität der Arbeit zunehmen, sodass entsprechend dem WDGM das Lernen angeregt wird. In diesem Beitrag soll eine integrative Betrachtung basierend auf den Erkenntnissen der Fallanalyse sowie quantitativen Ergebnissen erfolgen, um denkbare praktische Implikationen zu diskutieren.

Einsatz von KI durch Lehrkräfte: Faktoren und Auswirkungen einer berufsbegleitenden KI-Fortbildung
Pauline Czora | Uni Frankfurt | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Pauline Czora | Uni Frankfurt | Germany
Dr. Maria Zirenko | Uni Frankfurt | Germany
Pauline Naumann | Uni Frankfurt | Germany
Dr. Carmen Heckmann | Uni Frankfurt | Germany
Prof. Dr. Holger Horz | Uni Frankfurt | Germany

Da KI zunehmend Einzug in Schulen hält, untersucht diese Studie Faktoren, die einen kritischen, pädagogisch fundierten und verantwortungsvollen Einsatz von KI durch Lehrkräfte unterstützen oder behindern, um daraus gezielte Fortbildungsmaßnahmen ableiten zu können. In Anlehnung an das „DOIT“-Modell (Horz & Schulze-Vorberg, 2017), einem etablierten Rahmenkonzept für erfolgreiche digitalisierte Lehr- und Lernprozesse, untersuchen wir die Auswirkungen der Faktoren Didaktik (D), Organisation (O), Individuum (I) und Technologie (T) auf die Nutzung von KI im Unterricht und ordnen diesen Faktoren Maßnahmen zu. Die Verbindung zwischen individuellen und organisatorischen Faktoren unter besonderer Berücksichtigung von KI ist ein Alleinstellungsmerkmal unserer Studie. Die Datenerhebung begann im November 2025 und dauert derzeit noch an. Für diesen Beitrag haben wir einen vorläufigen (Cut-off) Datensatz analysiert, der eine Stichprobe von 63 Lehrkräften (55 % weiblich; M = 46.4, SD = 10.8) umfasst. Vorläufige Ergebnisse zeigen, dass KI-Angst negativ mit Aspekten der Selbstwirksamkeit in Bezug auf die didaktische Integration von KI in den Unterricht (r = -.46) und dem Einsatz digitaler Diagnostik (r = -.35) korreliert. Die Verhaltensabsicht KI einzusetzen, korreliert positiv mit Selbstwirksamkeitserleben beim Unterrichten mit KI (r = 0.44) und auf die interne Zusammenarbeit unter Lehrkräften (r = 0.29). Die weitere Datenanalyse (ca. 300 Lehrkräfte) untersucht zusätzlich die Wirksamkeit der berufsbegleitenden Fortbildungen in Abhängigkeit organisatorischer Aspekte. Die Ergebnisse können zur Optimierung von KI- Fortbildungen für Lehrkräfte genutzt werden und liefern eine evidenzbasierte Grundlage für Schulentwicklungen.

Arbeitsbezogenes Lernen mit Augmented Reality: Evidenz aus einer experimentellen Studie mit generativen Lernaktivitäten
Rabea Bödding | Uni Bielefeld | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Rabea Bödding | Uni Bielefeld | Germany
Prof. Dr. Günter Maier | Uni Bielefeld | Germany

Augmented Reality (AR) ermöglicht die Visualisierung digitaler Informationen in realen Umgebungen und hat Potenzial zur Unterstützung arbeitsbezogenen Lernens gezeigt. Ein Großteil der bisherigen AR-Forschung stützt sich auf medienvergleichende Ansätze, während es an theoriegeleitetem Instruktionsdesign fehlt, welches erklären könnte, wie AR effektiv Lernen unterstützen kann. Generative Lernaktivitäten (GLAs) bieten einen theoretischen Rahmen, um diese Lücke zu schließen. GLAs fördern die kognitive Verarbeitung von Lerninhalten und damit das Lernen mithilfe von z.B. Selbsterklärungen, Vorhersagen. Forschungsergebnisse zu GLAs zeigen, dass diese Lernergebnisse sowohl in analogen als auch in digitalen Umgebungen verbessern können. Zudem sind GLAs besonders gut für AR-basiertes Lernen geeignet, da sie zentrale Affordanzen von AR, wie z.B. Präsenz, aufgreifen können.
Diese präregistrierte Studie untersucht, ob die Einbettung von GLAs in AR das Lernen über AR ohne solche Aktivitäten und über eine nicht-augmentierte Lerneinheit hinaus verbessert. In der Studie werden 180 Teilnehmer einer von drei Versuchsbedingungen zugewiesen: AR mit GLAs, nur AR oder eine Kontrollgruppe. Nach einer informierten Einwilligung in die Studie werden die Teilnehmer einen ersten Fragebogen ausfüllen, der auch einen ersten Wissenstest enthält, und anschließend mithilfe textbasierter Lernmaterialien zur Gesundheit des Bewegungsapparats von Büroangestellten lernen. Während der Lernintervention werden die Teilnehmer über Smartphones auf Inhalte zugreifen, entweder über AR mit oder ohne GLAs oder über Bilder in der Kontrollbedingung. Der Lernerfolg, die kognitive Belastung und die Präsenz werden unmittelbar nach der Unterweisung bewertet. Der Lernerfolg und ein verhaltensbezogener Indikator, der auf den Lerninhalt abgestimmt ist, werden in einer Nachbefragung erneut gemessen. Die Datenerhebung wird voraussichtlich bis April 2026 abgeschlossen sein.

Mikro-Interventionen als Impuls zum Weiterlernen und Wissenstransfer
Prof. Dr. Simone Kauffeld | TU Braunschweig | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Simone Kauffeld | TU Braunschweig | Germany
Leoni Senkbeil | TU Braunschweig | Germany
Kristien Klaka | TU Braunschweig | Germany
Dr. Marie Ritter | TU Braunschweig | Germany

Im digitalen Wandel gewinnt informelles Lernen zunehmend an Bedeutung. Die Konvergenz von Lern- und Arbeitswerkzeugen sowie das Potenzial digitaler Lernformate eröffnen neue Gelegenheiten, informelles Lernen situativ zu aktivieren, wenn Wissen im Arbeitsprozess geteilt wird. Kurze, ca. achtminütige TechTalk-Videos lassen sich als Mikrointerventionen in virtuelle Lernumgebungen einbetten und ermöglichen es Mitarbeitenden, Lernbedarf und -methoden eigenverantwortlich zu nutzen und weiterzugeben. Bislang ist jedoch unklar, wie der Spillover-Effekt von Lernaktivitäten erfolgt – erste Untersuchungen des Spillovers heben die Rolle der Reflexionsprozesse hervor.
In unserer qualitativen Studie (N = 23) haben Berufstätige aus unterschiedlichen Organisationen einen TechTalk zu Meetings genutzt und leitfadengestützt Reflexionsberichte angefertigt. Die Antworten wurden in MAXQDA qualitativ auf förderliche und hinderliche (Transfer-)Faktoren, informelles Lernen, Wissenstransfer und Kooperation des TechTalks ausgewertet werden. Erste Ergebnisse zeigen, dass TechTalks als formaler Impuls als Auslöser für den Spillover in informelles Lernen und Wissensaustausch dienen können, und Persönlichkeitsmerkmale und Selbstregulationsprozesse den Effekt verstärken. Mit der Studie tragen wir zu einem differenzierten Verständnis von informellem Lernen und des Spillover-Effekts bei.

08:00 am
iCal
Promoting Healthy Ageing Through Innovative Technology
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Isabelle Albert (University of Luxembourg)
Co-chair(s) Dr. Martine Hoffmann (geroResearch)
Room: AT
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Coupled symposium
Duration: 195 Minutes

In the light of population ageing and growing life-expectancies, the question of how well-being in older age can be effectively supported has gained growing interest, both in research and practice. The World Health Organization refers to healthy ageing as “the process of developing and maintaining the functional ability that enables wellbeing in older age.” In this context, innovative technologies offer promising tools for the personalized assessment and monitoring of needs as well as for prevention and intervention. Technological innovations can support older adults to meet their needs and desires even when they are confronted with health challenges.
The present double symposium brings together scholars from psychology, medicine, and sport science/neuroscience to present their work on how current technological advancements can support healthy ageing and well-being. Contributions in the first part will address, among other topics, digital approaches to assessing health indicators, technology-supported cognitive-motor testing and training for fall prevention in older people. In the second part, we will focus more closely on digital approaches regarding well-being of older patients with Parkinson’s disease. By integrating interdisciplinary perspectives, the symposium will highlight how digital tools can contribute to maintain physical, cognitive, social, and emotional functioning, thereby supporting autonomy and quality of life in older adulthood.

Empowering Healthy Aging Through Digital Health Technologies: A Capability-Centered Perspective
Messaline F. Fomo | Digital Medicine, Department of Precision Medicine, Luxembourg Institute of Health, Strassen & Digital Medicine, Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine, University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Messaline F. Fomo | Digital Medicine, Department of Precision Medicine, Luxembourg Institute of Health, Strassen & Digital Medicine, Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine, University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Dr. Liyousew Borga | Digital Medicine, Department of Precision Medicine, Luxembourg Institute of Health, Strassen & Digital Medicine, Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine, University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. Thomas Abel | Institute of Social and Preventive Medicine (ISPM) | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Philip Santangelo | Luxembourg
Dr. Sara Riggare | Participatory eHealth and Health Data Research Group, Department of Women’s and Children’s Health | Sweden
Prof. Dr. Jochen Klucken | Digital Medicine, Department of Precision Medicine, Luxembourg Institute of Health, Strassen; Digital Medicine, Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine, University of Luxembourg & Centre Hospitalier de Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Dr. Ivana Paccoud | Digital Medicine, Department of Precision Medicine, Luxembourg Institute of Health, Strassen & Digital Medicine, Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine, University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg

As populations age, supporting older adults in maintaining health, autonomy, and quality of life is a growing societal priority. Digital health technologies are increasingly promoted as tools to support healthy aging, yet their value depends on whether they address what older adults themselves consider meaningful for their daily lives. This work draws on a capability-based framework to examine how digital health technologies support empowerment in people living with chronic conditions. Results can be used to inform approaches to healthy aging. Using evidence from a scoping review of digital health use among people with chronic conditions, we identified key empowering capabilities, including the ability to access and understand health information, confidence in self-management, engagement in healthcare decisions, and emotional and social support. These capabilities align closely with core dimensions of healthy aging, such as maintaining functional ability, autonomy, psychological well-being, and social participation. The results also highlight how digital tools functionalities such as symptom tracking, personalized feedback, remote communication with healthcare professionals, and peer support platforms serve as resources that can enable these capabilities when they are accessible, usable, and adapted to individual contexts. Additionally, conversion factors such as digital literacy, health status, and the availability of supportive social and care networks shape whether individuals can translate digital resources into valued outcomes. This work provides a conceptual framework for understanding how innovative technologies can support health and well-being across diverse populations and stages of aging.

VR-Health: Integrative Immersive Technologies for Mental Well-Being and Self-Regulation in Older Adults
Dr. Martine Hoffmann | geroResearch | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Martine Hoffmann | geroResearch | Luxembourg
Prof. Matthias Pfaff | Germany

As populations age and life expectancy rises, strengthening mental well-being, emotional regulation, and resilience in older adults has become a pressing societal and public health priority. The interdisciplinary VR-Health framework, developed in cooperation with geroRESEARCH and Hochschule Kaiserslautern, aims to design and pilot innovative immersive mental-health solutions to address this growing need.
The presentation highlights two innovative prototype VR-based solutions, co-designed with a user-centered, participatory approach, to support preventive mental health in older adults. The VR-Hypnosis prototype immerses users in minimalist, attention-guiding virtual environments enriched with guided verbal suggestions and multisensory stimuli, enabling deep trance states and the activation of individual psychological resources. NeuroVR incorporates EEG-based neurofeedback into immersive virtual reality, allowing the virtual environment to adapt in real time to users’ neurophysiological signals, supporting personalised self-regulation and resilience training. Both solutions were co-created through a participatory design process involving virtual environment designers, psychotherapists and older adults, ensuring high usability, accessibility, engagement, and real-world applicability.
Early pilot testing demonstrates feasibility, high acceptance, and promising indications of improving relaxation and wellbeing. Findings highlight the potential of user-centered, immersive VR interventions to promote mental health, paving the way for evidence-based preventive solutions.

FLUX2: Innovate Fall Prevention Using Motor-Cognitive Training Technology
Beatriz Jordao | Department of Sport, LUNEX, Differdange, Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Beatriz Jordao | Department of Sport, LUNEX, Differdange, Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. Thorben Hülsdünker | Department of Sport, LUNEX, Differdange, Luxembourg & Luxembourg Health & Sport Sciences Research Institute (LHSSRI), Differdange, Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. Isabelle Albert | Luxembourg
Dr. Martine Hoffmann | geroResearch | Luxembourg

Falls are a major cause of injury and mortality in adults > 65 years of age and are strongly associated with reduced independence, lower quality of life, and substantial healthcare costs. Worldwide, falls and neurodegenerative diseases result in the largest number of life years with disability. Luxembourg shows one of the highest fall rates in Europe, ranking 5th in fall incidence and 7th in fall-related mortality. With ongoing population ageing and demographic change, falls are expected to become an even greater challenge, underscoring the need for effective fall prevention strategies to preserve independence and quality of life in older adults in Luxembourg.
Building on the FLUX project on fall risk prediction, the FLUX2 project aims to develop and evaluate a technology-supported fall prevention program for older adults in Luxembourg. In a collaboration between GERO, the University of Luxembourg, and the Luxembourg Institute for Health and Sport Science Research, a 10-week intervention program is being implemented.
Participants are assigned to one of three training conditions targeting motor and balance performance, cognitive functions, or integrated cognitive-motor abilities. The fall risk of participants will be evaluated prior to and after the training to determine the most effective form of fall prevention training.
The project investigates which training modality is most effective in reducing fall risk and improving functional abilities. The results will inform evidence-based, training recommendations for the Luxembourgish elderly population. FLUX2 contributes to the development of innovative, data-driven strategies to maintain autonomy, functional capacity, and quality of life in the senior population.

A Scoping Review of the Scientific Literature on Digital Technology for Healthy Ageing in Migrant Populations
Prof. Dr. Adrian Stanciu | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Adrian Stanciu | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. Alejandro Dominguez-Rodriguez | Faculty of Behavioral, Management and Social Sciences (BMS) | Netherlands
Prof. Dr. Gerben J. Westerhof | Faculty of Behavioral, Management and Social Sciences (BMS) | Netherlands

The scientific literature is scarce and unsystematic considering the role of digital technology in healthy ageing of migrants. We still do not know what works, when, and for whom, and this knowledge gap delays the development of inclusive personalized interventions. We present the results of a scoping review of scientific articles published in English, German, and Spanish after 2010 carried out across specialized and interdisciplinary databases (EBSCO, IEEE Xplore, IET Digital Library, PsychINFO, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science). We included articles in the quantitative and qualitative method reporting on data from individual first generation migrants aged 55+. We reviewed only explicit findings regarding the adoption, use and effectiveness of digital technology in view of improving health in older migrant populations. The piloted search strategy resulted in approximately 1,000 initial articles, which were subsequently screened by two independent reviewers. Preliminary findings suggest that less than ten articles met our inclusion criteria. Moreover, we observe that communication and information technology (e.g., instant communication) as well as technology specifically designed for disease management (e.g., cancer) contribute to improvement of health indicators in older migrants. Finally, we note an underlying assumption in many of the excluded articles that existent technologies can be adjusted (i.e., translated) to accommodate the specifics in migrants. We argue that this is a problematic approach as migrant populations have specific healthcare needs and limitations due to, for instance, culturally informed expectations that must be taken into account at early stages of technology development.

Monitoring Functional Quality of Life Using a Geriatric Composite Score
Alan Castro Mejia | Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Alan Castro Mejia | Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine | Luxembourg

Prof. Dr. Isabelle Albert | Luxembourg

Prof. Dr. Jochen Klucken | Digital Medicine, Department of Precision Medicine, Luxembourg Institute of Health, Strassen; Digital Medicine, Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine, University of Luxembourg & Centre Hospitalier de Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Dr. Jean-Paul Steinmetz | Zitha SA, Luxembourg, Luxembourg | Luxembourg

Introduction: Clinicians generate data from standard assessments, biomarkers, and technologically assisted functional tests that could be used to characterize the patient’s functional health. We hypothesize that patient-centered data can estimate the drivers of functional impairments that significantly affect a patient’s quality of life and activities of daily living.
Methods: Cross-sectional clinical data from geriatric-age patients (≥ 60 years) living in long-term care homes was collected, including demographics, treatment regimen, functional mobility, independence, cognition, affective state, and patient-reported global and physical health, and digital mobility assessment. Using a data-driven approach, we developed a multi-parametric composite scores to predict functional impairment via a linear sparse group LASSO regression.
Results: Sixty-five patients were enrolled (19 females) with a mean age of 81.62 ± 10.01 years, Functional Independence Measure 90.01 ± 12.45, and a Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment of 20.22 ± 4.35. Estimation of functional impairment (R2 = 0.81) were primarily driven by the affective state and mobility in the balance domain.
Conclusion: Our data-driven approach produced an interpretable composite score that reflects multidimensional health in older adults. Mobility, autonomy, and treatment regimen are primarily responsible for the score’s monitoring performance. Its application could assist in personalized patient tracking and flagging early signs of deterioration. The second phase of the project will explore the score’s sensitivity to change and its ability to predict negative outcomes of interest (e.g., falls).

Evaluations of Disease Consequences Predict Affective Well Being Beyond Functional Impairments in Parkinson’s Disease
Ella Abri | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Ella Abri | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. Thomas Boll | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. Isabelle Albert | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. Anna Kornadt | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. Jochen Klucken | Digital Medicine, Department of Precision Medicine, Luxembourg Institute of Health, Strassen; Digital Medicine, Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine, University of Luxembourg & Centre Hospitalier de Luxembourg | Luxembourg

Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor and non-motor symptoms that impair functioning, limit activities of daily living, and restrict participation across important life domains. As health and functioning are key determinants of subjective well-being (SWB), PD impairments are likely to reduce SWB. SWB comprises affective well-being (positive and negative emotions) and cognitive well-being (global and specific domains of life satisfaction).
Guided by the Wilson and Cleary model of health-related quality of life, the International Classification of Functioning, and cognitive theories of SWB, we examined how functional impairment, activity limitation, and evaluations of PD consequences contribute incrementally to the prediction of affective well-being.
We analyzed cross-sectional data from N = 850 individuals with PD (33.3% female; mean age 70.7 years). All variables were assessed using validated clinician ratings or self-report measures. A hierarchical multiple regression analysis was conducted with predictors entered in theoretically informed blocks: (1) functioning, (2) activity limitation, and (3) evaluations of PD consequences. Changes in explained variance (ΔR²) were examined at each step.
Functioning accounted for 25.8% of the variance in affective well-being. Activity limitation explained an additional 3.8% variance. Adding evaluations of PD consequences produced a substantial further increase, resulting in a total amount of explained variance of R² =.478. These results indicate that PD-related impairments alone do not predict affective well-being; rather, patients´ evaluations of how their condition affects important life domains relative to their desires, preferences, or needs are the strongest predictor of affective well-being.

Evidence-based Design Translation for Mood Management in Newly Diagnosed People with Parkinson's Disease
Niloofar Kheradbin | Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine (LCSB) | Luxembourg

Prof. Dr. Jochen Klucken | University of Luxembourg, Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine (LCSB), Esch-sur-Alzette, Luxembourg & Centre Hospitalier de Luxembourg, Luxembourg | Luxembourg

This study aims to define evidence-based educational content tailored to the specific needs of newly diagnosed people with Parkinson’s disease (PwPD), with the goal of motivating proactive engagement in mood management and ultimately improving Quality of Life (QoL).
A systematic literature search and analysis were conducted to identify existing digital health solutions supporting mood management in Parkinson’s Disease (PD) care. Using a thematic analysis approach [1], we identified key content requirements and user engagement elements relevant to platform and content design. An evidence informed design synthesis [2] was then applied to map these findings, resulting in the formulation of design principles.
Telehealth platforms were the most frequently reported solutions, followed by mobile applications and social robots. Depression, anxiety, and sleep disturbances were the most commonly addressed conditions, whereas shame and social isolation were rarely targeted (n=2 studies). Two major content themes emerged: (1) Patient-Empowered Disease Management, including self-management, motivation, education, and interaction; and (2) Interventional Disease Management, encompassing treatment and assistance. The main themes on user engagement included: Access and Communication, Technological Integration and Support, Tailored and Personalized Content, Social Engagement and Community, and Barriers to Engagement.
Design principles which are grounded in evidence-based and need-based analysis will be next mapped to clinical data from the Luxembourg Parkinson cohort study, providing a solid foundation for the participatory design [4] of MoodAid; a digital coach for mood management in newly diagnosed PwPD.

PARKINSONNET Luxembourg: Towards a Digital Supported Integrated Care Network for People With Parkinson's Disease
Dr. Patricia Martins Conde | Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine (LCSB) | Luxembourg
Show details

Dr. Ivana Paccoud | Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine (LCSB) | Luxembourg
Dr. Sylvia Herbrink | Centre Hospitalier de Luxembourg, Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. Anne Kaysen | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. Rejko Krüger | Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine (LCSB), University of Luxembourg, Luxembourg; Centre Hospitalier de Luxembourg, Luxembourg & Luxembourg Institute of Health, Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. Jochen Klucken | Digital Medicine, Department of Precision Medicine, Luxembourg Institute of Health, Strassen; Digital Medicine, Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine, University of Luxembourg & Centre Hospitalier de Luxembourg | Luxembourg

Digital solutions offer the possibility to improve the management of patient care by increasing and facilitating the communication within multidisciplinary care teams. However, integrating digital medical devices and services into integrated care models comes with several challenges such as the resistance to change by healthcare professionals (HCPs), and the disruption of care pathway workflows, among others1.
We co-designed an initiative with local stakeholders targeting the improvement of the communication between the multidisciplinary care team and people with PD, members of the integrated care network “Réseau de Compétences – Maladies neurodégénératives2 dénommé ParkinsonNet Luxembourg”, by leveraging the use of digital management solutions and the Luxembourgish Electronic Health Records (EHR)3. To test feasibility and inform better engagement, an anonymous online survey was distributed among the ParkinsonNet Luxembourg HCPs to understand their perspectives on the usage of digital solutions to support patient care.
Among the 45 respondents, 82.2% confirmed their willingness to use medical software to document clinical information, and among these, 78.4% are willing to collect clinical information in a structured way. Furthermore, 72.7% agreed that clinical information should be stored in the EHR. However, 51.2% believe that the lack of time during a consultation or EHR complexity will be the biggest barriers to integrate EHR into their daily work. These results demonstrate the planned initiative is feasible within ParkinsonNet Luxembourg, provided that enough guidance is given to HCPs and that the integration of these solutions is done without major adjustments to the care pathway and related workflows.

Background: Electronic Health Records (EHRs) enable information-sharing between healthcare professionals (HCPs) and patients—especially relevant in countries like Luxembourg, given its high cross-border patient mobility. EHRs are vital for managing chronic conditions such as Parkinson’s disease (PD), which require coordinated, multidisciplinary care. Despite the national EHR rollout in 2020, only 7.5% of the general population used the EHR in 2021. Beyond technical barriers for HCPs, little is known about whether low uptake among people with Parkinson’s disease (PwPD) is linked to limited digital health literacy, insufficient HCP support or lack of technical support.
Objectives: To examine how sociodemographic and clinical characteristics, digital health literacy, and HCP support influence EHR use among PwPD in Luxembourg.
Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among PwPD enrolled in the NCER-PD cohort (July–December 2024). Respondents were analyzed across digital health literacy domains (eHLQ), EHR usage patterns (HINTS), co-dependence (EHIS), and demographic/clinical factors. Logistic regression identified key predictors of EHR use.
Results: Among 191 respondents, 30% accessed their EHR at least once in the past year, and only 19% were regular users. EHR users reported higher confidence in five digital health literacy domains, including ability to engage with technology and accessing reliable technology. They also received more encouragement from HCPs, reported greater trust in HCPs, were less co-dependent on family, were more likely to be born in Luxembourg, and were at earlier stages of disease. Logistic regression showed that confidence in engaging with technology (OR=3.89), access to reliable technology (OR=3.74), and HCP support (OR=3.63) were significantly associated with EHR use. Interestingly, higher trust in HCPs (OR=0.20) and confidence in understanding health concepts (OR=0.26) were associated with lower EHR use.
Conclusions: EHR uptake among PwPD remains low. Improving usability, digital skills training, and active HCP support are key to boosting engagement. Special attention is needed for vulnerable groups, including immigrants, those with lower income, and individuals in advanced disease stages. Future research should explore how support needs evolve with disease progression, to inform education campaigns within care networks.

How Learners Process and Evaluate Multiple Documents: Evidence From Instructional, Cognitive, and Technological Perspectives
Chair(s) Dr. Corinna Schuster
Dr. Veit Kubik
Room: BG
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Learning from multiple, partially conflicting documents poses substantial challenges for learners. Successful performance requires not only the integration of information across sources, but also the evaluation of claims, the handling of inconsistencies, and the effective use of instructional and technological support. This symposium brings together four contributions that examine how learners process, evaluate, and learn from multiple documents under varying cognitive, instructional, and technological conditions.
The first contribution examines how prior beliefs and factual accuracy jointly influence the evaluation of socioscientific information. Across four experiments, findings demonstrate that belief-consistent misinformation is more likely to be accepted and processed fluently than belief-inconsistent information, even when controlling for prior knowledge. This highlights the powerful role of beliefs not only in strategic evaluation but also in basic comprehension processes.
The second contribution focuses on post-reading generative learning activities. Across two studies, generative tasks such as argument validation or summarization did not enhance comprehension of conflicting documents compared to non-generative activities and, in some cases, even impaired the text base. Ongoing work examines whether scaffolding generative learning activities and increased task engagement can yield delayed benefits.
The third contribution investigates whether rubrics can foster metacognitive monitoring while writing from multiple documents. Results show that rubrics do not generally improve monitoring accuracy; instead, benefits emerge primarily for high-performing learners, indicating that rubric-based support may differentially affect learners’ monitoring performance depending on their competence level.
The fourth contribution addresses the role of emerging technologies by examining how the use of generative AI (ChatGPT) affects learning from multiple documents. Focusing on metacomprehension accuracy, cue use, and regulation, the study investigates whether AI support alters learners’ reliance on diagnostic cues and their ability to regulate learning effectively.
Together, the contributions provide an integrated perspective on how evaluation, comprehension, and instructional support shape learning from multiple documents, highlighting both opportunities and limitations in contemporary educational contexts.

Effects of Prior Beliefs and Factual Accuracy on Strategic Evaluation and Non-Strategic Acceptance of Socioscientific Claims from Multiple Documents
Dr. Johanna Abendroth
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Johanna Abendroth
Tobias Richter

When engaging with multiple socioscientific documents online, readers are often confronted with conflicting information as well as misinformation. Based on the notion that knowledge and beliefs not only influence strategic evaluation, but also the comprehension of information through validation, four experiments investigated the influence of knowledge and beliefs influence when belief-consistency and factual accuracy of claims interact. Experiment 1 (n = 73) used a validity judgement task and found that participants made more errors in judging false belief-consistent claims (β = -0.78, z = -6.30, p < .001) and needed more time to correctly respond to true but belief-inconsistent (β = -15.60, t(2,378) = -2.57, p = .005) and to false but belief-consistent claims (β = 23.16, t(2,331) = 3.23, p < .001). Experiment 2 (n = 50) fully replicated these results in a broader sample. Experiment 3 (n = 84) used the epistemic Stroop task to investigate the influence of beliefs and knowledge in a nonepistemic task and found that affirmative responses were not influenced by their factual accuracy for belief-consistent claims (β = -4.03, t(472) = -0.35, p = .725), whereas factual accuracy was crucial for belief-inconsistent claims (β = -31.55, t(472) = -2.77, p = .006). Experiment 4 (n = 226) replicated the results for both tasks, controlling for readers’ prior knowledge. The results suggest that beliefs not only exert a strong influence on the strategic evaluation of socioscientific information, but also on the acceptance of belief-consistent false information beyond motivated reasoning.

Can Generative Learning Activities After Reading Enhance Comprehension of Conflicting Multiple Documents?
Veit Kubik
Show details
Authors:
Veit Kubik
Mandy Krüger
Dr. Johanna Abendroth
Tobias Richter

Constructing knowledge from partially conflicting multiple documents is challenging as it requires the readers to construct an integrated mental model of the documents and their prior knowledge. Such knowledge construction requires readers not only to activate and integrate textual information into a coherent representation but also to validate its consistency with currently activated knowledge and beliefs. Based on this notion, we hypothesized that argument validation as a post-reading generative task can support readers in text integration and validation. In addition, we examined whether possible positive effects of argument validation persist over time. In two experiments, we compared post-reading generative learning tasks (i.e., argument validation, argument summary) versus nongenerative tasks (restudy, facts summary). In Experiment 1 (in the lab; n = 159) and Experiment 2 (online: n = 204) we assessed the effects for comprehension and memory using immediate verification and recognition tests. In both studies, generative learning tasks did not improve comprehension relative to nongenerative tasks and even led to lower memory for texts. Experiment 3 (data collection ongoing) introduced informed training and extended the execution time for the learning task to test whether higher-quality generative learning yields long-term benefits for comprehension and retention after one week. Theoretical and practical implications for post-reading interventions for multiple-document comprehension are discussed.

Supporting Writing From Multiple Documents Using Rubrics
Rebecca Krebs
Show details
Authors:
Rebecca Krebs
Corinna Schuster | Germany
Marc Stadtler

Rubrics are widely used to support learning and performance, yet their effects on metacognitive processes in complex tasks such as writing from multiple documents remain unclear. From a metacognitive perspective, rubrics are assumed to facilitate accurate self-assessment and thereby support effective regulation of learning. This study investigated whether rubric use affects monitoring accuracy and regulation decisions in a writing-from-multiple-documents task. A total of 245 university students completed an argumentative essay based on multiple historical texts. Learners either received a rubric including quality levels and detailed descriptions or no additional support. Moderation analyses examined whether effects of rubric use depended on essay performance. Results revealed no overall main effect of rubric use on monitoring accuracy. However, a significant interaction between rubric use and essay performance indicated that high-performing learners benefited from rubrics in terms of monitoring accuracy, whereas lower-performing learners did not. No effects of rubric use were found for regulation decisions, pointing to potential limits of rubric-based support for regulating learning. These findings suggest that rubrics do not uniformly support metacognitive processes and highlight the need for differentiated instructional support that accounts for learners’ performance levels in complex writing tasks.

Does AI Support Change How Learners Judge Their Understanding? How ChatGPT Affects Metacomprehension, Cue Use, and Regulation in Multiple-Document Reading and Writing
Corinna Schuster | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Corinna Schuster | Germany
Marc Stadtler

The increasing use of large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT is reshaping how students engage with multiple sources during reading and writing. While prior research indicates that AI assistance can enhance task performance and reduce perceived cognitive effort, little is known about its impact on learners’ metacomprehension—particularly in epistemically complex tasks that require integrating conflicting information. Understanding these effects is crucial, as accurate metacomprehension underlies effective self-regulated learning.
Grounded in the cue-utilization framework (Koriat, 1997) and the MD-TRACE model (Rouet & Britt, 2011), this study examines how ChatGPT use influences metacomprehension accuracy and regulation during multiple-document reading and writing. We investigate whether ChatGPT use is associated with lower metacomprehension accuracy and whether this relationship is mediated by reduced cognitive effort. Furthermore, we examine whether ChatGPT use is linked to less adaptive regulation decisions (allocating further study), and whether this effect is mediated by metacomprehension accuracy.
In a randomized experimental design, university students read conflicting historical texts and wrote an integrative essay either with or without ChatGPT support. Participants provided metacognitive judgments before and after writing, completed comprehension and inference measures, reported subjective cognitive effort, and indicated how they would regulate further learning. Metacomprehension accuracy was operationalized as the correspondence between judgments and performance, and regulation quality as the alignment between judgments and subsequent learning decisions.
By testing a theoretically specified mediation model, this study aims to clarify whether and how generative AI shapes metacomprehension accuracy and regulation in complex information environments. Data collection will be completed in February 2026, allowing results to be presented at the conference.

Advances in Research on Pedophilia and Child Sexual Abuse
Chair(s) Frederic Maximilian Gnielka (Medical School Berlin)
Room: RO
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

This symposium brings together current advances in research on child sexual offending, pedophilia, and child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM). One contribution directly tests assumptions about sexual interest in children being disproportionately associated with the ethnically white population by using a globally diverse online sample and a combination of direct and indirect measures, thereby addressing pedophilia as a potential cultural phenomenon.
The session also introduces an important methodological advance for experimental sexual preference research: a validation study of a new, ethnically diverse AI-generated pictorial stimulus set covering the full range of developmental stages.
In addition, two contributions address new trends in CSEAM research by examining how written narratives depicting minors relate to adult sexual stories on the clear web and by testing whether engagement with text-based CSEAM is associated with distinct psychological risk profiles compared with exclusive use of images and videos.
Another talk focuses on offenders in the dark web, applying computer science and machine learning techniques to identify individuals across CSEAM forums, which allows research questions about the consistency of behavior across forums to be addressed.
The final talk shifts attention to recidivism assessment by examining how forensic experts implicitly weigh dynamic risk factors in sexual recidivism judgments using choice-based conjoint analysis, shedding light on overlap and discrepancies between evidence-based classifications and professional decision-making.

Do White men Have Disproportionately High Pedophilic Interests? A Direct Test in a Globally Diverse Sample
Prof. Dr. Alexander F. Schmidt | Institute of Psychology | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Alexander F. Schmidt | Institute of Psychology | Germany
Prof. Dr. Robert J. B. Lehmann | Medical School Berlin | Germany
Prof. Kelly Babchishin | Carlton University | Canada
Dr. Laura Quinten | Medical School Berlin | Germany

In the international literature on child sexual abuse, it is assumed that disproportionately more White men, compared to non-White men, are sexually interested in children. This is also reflected in an initial meta-analysis that finds a disproportionate accumulation of paraphilic offenses and, in particular, child sexual abuse offenses among Whites (Thompson & Hanson, 2025; k = 35, N > 20,000, OR = 2.3). However, a conceptual problem is that the literature usually infers pedophilic sexual interests indirectly from child sexual abuse offenses, and that the pedophilia-child sexual abuse link empirically shows at most moderate effect sizes outside of forensic populations. In this talk, results from a global online study from six different countries of the Global North and South (N > 3,500 community men) are presented, testing systematic prevalence differences between White and various non-White groups and in which sexual interest in children was measured using theoretically more informative direct self-report measures (subjective sexual attractiveness ratings) and indirect reaction-time-based measures (Viewing Time). In addition, associations with self-reported past child sexual abuse offenses and the propensity to commit such offenses if there were no personal negative consequences are also reported. The results are critically discussed against the background of existing theoretical attempts to explain a link between race (as operationalized via skin colour) and pedophilic interest.

Do AI-Generated Humans Look Like Intended? Validating the RAPPID Picture Set for Sexual Preference Research
Dr. Laura Quinten | Medical School Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Laura Quinten | Medical School Berlin | Germany
Prof. Dr. Alexander F. Schmidt | Johannes Gutenberg Universität Mainz | Germany
Prof. Babchishin Kelly | Carlton University | Canada
Prof. Dr. Thomas Schäfer | Health and Medical University Erfurt | Germany
Prof. Dr. Robert J.B. Lehmann | Medical School Berlin | Germany

Age-related sexual interest is a key component in sexuality research and forensic evaluations. Indirect assessments via physiological or cognitive responses avoid social desirability bias, but require suitable stimuli depicting minimally clothed artificial individuals of different ages. The RAPPID Picture Set was developed using artificial intelligence to overcome the lack of ethnic diversity and full age representation in existing picture sets. It comprises 96 images systematically varied by sex (50% female) and ethnicity/skin tone (Asian, Dark Brown, Medium Brown, White), covering all six chronophilic age categories. In a first validation study, each stimulus was evaluated by 50 of 200 German psychology students (naïve) and by four pediatricians (experts) along multiple perceptual dimensions. Results indicate that the depicted individuals generally reflect the intended features. Age ratings matched the target ranges, with male stimuli being perceived as slightly older than female stimuli. Physical development ratings were highly accurate for the youngest and oldest categories, with lower accuracy in transitional age categories. Skin tone ratings were accurate, whereas ethnicity classification was more variable, particularly for medium brown skin tones. Attractiveness ratings were consistent within each age–sex category. Dark and medium brown stimuli were rated as more attractive than white or Asian stimuli, and attractiveness ratings followed a U-shaped trajectory across age categories, peaking in young adulthood. Overall, the findings demonstrate the utility of the RAPPID Picture Set for studying chronophilic variation and various other stimulus-related research questions.

Text-Based CSEAM – What is it and how Does it Relate to Adult Sex Stories?
Frederic Maximilian Gnielka | Medical School Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:

Dr. Laura Quinten | Medical School Berlin | Germany
