Research on child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) has predominantly concentrated on photographic and video formats. However, substantial amounts of textual material—child sex stories or text-based CSEAM—circulates through both the clear and dark web.
Text based material may reveal unique insights into the desires and beliefs of its producers and consumers, as reading and writing of these stories has no direct child victim and is in many countries not illegal. Therefore, legal and social inhibitions that are imposed on the producers and consumers of CSEAM are likely reduced for of text-based CSEAM (e.g. fear of persecution or feelings of guilt). This form of CSEAM has not yet beensystematically investigated empirically.
We analyze a large corpus of sexually explicit narratives scraped from nifty.com, a semi-moderated story platform on the clear web, and identify texts depicting minors or youth characters. Building on a pilot study of 133 darknet narratives, we will (1) map recurring themes and stylistic features using the BERTopic pipeline (transformer embeddings and clustering) and (2) compare text-based CSEAM to adult-only sexual stories from the same platform. These comparisons will test whether text-based CSEAM shows distinct topic distributions, or whether these narratives largely reproduce adult narrative patterns.
Results are expected to generate empirically grounded hypotheses regarding differences between teleiophilic and pedo-/hebephilic sexual interests and to inform scalable content-analysis tools for research and prevention.

Psychological Risk Profiles of Text-Based Versus Image-Based Child Sexual Exploitation Material Users
Robert J. B. Lehmann | Medical School Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Robert J. B. Lehmann | Medical School Berlin | Germany
Dr. Laura Quinten | Medical School Berlin | Germany
Prof. Dr. Joscha Hausam | Psychologische Hochschule Berlin | Germany

The legal and clinical significance of text-based child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) remains contested, reflecting uncertainty about whether written narratives indicate meaningful risk beyond image- and video-based material. While visual CSEAM is consistently criminalized, fictional depictions occupy a legal grey zone in many jurisdictions. Empirically, little is known about whether individuals who engage with text-based CSEAM differ psychologically from those who consume only visual material.
Guided by the Motivation–Facilitation Model (Seto, 2017, 2019), this study examined whether convicted CSEAM users who report using text-based material exhibit distinct psychological profiles compared with those who report exclusive use of images or videos. Adult men convicted of CSEAM-related and/or contact sexual offenses against children (N = 76) were recruited from forensic and correctional settings and completed a multi-method assessment battery assessing motivational, trait, and situational risk factors.
Text-based CSEAM use was assessed via structured interview and analyzed as a dichotomous outcome. Because of the base rate of text-based CSEAM use, group differences were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analyses rather than conventional correlations, focusing on discriminatory accuracy.
By systematically testing whether the inclusion of text-based material is associated with a distinct configuration of psychological risk factors, this study provides an empirical foundation for ongoing debates about the forensic and legal relevance of narrative CSEAM.

Tracking User Behaviours Across Darknet Child Sexual Abuse Material Forums
Rebecca Reichel | Medical School Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Rebecca Reichel | Medical School Berlin | Germany
Frederic Maximilian Gnielka | Medical School Berlin | Germany
Prof. Dr. Arjan Blokland | Netherlands Institute for the Study and Law Enforcement | Netherlands
Prof. Dr. Robert J. B. Lehmann | Medical School Berlin | Germany

Both researchers and law enforcement have an interest in matching user profiles across different darknet forums dedicated to child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) to facilitate investigative efforts and offer insights into user behaviours over time and between different forums. One intuitive way to match user profiles is via their usernames, assuming that the same username belongs to the same person – especially in the context of the darknet, where reputation and trustworthiness play an important role. Previous research on social media platforms and online drug markets has shown that this strategy can indeed yield accuracy levels as high as 77%. This is the first study to match user profiles across different CSEAM forums to answer the following questions: How can users across different darknet CSEAM forums be matched? How many users are active on multiple forums? Do users behave differently between forums? We use data from ten darknet CSEAM forums that were seized by law enforcement, including usernames and posting behaviour of registered users and sometimes meta-data such as passwords or email addresses. The usernames of profiles who contributed at least one post are compared across all forums. Minhashing, locality-sensitive hashing, a normalised Levenshtein distance and component detection are used to find identical and highly similar usernames. The activities among matched user profiles are then compared to test the plausibility of the obtained matches and to track the development of users’ behaviours and movements across forums.

Implicit Weighting of Dynamic Risk Factors in Sexual Recidivism Assessment: A Choice-Based Conjoint Analysis
Prof. Dr. André Körner | Medical School Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. André Körner | Medical School Berlin | Germany
Ulla Redwan | Medical School Berlin | Germany

Accurate assessment of sexual recidivism risk relies not only on empirically validated risk factors but also on how these factors are weighted in professional judgment. While actuarial tools are based on evidence-based classifications (e.g., Mann et al., 2010), little is known about the implicit weighting processes used by forensic experts when multiple risk factors co-occur. We therefore investigated how forensic experts prioritize dynamic risk factors when assessing the likelihood of sexual reoffending among individuals with pedophilic disorder. Using a choice-based conjoint analysis, 13 forensic experts evaluated fictitious offender profiles that systematically varied across four dynamic risk factors: impulsivity, non-compliance with supervision, offense-supportive attitudes, and lack of victim empathy. Participants repeatedly selected the profile they perceived as having the highest risk of reoffending across 12 choice sets. Relative importance scores and part-worth utilities were estimated to reconstruct implicit decision weights. Results indicated that impulsivity and non-compliance were weighted most strongly in recidivism judgments, whereas offense-supportive attitudes and lack of victim empathy played a comparatively smaller role. This weighting pattern partially aligned with the empirical risk classification, though impulsivity was prioritized more strongly than theoretically expected. The findings suggest that observable, behavior-oriented factors exert a disproportionate influence on expert risk judgments, potentially reflecting heuristic decision processes in applied forensic contexts. Overall, the study highlights systematic discrepancies between empirical risk classifications and intuitive professional weighting. Conjoint analysis proved to be a promising approach for examining implicit decision-making in forensic risk assessment and may inform training efforts aimed at improving structured and evidence-based evaluations.

Effectiveness of Self-Stigma–Reducing Interventions for Mental Health: A Meta-Analysis
Christine Emmer | University of Mannheim | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Christine Emmer | University of Mannheim | Germany
Nicolas Krumpe | University of Mannheim | Germany
Jutta Mata | University of Mannheim | Germany

Self-stigma, the internalization of negative stereotypes about one’s own social identity, is consistently associated with poorer mental health. Although various interventions reduce self-stigma, their broader impact on mental health and which interventions are most beneficial for whom remain unclear. To address this gap, we conducted a preregistered meta-analysis of RCTs examining the effects of self-stigma–reducing interventions on mental health across stigmatized populations. Preliminary analyses are based on 17 RCTs (3,992 participants; 56 effect sizes) using a three-level random-effects model. Overall, interventions produced a significant small-to-moderate improvement in mental health (g = .23), which remained robust when controlling for publication year, region, and methodological quality. Moderator analyses of study characteristics showed larger effects for interventions compared with passive (g = .34) than active control groups (g = .11). Intervention setting also mattered: individual face-to-face interventions yielded the strongest effects (g = .47), whereas group-based (g = .20) and individual remote interventions (g = .16) did not differ significantly from each other. No differences emerged for intervention exposure time or duration. No differences were observed for gender, age, or ethnicity. Exploratory subgroup analyses indicated particularly strong effects for third-wave psychotherapy interventions (g = .31) and social support–based interventions (g = .48), whereas evidence for cognitive behavioral, positive psychology, and narrative interventions remains inconclusive. These findings suggest that self-stigma–reducing interventions can improve mental health and should be considered in care for stigmatized individuals; they also identify effective intervention characteristics and highlight evidence gaps to guide future research and intervention development.

Perspektiven deutscher Mental Health Professionals auf Ursachen und Verantwortung für die Entstehung und den Verlauf von Depressionen
Dr. Angelika Augustine | Bielefeld University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Angelika Augustine | Bielefeld University | Germany
Prof. Doreen Reifegerste | Bielefeld University | Germany

Ärzt*innen vertreten bei Depressionen das biopsychosoziale Modell, welches Depressionen multifaktoriell verursacht sieht. Sie können jedoch den Anteilen spezifischer Ursachen unterschiedliche Bedeutungen zumessen (Engert et al., 2020; Marx et al., 2023). Diese Überzeugungen beeinflussen Behandlungsentscheidungen und die Arzt-Patienten-Kommunikation (Lebowitz & Ahn, 2014).
Laut Attributionstheorie ist die wahrgenommene Kontrollierbarkeit einer Krankheit zentral für Schuldzuweisungen und Stigmatisierung von Betroffenen (Weiner, 1995). Bei Kliniker*innen wird verstärkte wahrgenommene persönliche Verantwortung mit einer stigmatisierenden Haltung assoziiert (Wolgast et al., 2025). Biomedizinische Erklärungen für Depressionen verringern Schuldzuschreibungen, aber erhöhen gleichzeitig die Wahrnehmung von Chronizität und prognostischen Pessimismus (Deacon & Baird, 2009, Nolan & O'Connor, 2019).
Die Perspektive von Psychiater*innen hinsichtlich der Ursachenanteilen (beispielsweise genetisch, umweltbezogen, lebensstilbezogen) von Depressionen und der Zuweisung von Verantwortung für Entstehung und Verlauf der Depression ist bisher wenig erforscht (Jauch et al., 2023).
Um dies zu beleuchten wurden im Jahr 2025 qualitative, halbstrukturierte Interviews online mit N = 24 Psychiater*innen und Neurolog*innen in Deutschland durchgeführt. Wir wandten eine qualitative Inhaltsanalyse mit induktiven und deduktiven Anteilen an.
Alle Teilnehmer*innen nannten ein biopsychosoziales Entstehungsmodell der Depression. Die Kliniker*innen neigten zu wenig Verantwortungsattribution für die erste Entstehung der Depression, jedoch zu mehr Verantwortungsattribution für das Abklingen und rezidivierende Depressionen. Die jeweiligen zugeschriebenen Ursachenanteile von Genen, der Umwelt und deren Interaktion variierten.
Unseren Ergebnissen zufolge attribuieren Kliniker*innen bei rezidivierenden depressiven Episoden mehr Verantwortung bei Betroffenen, was zu einer verstärkten Stigmatisierung dieser Betroffenen führen könnte. Anti-Stigmatisierungskampagnen für Psychiater*innen könnten sich daher vermehrt auf die Entstigmatisierung rezidivierender Depressionen durch Informationen darüber, warum Depressionen trotz Behandlung bestehen bleiben, fokussieren.

Hype vs Hope: Evaluating the Promise of Network-Informed Interventions for Psychopathology
Dr. René Freichel | University of Amsterdam | Netherlands
Show details
Authors:
Dr. René Freichel | University of Amsterdam | Netherlands
Prof. Dr. Claudi Bockting | University of Amsterdam | Netherlands

According to network theory, mental disorders arise from dynamic interactions between symptoms rather than from a single underlying disease entity. Identifying highly interconnected nodes or clinically relevant edges within a patient’s symptom network may offer actionable treatment targets. In recent years, network models have moved beyond descriptive analyses toward applied, personalized treatment approaches.

In this talk, I discuss recent empirical developments to evaluate whether network-informed interventions represent genuine clinical innovation or premature enthusiasm. Drawing on completed and ongoing studies for eating disorders and depression/anxiety, I discuss several network-informed intervention studies, in which participants completed intensive ecological momentary assessment and received personalized treatment modules targeting their most central symptoms. I present preliminary findings and address key conceptual, methodological, and pragmatic challenges, including questions about causal interpretation, added value beyond established treatments, scalability, and clinical implementation.

The clinical neuroscience of lateralization – An update
Prof. Dr. Sebastian Ocklenburg | MSH Medical School Hamburg | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Sebastian Ocklenburg | MSH Medical School Hamburg | Germany

Functional and structural brain asymmetries are fundamental principles of brain organization, and a large body of research suggests a higher prevalence of atypical hemispheric asymmetries in various groups of patients with mental and developmental disorders. In this talk, I will give an overview about several recent theoretical developments, empirical studies and meta-analyses that focused on hemispheric asymmetries in clinical groups. In general, atypical asymmetries are more prevalent in patients with mental and developmental disorders compared to healthy controls. However, case-control differences vary substantially with diagnosis. Some diagnoses, like schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorders and dyslexia are associated with a higher prevalence of atypical asymmetries than other diagnoses. Specifically, the data suggest that neurodevelopmental conditions, nonneurodevelopmental conditions with an early age of onset, and conditions that include symptoms related to language were all associated with higher rates of atypical functional asymmetries. These finding suggests that the association between atypical asymmetries and clinical conditions is best understood from a transdiagnostic, developmental, and symptom-focused perspective.

Emotional and Behavior Problems in Children and Adolescents with Chronic Physical Health Conditions: An Updated Meta-Analysis
Prof. Martin Pinquart | Philipps Universität Marburg | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Martin Pinquart | Philipps Universität Marburg | Germany

About 15% of children and adolescents have chronic physical health conditions. These conditions are risk factors for emotional and behavioral problems. Monitoring the prevalence of these problems and identifying related risk factors is important for understanding the psychosocial consequences of chronic physical conditions and identifying groups with the highest need to be screened, as well as the main targets for prevention and intervention.
The present study updated a meta-analysis on emotional and behavioral problems among children with chronic physical health conditions as assessed with the Achenbach System of Empirically Based Assessment. A systematic search in electronic databases (PsycInfo, Medline, Web of Science, and PSYNDEX) identified 1337 studies that were analyzed with multilevel meta-analysis.
Young people with chronic physical health conditions had, on average, higher levels of internalizing (g=.51 standard mean difference), externalizing (g=.25), and total behavior problems (g=.49) than peers without such conditions or test norms. Elevations of total problems were larger than in a previous meta-analysis. Effect sizes were larger when parent reports were used rather than adolescent self-reports. Largest elevations of internalizing problems were found for chronic fatigue syndrome, while largest elevations of total and externalizing problems were observed in the case of thalassemia. Effect sizes also varied by country and, in part, by duration of the chronic health condition, sampling, target of comparison, equivalence of the compared groups, response rate, age, and gender. The present results call for regular screening for psychological distress in children with chronic physical health conditions.

Dr. Sonja Hahn | DIPF | Germany

In psychological research, artificial intelligence (AI) has been applied to a wide range of tasks, e.g., to evaluate answers to open ended items. These approaches rely largely on deep neural networks that come along with several methodological constraints, e.g. the lack of transparency and the amount of data necessary for training, while available information (e.g., from theory or empirical findings) does not enter the models. A current development addressing these and further issues are neuro-symbolic (also neuro-explicit or hybrid) approaches. They handle a part of the information in neural networks in a more accessible and direct manner, for example by using neural networks and other approaches (e.g., expert systems, statistical data mining approaches) in a temporal order or by restricting features of the neural network.
The present contribution first gives an overview of different frameworks for neuro-symbolic approaches. I illustrate these approaches in an example for evaluating learners’ free hand drawings with different AI approaches (N=95, weighted F1=.021-.984), focusing on 1) how information from a rating rubric can be incorporated into the AI evaluation, and 2) how the frameworks can be applied to gain a deeper methodological understanding of the respective approaches (e.g., explain low performance of specific approaches). The last part shows where neuro-symbolic AI was or might be applied in psychological fields and discusses the relevance of this stance for selection and construction of the AI architectures as well as limitations and future directions in terms of substantive and methodological research.

The development of strong artificial intelligence (AI) is gaining momentum, and questions arise about how it will evolve after it becomes superintelligent. At this level of intelligence, direct oversight and control of actions and consequences is impossible. Hence, the question arises of which values such systems should be aligned with to help control itself. This question is different - and much more complex - than with present large language models, whose benevolent interaction styles result from supervised training and oversight, both of which become insufficient once AI surpasses human-level intelligence.
I will show that even simple (unconscious) developer decisions incorporate hidden preferences into AI, potentially biasing it towards certain values. I present an exemplary study (N = 766) that shows how developers’ environmental motivation affects the training of AI email spam filters, potentially impacting the sorting of billions of emails such as petitions as spam or not.
On a more general level, I present the relationship between personality traits (i.e., HEXACO), and attitudes towards AI in three studies (N = 138, N = 176, N = 1,571). Consistently across all studies, the strongest relation emerged between Honesty-Humility and a positive attitude towards AI (β = -0.36, β = -0.20, β = -0.28), suggesting that individuals lower on Honesty-Humility are more inclined to view AI favorably and may adjust it to their values.
Based on this evidence, I will discuss which personality strong AI could have and how to potentially support developers on AI alignment and control from a psychological perspective.

Psychische Gesundheit, sichere Arbeitsbedingungen und nachhaltige Leistungsfähigkeit von Organisationen gehören zu den zentralen Herausforderungen moderner Arbeitswelten. Zugleich gerät der Arbeitsschutz derzeit politisch und medial unter Druck: Unter dem Leitmotiv der Entbürokratisierung werden zentrale Schutzstandards infrage gestellt, während die Lockerung arbeitszeitrechtlicher Regelungen öffentlich diskutiert wird. Diese Entwicklung trifft auf eine Praxis, in der gesetzliche Anforderungen bereits heute häufig unzureichend umgesetzt werden. So zeigt die Betriebs- und Beschäftigtenbefragung der Gemeinsamen Deutschen Arbeitsschutzstrategie, dass nur 44 Prozent der Unternehmen eine Gefährdungsbeurteilung psychischer Belastung durchführen. Parallel steigen psychisch bedingte Fehlzeiten seit Jahren an.
Vor diesem Hintergrund fragt das Panel, wie psychologische Expertise im Arbeits- und Gesundheitsschutz wirksamer, sichtbarer und politisch durchsetzungsfähiger werden kann. Im Mittelpunkt steht die neue strukturierte Kooperation von BDP, DGPs und PASiG. Erstmals sollen berufspolitische Vertretung, wissenschaftliche Exzellenz und spezialisierte Fachkompetenz im Feld der Arbeits- und Organisationspsychologie systematisch gebündelt werden. Ziel ist es, Ressourcen und Netzwerke zusammenzuführen, gemeinsame Positionen zu entwickeln und Qualitäts- sowie Qualifizierungsstandards weiter auszubauen.
Das Panel diskutiert diese Kooperation als Antwort auf eine doppelte Herausforderung: auf wachsende psychische Belastungen in der Arbeitswelt und auf die Notwendigkeit, psychologische Fachlichkeit im Arbeitsschutz endlich mit größerer Geschlossenheit zu vertreten. Damit rückt nicht nur die Profession, sondern auch ihre gesellschaftliche Verantwortung in den Fokus.

Room: Workshop 0
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Fachgruppensymposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

The goal of this symposium is to provide a forum to discuss research and theoretical perspectives on two intertwined societal challenges - the digital transformation of society and the erosion of democratic principles such as separation of powers, political equality, and minority rights. Contributors address these challenges from various, complementary angles. We start by discussing the societal consequences of artificial intelligence and derive some first implications and recommendations from a social psychological perspective (Glöckner et al.). Zooming in on communicative styles of political actors in offline and online contexts, we consider the question what makes radical right digital communication so effective (Rothmund et al.). In the next talk, we address the role of media consumption for increasing polarization across the political spectrum (Walther & Sassenberg). We move on to an in-depth study of political discussion on Reddit, which demonstrates the viability of lab-in-the-field experiments for reducing participation inequality (Oswald et al.). Toward the end of the symposium, we consider the possibility that digital transformation requires treating concepts such as “attitudes” not as variables but as “ant-trails” (Quayle). We close by returning to the policy level and discussing the implications of four “pressure points” between technology and cognition, especially algorithmic content curation, for possible future policy frameworks (Lewandowsky).

Digital media have become increasingly influential in political communication. Populist radical right actors and parties are particularly successful not only in reaching large audiences online, but also in shaping political agendas in the digital sphere and radicalizing segments of the public in liberal democracies. Yet it remains unclear what accounts for this success.
We tested the claim that the success of radical right digital communication is driven less by argumentative content than by communicative style and introduce the concept of experience-based social imagining as a distinctive stylistic feature of political communication. This style (a) resonates with recipients’ sensory and affective experiences and (b) relies on social imaginations rather than rational arguments.
Empirically, we analyzed a large text corpora of parliamentary speeches from multiple European countries and social media posts by the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in Germany. Using Large Language Models (LLMs) as automated coders, we examined systematic differences in rhetorical style across the political spectrum. Our findings indicate that representatives of radical parties—on both the right and the left—are significantly more likely to employ System-1-oriented rhetoric style and less likely to use System-2-oriented rhetoric style in parliamentary speeches compared to politicians from centrist parties. We further outline how these differences in rhetorical style manifest as experience-based social imagining and distinguish between several prototypical expressions.
The presentation concludes by discussing the theoretical implications for understanding experience-based social imagining in contemporary political communication, as well as the methodological potential of LLM-based approaches for studying the digital transformation of public opinion formation in liberal democracies.

Polycrises, Polarization and the Media
Prof. Dr. Eva Walther | Germany
Show details

Prof. Dr. Eva Walther | Germany

After decades of relative stability in many Western democracies, societies are currently facing a period of profound upheaval driven by overlapping global crises. This condition is often described as a polycrisis, defined by the simultaneous and mutually reinforcing occurrence of multiple crises that strain political systems, social cohesion, and scientific institutions alike. Governments face increasing pressure to secure a livable future while competing with anti-democratic actors offering simplistic solutions to complex problems. Because policy responses to one crisis often intensify others, political action is frequently perceived as insufficient or ineffective. Whether and how agency is perceived, however, depends largely on the political orientation of citizens and their needs. Policy measures such as stricter migration controls may be experienced by some as necessary state action that enhances security, while others perceive them as violations of human rights and symptoms of authoritarian drift. This divergence contributes to rising political polarization, complicating majority-building, particularly in the political center, and threatening democratic processes. Media play a pivotal role in shaping these perceptions, as many crises are experienced primarily through mediated communication. At the same time, traditional media are undergoing structural transformations due to shifting information practices and competition from social media platforms. Using data from a representative German survey (N = 1,062), we examined the relationship between crisis perception, media consumption, openness to new technologies, and political orientation. The findings indicate that political orientation and media use do not shape the intensity of crisis perception, but rather which specific crises are perceived as most threatening. These findings underscore the importance of the media in the perception of polycrisis-like conditions and their impact on democratic resilience.

Digital technology has fundamentally transformed social interaction, including political communication. This visibility gap can distort perceptions of public opinion and fuel polarization. We tested whether participation inequality can be reduced with norm- or incentive-based interventions. We recruited 520 U.S. participants, randomly assigned them to conditions in six private communities, and asked them to discuss 20 political issues over four weeks while completing weekly surveys. Lurking (posting nothing) was most common among users who perceived discussions as toxic, disrespectful, or unconstructive. However, these same perceptions also predicted power-usership (more posting, conditional on not lurking). Experimentally, financial incentives for commenting reduced participation differentials whereas we did not find effects from a civility norm treatment.

Ant-trails and attitudes: how digital technologies rewire human stigmergy
Prof. Dr. Michael Quayle | Ireland
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Michael Quayle | Ireland

In evolutionary history, cognition emerged before neurons. Simple organisms can operate as a collective by offloading memory to their environment and performing computation by writing and reading information traces. In this way, they can collectively search and exploit their environment, allowing the collective to process and exploit information far surpassing individuals’ cognitive and physical limitations. This is stigmergy: an efficient social mechanism for collective information processing and coordination over physical and temporal distances with no top-down control, no agent needing more than local knowledge—and even without direct social interaction. Using ant-trails as an example, I show how stigmergy produces compressed representations of information in the environment. Stigmergy operates similarly in human societies, where our physical and symbolic environment operates as a loosely coupled distributed social information system in which traces of group identity are written and read (and where new technologies introduce new trail-making abilities). The ability to decode useful social information from this system depends on it being compressible in group terms, in much the same way that a useful ant trail requires concentration of pheremones. To the extent that it is compressible, the social information system allows people to 'read' group identity from minimal information, and redundancies facilitate recognition even where communication is noisy or lossy. I discuss how digital communication systems, especially online social media, have rewired human stigmergy by providing new mechanisms for making, discovering and reading traces, and exploiting stigmergic signals for (usually profit-motivated) algorithms that impose themselves on the stigmergic process. I discuss how concepts such as "attitudes" should be conceptualized in these terms as supra-individual distributed information systems more like ant-trails than variables.

Prof. Dr. Stephan Lewandowsky | United Kingdom

Author:
Prof. Dr. Stephan Lewandowsky | United Kingdom

We live in an era of democratic backsliding and autocratization. Online technologies and social media have frequently been implicated in causing these concerning trends, but the relevant evidence appears fragmented and heterogeneous at first glance. To resolve the heterogeneity, I approach the problem through the lens of four pressure points between human cognition and online technologies that have potentially adverse consequences for democracy: the attention economy, choice architectures, algorithmic content curation, and dis- and misinformation. For illustration, I then focus on algorithmic content curation, and in particular the implications of “microtargeting” and what countermeasures might exist. I discuss the implications within existing and possible future policy frameworks.

Artificial Intelligence and Children – mapping the digital transformation with multiple methods
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Louisa Kulke (University of Bremen)
Room: Workshop +1
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Fachgruppensymposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Artificial intelligence (AI) has quickly become omnipresent in everyday life within the last years. Children encounter robots at restaurants and supermarkets, ask Alexa about the weather and use chatbots to finish their homework. But how do they perceive interactions with AI and how can their guardians support them through the digital transformation when navigating an environment full of AI? The current symposium brings together findings from multiple methods to map how children navigate AI environments, combining quantitative and qualitative methods, questionnaires, eye-tracking, human-robot interaction and physiological markers. Qualitative surveys indicate that parents are trying to guide their children through using AI while not being experts on AI themselves (Sahura Ertugrul). Qualitative research shows that providing teaching resources to inform children and parents about AI can help to navigate the novel world of AI (Ira Diethelm). Understanding AI also opens up new possibilities to profit from its benefits, for example, by using educational resources such as AI-based tutoring software (Larbi Abdenebaoui). But how do children perceive AI? Human-robot interaction studies using eye-tracking and physiological measures show how children respond to robots as social agents (Niloofar Goharbakhsh) and how robots are perceived more similarly to children than to adults (Louisa Kulke). In a world of digital transformation with rapidly developing AI systems, the current symposium provides a basis to map interactions of children with AI and contrasts the caveats and the benefits of AI use in children.

Teaching about AI principles from primary school is crucial to foster digital literacy, critical thinking, and understanding of AI's societal impact. It empowers children to actively shape technology and the future world. Therefore, suitable teaching materials are essential to enable teachers of all subjects to teach about AI concepts and not only to use AI tools. In this session, we will present exemplary parts of the German IT2School material set and its conception that is used by approximately 1000 schools to date.

IT2School is an educational project developed and curated by the University of Oldenburg and OFFIS, offering comprehensive materials to help teachers with selection and preparation for over 10 years. It provides free CC-licensed resources for grades 4–10, covering topics like digitalization, automation, and networking and also many aspects of artificial intelligence and different types of machine learning. The materials include lesson plans, worksheets, and sample solutions, with some modules functioning "unplugged" (without technology), e.g., a paper-based roleplay to understand how digital home assistants like Alexa or Siri are able to answer questions or execute commands. It aims to help students understand how IT and AI systems in general work, create their own AI-based applications, experience their power and limitations and enable them to judge on a solid basis on AI's impact on daily life.

The increasing use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in educational contexts raises critical questions about how such systems can support children’s learning while respecting pedagogical values, agency, and well-being. EduMind addresses these challenges by developing a value-driven, human-centred AI tutoring module designed as an extension for existing digital learning platforms used by children and adolescents.

EduMind combines generative AI with didactic expertise from teachers to create personalized, everyday-relevant learning experiences. Learning content is contextualized using children’s interests (e.g., sports, music, daily situations) and presented through pedagogical strategies such as storytelling or Socratic dialogue, following the Anchored Instruction principle. Rather than fully automating teaching, EduMind positions teachers as key actors who curate content, define instructional styles, and guide AI behavior.

From a value-driven AI perspective, EduMind follows a systematic design pipeline that spans from early value elicitation to technical implementation. Core values are first identified through workshops and interviews with key stakeholders, including children, teachers, and parents. These values are then translated into value-based quality requirements that guide interaction design, data handling, and system behavior. In the resulting implementation, children’s autonomy is supported through transparent interactions and age-appropriate explanations; data minimization and privacy by design principles reduce risks associated with profiling minors; and inclusivity is fostered by adapting language complexity and examples to diverse learning backgrounds. A community-based approach allows teachers to share materials and experiences, ensuring that the system evolves in alignment with educational practice rather than purely data-driven optimization.

Ostracism, being excluded from social interaction, is a common experience across the lifespan (Williams et al., 2013). As the prevalence of robots in social situations has been increasing among children (Xu & Ouyang, 2025), it is a necessity to understand how children perceive ostracism in interaction with robots.

Children show more prosocial behaviours to fortify the ostracized person’s threatened needs (Correia et al., 2024). However, there is no study to investigate how children respond to the ostracized robot compared to the ostracized human. Findings suggest that children behave differently toward robots with different levels of anthropomorphism; children share their costly resources with the affective robot compared to the robot without affective state (Nijssen et al., 2021). Yet theoretical accounts of anthropomorphism also suggest a dual-process model: people reflexively respond to robots as if they were social beings, but at a reflective stage may discount them as “not truly human” (Złotowski et al., 2018). Therefore, it is unknown whether children make this distinction or respond to robots consistently as social partners during ostracism.

This study aimed to compare responses towards low anthropomorphic robots, high anthropomorphic robots, and humans in three stages: reflexive, reflective (resource-allocation task), and self-report during and after ostracism. Eye movements and pupil dilation as a physiological marker of arousal and behaviour are compared between agents varying in anthropomorphism. This study clarifies to what extent children apply prosocial responses to robots, thereby addressing fundamental questions of anthropomorphism and informing the design of child-robot interaction during ostracism.

Show details
Authors:

In social contexts, implicit rules are in place. People avoid staring at strangers in a waiting room context, yet they readily look at videos of strangers. However, it is unclear whether and how social rules are applied to artificial intelligences and robots. The current set of studies investigated social inhibition of gaze towards robots compared to humans.

In Study 1, social gaze towards an android robot compared to a human was measured using mobile eye-tracking. N = 49 participants were asked to sit in a waiting room, where they either saw a human sitting in the room, an android sitting in the room or a video of an android. Participants looked significantly more at the android robot than at the human, suggesting that they inhibit their gaze towards humans but not robots.

Study 2 aimed to investigate whether adults’ gaze behaviour towards robots is comparable to interactions with human children. Seventy-two adults were seated in a waiting room where either a toddler, a toddler-sized robot (Nao) or an adult was present live or as a video. Mobile eye-tracking showed that adults looked significantly less at the live adult than at the video. However, they looked more at the live toddler and live robot than the live adult and interacted with the toddler significantly more frequently than with the adult.

In summary, humans follow different social rules when interacting with humans, compared to robots, and they seem to act towards robots comparably as they would to human children.

Envisioning the future is crucial for motivating climate protection, yet psychological mechanisms linking future thinking to climate action remain unclear. Drawing on Query Theory, two online experiments examined how the content, valence, and structure of future-related thoughts shape future vision and readiness to act against climate change, operationalized as climate policy acceptance and political participation intention.

In Study 1 (N = 1,049), participants either listed future thoughts freely (nondirected), began with positive thoughts, began with negative thoughts, or received no thought-listing instruction (control). Participants in the nondirected condition reported a more negative future vision than the other groups. At the same time, they showed higher climate policy acceptance than the control group, as did participants in the positive-first condition. Political participation intentions were not affected. Exploratory analyses revealed that most thoughts were climate-related; participants generated more negative than positive thoughts and tended to list negative thoughts earlier.

Study 2 (N = 517) compared nondirected future thinking with a control group. Overall, no group differences emerged for future vision or climate action. However, participants who naturally began with positive thoughts envisioned the future more positively. A higher proportion of positive thoughts was positively associated with all outcome variables. Thought order showed a curvilinear relationship with policy acceptance and participation: participants listing either positive or negative thoughts first displayed greater readiness for action than those with randomly dispersed thoughts.
Overall, findings provide partial support for Query Theory and suggest that structured future thinking may influence climate action. Underlying mechanisms require further investigation.

Sufficient consumer decisions involve avoiding new purchases and support the sustainable use of existing consumer goods. Thereby, they contribute to reducing the environmental impacts associated with the production of new consumer goods. Reflection in Consumption (RIC) captures considerations of the necessity of new consumer goods (“Do I need this?”) and personal consumption desires (“Why do I want this?”). It also includes strategies to avoid new purchases (“Do I already own something similar?”). Thus, RIC can play a crucial role in sufficient consumer decisions. To date, however, no validated scale has been available to measure RIC. In the present study, a scale for the assessment of RIC was therefore developed based on a qualitative study and two quantitative studies. The factor structure was examined in two independent samples using exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis. Initial validation results revealed a positive association between RIC and sufficient consumer decisions, as well as a negative association with consumer expenditure. The current findings suggest high reliability and validity of the scale. A short version was developed to enable the efficient application of the RIC scale. The RIC scale contributes to sufficiency research by enabling a deeper understanding of the processes underlying sufficient consumer decisions. Moreover, it provides a starting point for future interventions fostering sufficient consumer decisions. The RIC scale is a promising instrument for environmental education, environmental communication, and health psychology.

Explaining behavioral plasticity of circular consumer practices
Marie Brüggemann | Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Marie Brüggemann | Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg | Germany
Karolin Schmidt | Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg

Changes in consumer practices are essential for the transition towards a circular economy. Beyond theoretical CO₂ savings, the impact of interventions depends on the proportion of people who change their behavior—the behavioral plasticity. People engage in a circular consumer practice (CCP) when they are sufficiently motivated to overcome the barriers of the behavior (i.e., the behavioral costs; e.g. money, effort). Change occurs when costs are reduced—allowing more individuals to meet the required motivational threshold—or when motivation increases sufficiently to offset existing costs. Behavioral plasticity thus describes how many people hold a motivation higher than the costs of engaging in a specific CCP following an intervention. In an online study with a representative sample of German consumers (N=984), participants reported their current engagement in 72 CCPs and their willingness to adopt them if financial costs and convenience matched conventional alternatives, i.e., if behavioral costs were reduced. A Rasch model was calibrated to estimate behavioral costs under current and altered conditions, as well as the sample’s motivation. Results showed that behavioral plasticity depends not only on the absolute reduction in costs but also on the proportion of individuals whose motivation was insufficient under current conditions yet sufficient under reduced costs. Plasticity was highest for behaviors with current costs slightly above the sample’s mean motivation. Considering behavioral costs alongside a target group’s motivational level provides a parsimonious strategy for identifying promising intervention targets: behaviors for which modest cost reductions enable a substantial number of people to cross the motivational threshold.

Basierend auf den Theorien zu place attachement und der sozialen Identität erwarten wir, dass der so entwickelte Bürgerentwurf als passender zur Region und Heimat empfunden wird. Prozess und Ergebnisse wurden auf einer öffentlichen Bürgerveranstaltung präsentiert und im Anschluss in einer telefonischen Bürger-Befragung evaluiert (N = 110). Die Idee, eine unabhängige Bürgergruppe in die EE Planungen einzubeziehen, wurde begrüßt, der Gruppe ein ähnlich hohes Vertrauen wie der Kommunalvertretung entgegengebracht. Zudem zeigen die Ergebnisse, dass der Bürgerentwurf, verglichen mit einem Expertenentwurf nach konventionellen Planungsregeln, bevorzugt wird. Wie erwartet wurde er als passender zur Region (M = 2.38 vs. M = 1.33, Skala 0-4), als positiver für die Heimat (M = 0.71 vs. M = 0.20, Skala –3 bis +3) und den Strukturwandel (M = 1.39 vs. M = 0.84) eingeschätzt. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass der stärkere Einbezug von Bürger:innen und deren lokaler Erfahrungen lokale Veränderungen positiv gestalten können.

The Widening Gap of Selective Digitalization: Trends in Technology Adoption and Work Design (2019–2025)
Prof. Dr. Christian Härtwig | FOM Hochschule für Oekonomie & Management | FOM University of Applied Sciences for Economics & Management | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Christian Härtwig | FOM Hochschule für Oekonomie & Management | FOM University of Applied Sciences for Economics & Management | Germany

Digitalization is a central driver of organizational change, reshaping work conditions across all industries. This study presents core findings from the “Monitor Digitization”, a large-scale longitudinal trend study (N > 30,000 participants from >1,500 firms) conducted across German industrial sectors in three waves (2019, 2022, 2025). Covering pre- and post-Covid eras and the recent rise of AI, we analyze developments over time regarding work design, health, and well-being, focusing on distinct group differences between sectors and activity fields.
Results reveal a phenomenon of "selective digitalization": While classical ICT usage has saturated, AI adoption remains low overall and is highly stratified. A significant divide exists between white-collar domains (e.g., IT, R&D), where AI is increasingly integrated, and blue-collar domains (e.g., Production, Logistics), which remain largely disconnected. Contrasting the current "technology hype," perceived support from digital tools has stagnated or declined since 2022. Crucially, most employees report no productivity gains. While quantitative strain decreased and qualitative strain rose slightly, self-rated digital competence in 2025 was perceived as less adequate than in 2022, suggesting technological complexity is outpacing skill development.
Furthermore, the gap in organizational support is widening. White-collar workers report higher autonomy and participation, whereas production workers feel increasingly detached. With continuing professional development and supportive leadership remaining low, findings suggest the digital transformation is solidifying a two-tier workforce, necessitating targeted interventions to bridge the gap between occupational groups. Finally, we discuss implications for organizations and derive specific support strategies based on the Systemic Work Coping Model (SAB Model).

Casper Haak | Catholic University Eichstätt-Ingolstadt | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Casper Haak | Catholic University Eichstätt-Ingolstadt | Germany
Dr. Patricia Zieris | Catholic University Eichstätt-Ingolstadt
Prof. Dr. Elisabeth Kals | Catholic University Eichstätt-Ingolstadt

Rising burnout rates necessitate new approaches in organizational and health psychology research to analyze the work stress of employees. This study supplements classic models of work stress – specifically, the job demand–control model and the effort–reward imbalance model – with four dimensions of justice (distributive, procedural, interpersonal, and informational justice) to further explain emotional exhaustion, the core characteristic of burnout.
The data set consisted of a cross-sectional survey of employees in Germany (N = 942). The results of the hierarchical regression analyses show that the classic workplace stress models already explained a substantial portion of emotional exhaustion, and adding the dimensions of justice further increased explained variance (ΔR2 = .05, final model R2 = .45). Specifically, only interpersonal justice – reflecting respectful and dignified treatment by supervisors and colleagues – contributed significantly. Building on this, moderation analyses revealed a significant interaction: initiated interdependence (others depend on the participant’s work) influenced the relationship between interpersonal justice and emotional exhaustion (interaction ΔR2 = .003). Specifically, high levels of interpersonal justice are particularly protective, whereas low levels are especially detrimental when others depend on the participant’s work.
This study contributes to clarifying the relevance of organizational justice in the investigation of work structures and burnout. The results suggest that, beyond a balanced relationship between demands and rewards, respectful treatment in the workplace is essential for employee health, especially when they are mutually dependent on each other's work.

Views on spatial skills affect confidence and math anxiety in pre-service early educators
Dr. Jonas Schäfer | University of Education Schwäbisch Gmünd | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Jonas Schäfer | University of Education Schwäbisch Gmünd | Germany

Spatial skills are cognitive abilities involved in understanding and reasoning about relations among objects and scenes. They are closely associated with STEM abilities in early childhood, making educational support indispensable. However, several early educators neglect that spatial skills are trainable (static views), while others view spatial skills as improvable (incremental views). Holding incremental views might positively affect self-perception, confidence, and performance in spatial tasks, while acting as a protective factor against math anxiety. Despite the documented link between mindset and teaching behavior in early educators, few is known about the effects of their views on spatial skills.
We tested 76 pre-service educational practitioners (Mage=22.74 years, SD=4.58; 97% female) by assessing their views on spatial skills, self-perceived spatial skills, and math anxiety. Moreover, participants solved spatial tasks (objective spatial performance) and indicated their confidence and trainability beliefs in these tasks.
Regression analyses revealed that incremental views significantly predicted confidence (β=.27*), trainability beliefs (β=.33**), and lower math anxiety (β=–.25*), but neither self-perceived spatial skills nor objective spatial performance.
Findings suggest that the impact of views on spatial skills is multifaceted: educators with incremental views believe that they could train their spatial performance and are more confident when solving spatial tasks, even though their objective spatial performance resembles that of educators with static views. The finding that incremental views on spatial skills were related to lower math anxiety emphasizes the central role of spatial cognition for math. Our study highlights the importance of considering an educator’s mindset when it comes to spatial cognition.

AI Empowers and Exhausts: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on the Double-Edged Role of AI at Work
Marie-Claire Joyeaux | EBS Universität für Wirtschaft & Recht | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Marie-Claire Joyeaux | EBS Universität für Wirtschaft & Recht | Germany
Prof. Dr. Myriam N. Bechtoldt | EBS Universität für Wirtschaft & Recht

This meta-analysis examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) at work by integrating emerging evidence within the Job Demands-Resources framework to explain whether, to what extent, and under which circumstances AI implementation and usage can simultaneously generate strain-inducing demands, resource-enhancing opportunities, and corresponding negative or positive employee outcomes. Across 118 studies with a total sample size of 127,811 participants, Meta-Analytic Structural Equation Modelling shows AI implementation and usage to be significantly correlated with increased job demands and more negative employee outcomes such as stress, anxiety, or burnout. Simultaneously, AI demonstrates a significant and even stronger positive correlation with job resources, prompting more positive employee outcomes including engagement, well-being, and job satisfaction. An additional review-based typology highlights the health-impairment pathway to be particularly pronounced when employees engage with monitoring-intensive and responsibility-heavy AI systems. By contrast, AI systems relying on active employee expertise and judgement are less likely to be experienced as demand-escalating technologies. Further subgroup analyses reveal these effects to be significantly different by employee age and industry type, and different gender patterns suggest men and women to subjectively emphasise different aspects of AI-related work experiences. By applying the Job Demands-Resources model, this study underscores AI’s dual capacity as both a job demand and resource, highlighting the multifaceted way in which employees experience and interact with AI in the workplace. These findings suggest that organisations should consider the specific types of AI employed, as well as gender inclusivity, age, and industry-specific contexts, to maximise AI’s potential benefits while managing stress-related risks.

Technostress and Work Ability During Digital Transformation: The Role of Inclusive Leadership in Demographic Change
Prof. Dr. Daniel Thiemann | TH Köln (Cologne University of Applied Sciences) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Daniel Thiemann | TH Köln (Cologne University of Applied Sciences) | Germany
Prof. Dr. Irmgard Mausz | International School of Management ISM | Germany

Insufficient adaptation to technological demands can trigger technostress, which is linked to emotional exhaustion (Tarafdar et al., 2019). Employees differ in their ability to adapt to digital technologies. Under demographic change, this heterogeneity matters because sustaining work ability central to sustainable working lives (Giesert et al., 2017). Early evidence indicates that leadership styles influence technostress (Thiemann, 2022); inclusive leadership may therefore help manage diverse adaptation capacities.
We conducted two two-wave online surveys among employed adults in Germany (Study 1: N_T1=196, N_T2=118; Study 2: N_T1=726, N_T2=320). Study 1 examined technostress, emotional exhaustion, and overall work ability, and tested whether inclusive leadership buffers these relationships. Study 2 replicated and extended the model by adding cognitive work ability, job satisfaction, turnover intention, and disengagement as an alternative mechanism.
Preliminary results suggest that technostress at T1 predicts lower cognitive work ability and job satisfaction at T2 and higher turnover intention. Emotional exhaustion mediates these effects, whereas disengagement does not. Inclusive leadership is directly associated with lower technostress and higher cognitive work ability, but it does not moderate the indirect pathway via exhaustion, suggesting it operates more as a general resource than as a stress-buffer in this process.
Longer follow-up periods are needed to capture long-term effects of technological demands and to evaluate protective factors more robustly. The findings suggest prioritizing exhaustion-focused risk management alongside efforts to reduce technostress, while viewing inclusive leadership primarily as a direct resource rather than a buffering factor.

Random Effects Misspecification in Multilevel IRT Models: Implications for Estimations Using Plausible Values
Eva Zink | Leibniz Institut für Bildungsverläufe | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Eva Zink | Leibniz Institut für Bildungsverläufe | Germany
Dr. Timo Gnambs | Leibniz Institut für Bildungsverläufe

Multilevel item response theory (IRT) models are a standard analytic framework in large-scale assessments, as hierarchical data structures are induced by design (e.g., students nested within schools). In these models, random effects at higher aggregation levels are typically assumed to follow a normal distribution. This assumption is rarely questioned in applied research, despite systematic differences between institutions such as selective admission practices, tracked school systems, or uneven performance distributions.
The present study investigates the consequences of misspecifying the distribution of cluster-level random effects in multilevel IRT models for regression inference based on plausible values. Plausible values are widely used in secondary analyses while accounting for measurement error, yet they depend directly on the assumed structural model, including the specification of random effects.
Using a preregistered Bayesian simulation study, data are generated under realistic conditions while systematically varying the distributional shape of cluster-level random effects. Modeling strategies are compared, including a standard specification assuming normally distributed cluster effects, distribution-matched models assuming skewed or heavy-tailed cluster effects, and a cluster-specific fixed-effects approach commonly used in practice.
The evaluation focuses on parameters central to substantive research questions, such as regression coefficients and variance components capturing between-cluster differences. Performance is assessed in terms of estimation accuracy and precision across simulation conditions.
Overall, the study demonstrates that assumptions about normally distributed cluster-level effects are not merely technical defaults but can meaningfully shape conclusions about between-institution differences in psychological and educational research based on plausible values.

Benchmarking Psychological Longitudinal Forecasting: Neural Network Forecasters vs. Established RI-CLPM Approaches
Andre Nedderhoff | Helmut-Schmidt Universität Hamburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Andre Nedderhoff | Helmut-Schmidt Universität Hamburg | Germany
Prof. Steffen Zitzmann | Medical School Hamburg
Prof. Martin Hecht | Helmut-Schmidt Universität Hamburg

Longitudinal designs constitute a core methodological paradigm in psychological science. The proliferation of mobile and ambulatory assessment technologies has accelerated the adoption of (intensive) longitudinal protocols, thereby motivating renewed attention to the dynamics of intraindividual processes. Conventionally, such data have been interrogated with parametric time-series frameworks, such as the Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM) in discrete- or continuous-time formulations, to disentangle within-person temporal dependencies from stable between-person heterogeneity and to quantify lagged dependencies among constructs.

Concurrently, recent methodological advances in machine learning (ML) have introduced flexible, data-adaptive alternatives that are particularly attractive for prospective forecast. In the present work, we examine the forecasting utility of ML-based forecasters via a simulation study. We generated synthetic time series from a discrete-time data-generating mechanism, while systematically manipulating design and process characteristics, including the number of observed time points, forecast horizon, sample size, and the autocorrelation.

We benchmarked two canonical dynamic specifications, namely the discrete-time and continuous-time RI-CLPM, against neural forecasters (LSTM and Transformer). Univariate forecasting accuracy was assessed via bias and root-mean-square error (RMSE). Across simulation conditions, both RI-CLPM variants and the LSTM yielded the lowest RMSE, whereas the Transformer and a pretrained Transformer (TimeGPT) exhibited the highest RMSE. These findings indicate that RI-CLPM dynamics and the LSTM provide superior forecast performance for intraindividual univariate processes compared to a Transformer and a pretrained Transformer (TimeGPT), which are therefore preferred for applied forecasting.

Real-time cognitive-affective dynamics of failure feedback in a technology-based learning task
Helene Ackermann | Universität Potsdam | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Helene Ackermann | Universität Potsdam | Germany
Anna L. Lange | Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin
Prof. Dr. Verena V. Hafner | Humbold-Universität zu Berlin
Prof. Dr. Hanna Dumont | Universität Potsdam
Prof. Dr. Rebecca Lazarides | Universität Potsdam

As technology-based learning environments increasingly rely on automated feedback, understanding how learners process feedback in real time is essential. This study examined how cognitive and metacognitive failure feedback delivered by a humanoid robot affected performance and how effects were moderated by feedback characteristics (frequency; content) and learner characteristics (on-task emotions; cognitive ability). Ninety adults (18-59 years, Mage = 29.53, 67.8% female) completed a learning task in one of three conditions: (1) fixed guidance condition with fixed-frequency, content-generic feedback, (2) basic-adaptive condition with content-generic feedback adapting frequency based on performance and on-task enjoyment, or (3) personalized-adaptive condition with frequency-adaptive and content-personalized feedback adjusting content to learners prior errors. A three-level generalized path model showed that cognitive and metacognitive failure feedback increased the likelihood of a correct subsequent response across conditions. Relative to the fixed-guidance condition, frequency-adaptive feedback (basic-adaptive condition) did not enhance this effect, whereas content-personalized feedback (personalized-adaptive condition) led to reduced immediate performance but improved overall performance compared to the basic-adaptive condition. Across conditions, learners with higher cognitive ability benefited less, while those reporting higher momentary on-task boredom benefited more from cognitive feedback. Findings highlight how situational cognitive-affective mechanisms can shape the effectiveness of automated feedback in technology-based learning.

Peer-, KI- und hybrides Feedback in der Lehramtsausbildung: Effekte auf evidenzorientiertes Problemlösen
Dr. Martin Greisel | Universität Augsburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Martin Greisel | Universität Augsburg | Germany
Alina Sheppard-Bujtor | Universität Augsburg | Germany
Julia Hornstein | Universität Augsburg | Germany
Ingo Kollar | Universität Augsburg | Germany

Lehramtsstudierende haben häufig Schwierigkeiten, problematische Unterrichtssituationen evidenzorientiert zu analysieren und zu lösen. Als Unterstützungsformen gelten sowohl Peer-Feedback, bei dem Studierende gegenseitig Rückmeldungen zu ihren Problemanalysen geben und diese überarbeiten, als auch KI-basiertes Feedback durch große Sprachmodelle. Letzteres birgt jedoch die Gefahr, dass lernwirksame Prozesse wie das aktive Geben von Feedback an die KI ausgelagert werden und damit an Effektivität verlieren. Vor diesem Hintergrund untersuchte die Studie, wie sich Peer-Feedback, KI-Feedback und unterschiedliche Mischformen (hybrides Feedback) auf Feedbackqualität, Feedbackwahrnehmung, Revisionsverhalten und den Erwerb evidenzorientierter Problemlösefertigkeiten auswirken.

N=275 fortgeschrittene Lehramtsstudierende analysierten theoriebasiert eine problematische Unterrichtssituation. Anschließend wurden sie zufällig einer von vier Bedingungen zugewiesen: reines Peer-Feedback, reines KI-Feedback, KI-Feedback-plus-Peer-Feedback oder KI-Feedback-auf-Peer-Feedback. Alle drei Peer-Feedback-Bedingungen entwarfen Peer-Feedback, aber nur die hybriden Bedingungen überarbeiteten dieses mithilfe von KI-generiertem Feedback entweder auf die ursprüngliche Problemanalyse oder auf das eigene Feedback. Danach erhielten alle Studierende das Feedback und überarbeiteten ihre ursprünglichen Problemlösungen. Erfasst wurden strukturelle Aspekte der Feedbackqualität (u.a. Länge, Lob, Kritik, Erklärungen, Verbesserungsvorschläge), die wahrgenommene Angemessenheit des Feedbacks, der Umfang und die Qualität der Revisionen sowie die evidenzorientierte Problemlösefertigkeiten in einem Posttest.

Vorläufige Ergebnisse zeigen, dass Studierende in den hybriden Bedingungen ihr Feedback deutlich stärker überarbeiteten als in der reinen Peer-Feedback-Bedingung, was sich in signifikant längeren Feedbacktexten und mehr Verbesserungsvorschlägen äußerte. Diese strukturellen Verbesserungen führten jedoch weder zu umfangreicheren Revisionen noch zu einer höheren wahrgenommenen Feedbackangemessenheit oder besseren evidenzorientierten Problemlösefertigkeiten im Posttest. Auffällig ist, dass reines KI-Feedback ähnlich angemessen wahrgenommen wurde und zu vergleichbaren Lernleistungen führte, was auf das Potenzial qualitativ hochwertigen KI-gestützten Feedbacks hinweist.

Asymmetric Confidence Intervals for Difference- and Ratio-Based Average Effects on Binary Outcomes
Kevin Hoppe | Bielefeld University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Kevin Hoppe | Bielefeld University | Germany
Dr. Christoph Kiefer | Bielefeld University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Axel Mayer | Bielefeld University

Average effects on binary outcomes can be defined as functions of average true outcomes. Kiefer, Lugauer, and Mayer (2024) propose difference- and ratio-based specifications of average effects which can be estimated from logistic regression models. Symmetric confidence intervals can be obtained using the Delta method. However, due to the local linearization of the effect function, these may violate true effect bounds, rendering them invalid. We present a simulation study that compares this approach with two methods of constructing asymmetric confidence intervals that can adhere to these natural effect limits: a) applying the Delta method to unbounded transformations of the point estimates, then transforming symmetric interval boundaries back onto the original effect scale, and b) using bootstrapping to estimate the distribution of point estimates. Results show that symmetric intervals often fail to adhere to natural effect bounds when dealing with large ratio-based average effects and large standard errors. Asymmetric intervals remain valid and improve statistical inference in these conditions.

Beyond Body Weight: The Role of Internalized Weight Bias in Sexual Functioning
Dr. Laura Pietras | University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Laura Pietras | University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf | Germany
Dr. Thula Koops | University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf | Germany
Dr. Arne Dekker | University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf | Germany
Prof. Dr. Peer Briken | University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf | Germany

Obesity has repeatedly been linked to impairments in sexual functioning. However, the mechanisms underlying these associations remain unclear. Beyond biomedical explanations, internalized weight bias (IWB)—the internalization of negative societal attitudes toward higher body weight—may represent a psychological pathway influencing the experience of sexual distress due to a sexual problem. This study examined whether body mass index (BMI) and internalized weight bias are independently associated with sexual distress due to a sexual problem across multiple domains of sexual dysfunction in women and men. A quota sample of German individuals (N = 9,725; 49.9% women, 50.1% men; ages 18–75 years) completed an online survey in October/November 2024. Quotas were set for gender, age, education and German federal states. BMI was calculated from self-reported height and weight. IWB was assessed using the WBIS-3. Sexual dysfunctions and associated distress (in the past 12 months) were operationalized according to ICD-11 criteria. Hierarchical regression models were conducted separately by gender and sexual problem, controlling for age, depressive symptoms (PHQ-2), and anxiety (GAD-2).
Across most sexual problems and both genders, IWB demonstrated significant incremental effects. beyond BMI and psychological covariates, explaining additional variance in distress across female desire, arousal, orgasmic, and pain-penetration problems, as well as male erectile and ejaculatory problems. Sexual distress due to a sexual problem appears to be more strongly associated with internalized weight bias than with BMI itself. These findings support a stigma-informed perspective on sexual health.

Do women respond differently to hormonal contraceptive use? Evidence from five large-scale analyses of sexuality and well-being across multiple dataset

Show details
Authors:

Chiara N. Draxler | University of Göttingen - Georg-August-Universität Göttingen
Nelly Schmidt | University of Göttingen - Georg-August-Universität Göttingen
Julie C. Driebe | University of Göttingen - Georg-August-Universität Göttingen
Tanja M. Gerlach | Leibniz Institute for Educational Trajectories (LIfBi)
Julia M. Rohrer | Leipzig University
Lars Penke | University of Göttingen - Georg-August-Universität Göttingen
Ruben C Arslan | University of Witten/Herdecke

Hormonal contraceptive use is common, yet women appear to differ substantially in their psychological and behavioral responses to it. This presentation focuses on whether and how women respond differently to hormonal contraceptive use in the domains of sexuality and well-being. Across five large-scale correlational analyses drawing on multiple datasets, we examined potential causal effects of hormonal contraceptive use, with a focus on individual differences in responses. (1) A cross-sectional study (N = 1,179) found positive effects of hormonal contraceptive use on sexual frequency and negative effects on masturbation frequency, even after controlling for confounders. (2) A longitudinal analysis (N = 5,041; 23,130 observations) demonstrated positive average effects on sexual frequency and high heterogeneity in individual effects. (3) A second longitudinal analysis based on the same dataset (N = 5,232; 24,306 observations) showed no average effects on well-being outcomes and low heterogeneity in individual effects. (4) A cross-sectional study (N = 1,299) found no robust effects on ideal partner personality traits once confounders were controlled for. (5) Finally, a longitudinal study (N = 1,993; 3,787 observations) showed that dissatisfaction with the contraceptive method—but not sexual satisfaction—predicted method switching. Together, these findings highlight the importance of taking individual differences into account when trying to understand how women respond to hormonal contraceptives. From a public health perspective, our results suggest that hormonal contraceptives are psychologically safe for most women, with important implications for mental health, while also underscoring the importance of monitoring and communicating individual variability in response.

“Masculine Sexual Entitlement“ (MSEN) is defined as “personal and collective attitudes, norms, and behaviors involving an exaggerated belief in masculine individuals’ right to or deservingness of sex and upholding or reinforcing patterns that contribute to these dynamics”. The present study translated the 25-item Masculine Sexual Entitlement Norms Scale (MSEN25) from English to German. Exploratory structural equation modeling (ESEM) was employed for the purpose of analyzing the underlying factor structure and obtaining fit indices. Internal consistency was assessed as well as convergent correlations with the Hostility Towards Women Scale (HTW), the Sexual Narcissism Scale (SNS), and the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory (CMNI). The Interpersonal Sexual Objectification Scale (ISOS-P) was used to assess predictive validity of the MSEN25 with regard to sexual coercive behavior. The German version exhibited a five-factor structure closely aligned with that of the original English version, supported by robust fit indices, but several factor loadings differed from the original version. The MSEN25 significantly added to the prediction of HTW beyond the SNS, and to the prediction of interpersonal sexual objectification. Additional studies regarding the association with rape proclivity and the developement of a second version for forensic research are being presented.

Hintergrund:
Auch im 21. Jahrhundert ist Sexualität im postsowjetischen Raum noch stark schambesetzt und daher weiterhin nur unzureichend erforscht, während im englisch- und deutschsprachigen Raum bereits eine umfangreiche Forschungsliteratur zu diesem Themenfeld vorliegt (z.B. Buzwell & Rosenthal, 1996; Deutsch et al., 2013). Im postsowjetischen Raum existieren bislang lediglich wenige Studien zum sexuellen Selbstkonzept, insbesondere bei Frauen. Die wenigen Untersuchungen konzentrieren sich überwiegend auf einzelne Teilaspekte wie den Beziehungsstatus oder sexuelle Funktionsstörungen. Ziel der vorliegenden Studie ist es daher, Aufschluss darüber zu erhalten, wie sich das sexuelle Selbstkonzept ukrainischer Frauen darstellt und welche Akzentuierungen es aufweist.
Methode:
Auf Grundlage einer qualitativen Präanalyse (n=6 Interviews) wurde ein Fragebogen entwickelt und dann online an eine Gelegenheitsstichprobe von n=194 ukrainische Frauen im Alter von 18 bis 44 Jahren vorgegeben. Zur Identifikation der zugrunde liegenden Dimensionen des sexuellen Selbstkonzeptes wurde eine explorative Faktorenanalyse durchgeführt und die jeweiligen Ausprägungen deskriptiv beschrieben. Zusätzlich erfolgte eine Clusteranalyse auf Basis der extrahierten Faktoren sowie ausgewählter soziodemographischer Variablen.
Ergebnisse:
Die Faktorenanalyse ergab 13 Dimensionen des sexuellen Selbstkonzepts, darunter u. a. Bedürfnisbefriedigung und Entspannung(α=.86), Selbststärkung durch sexuelle Aktivität(α=.50), emotionale Aspekte des Sexuallebens(α=.74), Kommunikation über Sexualität(α=.84), sowie Umsetzung eigener sexueller Bedürfnisse (α=.67). Die Clusteranalyse identifizierte vier homogene Gruppen mit unterschiedlichen Profilen sexueller Entwicklung und Selbstwahrnehmung. Diese unterschieden sich insbesondere hinsichtlich des Alters der ersten sexuellen Erfahrung(F(3;141)=6.43,p=.000,ῃ²=.12) und Masturbationsfrequenz (F(3;141)=7.07,p=.000,ῃ²=.13), der emotionalen Bedeutung von Sexualität(F(3;141)=29.80,p=.000,ῃ²=.39) sowie der Umsetzung eigener sexueller Bedürfnisse(F(3;141)=14.95,p=.00,ῃ²=.24).
Schlussfolgerung:
Die Ergebnisse unterstreichen die Multidimensionalität des sexuellen Selbstkonzepts ukrainischer Frauen und leisten einen wichtigen Beitrag zur kulturvergleichenden psychologischen Sexualforschung.

Mental Labor: Scale for measuring invisible household management.
Dr. Jan-Bennet Voltmer | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Jan-Bennet Voltmer | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany
Dr. Natalia Reich-Stiebert | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany

Mental labor in the household refers to the cognitive, managerial, other-directed, anticipatiory, and invisible processes required to keep everyday life running. Despite its relevance for understanding gendered inequalities in couple relationships, mental labor has so far been insufficiently operationalized psychometrically and is often conflated with physical household tasks. In a two-stage research program, we aimed to conceptualize mental labor as an independent, multidimensional construct. In an exploratory preliminary study, mental labor was initially assessed via responsibility for a wide range of household tasks. The results revealed pronounced gender differences, only moderate agreement between partners, and differential associations with fairness beliefs and relationship satisfaction. At the same time, this task-based approach exposed clear limitations in terms of instrument length and generalizability. Building on our previous literature review, our main study therefore focused on developing a theory-driven mental labor scale. Items were generated to capture five core dimensions of mental labor: cognition, management, anticipation, other-directedness, and invisibility. Two independent samples (n₁ = 396, n₂ = 361) completed an initial and a revised version of the scale. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a stable five-factor structure with good internal consistency. For validation, associations with mental load, prospective memory ability, agency/communion, personality traits, and relationship satisfaction were examined. The results showed theoretically consistent patterns of convergent and discriminant validity; moreover, mental labor predicted relationship satisfaction beyond physical household labor. Overall, findings support mental labor as a distinct construct and provide a parsimonious instrument for research on couple relationships, gender roles, and domestic inequality.
