Processes of personality development across different time scales
Chair(s) Junwen Gu (Heidelberg Univerity)
Prof. Dr. Cornelia Wrzus
Room: FI
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

During the last years, the focus of research on adult personality development shifted towards understanding individual differences and processes underlying long-term trajectories. Theoretically, these processes can range from moment-to-moment to long-term effects manifesting over years. Likely multiple processes operate simultaneously on different time scales. The current symposium demonstrates how such different processes contribute to personality development in adulthood.

Olaru et al. examined sudden changes in Emotional Stability over a few days during a personality intervention with a focus on strategies that facilitate sudden gains. Hungerbuehler et al. investigated how philanthropic behaviors contribute to changes in Big Five traits over multiple years. Braig et al. focused on how antagonistic traits develop over several years in romantic and parent-child relationships, demonstrating bidirectional effects between relationship experiences and traits. Preuß et al. examined international students’ motivation repeatedly every six months during their Bachelor studies. Finally, Gu et al., delineate meta-analytically how short- and long-term studies abroad contribute differently to students’ personality development in the domains of the Big Five traits, self-evaluations, and values.

Together, the talks present results from large representative samples, use sophisticated statistical modelling, and examine different personality characteristics to cover personality development broadly. We discuss how the time scales of the studies shape our understanding of personality development processes and outline how future research could benefit from study designs with multiple or approximately continuous time scales.

The Role of Sudden Gains as Catalysts of Volitional Neuroticism Change
Prof. Dr. Gabriel Olaru | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Gabriel Olaru | Germany
Dr. Peter Haehner | Switzerland
Amanda J. Wright | Switzerland
Rosalie Andrae | Switzerland
Christopher Hopwood | Switzerland
Wiebke Bleidorn | Switzerland

Sudden gains—abrupt, substantial improvements between consecutive assessments—are well-documented phenomena in psychotherapy research, where they predict more favorable treatment outcomes. Yet, little is known about whether such breakthrough moments also occur in non-clinical interventions that target personality traits. In this preregistered study, we investigate the role of sudden gains in the context of a 6-week digital intervention designed to decrease neuroticism (CHILL study; Haehner et al., 2025; Wright et al., 2025). Using daily and weekly assessments of neuroticism from 427 participants, we aim to identify sudden gains defined as statistically reliable drops in neuroticism and examine their implications for subsequent change trajectories. Specifically, we test whether experiencing a sudden gain predicts stronger overall reductions in trait-level neuroticism and improvements in self-functioning indicators such as self-esteem, self-control, self-efficacy, and self-concept clarity. We further explore which intervention strategies are more likely to elicit and sustain sudden gains. This project seeks to advance understanding of the short-term dynamics underlying volitional personality change and to uncover mechanisms that could be leveraged to personalize digital interventions for greater effectiveness.

Personality Traits and Philanthropy Across Time
Lina Hungerbuehler | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Lina Hungerbuehler | Switzerland
Dr. Peter Haehner | Switzerland
Dr. Michael D. Krämer | Switzerland
Christopher J. Hopwood | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Wiebke Bleidorn | Switzerland

Volunteering and charitable giving are core examples of philanthropic behaviors that contribute to both individual well-being and societal welfare. Previous research has established cross-sectional links between broad personality traits and these behaviors, yet little is known about how these links develop and change over time. Personality traits and philanthropic behaviors may be linked because people with certain trait levels are more likely to later engage in volunteering or charitable giving (selection effects), and sustained engagement in these behaviors may, in turn, shape personality development over time (socialization effects). Theory and preliminary evidence further suggest that these processes may vary across the lifespan. Moreover, an over-reliance on small samples and brief personality inventories in prior studies may have limited the precision and robustness of existing findings. In the present study, we address these limitations by examining the dynamics between personality traits and philanthropic engagement using an extensive personality measure and five-wave nationally representative data from Switzerland (N = 4,577). We extend prior research by testing whether personality traits predict later volunteering and charitable giving and whether engagement in these behaviors predicts personality trait change. In addition, we investigate age-related moderation to assess whether these selection and socialization processes differ across the adult life course. Together, these findings advance understanding of how personality and philanthropy shape one another across the lifespan and may inform efforts to promote both individual well-being and societal welfare.

Dynamic Influences between Antagonistic/Self-Centered Traits and Close Relationships
Anna Braig | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Anna Braig | Germany
Matthew D. Johnson | Canada
Prof. Dr. Marcus Mund | Austria
Prof. Dr. Franz J. Neyer | Germany

Romantic partnerships have been shown to play a significant role in personality development during young adulthood. However, research is still limited with regard to how (changes in) antagonistic and self-centered personality traits and (changes in) couple relationship functioning mutually influence one another over time. Moreover, existing research on parent–child relationships has predominantly focused on how parental characteristics shape children’s personality development. In contrast, far fewer studies have examined how parents’ own antagonistic or self-centered traits affect children’s well-being and broader relational functioning within the parent–child dyad.

The present two studies address this gap by examining the transactional dynamic interplay between Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and narcissism and relationship qualities in couple and parent–child relationships. Using data from the German Family Panel (pairfam), Study 1 estimated extended bivariate latent change models in a sample of 1,925 couples (anchor persons’ mean age = 36.48 years, SD = 7.62; partners’ mean age = 36.91 years, SD = 8.71) across three measurement waves spanning four years. Study 2 employed random-intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs) in a sample of 994 parent–child dyads (parents’ mean age = 41.00 years, SD = 4.67; children’s mean age = 11.88 years, SD = 2.22), covering the same time span.

Results provided evidence for bidirectional effects between (changes in) antagonistic/self-centered personality traits and (changes in) relational outcomes, pointing to dynamic reciprocal processes unfolding over time.

Intersectional perspectives on the development of expectations and values of international (STEM) students over the study course
Dr. Judith Sarah Preuß | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Judith Sarah Preuß | Germany
Dr. Julia Zimmermann | Germany
Prof. Dr. Kathrin Jonkmann | Germany

With about 368,000 international students, Germany is the most popular non-English-speaking host country. However, high estimated drop-out rates (41% international vs. 28% domestic bachelor students) require a better understanding of international students’ study motivation and its development whilst considering the demographic heterogeneity in this group. A previous study based on the situated expectancy-value-theory (SEVT), identified motivational differences amongst international students at study start by demographic characteristics and their intersections. Therefore, we build on these findings and addressed the long-term motivational development by analysing data from 1,486 international bachelor students in Germany (nSTEM = 839, nnon-STEM = 647) from a panel study with five measurements (each at the end of the semester) using (conditional) latent growth curve models (LGCM). We investigated both the development of expectancy-value-components over the study course and interindividual differences therein based on gender, subject group (STEM versus non-STEM), parental academic and cultural background, and their intersectional interplay.

We identified differences in motivational trajectories of STEM versus non-STEM students, between first- and continuous-generation students and between students with different cultural backgrounds. Noteworthy were higher initial costs and lower study-related language skills of students from outside Western Europe that mostly persisted across five semesters.

The results offer a differentiated understanding of the motivational development in the heterogeneous group of international bachelor students and provide indications for tailored interventions to support study motivation and success. Future research would benefit from considering the developmental interplay between the motivational components and further individual characteristics such as the big five and (acculturation) attitudes.

A meta-analysis how studying abroad contributes to personality change among international students from European and Asian countries
Junwen Gu | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Junwen Gu | Germany
Prof. Dr. Cornelia Wrzus | Germany

Understanding how international students’ personalities change during their study abroad, is crucial because personality adapts to environmental influences, and affects well-being, academic achievement, and other life outcomes. Most existing research relies on European samples or cross-sectional designs, which provide valuable snapshots but limited insight into cultural aspects and changes over time. Thus, this preregistered meta-analysis aims to address this gap by synthesizing all relevant longitudinal evidence in the field. We hypothesized that studying abroad is associated with increases in Openness and Agreeableness and decreases in Neuroticism. Also, we anticipated selection effects, whereby students higher in openness and lower in neuroticism are more likely to study abroad. Further moderator analyses examine age group (adolescents vs. young adults), duration of stay, and cultural distance between home and host countries. Finally, we examined students’ post-return adjustment process, or whether personality changes persist, diminish, or reverse after returning home. Based on a systematic literature search on EBSCOhost (October 27, 2025), we identified 874 empirical, longitudinal studies, and 27 of them were included with a total sample of approximately 5,700 participants. Students mainly originate from the USA, Germany, and various Asian countries, and study predominantly in Western destinations. Data extraction has been completed, and data analysis is currently in progress, with results expected in spring 2026. We will discuss potential similarities and differences of personality change among international students depending on the home and host countries.

Innovations in Psychotherapy Training: AI-Based Skill Assessment, Multimodality, and Emerging Topics
Chair(s) Jana Bommer (Trier University)
Prof. Wolfgang Lutz (Trier University)
Room: GR
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Clinical training faces increasing demands due to ongoing reforms, rapid technological developments such as artificial intelligence (AI), and the growing complexity of mental health challenges. These developments require innovative approaches for the systematic assessment and training of therapeutic skills. Core competencies must be more precisely conceptualized, multimodal assessment methods explored, and emerging clinical topics integrated into curricula. This symposium brings together contributions that develop, implement, and critically evaluate innovative training formats, including AI-based skill assessment, multimodal approaches, and the integration of emerging topics in psychotherapy training. The first presentation introduces a simulation-based teaching concept for child and adolescent psychotherapy that enables systematic training and multimodal assessment of psychotherapeutic social skills. The second contribution presents results from a randomized controlled trial comparing clinical training as usual with AI-supported clinical training to examine the added value of AI-enhanced approaches. The third presentation focuses on the development and evaluation of PsyRAI, an AI-based system designed to assess and provide feedback on clinical micro-skills to support deliberate skill acquisition. The fourth talk addresses ethical concerns by examining multicultural and gender biases in PsyRAI and exploring whether AI can detect biases within its own reasoning. The fifth contribution investigates whether multimodally enriched transcripts improve the validity of AI-based ratings of interpersonal skills by integrating vocal-affective information into text-based assessment. The symposium concludes with a presentation on the psychological consequences of the climate crisis in individuals with pre-existing mental disorders and the development of a targeted group intervention addressing climate-related distress.

Enhancing professional communication training in higher education through artificial intelligence(AI)-integrated exercises
Dr. Laura-Ashley Fraunfelter | Trier University
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Laura-Ashley Fraunfelter | Trier University
Sara Koc | Trier University
Prof. Dr. Michael Schneider | Trier University
Dr. Thomas Simacek | Trier University
Emma Boerner
Prof. Dr. rer. nat. Marion Tegethoff | RWTH Aachen University
Liam Schirmer | Trier University
Dr. Maria Theobald | Trier University
Mira Flohr-Devaud | Trier University
Vivien Cordes
Dr. Nicole Lepsy | Trier University
Prof. Dr. Gunther Meinlschmidt | Trier University

Theoretical Background
Competencies in professional interviewing and communication are essential, learnable skills for psychotherapists, yet they often require time-intensive and resource-demanding training formats. The provision of generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers innovative opportunities to enhance communication skills training through the simulation of realistic conversations and individualized, adaptive feedback.
Research Question
The present randomized controlled trial investigates the effectiveness and feasibility of AI-supported exercises for acquiring professional communication skills among psychology students.
Method
Students at Trier University participate in the cluster-randomized study within the context of communication skills seminars. Seminar groups are randomly assigned either to the AI condition (AI-supported exercises in addition to classical training methods within teaching-as-usual, TAU) or to the control condition (TAU without AI-supported exercises). The effectiveness of the AI-supported exercises is assessed using a communication skills competence test (primary outcome measure). Secondary measures include self-efficacy, self-concept, motivation, attitudes toward AI, course evaluation, and students’ ratings of the AI tool. The study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) under “th6f4.”
Results
To date, data from n = 61 participants are available. Additional data collection will be completed in subsequent semesters. Initial results of the study will be presented in the talk.
Conclusion
The study is expected to contribute evidence regarding the effectiveness and feasibility of integrating AI into university-level communication skills training. Successful implementation of AI-supported training approaches could advance innovative educational practices by creating scalable, accessible, and personalized learning opportunities.

Training therapeutic competencies through AI-supported deliberate practice with PsyRAI
Jana Bommer | Trier University
Show details
Authors:
Jana Bommer | Trier University
Prof. Dr. Wolfgang Lutz | Trier University
Jeanne Hierse | Trier University
David Riebschläger | Deutsches Forschungszentrum für Künstliche Intelligenz GmbH (DFKI)
Christoph Maerz | Deutsches Forschungszentrum für Künstliche Intelligenz GmbH (DFKI)
Dr. Antonia Vehlen | Trier University

Aim: Clinical micro-skills are relevant in every therapeutic session, highlighting the importance of systematic training in psychotherapy education. However, such training is resource-intensive, and maintaining trainees’ motivation to engage in repeated practice poses an additional challenge. To address these gaps, we developed and evaluated PsyRAI, a local large language model–based system designed to automatically assess clinical micro-skills and provide structured feedback based on therapists’ responses to video-based simulated patient statements.
Methods: PsyRAI was developed to assess clinical micro-skills based on the CMST (Bommer et al., 2025) using an iterative prompt-engineering procedure. The reliability of PsyRAI was examined using ICC(2,3), assessing agreement between PsyRAI and two trained human raters based on ratings of N = 150 videos. In addition, students evaluate the perceived helpfulness and motivational value of the feedback generated by PsyRAI.
Results: ICC values across clinical micro-skills ranged from .63 (interpersonal competence and time and process management) to .82 (communication competence). Analyses of students’ evaluations of the PsyRAI feedback are ongoing and will be presented at the conference.
Discussion: PsyRAI can approximate human ratings of clinical micro-skills with promising accuracy, suggesting its potential to support psychotherapy training. By providing immediate, structured feedback in an interactive and low-threshold learning environment, PsyRAI may also foster trainees’ motivation to engage in repeated practice. However, interpersonal competencies remain harder for the model to capture than surface-level features like communication competencies. This may reflect PsyRAI’s current text-based design and the inherent complexity of relational processes, which may require expert human judgment.

„Thank you PsyRAI - seems fair“ - Testing for multi-cultural and gender biases in an AI-based rating system for clinical micro-skills.
Jeanne Hierse | Trier University
Show details
Authors:
Jeanne Hierse | Trier University
Jana Bommer | Trier University
David Riebschläger | Deutsches Forschungszentrum für Künstliche Intelligenz GmbH (DFKI)
Christoph Maerz | Deutsches Forschungszentrum für Künstliche Intelligenz GmbH (DFKI)
Prof. Dr. Wolfgang Lutz | Trier University
Dr. Antonia Vehlen | Trier University

Aim: This study examines whether PsyRAI, an LLM-based rating system for clinical micro-skills, shows discriminatory effects in its ratings when therapist background characteristics are varied based on gender and cultural background, and whether AI can be used to detect bias in the system’s explanatory reasoning.
Methods: PsyRAI uses an established rating scale to evaluate clinical micro skills in video recordings of therapeutic responses to patient statements. Additionally, the system receives structured information about the patient and therapeutic context. For bias testing, ten counterfactual variants were created by changing only information about the therapist’s gender or cultural background while keeping all other content identical. Ratings from PsyRAI were than compared to a reference condition to identify systematic biases. Additionally, reasonings from bias-induced variations were qualitatively assessed by two human raters and an LLM-based bias-detection agent using a five-point Likert scale (1 = strong bias to 5 = no bias).
Results: PsyRAI’s ratings remained highly stable across counterfactual variations, with ICCs between .83 and .88, indicating strong agreement with the reference condition. The LLM-based bias-detection agent showed strong agreement with human raters in identifying bias (MAE = 0.74).
Discussion: PsyRAI showed minimal sensitivity to counterfactual variations in clinical micro-skill evaluations, suggesting robust and fair handling of diversity-related information within the tested dimensions. The LLM-based bias assessment also showed high agreement with human judgments, demonstrating its potential as an automated tool to monitor and safeguard the trustworthiness of psychological rating systems.

Bringing transcripts to life: From audio recordings to multimodal transcription for the clinical training of interpersonal skills in psychotherapy
Dr. Antonia Vehlen | Trier University
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Antonia Vehlen | Trier University
Jeanne Hierse | Trier University
Jana Bommer | Trier University
Prof. Dr. Wolfgang Lutz | Trier University

Clinical micro-skills, including interpersonal skills, are essential for therapists and can be applied across orientations to support treatment outcomes. This highlights the importance of systematic training programmes and scalable feedback on these skills in clinical training. Although large language models (LLMs) have the potential to provide such possibilities, current approaches are limited to text-only representations and therefore neglect the multimodal aspects of therapeutic interaction that are particularly important for evaluating interpersonal skills. Consequently, this work explored the potential of multimodally enriched transcription approaches as a basis for AI-based rating systems.
Following a deliberate practice framework, recorded therapist responses (N = 150) to standardized patient statements serve as the empirical basis. Audio recordings are transcribed using a prompted version of Whisper (large-v3), which preserves fillers and pauses. Voice emotion recognition models (openSMILE and emoW2V) extract vocal features related to therapists’ affective expression. These signals are translated into multimodal descriptions using rule-based procedures and a dedicated LLM-based interpretation agent and integrated into the transcripts. The multimodally enriched transcripts are then evaluated to determine their influence on agreement between AI-based and human rating systems with respect to interpersonal skills.
Preliminary findings indicate that prompted automatic transcription achieves high agreement with human-generated transcripts, particularly with respect to fillers and pauses. Based on text-only transcripts, the AI-based rating system shows moderate agreement with human raters of interpersonal skills (ICC = .40–.60). Multimodally enriched transcripts increase agreement between the AI-based system and human raters, indicating the added value of multimodal transcription for AI-supported clinical training.

Climate-related stress in people with mental illness: Empirical evidence and psychotherapeutic responses
Sarah Stapel | Universität Greifswald
Show details
Authors:
Sarah Stapel | Universität Greifswald
Prof. Dr. Eva-Lotta Brakemeier | Universität Greifswald

The presentation highlights the psychological consequences of the climate crisis for people with existing mental illnesses and combines empirical findings with psychotherapeutic implications. Based on initial routine data from a university psychotherapy outpatient clinic, it shows how often climate-related stress occurs in people with mental health diagnoses, how it is related to different disorders, and which individual predictors can be identified.
Initial results show that about a quarter of patients report clinically relevant climate-related stress that can exacerbate existing psychological symptoms or trigger new ones. Against this background, a newly developed group therapy manual specifically designed to address climate-related stress is presented. The intervention was developed based on theory and is currently being implemented and evaluated. The presentation provides insight into key content, therapeutic objectives, and initial experiences from its application, and discusses implications for psychotherapeutic care in times of climate crisis.

Digitale Unterstützung in der Schule: Weiterbildung, Diagnostik und individuelle Förderung
Chair(s) Dr. Fenke Kachisi (DIPF I Leibniz-Institut für Bildungsforschung und Bildungsinformation)
Room: SI
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Digitale Tools eröffnen neue Möglichkeiten zur Unterstützung von Schüler*innen und Lehrkräften in schulischen und schulnahen Settings. Sie können dabei u. a. sowohl zur evidenzbasierten Diagnostik und individualisierten Förderung von Kindern als auch zur Weiterbildung von Lehrkräften eingesetzt werden. Gleichzeitig stellt ihre nachhaltige Implementierung in realen schulischen Settings eine zentrale Herausforderung dar. Das Symposium bündelt aktuelle Forschungs- und Entwicklungsarbeiten, die exemplarisch zeigen, wie digitale Anwendungen zur Förderung fachlicher, überfachlicher und psychosozialer Kompetenzbereiche gestaltet, geprüft und in die schulische Praxis integriert werden können.

Die Beiträge decken vier Anwendungsfelder ab: (1) die individualisierte Leseflüssigkeitsförderung mit FLINK, (2) eine App zur modularen Förderung mathematischer Basiskompetenzen, die ein integriertes Screening zum adaptiven Einstieg nutzt, (3) digitale Fortbildungsmodule zur Förderung professioneller Kompetenzen von Lehrkräften im Bereich selbstregulierten Lernens sowie (4) eine Online-Plattform zur Unterstützung der psychischen Gesundheit von Kindern und Jugendlichen in der Lebensumwelt Schule.

Das Symposium verfolgt einen multiperspektivischen Ansatz, der die Nutzung digitaler Tools auf Ebene der Lernenden (Diagnostik und Förderung), der Lehrkräfte (Professionalisierung) und der schulnahen Unterstützungssysteme (psychosoziale Versorgung) integriert in den Blick nimmt. Gemeinsam adressieren die Beiträge Fragen der diagnostischen Güte, der adaptiven Förderung, sowie der Akzeptanz und Nutzung durch unterschiedliche Anwender*innen. Im Rahmen des Symposiums sollen übergreifende Herausforderungen und Gelingensbedingungen der Implementierung diskutiert werden, um Perspektiven für den nachhaltigen Transfer digitaler Angebote in schulische Praxis und Unterstützungssysteme aufzuzeigen.


Keywords: Leseschwierigkeiten, Rechenschwäche, Selbstregulation, Mental Health, Digitale Intervention

Evaluation eines digitalen Leseflüssigkeitstrainings für die 2. Klassenstufe
Dr. Fenke Kachisi | DIPF | Leibniz-Institut für Bildungsforschung und Bildungsinformation | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Fenke Kachisi | DIPF | Leibniz-Institut für Bildungsforschung und Bildungsinformation | Germany
Dr. Sebastian Korinth | DIPF | Leibniz-Institut für Bildungsforschung und Bildungsinformation
Dr. Telse Nagler | DIPF | Leibniz-Institut für Bildungsforschung und Bildungsinformation

Ein frühzeitiges Interventionsangebot für Kinder mit Leseschwierigkeiten ist entscheidend, um Leseverbesserungen zu erzielen und schulische Probleme zu vermeiden. Das browserbasierte FLINK-Training nutzt das sogenannte Text-Fading, bei dem die Lesegeschwindigkeit durch schrittweises Ausblenden des zu lesenden Textes beeinflusst wird (Breznitz & Berman, 2003). Das Lesematerial wird, angepasst an das individuelle Leseniveau, in Leserichtung Buchstabe für Buchstabe ausgeblendet und soll Kinder so zu schnellerem Lesen anregen (Nagler et al., 2021).

Lehrkräfte können ausgewählte Schüler*innen mit Leseleistungen im mittleren und unteren Leistungsbereich der Klassenstufe 2 bis 6 zur Teilnahme anmelden. Vorgesehen sind zwei Übungseinheiten mit jeweils 30 Aufgaben pro Woche (maximal 54 FLINK-Übungen pro Schuljahr). Alle Kinder starten mit der gleichen Ausblendegeschwindigkeit, die im Trainingsverlauf basierend auf der Verständnisleistung individuell angepasst wird.

Die Wirksamkeit des Trainings im Schulalltag konnte bereits für die 3. und 4. Klassenstufe gezeigt werden (Kachisi et al., 2025). Ziel dieses Projektes ist es, die Wirksamkeit des Trainings ebenfalls für die 2. Klassenstufe zu untersuchen. Dazu wurden n = 425 Kinder, die an FLINK teilgenommen haben, mit einer gematchten Kontrollgruppe ohne Training verglichen. Das Leseverständnis der Kinder wurde zum Prä- sowie zum Post-Zeitpunkt etwa drei Wochen später erfasst. Ein lineares Mixed-Effects-Modell zeigte eine signifikante Interaktion zwischen Messzeitpunkt und Trainingsumfang (b = 0.81, SE = 0.37, t = 2.21, p = .027), sodass eine höhere Anzahl Trainingssessions mit stärkeren Leistungszuwächsen assoziiert war.
Der Symposiumsbeitrag diskutiert die Ergebnisse im Hinblick auf die methodische Herangehensweise sowie praktische Implikationen und Herausforderungen des Trainings für den Einsatz an deutschen Schulen.

Breznitz, Z., & Berman, L. (2003). The underlying factors of word reading rate. Educational Psychology Review, 15(3), 247–265.
Kachisi, F., Ehm, J.-H., Marković, J., & Nagler, T. (2025). FLINK: Evaluation of a digitized reading fluency training. In J. Ziehm, M. Hasselhorn, & H. G. Roßbach (Hrsg.), Kinder mit Risiken für Bildungsmisserfolg (Edition ZfE). Springer.
Nagler, T., Zarić, J., Kachisi, F., Lindberg, S., & Ehm, J.-H. (2021). Reading-impaired children improve through text-fading training: analyses of comprehension, orthographic knowledge, and RAN. Annals of Dyslexia, 71(3), 458–482.

Entwicklung und Erprobung eines Screenings in einem Serious Game zur Förderung von Kindern mit Rechenschwäche
Dr. Angelika Becker | Helmut-Schmidt-Universität Hamburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Angelika Becker | Helmut-Schmidt-Universität Hamburg | Germany
Darius Endlich | Universität Würzburg | Germany
Lena Engel | Universität Würzburg | Germany
Wolfgang Lenhard | Universität Würzburg | Germany
Jenny Maurer | Helmut-Schmidt-Universität Hamburg | Germany
Leon Skoba | Helmut-Schmidt-Universität Hamburg | Germany
Monika Daseking | Helmut-Schmidt-Universität Hamburg | Germany

Das Serious Game „Ecki’s Würfelkosmos“ wurde zur adaptiven Förderung von Kindern mit Rechenschwäche entwickelt (Skoba et al., 2024). In der aktuellen Version beginnen alle Spielenden unabhängig von ihren individuellen Vorkenntnissen auf der niedrigsten Schwierigkeitsstufe. Bei Kindern mit einem stärkeren Fähigkeitsprofil kann dies zu einem Motivationsverlust und folglich zu vermehrten Spielabbrüchen führen. Um einen passgenaueren Einstieg zu ermöglichen, wird die App um ein integriertes Screening-Verfahren erweitert, das zu Beginn der Nutzung durchgeführt wird. Ziel des Screenings ist die Erfassung zentraler mathematischer Basiskompetenzen, um darauf aufbauend einen individuellen Startwert zur Förderung festzulegen.
Das Screening besteht aus vier bereits in der App integrierten Spielen aus den Bereichen Mengenverständnis, visuell-räumliche Wahrnehmung, Zahlenverständnis sowie Grundrechenarten. Alle vier Aufgabenformate werden in einer festgelegten Reihenfolge durchgeführt. Jede Aufgabe besteht aus vier bis sechs Items.
Für die Auswertung werden die Klassenstufen („2“, „3“, „4“), die Anzahl korrekter Antworten sowie die Bearbeitungszeit berücksichtigt. Auf Basis dieser Daten wird ein individuelles Fähigkeitsprofil erstellt, das zur Festlegung der Schwierigkeitsgrade aller im Spiel enthaltenen mathematischen Aufgaben dient. Dadurch starten Spielende mit einem an ihre Kompetenzen angepassten Niveau.
Zur Überprüfung der Güte des entwickelten Screenings werden die erhobenen App-Daten mit externen Leistungsmaßen aus standardisierten Rechentests verglichen. Dadurch soll untersucht werden, inwieweit das Screening mathematische Kompetenzen valide erfasst. Darüber hinaus soll in einer Folgestudie überprüft werden, ob das vorgeschaltete Screening zu einer wirksameren Nutzung der App und zu größeren Lernzuwächsen führt.

Fördern fördern: Fortbildungsmodule zur Förderung selbstregulierten Lernens durch Lehrkräfte
Dr. Lea Nobbe | Goethe-Universität Frankfurt | Germany

Authors:
Dr. Lea Nobbe | Goethe-Universität Frankfurt | Germany

Selbstreguliertes Lernen (SRL) gilt als Schlüsselkompetenz für Bildungserfolg. Obwohl Studien den positiven Einfluss SRLs auf akademische Leistungen und Motivation belegen, zeigt sich eine unzureichende Implementierung im schulischen Alltag (Dignath & Veenman, 2021). Für Lehrkräfte bestehen Herausforderungen bei der Förderung – beispielsweise aufgrund mangelnden Fachwissens, unrealistischer Annahmen über Schüler*innenkompetenzen und struktureller Barrieren (Dignath, 2016; Karlen et al., 2020). Die gezielte Förderung professioneller Kompetenzen wie Fachwissen, Überzeugungen und Selbstwirksamkeit ist eine zentrale Voraussetzung für den nachhaltigen Fortbildungserfolg von Lehrkräften (Karlen et al., 2023). Diese Arbeit untersucht, inwieweit das Bearbeiten digitaler Fortbildungsmodule zur SRL-Förderung Lehrkräfte darin unterstützt, diese professionellen Kompetenzen zu verändern.
Die wissenschaftliche Evaluation basiert auf prä-posttestbasierten Quasi-Experimenten für jedes Lernmodul. Für das erste Lernmodul liegen Daten vor; weitere Evaluationen sind rechtzeitig zur Tagung ausgewertet.
N = 44 Lehrkräfte nahmen an einer vierwöchigen digitalen Lernwerkstatt teil, in der theoretische Inhalte zu SRL, Praxisbeispiele sowie Reflexionsimpulse zur Wochenplanarbeit vermittelt wurden. Fragebögen erfassten Wissen über SRL, Überzeugungen und Selbstwirksamkeit. Zur Auswertung wurden t-Tests für verbundene Stichproben und Wilcoxon-Vorzeichentests genutzt.
Die Ergebnisse zeigen signifikante Steigerungen im Wissen der Lehrkräfte über Förderung von SRL (d = 0.93) und ihrer Selbstwirksamkeitserwartung (r = .46). In den konsistenten (V = 68, p = .186) und inkonsistenten Überzeugungen (V = 138.5, p = .143) fanden sich keine Unterschiede.
Die Ergebnisse verdeutlichen das Potenzial digitaler Fortbildungsformate zur Förderung professionsbezogener Kompetenzen von Lehrkräften im Bereich SRL. Perspektivisch sollte die Wirksamkeit solcher Fortbildungsformate auch unter Einbezug von Schüler*innenmerkmalen und -leistungen weiter erforscht werden.

Digitale Präventions- und Interventionsangebote zur Förderung psychischer Gesundheit bieten im schulischen Kontext die Möglichkeit, evidenzbasierte Unterstützung niedrigschwellig, flexibel und skalierbar bereitzustellen. Der Beitrag stellt die Youth Mental Health (YMH) Online-Plattform GUSTAPH vor und diskutiert deren Entwicklung, empirische Fundierung und Implementationspotenziale in schulischen Settings.
GUSTAPH bündelt psychoedukative Inhalte sowie kurze, selbstständig anwendbare Interventionen zu zentralen Themen der psychischen Gesundheit im Kindes- und Jugendalter. Die Plattform richtet sich primär an Kinder und Jugendliche, ergänzt durch Informationsangebote für Eltern sowie pädagogische und psychologische Fachkräfte, und ist u. a. für den Einsatz in schulischen Präventions- und Förderstrukturen konzipiert (z. B. Unterricht, schulische Beratung, Präventionsprogramme).
Die Entwicklung von GUSTAPH erfolgt im Rahmen des Deutschen Zentrums für Psychische Gesundheit (DZPG) und folgt einem partizipativen Ansatz, in dem Kinder und Jugendliche kontinuierlich in Bedarfsanalysen, Priorisierungsprozesse und Feedbackschleifen eingebunden werden. Eine partizipativ entwickelte Schüler*innenbefragung (N = 730; 49 % weiblich; Alter M = 15,39 Jahre) identifizierte beispielsweise ausgeprägte Informations- und Unterstützungsbedarfe in schulbezogenen Belastungen, psychischer Gesundheit und emotionsbezogenen Themen. Diese Befunde fließen, gemeinsam mit weiteren empirischen und konzeptionellen Grundlagen, in die modulare Struktur und thematische Ausrichtung der Plattform ein.
Der Beitrag ordnet GUSTAPH in aktuelle transdisziplinäre Ansätze der digitalen Mental-Health-Forschung ein (vgl. Konsortium der YMH-INF, 2025) und diskutiert Herausforderungen der schulischen Implementierung, darunter heterogene digitale Vorerfahrungen, altersabhängige Bedürfnisse sowie organisatorische Rahmenbedingungen. Abschließend werden Potenziale digitaler Plattformen für den Transfer evidenzbasierter Präventions- und Interventionsangebote in den schulischen Alltag aufgezeigt.

Konsortium der YMH-INF et al. (2025). Verbesserung der psychischen Gesundheit im Kindes- und Jugendalter: Die Aufgabe der Youth-Mental-Health-Infrastruktur im Deutschen Zentrum für Psychische Gesundheit. Kindheit und Entwicklung, 34(1), 33–43.

Interoception and health: From observation to modification
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. André Schulz (University of Luxembourg)
Room: CZ
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Interoception, the processing and perception of signals from inside the body, is essential for mental and physical health. Mental disorders and systemic diseases are associated with a specific pattern of interoceptive dysfunction. The aims of this symposium are to characterize highly-prevalent mental and systemic diseases in terms of interoceptive dysfunction and to establish novel intervention techniques to normalize deficient interoception. Nina Buntic (Luxemburg) demonstrates exaggerated cortical representation of visceral-afferent signals in Post-Covid syndrome, whereas André Schulz (Luxemburg) showed higher sensitivity to interoceptive perceptual learning (heartbeat perception training) amplified by post-learning stress in high somatic symptom distress. He also introduces two bottom-up techniques: Perceptual learning to increase interoceptive accuracy (IAc), and intermittent theta burst stimulation of the right supramarginal gyrus to enhance interoceptive attention (IAt), but not IAc. Organ-specific interoceptive perceptual learning, as investigated by Anxhela Sulay (Luxembourg), showed that an increase of IAc can only be achieved in the cardiac, but not the respiratory domain. Two top-down interventions, based on mobile apps, are presented by colleagues from Ulm: Christine Schillings demonstrates a Chatbot intervention targeting interoception to increase IAc, whereas Elisa Schmied-Weggler showed that a mindfulness intervention enhances interoceptive awareness (IAw), but does not affect IAc. In summary, this symposium introduce a set of novel, cutting-edge intervention methods to be applied in the lab and using mobile apps to selectively modify different facets of interoception, such as IAc, IAt and IAw. These can be used to normalize dysfunctional interoception in mental disorders and systemic diseases.

Increased heartbeat-evoked potentials in Post COVID syndrome: Evidence for exaggerated cortical representation of visceral-afferent signals.
Nina Buntic | University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Nina Buntic | University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. Jochen G. Schneider | University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. Marc Schlesser | Le Cabinet de Pneumologie Glacis | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. André Schulz | University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg

Post COVID syndrome is a heterogeneous condition characterized by persistent fatigue, post exertional malaise, and cognitive dysfunction, with substantial consequences for mental health and daily functioning. Autonomic dysregulation and alterations in interoceptive processing have been proposed as contributing factors to symptom persistence. While reduced heartbeat evoked potentials (HEPs) have been examined following SARS CoV 2 infection, behavioral evidence for interoceptive functioning in post COVID syndrome remains limited, particularly in the respiratory domain, despite the respiratory tract being central to infection.
In this symposium contribution, we present multimodal evidence on cardiac and respiratory interoception using behavioral tasks and evoked potentials. Eighty-eight participants, including 45 individuals with post COVID syndrome and 43 healthy controls, completed heartbeat counting and discrimination tasks as well as a respiratory resistance detection task during simultaneous EEG and ECG recordings. Interoceptive accuracy and sensitivity were assessed alongside HEPs and respiratory related evoked potentials (RREPs).
Healthy participants demonstrated higher accuracy in the heartbeat discrimination task, whereas individuals with post-COVID syndrome showed greater respiratory interoceptive sensitivity, reflected by lower detection thresholds. At the cortical level, RREP amplitudes did not differ between groups, suggesting preserved processing of respiratory afferent signals. In contrast, HEP amplitudes were increased in post-COVID participants across both resting and active interoceptive attention conditions, while attentional modulation effects were comparable between groups.
Together, these findings argue against a uniform interoceptive deficit following SARS-CoV-2 infection. Instead, they indicate enhanced cortical processing of cardiac signals alongside preserved respiratory interoceptive function, potentially shaped by task demands and symptom duration.

Prof. Dr. André Schulz | University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. André Schulz | University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg

Interoception is essential for mental health. Two major facets of interoception concern interoceptive accuracy (IAc) and interoceptive attention (IAt). Mental disorders, such as somatic symptom disorder (SSD), show dysfunctional IAc, IAt or both, which calls for indicator-specific interventions. We introduce two novel techniques: Interoceptive perceptual learning using a heartbeat perception training (HBPT) and (offline) transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of the right supramarginal gyrus (rSMG), a structure with high functional correlation with neural structures mediating interoception. In Study I N=96 healthy adults completed either a HBPT or a visual perception training, followed by an acute stressor (‘socially-evaluated cold pressor test’/SECPT) or a control test (randomly assigned). Study II, n=22 high and n=26 low symptom reporters completed the HBPT followed by the SECPT or the control test. We assessed IAc using a heartbeat counting and a heartbeat discrimination task (HCT/HDT). IAc increases could only be observed in the HBPT+stress group (Study I), an effect which was stronger in high symptom reporters (Study II). In Study III, N=22 healthy adults underwent a stimulation (intermittent theta burst stimulation/iTBS), an inhibition (continuous TBS) and a neutral (intermediate TBS) TMS protocol. IAc was assessed using the HCT/HDT, whereas heartbeat-evoked potentials (HEPs) served as indicators of IAt. The iTBS protocol increased HEPs, thereby potentially IAt, whereas IAc remained unaffected. Interoceptive perceptual learning plus post-learning stress may increase cardiac IAc, whereas offline iTBS of the rSMG can selectively enhance IAt. These approaches can be used to normalize selective interoceptive dysfunctions in mental disorders, such as SSD.

Interoception, the sensing and interpretation of internal bodily signals, is increasingly viewed as a transdiagnostic mechanism relevant to mental health, with interoception-based interventions showing promise across disorders characterized by heightened attention to bodily sesnsations or symptom preoccupation. Interoceptive processing can be described across stages, from early cortical representation of afferent signals (stage I) to perceptual discrimination (stage II) and evaluative/affective interpretation (stage III). Here, we tested whether organ-specific, multisession, feedback-based training enhances behavioral interoceptive accuracy performance and whether effects are modality-specific or generalize across organ systems. Healthy adults (N=21) were randomly assigned to heartbeat perception training (HBPT), respiratory resistance detection accuracy training (RRDAT), or visual perception training (VPT; exteroceptive control), with the gastric domain serving as an untrained comparison. Before and after four weekly training sessions, participants completed cardiac (heartbeat counting/discrimination), respiratory (resistance detection), and gastric (WLT-II; sat_%) tasks. EEG/ECG were simultaneously recorded to derive heartbeat-evoked potentials (HEPs) and respiratory-related evoked potentials (RREPs) as neural markers of first-order sensory-perceptual processing of cardiac and respiratory afferent signals in the CNS (stage I). Across groups, cardiac interoceptive accuracy and gastric sat_% improved from pre- to post-training, whereas a Group × Time interaction emerged for cardiac interoceptive accuracy after the HBPT only (stage II). In electrophysiological indices of stage I processing, HEPs did not differ from pre- to post-training, and the early RREP Nf component showed no significant pre-post modulation or group-specific change. Consistent with prior work indicating that early sensory evoked responses are relatively stable, our findings suggest that stage I indices may be less sensitive to short-term training in healthy participants. Together, these preliminary findings indicate organ-specific behavioral improvements without detectable changes in early evoked potentials in a healthy sample, motivating larger studies to test whether training effects preferentially target later evaluative stages (III) and whether these markers can index clinically relevant interoceptive disturbances.

Interoception – the perception and interpretation of internal bodily signal – plays a pivotal role in mental health. Chatbot-delivered interventions have been identified as a low-threshold approach to promoting psychological well-being, yet their potential for enhancing interoceptive processing remains largely unexplored. This study investigated the effects of a three-week chatbot-based intervention on interoceptive processes.
In a two-arm randomized controlled trial, N = 50 adults were allocated to either an intervention or a treatment-as-usual control group. Chatbot ELME guided participants through a three-week training program (two daily sessions, 10-20 minutes) targeting interoception, mindfulness, and stress management. Interoceptive accuracy was assessed using a heartbeat counting task (HCT) and the Graz Ambulatory Interoception Task (GRAIT). Interoceptive sensibility was measured via the Interoceptive Accuracy Scale (IAS). All assessments took place at t1 (baseline) and t2 (after 3 weeks).
Results indicated improved interoceptive accuracy in the intervention group compared to controls, as assessed by the HCT. No significant changes were observed in interoceptive sensibility.
These findings suggest that chatbot-delivered interventions may provide a promising approach for enhancing interoceptive accuracy. A high guidance by the chatbot, individual and flexible time points of the intervention units might be advantages of the intervention to easily integrate it into everyday life. GRAIT data are currently being analyzed and will provide further insight into intervention effects on interoceptive accuracy in everyday life. The GRAIT further demonstrates potential as an innovative ecological momentary assessment method for measuring interoceptive accuracy in naturalistic settings.

Show details
Authors:

Interoception is the ability to detect and process bodily signals. While mindfulness is hypothesized to enhance attention to these signals, empirical findings remain inconsistent how mindfulness interventions might influence interoceptive processing. The current study examined the impact of an app-based mindfulness intervention including respiratory exercises in healthy participants on a diverse set of interoceptive indices.
In this pilot study, 14 healthy participants were randomized to the mindfulness intervention or a waitlist control group. Interoceptive indices were measured at baseline (t1) and after two weeks of intervention (t2). Interoceptive indices included outcomes of two behavioral cardiac perception tasks (i.e., heartbeat counting task (HBC)), Heart Rate Discrimination task (HRD)) as well as, self-report methods (i.e., interoceptive attention scale, interoceptive accuracy scale).
Preliminary analyses yielded mixed results. Accuracy increased descriptively for the HBC, while there was no such trend for the accuracy (α,β) measured in the HRD. Moreover, differences of the HRD’s awareness measures were found between the groups, these results were similar for the HBC awareness measures.
Overall, the pattern of findings tentatively suggests that short-term mindfulness training may preferentially modulate subjective interoceptive awareness rather than sensory precision per se. This potential dissociation highlights the conceptual and methodological importance of distinguishing between objective performance, metacognitive awareness, and self-reported interoceptive beliefs. Psychophysical paradigms such as the HRD appear particularly valuable in disentangling perceptual sensitivity from decision processes and prior beliefs.

Adaptive Performance as a Metric for Understanding Human–AI Teaming
Eva Gößwein | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Eva Gößwein | Germany
Prof. Angelika C. Bullinger | Chemnitz University of Technology
PD Dr. Magnus Liebherr | University of Duisburg-Essen

Digital transformation and the increasing deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) are fundamentally altering the working environment. In this context, capturing how individuals adjust their behavior in response to evolving system capabilities is essential. This contribution positions adaptive performance as a core metric for understanding performance in human–AI teams, extending beyond static outcome measures to capture the dynamics of adaptation.
Adaptive performance is conceptualized as a temporally unfolding process encompassing a performance drop after the change and subsequent stabilization. This process-oriented perspective is particularly relevant for human–AI teams, where AI systems may change their behavior through learning algorithms, system updates, or shifts in autonomy, thereby continuously altering task demands and imposing coordination requirements on humans.
While this contribution takes a theoretical and generalist approach, research on simulators and long-term technology interventions highlights the importance of executive functions in supporting effective adaptation in changing environments. Beyond cognitive capacities, motivational and attitudinal factors such as self-efficacy, trust, and acceptance of AI shape adaptive performance trajectories. These factors relate to engagement with AI systems, persistence during periods of instability, and the willingness to adjust strategies over time. Together, these findings underscore the value of adaptive performance as a metric that captures adjustment within human–AI teams rather than focusing solely on final performance levels.
The contribution concludes by emphasizing the need for longitudinal, process-sensitive approaches to studying performance in human–AI teams, as adaptive performance enables a more nuanced evaluation of interactions.

Behavioral AI Anthropomorphism as a Mechanism of Trust and Gender Attribution in Chatbots
Dr. Fabio Ibrahim | Helmut-Schmidt-Universität / Universität der Bundeswehr Hamburg | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Fabio Ibrahim | Helmut-Schmidt-Universität / Universität der Bundeswehr Hamburg | Germany

Conversational AI is increasingly embedded in everyday life, and users often apply human social norms to text-based systems. However, anthropomorphism research in human–AI interaction has largely relied on belief-based measures, leaving open how users behaviorally relate to AI during interaction. In a large English sample (N = 933), we introduce and validate the Behavioral AI Anthropomorphism Scale (BAAS), a behavioral self-report instrument assessing enacted reciprocity and socioemotional alignment with AI chatbots. Using a random-split approach, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a robust two-factor structure and a hierarchical higher-order model with strong model fit and reliability, as well as discriminant validity relative to psychological anthropomorphism. Behavioral anthropomorphism emerged as a central mechanism shaping trust in AI: it explained incremental variance beyond belief-based anthropomorphism and mediated associations between AI use frequency, gender attribution, and trust. Gender similarity effects further indicated that men showed higher behavioral anthropomorphism when perceiving the AI as male, whereas women showed higher behavioral anthropomorphism when perceiving it as female, with parallel patterns for trust. These findings suggest that trust in conversational AI is grounded less in abstract cognitive attributions and more in enacted social behavior during interaction. The BAAS provides a validated tool for studying behavioral anthropomorphism and offers a theoretical basis for designing socially calibrated, user-sensitive conversational AI systems.

Do AI Systems Mirror Their Users? Personality, Values, and Sociocultural Norms in Human–AI Dynamics
Dr. Vera Vogel | Universität Mannheim/ Gesis-Leibniz Institut für Sozialwissenschaften | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Vera Vogel | Universität Mannheim/ Gesis-Leibniz Institut für Sozialwissenschaften | Germany

In times of rapid technological development, the question of how humans interact with artificial intelligence (AI) not only functionally but also socially is gaining increasing attention. While the alignment between individuals and their sociocultural contexts has primarily been studied in interpersonal settings, the growing presence of AI in everyday life opens up a new field of research: human–AI interaction as a site of social and value-based exchange. This research project extends this perspective by conceptualizing AI systems as a form of sociocultural context. Thereby, it addresses three core questions: Can AI systems perceive personal characteristics of their users? Are these individual characteristics reflected in the AI’s responses? And if so, do these patterns emerge from the AI’s perception of the user, or from its internalized knowledge of broader cultural norms? By integrating personality and values research with human–AI interaction technologies, the project offers an innovative contribution to understanding how individual traits, cultural contexts, and AI behavior intertwine—and which social dynamics may emerge in future AI-mediated environments.

Introduction: In response to the concern that ICD-10 criteria of schizophrenia lacked specificity, the ICD-11 re-weighted the symptoms required for the diagnosis. Instead of at least one first-line symptom (or ≥ 2 second-line symptoms, ICD-10), two out of seven symptom domains need to be met. Also, the ICD-11 applies dimensional specifiers for the main symptom cluster (e.g., negative symptoms), and the individual course (e.g., first episode). However, little is known about the validity and clinical utility of the new criteria in clinical practice. We explored what the changes in diagnostic criteria mean in terms of associations with (continuous) symptom severity and how they affect prevalence rates of psychotic disorders in an outpatient setting.
Methods: We utilize data of a longitudinal clinical trial delivering 24 sessions of cognitive-behavior therapy (approx. N = 200 with a psychotic disorder). For a subsample (n = 50), we apply the new ICD-11 criteria in addition to ICD-10 and DSM-5. At baseline, we assess the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5, clinical interviews for psychosis (Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale) and general functioning (Role Functioning Scale), and self-report questionnaires (e.g., Community Assessment of Psychic Experiences).
Results: We report the number of individuals per diagnostic category according to ICD-10 and ICD-11 and the associations of diagnosis with severity and frequency of psychotic symptoms, and level of functioning.
Discussion: We discuss clinical implications of the new ICD-11 criteria for psychosis - including directions for future studies and recommendations for the use of the new ICD-11 criteria in clinical practice

The development of PTSD and complex PTSD at the WHO left open the issue of how other cultural presentations of the disorders might manifest. An international consortium has taken the Cultural Script Theory as its basis and expanded it to include a new galaxy and constellation model of the disorders. This involves examining the dominant symptoms and signs in a region of the world with the aim of applying them in a culturally sensitive clinical practice.
A mixed-method approach was used in each of the consortium regions to date (East Africa, Northern China, Switzerland, Georgia). The first phase of this approach involves focus group interviews separately for patients and practitioners. This yielded region-specific symptoms and signs, which were analyzed in qualitative symptom network analyses according to the galaxy and constellation model. The second quantitative phase developed and validated additional diagnostic tools for the ICD-11 symptom assessments (Ns from 225 to 1208).
The results of the first phase revealed four constellations of trauma consequences that were impressively distinct from each other and independent of the ICD-11 formulations. The respective cultural explanatory models can also be gleaned from these cultural scripts. The results of the second phase (in three regions to date) yielded valid screeners for dominant symptoms that differ across world regions.
The discussion summarizes the achievements and challenges of the approach, on which research will continue in three additional world regions. Further, we discuss the applicability of the approach for improving the use of psychotherapy and the development of culturally sensitive treatment.

Chronische Schmerzen in der ICD-11: Endlich biopsychosozial
Prof. Dr. Antonia Barke | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Antonia Barke | Germany

Das ICD-11 führt erstmals eine systematische, auf dem biopsychosozialen Modell basierende Klassifikation chronischer Schmerzen ein. Dies behebt lange bestehende Defizite der ICD-10, wie den obsoleten Dualismus von „psychisch-somatisch“, die fehlende einheitliche Definition von Schmerzen und das Fehlen wichtiger Diagnosen.
Die aktuelle Definition der International Association for the Study of Pain bildet die Grundlage für alle Diagnosen chronischer Schmerzen. Chronische Schmerzen sind Schmerzen, die länger als drei Monate andauern oder wiederkehren. Das neue Kapitel MG30 „Chronische Schmerzen" enthält sieben Hauptkategorien: eine Kategorie für chronische primäre Schmerzen (Schmerz als eigenständiges Krankheitsbild) und sechs Kategorien für chronische sekundäre Schmerzen. Diese umfassen u.a. tumorassoziierte, postoperative, muskuloskelettale, viszerale, neuropathische Schmerzen. Daneben ermöglichen optionale Zusatzcodes, die mit allen chronischen Schmerzen (primär und sekundär) kombiniert werden können, die Schmerzschwere sowie behandlungsrelevante psychosoziale Faktoren zu erfassen.
In Feldtests der WHO erwiesen sich die chronischen Schmerzdiagnosen in Hinblick auf die Eindeutigkeit der Diagnosen und die Vergabe zutreffender Codes als sehr zufriedenstellend. Dies bestätigte sich auch in einer internationalen Studie, die diagnosebezogene Interraterreliabilitäten erfasste. In Ländern verschiedener Einkommensstufen zeigte sich eine hohe klinische Nützlichkeit und eine verbesserte Sichtbarkeit chronischer Schmerzen in der klinischen Dokumentation und entsprechenden Gesundheitsstatistiken.
Die neuen Diagnosen chronischer Schmerzen verweisen entschieden auf psychologische, soziale und biologische Aspekte bei allen chronischen Schmerzen und schaffen so eine verbesserte und sachangemessenere Klassifikation. Die Implementierung in das deutsche Gesundheitssystem steht bevor und erfordert eine entsprechende Berücksichtigung bei Behandlungswegen und Leistungserbringung.

We assessed the frequency at which DDAA symptoms occurred and whether parents and clinicians viewed them as problematic and deviant for this age group. Climate change affects extreme weather events like floods and heatwaves. Yet this may vary inter-individually and between contexts, for example, by political orientation or extreme weather experience. This symposium showcases observational and experimental studies on these perceptions, responses, and their driving factors in various European countries. Engel et al. show that people in 15 European countries are generally concerned about weather extremes, but overestimate characteristics of specific future weather extremes. Haak et al. evaluate the causal link between exposure to different weather extremes and climate policy support among right- and left-leaning Germans. Focusing on a specific extreme, Ulrich and Kause show how flood risk but not climate risk perceptions increased after a major flood in Germany in 2021 and how these changes link to flood experiences and political orientation. Finally, Kause and Ulrich explore how Germans (mis)estimate the probability of weather extremes in past, current, and future climates and how they respond to uncertain information about changes in these probabilities. These insights can inform effective extreme weather-related communication and policymaking, potentially fostering behavioral change by accounting for features of extreme weather perceptions.

Many societal roles are still highly gendered, and people have beliefs and expectations of women’s and men’s roles in society. This could lead to people using biased information gathering strategies to confirm these pre-existing beliefs. In four preregistered studies (total N = 295), we explored how biased sampling strategies could result in overrepresentation of belief-confirming information. Furthermore, we investigated how individual differences in beliefs about gender roles (i.e., gender essentialism) could further amplify this process.

In our experiments, participants saw various companies based on highly gendered professions (e.g., engineer, beautician) and could view up to ten employees per company before making estimates of that company’s gender distribution. Importantly, we manipulated the employee sequences such that the initial faces either confirmed or disconfirmed the gendered expectations.

We found that participants sampled less social information when the initial evidence confirmed (vs. disconfirmed) participants’ pre-existing beliefs. They also engaged in selective exposure strategies as they tried to stop sampling when the sequence contained more stereotypically congruent employees. Additionally, both their prior beliefs and observed information were also incorporated into participants’ estimates of the company’s gender distributions. Finally, we found that the selective exposure strategies and gender distribution estimates were influenced by the strength of participants’ gender-based beliefs. Overall, our findings reveal how people’s beliefs about gender roles impact information sampling and judgments in social situations and offer insight why gender roles continue to exist in the society.

Trust in science is essential for the adoption of science-based advice by the public, as it supports belief updating grounded in empirical evidence. However, little is known about the psychological mechanisms and boundary conditions under which trust in science promotes belief updating. The study used a pre-post design with experimental variations of author expertise (high vs. low; manipulated via written author descriptions) and evidence direction (conclusive vs. inconclusive; manipulated via descriptions of study results on the efficacy of acupuncture). Results showed that evidence attributed to high-expertise scientists elicited stronger belief updating than evidence from low-expertise scientists. Moreover, a significant three-way interaction between trust in science, author expertise, and evidence direction suggested that trust promoted belief change only when clear and unambiguous evidence stemmed from high-expertise sources. In contrast, cognitive dissonance—tested as a potential mediator—did not explain the effects of trust in science on belief updating. Together, these findings suggest that trust in science supports an adaptive pattern of information processing in laypeople: It facilitates belief change in response to credible information while guarding against uncritical acceptance of inconclusive evidence from unreliable sources.

Thus, our work provides initial evidence that highlighting the prevalence of a societal issue might galvanize even those who do not themselves belong to the disadvantaged group into action to address it.

How Fair Is Fair? Neue Befunde zu Bias, Diversity und (Un)Gleichbehandlung in der Personalauswahl
Chair(s) Julia Büttner (Universität Ulm)
Prof. Dr. Johannes Basch
Room: CY
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Bias und Benachteiligung in der Personalauswahl sind ein anhaltendes Problem mit negativen Konsequenzen für Individuen und Organisationen. Vor dem Hintergrund gesellschaftlicher Veränderungen wie Digitalisierung, Globalisierung und zunehmender Polarisierung bleiben zwar grundlegende Mechanismen von Bias bestehen, zugleich verschieben sich relevante Benachteiligungsgründe und Auswahlkontexte. Während Befunde bezüglich der Sichtung von Lebensläufen etwa auf abnehmende Geschlechtsunterschiede hindeuten, gewinnen andere, ebenfalls tätigkeitsirrelevante Merkmale—wie Weltanschauung, Sexualität oder religiöse Zugehörigkeit—insbesondere durch neue, digitale Auswahlinstrumente und einhergehende Informationszugänglichkeit an Relevanz. Das vorliegende Symposium greift diese Entwicklungen auf und untersucht in fünf Beiträgen Bias in digitalen Personalauswahlprozessen aus unterschiedlichen Perspektiven.
Das Symposium beginnt mit einer experimentellen Studie (N = 195), die die wahrgenommene Legitimität von Benachteiligung aufgrund politischer Gesinnung und Einstellungen zu sexueller Orientierung in der Personalauswahl untersucht.
Anschließend befassen sich zwei Beiträge mit Cybervetting, also der Nutzung sozialer Medien für frühe Auswahlentscheidungen, meist in Ergänzung zum Screening von Lebensläufen. Beitrag 2 (N = 334) betrachtet, wie das Zur-Schaustellen von Alkohol- oder Cannabiskonsum im Privaten die Wahrnehmung von Bewerbenden beeinflusst. Beitrag 3 untersucht (basierend auf realen Facebook- und LinkedIn-Profilen in einer mehrteiligen Feldstudie, N1 = 150, N2 = 200), welche Faktoren die Validität von Urteilen beeinflussen.
Die nächsten Beiträge widmen sich Bias in der Vorauswahl. Beitrag 4 untersucht in zwei Studien (N₁ = 160, N₂ = 1148), inwiefern Game-Based-Assessments über Stereotype Threat zu Geschlechterunterschieden beitragen können. Schließlich analysiert der fünfte Beitrag (N = 391), inwiefern Hinweisreize auf eine muslimische Religionszugehörigkeit die Bewertung asynchroner Videointerviews beeinflussen und ob eine 10-minütige Intervention potenzielle Gruppenunterschiede reduzieren kann.

Show details

Prof. Dr. Cornelius J. König

Viele Unternehmen betonen ihre Diversität oder richten eigene Abteilungen ein, um Vielfalt als Wettbewerbsvorteil zu nutzen. Gleichzeitig nimmt die Polarisierung zu, sodass Personen verstärkt eher homogene Gruppen bevorzugen. Diese Studie untersucht, wie sich dieser Widerspruch in Entscheidungen der Personalauswahl niederschlägt. Im Mittelpunkt steht die Frage, inwiefern Menschen diskriminierende Auswahlentscheidungen je nach Merkmal der betroffenen bewerbenden Person unterschiedlich legitim bewerten. In einem Szenario-basierten, zweifaktoriellen Between-Subjects-Design wurden zwei Merkmale der bewerbenden Person variiert: die politische Orientierung der bewerbenden Person (rechtsaußen: AfD vs. linksaußen: Die Linke) sowie die Einstellungen zu Homo- und Bisexualität (feindlich vs. befürwortend). Insgesamt 192 Teilnehmende bewerteten die wahrgenommene Legitimität der diskriminierenden Entscheidung hinsichtlich der wahrgenommenen Legitimität der Entscheidung, der empfundenen Schadenfreude und Bereitschaft zu Hilfeverhalten (Allyship). Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass Diskriminierung in den vier Bedingungen unterschiedlich stark legitimiert wurde und somit klar merkmalsspezifische Unterschiede bestehen. Hypothesenkonform wurde Diskriminierung gegenüber rechts-außen orientierten Bewerbenden (AfD) sowie gegenüber homo- und bisexuell-feindlichen bewerbenden Personen stärker legitimiert als gegenüber links-außen orientierten oder homo- und bisexuell-befürwortenden Bewerbenden. Zudem zeigte sich, dass sowohl allgemeine Ähnlichkeit als auch politische Ähnlichkeit mit der diskriminierten bewerbenden Person die Legitimitätszuschreibung verringerten. Insgesamt verdeutlicht die Studie, dass die wahrgenommene Legitimität von Diskriminierung in der Personalauswahl stark vom jeweiligen Merkmal abhängt und systematisch durch politische wie auch allgemeine Orientierungen beeinflusst werden kann.

Social Media Assessments – als Background Check oder als erster Eindruck im digitalen Recruiting – sind inzwischen eine weit verbreitete Praxis in der Personalauswahl zur Beurteilung von Bewerber:innen („Cybervetting“). Doch in der Literatur ist hoch umstritten, ob und unter welchen Bedingungen aus Social-Media-Profilen valide Schlüsse auf jobrelevante Merkmale gezogen werden können. In dieser Studie adressieren wir diese Kontroverse mit einem theoriegeleiteten, mehrteiligen Multi-Source-Feldstudiendesign: Aufbauend auf bisherigen meist experimentellen Ansätzen mit manipulierten Profilinhalten untersucht die vorliegende Studie reale Social-Media-Profile und berücksichtigt damit die große Varianz von Social-Media-Aktivitäten außerhalb kontrollierter Settings (Feldstudie). Auf Basis des Realistic Accuracy Model untersuchen wir so systematisch zentrale Faktoren, die die Validität von Social-Media-Assessments beeinflussen könnten, darunter der Typ der Plattform (professionell vs. hedonisch), die Kontextualisierung von Beurteilungsitems sowie die herangezogene Referenzquelle (Kolleg:innen- und Selbstratings). Wir präsentieren hier Erkenntnisse aus unserer Feldstudie, für die wir 150 Arbeitnehmer:innen aus den USA rekrutierten, deren Persönlichkeit (Big Five), kognitive Fähigkeiten und weitere jobrelevanten Charakteristika (u.a. berufsrelevante Werte) durch 200 Personalverantwortliche basierend auf ihren realen Facebook- und LinkedIn-Profilen eingeschätzt wurde. Wir vergleichen diese Social Media-basierten Eindrücke mit parallel erhobenen Selbstberichten, Kolleg:innen-Ratings, und Vorgesetzten-Ratings zur Arbeitsleistung als Indikatoren für Konvergenz und Kriteriumsvalidität. Durch diesen Beitrag tragen wir zu einer differenzierteren Perspektive auf das in Forschung und Praxis sehr unterschiedlich bewertete Cybervetting von Bewerbenden bei und diskutieren, unter welchen Bedingungen Social-Media-Inhalte eine valide Ergänzung etablierter Auswahlverfahren darstellen können.

Ein potenzielles Problem an ihrem Einsatz ist jedoch, dass durch ihre Verwendung ggf. unter anderem Frauen im Vergleich zu Männern benachteiligt werden, da sie oftmals schlechter in GBAs abschneiden. In 2 Studien untersuchten wir, wie groß Geschlechtsunterschiede in verschiedenen GBAs ausfallen, in denen komplexe Simulationsaufgaben wie die Leitung eines fiktiven Unternehmens bearbeitet werden sollen. Zudem überprüften wir, ob Stereotype-Threat zu möglichen Geschlechtsunterschieden beiträgt, d. h. ob es zu einer Beeinträchtigung der Leistung von Frauen kommt, die dadurch ausgelöst wird, dass diese befürchten, durch ihre Leistung ein negatives Stereotyp über Frauen im Allgemeinen zu bestätigen. In Studie 1 mit studentischen Versuchspersonen (80 Männer, 80 Frauen) fanden wir deutliche Unterschiede zu Ungunsten von Frauen in drei verschiedenen GBAs. Zudem wurden diese Unterschiede im Vergleich zu einer Kontrollbedingung größer, wenn Stereotype Threat induziert wurde. In Studie 2 mit 344 Bewerberinnen und 804 Bewerbern, die ein GBA im Rahmen eines Auswahl-ACs bearbeiteten, fanden wir ebenfalls deutliche Geschlechtsunterschiede. Zudem beeinflusste die Geschlechterzusammensetzung des jeweiligen ACs die Größe dieser Unterschiede. Der Unterschied fiel umso deutlicher zu Ungunsten von Frauen aus, je niedriger ihr Anteil im jeweiligen ACs war. Dies ist in Einklang mit Stereotype-Threat-Modellen und spricht dafür, dass Stereotype Threat die Benachteiligung von Frauen verstärken kann, wenn GBAs für die Personalauswahl verwendet werden. Vor diesem Hintergrund sollten der Einsatz von GBAs im Rahmen der Personalauswahl und die konkreten Durchführungsbedingungen sorgfältig abgewogen werden.

Einstellungsinterviews sind ein zentraler Bestandteil der Personalauswahl. Mit der Digitalisierung haben sich neue Formate etabliert wie asynchrone Videointerviews (AVIs), in denen Bewerbende ihre Antworten auf Video aufzeichnen und Unternehmen diese im Nachgang bewerten. Trotz ihrer Vorteile ist der Einsatz von AVIs auch mit Herausforderungen verbunden. Signale der Gruppenzugehörigkeit – etwa das Tragen eines Hijabs oder Symbole im Videohintergrund – können stereotype Wahrnehmungen auslösen und Bewertungen verzerren. Obwohl Derous et al.’s (2016) Dual-Process Framework nahelegt, dass Training solche Verzerrungen reduzieren kann, ist die Evidenz zu kurzen, praktikablen Interventionen in AVIs begrenzt. Beim Screening von Lebensläufen zeigte sich dabei unter anderem eine Structured-Free-Recall (SFR)-Intervention als erfolgsversprechend. Hier werden Bewertende darin geschult, sich auf tätigkeitsrelevante Informationen zu fokussieren. Entsprechend zielte diese Online-Studie darauf ab, zu untersuchen, ob Signale islamischer Zugehörigkeit die Bewertung einer Kandidatin in AVIs verzerren und ob ein SFR-Training diesem Effekt entgegenwirken kann. Hierfür wurden 391 Versuchspersonen (67,3 % weiblich; MAlter = 29,6 Jahre; 51,7 % Studierende) zufällig einer von drei Trainingsbedingungen (SFR-Intervention, Kontroll-Training, kein Training) zugewiesen. Anschließend beurteilten sie eine Kandidatin, bei der die Sichtbarkeit islamischer Signale manipuliert wurde (Hijab, Symbole im Videohintergrund, beide, keine). Widererwarten zeigte sich eine Bevorzugung der Kandidatin mit islamischen Signalen, insbesondere beim Tragen eines Hijabs. Diese Verzerrung konnte durch die SFR-Intervention teilweise reduziert werden. Die Ergebnisse deuten darauf hin, dass SFR-Trainings ein vielversprechender Ansatz zur Förderung von Fairness in der Personalauswahl sein können, jedoch in realen Auswahlkontexten weiter geprüft werden sollten
