Agency, Control, and Efficacy Beliefs as Drivers of Collective Behavior
Chair(s) Dr. Fabian Heß ( Friedrich-Schiller-University Jena)
Room: BG
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

This panel examines how the human need for agency and control shapes collective action across contexts of socio-ecological transformation and ideological conflict. Integrating meta-analytic, theoretical, and experimental evidence, we position collective agency, group-based control restoration, and efficacy beliefs as core psychological mechanisms of mobilization in times of environmental and political crises. First, Karen Hamann presents a two-stage meta-analysis synthesizing 59 efficacy belief intervention studies (140 effect sizes). The meta-analytical findings reveal a small overall effect of efficacy beliefs on pro-environmental action and show that theory-based interventions yield the greatest effects. Next, Johannes Lautenbacher introduces the Agency-Indicator-Model as a framework for the emergence of collective agency beliefs. Findings from three studies show how perceptions of group goal consensus, capability of coordinated action, and group impact on the social environment initiate and motivate collective action. Then, Wanda Drabon demonstrates that threatened personal control polarizes support for climate activist groups. Left-wing individuals increase support under control threat, whereas conservatives respond with rejection, pointing to an ideological boundary condition of group-based control restoration. Finally, Fabian Hess contrasts significance-quest theory and group-based control theory as social psychological explanations for radicalization. Across two experiments disentangling control and significance threats, only control threat increased radical responses, challenging significance-quest accounts. Together, these contributions advance a unified perspective on collective action and behavior, positioning collective agency, efficacy, and group-based control restoration as central psychological mechanisms underlying pro-environmental engagement, activism, and radicalization.

Unveiling the Causal Antecedents and Consequences of Environmental Efficacy Beliefs: A Meta-Analytic Review of Interventions
Karen Hamann | Leipzig University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Karen Hamann | Leipzig University | Germany
Christina Juchem | Health and Medical University Potsdam | Germany
Anna Becker | Leipzig University | Germany
Eva Asselmann | Health and Medical University Potsdam | Germany
Immo Fritsche | Leipzig University | Germany

Efficacy beliefs are a major driver of individuals’ engagement in both private and collective action, especially in the context of socio-ecological transformation. Despite their central role, causal evidence linking efficacy beliefs to pro-environmental behavior remains somewhat ambiguous, with many experiments facing challenges in manipulating these beliefs. We present a two-stage meta-analysis synthesizing 59 intervention studies (140 effect sizes, 2009-2024) that targeted efficacy beliefs and pro-environmental action. The meta-analysis integrates data from diverse cultural contexts (e.g., Germany, Taiwan, Turkey, USA), from predominantly Western countries. The analysis includes both online and offline interventions, as well as both general public and student samples. Approximately 60% of participants across studies were female. Our analyses reveal a small overall effect (d = 0.19). Stronger effects occurred in female and student samples. Importantly, the efficacy type addressed in interventions moderated our results. We therefore systematically coded intervention characteristics, testing predictions from self-efficacy theory, the triple-A framework, and recent scholarly proposals. Our findings indicate that the main predictors proposed by self-efficacy theory hold (e.g., mastery experience, positive affect), and that direct manipulations of efficacy beliefs targeting the triple-A facets produce stronger effects than other manipulations. Based on this evidence, we aim to advance self-efficacy theory for understanding the antecedents and consequences of efficacy beliefs in large-scale collective crises.

The Agency-Indicator-Model (AIM)
Johannes Lautenbacher | Leipzig University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Johannes Lautenbacher | Leipzig University | Germany
Immo Fritsche | Leipzig University | Germany

Collective agency beliefs are pivotal in initiating and maintaining collective action. However, the underlying factors that determine their emergence are not well understood. Previous research primarily focused on the efficacy aspect of collective agency (i.e., the belief that a group can achieve its goals). We propose a broader construct of collective agency. Drawing on theories of personal control, we identify three central aspects constituting agency beliefs: agents that mobilize means to achieve desired ends. In the context of collective agency, this requires a group to perceive itself as a single agent, with a consensus on central group norms and goals. Moreover, the group must feel capable of coordinated action (means) to achieve these norms and goals. Only with these two aspects can the group's impact on its environment (ends) truly reflect collective agency. This new perspective emphasizes the importance of intragroup processes, such as the formation of group norms, rather than merely intergroup processes. We present three studies (N = 2,021) conducted in Germany and the United Kingdom, aiming to validate a new three-factorial measure of collective agency beliefs. These studies provide empirical support for our theoretical reasoning and offer novel insights into the antecedents and consequences of collective agency beliefs and, consequently, collective action.

Losing Control, Choosing Protest? Left-Wing Support for and Right-Wing Rejection of Climate Activist Groups in Response to Threatened Control
Wanda Drabon | Free University of Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Wanda Drabon | Free University of Berlin | Germany
Dr. Fabian Heß | Friedrich Schiller University Jena | Germany

The appeal of climate activist groups can be understood as a group-based response to threatened personal control, insofar as such groups may serve as “collective resources” for restoring a sense of control through identification and engagement. Rather than depending on whether these groups are perceived as moderate or radical, group support in response to threatened control may hinge on perceived collective agency (Stollberg et al., 2015) and ideological alignment with one’s political orientation (Hess et al., 2025). In Study 1 (N = 182), we manipulated the salience of personal control threat and assessed perceived attractiveness, identification, and engagement intentions toward a moderate (Fridays for Future) and a radical (Last Generation) climate activist group. When perceived group agency was low, control threat reduced identification with Fridays for Future, but had no effects on support for Last Generation. Across both activist groups, political orientation moderated threat effects: Among (far-)left-wing, but not conservative, participants, control threat increased support across groups. Study 2 (N = 266) manipulated control threat in the context of sustainable energy production and group radicalism (moderate vs. radical) using fictitious climate activist groups in a 2×2 design. Interaction effects with perceived agency were non-significant. However, political orientation again moderated threat effects: Irrespective of group radicalism, control threat increased group engagement intentions among (far-)left-wing respondents but reduced attractiveness and intentions to engage among conservatives. These findings identify political orientation as a key boundary condition for group-based control in the climate domain. For left-wing individuals, climate activist groups may function as control-restoring resources, whereas threatened control can elicit opposing effects (i.e, rejection) among more conservative individuals, potentially deepening ideological polarization. In contrast, whether perceived group agency facilitates effective control restoration may depend on broader contextual factors, such as societal acceptance of the group.

Radicalization: Significance-Quest or Group-Based Control Restoration?

Authors:

Significance-quest theory (SQT; Ellenberg & Kruglanski, 2024) explains radicalization as arising from a threatened (or incentivized) need for personal significance–the desire to matter and be respected–in interaction with social networks promoting radical narratives. Similarly, group-based control theory (GBCT; Fritsche et al., 2024) argues that radicalization results from a threatened need for personal control, particularly when one’s social identity is tied to radical group norms. An open question is whether these accounts reflect two distinct, independent motivational pathways to radicalization, or whether only one motive (significance vs. control) fundamentally drives radicalization–obscured by diffuse manipulations rendering both threat types simultaneously salient. Resolving this requires new experimental paradigms that disentangle threats to personal significance from personal control. In Study 1 (N = 289 opponents of the AfD), we manipulated control threat using an imagination task in which participants envisioned their megaphone failing at a political protest (vs. functioning properly); additionally, significance threat involved imagining being ignored (vs. admired) by the protest audience. Consistent with GBCT, but contrary to SQT, simple effects indicate that only threatened control increased support for radical anti-AfD actions. We replicated this pattern in Study 2 (N = 348 AfD-opponents) using compromise refusal toward the AfD as the outcome variable. Here, control threat was manipulated by imagining accidentally (vs. intentionally) donating groceries to homeless individuals; additionally, significance threat was manipulated by imagining being mocked as a show-off (vs. receiving social approval) for this donation. Again, the control-related rather than the significance-related threat increased radical responses, supporting GBCT. Finally, we discuss the conceptual and methodological challenges and prospects of disentangling the two types of threat.

Topic: Digital Transformation and AI

Digital interventions represent a promising frontier for promoting well-being and quality of life in later adulthood. The SMART-AGE randomized controlled trial (RCT; N = 648) examines the effects of a multi-domain, app-based intervention targeting social participation, technology acceptance, physical fitness, and health awareness among community-dwelling older adults. This symposium brings together four contributions that explore theoretical, empirical, and methodological insights from the study. Hans-Werner Wahl and Anna-Lena Schubert introduce the conceptual framework of digital interventions as psychological interventions in the context of aging. They discuss challenges related to sample representativeness, context effects (urban site differences), the modeling of intraindividual change, and the interpretation of technology use metrics as meaningful psychological outcomes. Nicole Memmer investigates whether a socially stimulating digital intervention leads to changes in analogue social-emotionally outcomes such as loneliness and social support in everyday life. Verena Kölsch focuses on health-related psychological outcomes, including awareness and health locus of control. Findings of both of these analyses highlight the potential of digital interventions to enhance health-related beliefs and behavior in older age. Finally, Alica Mertens explores whether digital stimulation outside the cognitive domain can lead to measurable cognitive change over a six-month period, using data from different intervention constellations. Together, the contributions provide a multifaceted view of digital interventions as tools for psychological change in later life.

Evaluating Digital Interventions for Older Adults: Conceptual, Methodological, and Analytical Challenges from the SMART-AGE Trial

Hans-Werner Wahl
Show details
Authors:
Anna-Lena Schubert
Hans-Werner Wahl

Experimental research on the psychological impact of prolonged digital technology use has focused almost exclusively on children and adolescents. Yet later adulthood represents another developmentally sensitive phase in which digital engagement may yield substantial benefits, but also reveal vulnerabilities, including limited technology skills and a social-emotional positivity effect that may foster uncritical acceptance of digitally provided information. The SMART-AGE RCT tested three app-based modules targeting social participation, health awareness, and physical fitness in 648 community-dwelling adults aged 67+, randomly assigned to full intervention, partial intervention, or active control. We address four issues central to ensuring psychological robustness in such evaluations. First, conceptually, we frame technology use as developmental self- and co-regulation, anchoring it within established developmental, motivational, health-related, and cognitive frameworks. Second, regarding recruitment, we analyze how variability in social-structural and psychological characteristics shifted across successive stages of sample development—from over 14,259 individuals initially contacted to 583 completers. Third, regarding validity, we discuss challenges in treating technology-generated data (e.g., frequency and duration of app use) as indicators of meaningful psychological processes. Fourth, regarding data analysis, we depart from common biomedical RCT practice by employing multi-group latent change score models within a structural equation modeling framework to estimate intraindividual change across study arms, increasing statistical power and enabling more rigorous assessment of intervention effects. Together, these considerations offer a methodological blueprint for future digital intervention research seeking to move beyond efficacy testing toward psychologically grounded evaluation.

Mental disorders are one of the most pressing health challenges of our time – in Germany and worldwide. In response to this crisis, the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR, formerly BMBF) established the German Center for Mental Health (DZPG, www.dzpg.org) in 2023 – the seventh German Center for Health Research, alongside existing centres focusing on neurodegenerative diseases, cancer, and cardiovascular disease.
The DZPG's long-term funding provides an exceptional opportunity to advance mental health research and improve prevention and early detection at all stages of life. Central to this endeavour is a genuinely interdisciplinary approach. From the outset, the DZPG has adopted a participatory approach, collaborating closely with individuals with personal experience of mental health issues to develop its research agenda.
The overarching goal is to measurably improve mental health in Germany throughout people's lives and strengthen the translation of research into practice. This keynote provides insight into the structure, vision, and early achievements of this nationwide initiative.

Live Long and Prosper: Behavioral Change for Planetary Health (Keynote Cornelia Betsch)
Room: Hemicycle
Topic: Psychology of Sustainable Behavior
Form of presentation: Keynote
Duration: 60 Minutes

Planetary health rests on a simple but demanding premise: human and planetary wellbeing are inseparable, and protecting one requires protecting the other. Climate protection and health prevention share a fundamental structure: both require decisions in which short-term individual costs are weighed against long-term, often collective benefits. Communication is an important (but not sufficient) link between scientific knowledge and behavioral change, and good intentions do not guarantee good outcomes. Drawing on psychological findings on vaccination decisions, the COVID-19 pandemic and climate action, this talk works through several intuitively appealing communication strategies (such as appealing to identity, correcting false memories, maximizing transparency about scientific uncertainty, or highlighting descriptive norms) that can backfire, deepening polarization or undermining trust rather than enabling coordinated action. Effective communication therefore has to start earlier: with the design of policies and interventions themselves, not merely with how they are explained. The talk closes with principles for behavioral-science-informed policy design, connecting psychological research on sustainable behavior to this congress's call to take responsibility in times of crisis and to build bridges toward a livable future.

Rethinking Edge Selection in Psychological Networks (Keynote Maarten Marsman)
Room: Room C
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Keynote
Duration: 60 Minutes

In psychology, graphical models are routinely used to study cross-sectional and longitudinal network relationships, including temporal relations in time series. In both settings, relationships are represented as edges in a network, and a central goal of the analysis is to determine which edges belong to the network and which do not. Contemporary approaches commonly combine regularized estimation with a model selection criterion for this purpose. I will argue that regularization is ill-equipped to answer this question, and support that argument with two empirical illustrations and a new preregistered simulation study comparing network estimation methods.

The central concern is that regularization cannot provide evidence for the absence of an effect. This matters in psychological networks because an absent relation may itself be a substantive finding: Conditional independence in a cross-sectional network, or the absence of a Granger-predictive relation in a temporal one. A regularized analysis estimates a network structure but cannot say whether a missing edge is supported by the data or merely lacks evidence for inclusion. Bayesian methods can make this distinction: They quantify the evidence for and against each edge and can therefore support an exclusion. A large-scale reanalysis of published psychological networks shows that for many edges the data provide compelling evidence for neither inclusion nor exclusion, making uncertainty about network structure part of the substantive conclusion. A Bayesian reanalysis of an empirical network further shows that violations of the sparsity assumption can substantially distort the estimated network and its structural features.

The preregistered simulation study, using generating models derived from eight empirical psychological datasets, compares Bayesian and regularized methods on edge weight estimation, uncertainty quantification, graph recovery, and out-of-sample prediction. Bayesian model averaging performed best overall, driven mainly by more accurate edge estimates and better-calibrated uncertainty intervals. Differences in graph recovery were concentrated in datasets with relatively small sample sizes, where it again performed best.

In sum, deciding which edges belong in a psychological network is a question of evidence, and regularization does not answer that question.

In den letzten Jahren konnte das Fach Psychologie einige Erfolge beim Einwerben größerer Verbundforschungsprojekte verzeichnen (z.B. DFG Graduiertenkollegs, Forschungsgruppen, Sonderforschungsbereiche, Exzellenzcluster). Trotz dieser erfreulichen Entwicklung besteht aber immer noch die für die Psychologie spezifische und wiederholt diskutierte Diskrepanz zwischen dem sehr erfolgreichen Einwerben von Einzelprojekten und dem oft ungenutzten Potential, wenn es um die federführende Initiierung und Leitung von koordinierten Programmen oder größeren Verbundprojekten geht. Psychological Research Methods in the Age of AI (in German)
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Andreas Frey (Goethe-Universität Frankfurt am Main)
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Mirka Henninger (Institute of Psychology, University of Basel)
Prof. Dr. Johannes Hartig (DIPF I Leibniz-Institut für Bildungsforschung und Bildungsinformation)
Dr. Dirk U. Wulff (Max Planck Institute for Human Developmen)
Prof. Dr. Andrea Hildebrandt (Carl-von-Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg)
Prof. Dr. Augustin Kelava (Universität Tübingen)
Room: Room C
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Panel discussion
Duration: 60 Minutes

Scientific Psychology stands at a turning point. Artificial intelligence (AI) methods are no longer just tools but are entering the core of psychological research itself. Large-language models, machine learning, and other AI methods already support hypothesis generation, study planning, test construction, data processing, statistical analysis, automated reporting, academic writing, and research synthesis. Used correctly and responsibly, these AI methods promise gains in efficiency, measurement precision, and more transparent workflows. At the same time, the integration of AI raises fundamental questions about good research practices and the skills required of psychological scientists. If central tasks of scientific inquiry such as theorizing, study design, operationalization, data collection, statistical analysis, and academic writing are outsourced to computer systems, the profile of human scientific expertise may drastically change, requiring new competencies in oversight, critical evaluation, and human–AI collaboration. The written word, as the traditional cornerstone of psychological cumulative knowledge acquisition, may be diluted by machine-generated texts. A potential result are texts that read well but that are not substantively precise and thus of limited value to describe, explain, and predict human experience and behavior. AI-assisted or automated statistical analyses may amplify biases in training data or overlook methodological aspects such as model assumptions or measurement scales. At the same time, carefully implemented AI systems could support assumption checks, robustness analyses, and error detection, strengthening methodological rigor. Furthermore, the increasing dependency of psychological research on proprietary software and infrastructures operated by global technology companies raises concerns about data protection, replicability, long-term accessibility, and autonomy of science. This panel brings together experts in psychological research methods who are using AI for scientific research or are examining AI in psychology as a research topic to critically discuss both the opportunities and the risks of AI in psychological research. Based on this, we will elaborate on potential future standards for a responsible and modern integration of AI into psychological research.

This meta-analysis updates and extends van Eerde and Klingsieck’s (2018) review of procrastination interventions by including studies published between September 2016 and December 2025.
Relevant records were identified through systematic searches in PsycINFO, Google Scholar, ERIC, Web of Science, Business Source Premier, and PubMed. Following Harrer et al. (2022), we calculate Hedges’ g as the group difference between experimental and control groups at post- and follow-up measurements, test for heterogeneity and potential risks of bias, and consider additional moderators such as the mode of delivery.
Until now, we have analyzed studies until September 2023. Of the 1,323 records identified, we included 18 control-group studies (k = 27 pre-post-comparisons, N = 2077; k = 11 post-follow-up-comparisons, N = 461). Overall effect size g when comparing experimental to control groups at post-measurement was -1.30, [-1.83; −0.78], p < .0001, being a larger effect size than in 2018. Contrary to the results in 2018, the follow-up measurements showed a significant decline −1.0405 [-1.76; −0.32], p = .0090.
The results reveal significant heterogeneity at post- (I2 = 90%) and follow-up measurement (I2 = 83 %). For intervention type, no significant moderating effect was found; however, in-person interventions showed a larger reduction of procrastination (g = -1.38, [-1.81; −0.94], p < .00; I2=75%) than digital or blended interventions. Eggert test results showed that a publication bias is likely (Z = -3.60 [-5.99; -1.21], p = .0071).
At the conference, all studies until December 2025 will be included, and results will be updated accordingly.

Dr. Iris Blotenberg | DZNE | Germany
Show details

High-resolution digital cognitive tools administered at frequent intervals enable the study of age-related cognitive change with unprecedented granularity, and computational modeling allows multiple aspects of performance to be examined simultaneously. Using the Boston Remote Assessment for NeuroCognitive Health Face–Name task in cognitively unimpaired older adults, we captured memory consolidation across seven days, repeated approximately every six months. Computational modeling of response times (RT) allowed us to separate age-related decline from practice effects and to deconstruct performance into process-based cognitive markers. We examined the paradigm’s sensitivity to age-related decline and estimated the direction of age effects on speed, stability, learning, and forgetting. Daily median RTs from participants in the Harvard Aging Brain Study and affiliated cohorts who completed multiple testing intervals over several years were modeled using a Bayesian double negative exponential model with embedded regressions for age, sex, education, and device. Peak speed slowed with age, and higher age was associated with steeper long-term slowing, greater day-to-day variability, reduced long-term learning, and greater forgetting. Higher educational attainment was linked to faster peak speed, less long-term slowing, and more long-term learning. These findings demonstrate that a digital multi-day learning paradigm combined with computational modeling of RTs sensitively detects age-related cognitive decline over relatively short timescales and identifies specific cognitive markers—slower speed, reduced stability, and diminished learning—associated with aging. Associations with education suggest that these markers may reflect modifiable influences and could serve as sensitive targets for interventions aimed at preserving cognitive function.

Show details

Behavioral experiments vary widely in design and reporting, limiting comparability and slowing cumulative theory building. Mapping the full space of task variables through large coordinated projects is informative but costly and difficult to scale. We therefore explore a complementary strategy: using a foundation model of human decisions as a domain-general cognitive simulator to study behavioral patterns in silico before collecting new data. If such a model generalizes beyond its training data, it can simulate behavior across broad combinations of environmental variables and help identify which paradigms produce meaningful differences before resource-intensive studies. To assess this possibility, we evaluate Centaur, a Llama 3.1–70B model with low-rank adapters fine-tuned on the Psych-101 behavioral dataset, together with two reference models, the base Llama model and a random-choice model. We focus on decision-from-experience tasks. Psych-101 serves as an in-sample benchmark. Out-of-sample tests use the large Decision-from-Experience database, a public resource developed by our team containing 3.8 million individual choices across 168 studies. It is divided into DfE-in, which shares feature structures with the training data, and DfE-out, which includes novel feature combinations. All tasks are converted into standardized prompts, and models generate trial-by-trial choices. We assess predictive accuracy and log-likelihood at the study level. Performance is expected to decline from training data to familiar and then novel paradigms, indicating generalization limits. Task-level differences will show where simulation remains reliable or breaks down, clarifying how LLM-based cognitive simulators can prioritize conditions, refine theories, and allocate empirical resources more efficiently.

We present the Extended Moral Foundations Vignettes (eMFV), a standardized, validated stimulus database for moral judgment research. The eMFV expands the original Moral Foundations Vignettes (Clifford et al., 2015) in important ways by systematically adding and varying three theoretically central features: moral foundation, actor agency, and moral valence. Each of 400 concise scenarios depicts a moral or immoral action reflecting one – and only one – of nine moral foundations reflecting recent theoretical advancements of Moral Foundations Theory: physical care/harm, emotional care/harm, equality/inequality, proportionality/disproportionality, liberty/oppression, loyalty/betrayal, authority/subversion, purity/desecration, and ownership/theft. The eMFV also contain social norm scenarios serving as a “morally neutral” control. Actor agency was manipulated along five dimensions (direct/indirect, active/passive, voluntary/coerced, individual/group, intentional/accidental). The full set was developed in English and also translated into German to broaden the applicability of the eMFV and to enable future cross-cultural comparisons. In validation studies conducted online via Prolific Academic, English (N = 800, 30 scenarios/participant) and German (N = 540, 20 scenarios/participant) participants rated pseudorandom subsets of vignettes on moral rightness/wrongness, realism, and the extent to which different moral foundations were represented. Results show high perceived realism and clear differentiation across moral foundations. The eMFV provide an open-access, standardized, and cross-linguistically validated tool for advancing research on moral cognition and judgment.

Age-discordance is defined using a norm-calibrated cutoff depending on country, survey year, and respondent age. We further test whether links between personality and age-discordant partnering vary by gender, couple gender composition (same- vs. different-gender), age, education, income, ethnicity, migration status, and country context, clarifying for whom and under which conditions personality is associated with age-discordant partnering. As such, this study provides the first cross-cohort and cross-national estimates of how personality is associated with age-discordant partnering, and identifies when these associations are amplified or attenuated across demographic and sociocultural contexts.

About 40% of the German population speak a dialect that differs from Standard German. Consequently, many children grow up hearing a dialect at home that is different from the language they encounter in school. However, these effects disappeared after two years of formal schooling. All effects were controlled for SES and sex. These findings suggest that although children who are exposed to dialect at home begin school with weaker Standard German spoken language skills, these early differences do not lead to lasting disadvantages in language or literacy development.

How to Replicate, Explain and Migitate the Minority Salience Effect
Kim Keller | Institute of Psychology Heidelberg University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Kim Keller | Institute of Psychology Heidelberg University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Andreas Voss | Institute of Psychology Heidelberg University | Germany

The minority salience effect describes the tendency to overestimate the prevalence of minority groups in perception and memory, observed in both laboratory experiments and naturalistic settings. This series of studies aims to replicate, explain, and mitigate the effect using a combination of behavioral experiments, field studies, and computational modeling.
First, we replicate the minority salience effect in a laboratory setting and in the field. Additionally, we examine whether perceptual exposure to population compositions, compared to providing accurate numerical base rates, affects support for diversity-related measures.
Second, we systematically test four proposed explanations for the effect. Using varied stimulus materials, we examine whether overestimation is driven by a general overestimation of small numbers, perceptual advantages of minority characteristics, the salience of unexpected stimuli, or a bias through motivated reasoning. We apply diffusion decision modeling to assess motivated reasoning and attentional mechanisms, testing whether salience is reflected in higher drift rates and whether preexisting biases manifest as response biases.
Finally, informed by these findings, we develop and evaluate interventions designed to reduce the minority salience effect. We present the results from an initial pilot study, which demonstrates the feasibility of a model-based explanatory approach.

Dr. Danna Oomen | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany
Teresa Nguyen | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg
Valerie Ferrari | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Oliver Genschow | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany

It is widely accepted that subtle differences in the wording of questions can influence eyewitness reports. One of the most influential studies supporting this claim was conducted by Loftus and Palmer in 1974. The authors showed that simply replacing a single word in a question about a car accident that participants witnessed changes how fast they remembered the cars to be. Despite its widespread impact for different research disciplines, close replication attempts of this misinformation effect have been sparse and evidence for it inconclusive. We conducted five high-powered and preregistered experiments (total N = 5,779) to closely replicate and extend the original research. Overall, we did not find support for the idea that the wording of questions asked about a witnessed car accident influence estimates of vehicular speed (Hedges’ g = 0.08) or related impressions. Only in cases where participants had no active memory of the accident, we found that more drastic words describing the accident were related to higher speed estimates and accident severity. These findings indicate that although slight variations in questions’ wordings influence reports about accidents, mere changes in wording cannot overwrite the memory representation of an actually witnessed accident.

Integrating the Fragmented Literature on Counterproductive Work Behavior: A Secondary Meta-Analysis of Antecedents and Outcomes
Sophia-Aileen Schadow | University of Rostock, Germany | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Sophia-Aileen Schadow | University of Rostock, Germany | Germany
Prof. Dr. Bernd Marcus | University of Rostock, Germany | Germany

Counterproductive work behavior (CWB) is pervasive and costly, impairing organizational effectiveness, employee well-being, and social functioning at work. Despite extensive research, the literature remains highly fragmented. Similar behaviors are examined under different umbrella constructs (e.g., counterproductive work behavior, workplace deviance, workplace aggression) and at varying levels of behavioral specificity. This terminological plurality and disciplinary segmentation have led to conceptual overlap, redundant empirical findings, and limited theoretical integration.
The present project addresses these challenges by conducting a large-scale secondary meta-analysis that synthesizes existing meta-analyses on CWB. The objectives are twofold: (a) to systematically integrate findings across related constructs and levels of specificity, and (b) to develop and empirically ground an integrative theoretical framework capturing antecedents and outcomes of both broad and specific forms of CWB. Eligible meta-analyses are classified into higher-order CWB constructs (e.g., counterproductive work behavior, workplace deviance, aggression) and specific behavioral categories (e.g., theft, abuse, absenteeism, sabotage).
A comprehensive literature search across major databases (1985–2025) resulted in approximately 100 eligible meta-analyses. The project is currently in an advanced preparatory phase. Ongoing work includes assessing overlap among primary studies, completing the systematic coding of antecedents, outcomes, and moderators, and finalizing the integrative theoretical framework. Quantitative synthesis will follow.
By integrating fragmented evidence, this project contributes to theory development in organizational behavior, represents one of the first comprehensive secondary meta-analyses in the CWB domain, and lays the groundwork for more coherent, evidence-based prevention and intervention strategies.
Keywords: Counterproductive work behavior; Secondary meta-analysis; Theoretical integration; Workplace deviance; Organizational behavior

Competing with Taylor Swift’s carbon emissions or: How a narrow focus of environmental psychological research prevents us from becoming relevant (Keynote Gerhard Reese)
Room: Plenary 1
Topic: Psychology of Sustainable Behavior
Form of presentation: Keynote
Duration: 60 Minutes

‘It’s the end of the world as we know it – and I feeeel fine.’ While it is quite debatable what former R.E.M. frontman Michael Stipe’s lyrics are really supposed to mean, they seem to capture what most people in the rich parts of the world may feel: Fine - because of the belief that whatever happens, there will be solutions. Technological, political, behavioural, or ‘saviour’-al. And the really bad things will happen to ‘them’, not to ‘us’. This thinking, however, is shortsighted at best, and doom-prone at worst. And we as psychologists? At least, we know what could have motivated us to do better. In the lab.
This talk will deliver a potentially uninspiring and truly bleak version of what our field should and could (not) do to understand, prevent and adapt to environmental crises. Among other issues, I will point out that a narrow focus on climate change mitigation left a void for understanding responses to other potentially life-threatening environmental crises, and that our collective ignorance as Western scholars is part of that problem. ‘All that time, we sat alone in our tower’, and sought to assess individual motivations, emotions and cognitions for change. And while these are all important parts of a system, we too often ignore the interlinkages within that very system and limit ourselves to few input and outcome variables. But hey – no such talk without a comprehensive model that resolves all these issues (not)! And what does all of that have to do with Taylor Swift? I am not sure, but we might figure out together, and no one needs to leave the talk crying in desperation.

Out of Our Minds: What is AI Doing to Us and for Us? (Keynote Yvonne Rogers)
Room: Room C
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Keynote
Duration: 60 Minutes

The phrase ‘out of our minds’ refers to how we externalise and offload various aspects of cognitive work through writing, drawing, talking and so on. In so doing, it helps us to articulate our half-baked ideas, partially-solved problems, generate new ideas and construct plans. AI is the latest technological tool that we use to do this. However, it is a very different kind of beast to the armoury of previously used computer-based tools. GenAI can amplify human cognition in extraordinary ways but sometimes at the expense of reducing the cognitive effort required to think, write, analyse, code, decide, and create, for ourselves. This can result in a paradox of effort where the extent to which we externalise is reduced leading to less satisfaction. Simply put, when we make the effort ourselves to perform a task it can be more rewarding than when we get AI to do it for us. How can we design AI tools to make cognitive tasks more effortful (rather than less) and in doing so more rewarding? In my talk, I will describe the research I have been doing investigating how best to extend human minds that can be both rewarding and challenging: enabling us to reason and make decisions more systematically through reflecting on our goals and intent.

Talent Development in the Context of Individual Differences: Intelligence, Personality, Motivation, and Creativity
Chair(s) Dr. Ann-Kathrin Jaggy (Hector Research Institute of Education Sciences and Psychology, University of Tübingen)
Co-chair(s) Dr. Benjamin Goecke (Hector Research Institute of Education Sciences and Psychology, University of Tübingen)
Room: HU
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Individual differences in intelligence, personality, motivation, and creativity are key drivers of talent development. Contemporary models postulate that the unfolding of talent is a multidimensional process where cognitive resources and non-cognitive traits interact to shape academic and creative achievement. This symposium explores how these characteristics contribute to the emergence, differentiation, and stabilization of talent across the lifespan, spanning from primary school to adulthood. The five contributions integrate diverse theoretical frameworks and innovative methodologies (e.g., machine learning, latent class analysis) to bridge research and practice. In the first contribution, Jaggy et al. employ a multimodal approach to identify key predictors of creative achievement in gifted adolescents. Goecke et al. then examine the early emergence and stability of gendered interest patterns in primary school children and how they relate to intelligence, personality, and academic performance. Meier et al. investigate the "mathematical cast of mind" as a specific predisposition for mathematical excellence beyond general intelligence. Shifting the focus to diagnostic challenges, Lellmann and Preckel address the operationalization of underachievement by comparing various statistical and person-centered methods. Finally, Preckel and Kauka provide evidence for the "hungry-mind hypothesis," demonstrating a systematic link between high cognitive ability and a high need for cognition. Taken together, these studies offer a broad perspective on how individual differences in key variables contribute to successful talent development. The symposium concludes with an open discussion of the individual contributions, led by Jörn Sparfeldt.

Prof. Dr. Ulrich Trautwein | Germany
Prof. Dr. Brent Roberts | United States

Extensive knowledge about creative achievements and their association with personality traits, motivation, and cognitive ability has been derived from univariate studies in adult samples. In contrast, research on children’s talent development often focuses narrowly on academic performance, overlooking creative achievements as developmental milestones early in life.
To better understand the nomological network of childhood creativity, this study took a comprehensive, multimodal approach to explore predictors of creative activities and (scientific and artistic) creative achievements (CAs) in N=431 gifted secondary school students. Using self- and parent-reports, performance tests, and a machine learning approach, over 40 theoretically derived predictors from personality, motivation, and cognitive domains were used to predict CAs.
Our results broadly aligned with the overall pattern of associations from adult samples but revealed important domain-specific differences. The most important predictors identified by the machine learning approach included openness, creative self-efficacy, artistic and investigative vocational interests, and divergent thinking. Beyond creative self-efficacy, which strongly predicted creative activities, structural equation modeling highlighted domain-specific predictive patterns: Intellectual curiosity (openness) and investigative interests were the strongest predictors of scientific creative achievement. In contrast, aesthetic sensitivity (openness) and artistic vocational interests were the strongest predictors of artistic creative achievement. Moreover, creative activities partly mediated the associations between personal characteristics and creative achievement.
Our findings underscore the multidimensional nature of creativity in gifted adolescents and highlight key factors by distinguishing robust predictors from simple correlates. We discuss the findings in relation to the nature of the gifted sample and the role of developmental context.

From an educational psychology perspective, interest is understood as a construct that is tied to subject matter, classroom experiences, and engagement in academic tasks. In contrast, interest research in adolescence and adulthood has primarily been shaped by vocational frameworks such as RIASEC. It remains unclear, how subject-related learning interests relate to later vocational interest structures, partly because interests are only beginning to take shape in early childhood and because age-appropriate measurement instruments are lacking. In this study, we present the development of a self-report RIASEC interest measure suitable for children in primary school. In a sample of more than 1,000 third graders, we assessed interests at the beginning and end of the school year. The items of the measurement instrument were constructed to theoretically align with the six facets underlying the RIASEC framework and were selected for the final instrument using Ant Colony Optimization. In addition to its psychometric properties, including structural validity, we report gender differences, developmental changes, and associations with fluid and crystallized abilities, parent-reported HEXACO personality dimensions, academic interests, and academic performance. Our findings revealed a RIASEC-like circumplex structure even in this young age group for both genders. Further, we found distinct interest profiles for girls and boys that are consistent with the gender-stereotypical patterns previously reported for older populations. Whereas general interest levels slightly decreased over time, profiles became more pronounced at the end of the school year. Associations with intelligence, personality, academic interests, and grades support the instrument’s convergent and discriminant validity.

Prof. Dr. Stephan Vogel | Austria
Prof. Dr. Roland Grabner | Austria

Understanding the sources of individual differences in mathematical abilities is considered essential by both researchers and society alike. Almost 50 years ago, the Russian psychologist V.A. Krutetskii proposed the concept of a mathematical cast of mind (MCOM), which he described as a predisposition to perceive the world through ‘mathematical eyes’. This MCOM should be particularly evident in gifted individuals, enabling them to acquire mathematical knowledge more rapidly and to achieve higher levels of mathematical performance. Although Krutetskii's concept is often referred to in models of mathematical giftedness, empirical attempts to measure it have been limited. Two consecutive studies aimed to identify tasks that capture aspects of the MCOM and to determine if these tasks contribute to an MCOM factor associated with mathematical achievement beyond intelligence. Austrian university students (Study 1: n = 80, mostly psychology students, data collection complete; Study 2: n = 80 STEM students, data collection ongoing) worked on tasks measuring the MCOM subcomponents of obtaining mathematical information (e.g., spontaneous focusing on numerosity, statistical learning), processing of mathematical information (e.g., mathematical creativity, switching between representations), retaining mathematical information (e.g., structured memory), and motivational tendencies. Results from Study 1 did not reveal an overarching MCOM factor, but the proposed subcomponents as separate latent factors. Additionally, motivational tendencies, but not the other subcomponents, were significant predictors of mathematical achievement. Together, these findings and the new results from Study 2 will provide further insight into the concept of MCOM and its potential as a reliable predictor of individual differences in mathematics.

Underachievement = Underachievement? A Comparative Study of Statistical and Non-Statistical Operationalization Methods
Julia Lellmann | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Julia Lellmann | Germany
Prof. Dr. Franzis Preckel | Germany

Academic underachievement refers to the discrepancy between an individual’s ability and actual achievement and is currently identified using various statistical (i.e., absolute split, simple difference, regression, Rasch) and non-statistical (i.e., nomination) methods. Previous research suggests that this variety results in divergent identifications, i.e., different methods produce different prevalences of underachievement and identify different students as underachieving. This impedes comparing research findings and deriving practical implications for interventions. However, findings are mixed depending on the methods studied. As previous comparative studies included only selected operationalization methods, an extended reanalysis appeared necessary. Our study systematically applies and compares the common methods to a sample of about 1,800 third and fourth graders and a subsample of high-ability students to describe overlaps and differences between the individuals identified as underachieving. In both samples, we expect the prevalences and identified students to vary by method with the smallest agreement between statistical and non-statistical methods. Continuous modeling of cutoff values complements our analysis. Further, we extend the variable-centered approaches with a person-centered approach (i.e., latent profile analysis) also considering emotional and social school experiences. We expect to find a latent student profile with high ability, low achievement, and maladaptive school experiences. The results aim at contributing to a better understanding of previous findings and might serve as an opportunity to rethink operationalizing underachievement and to conduct more informed future studies.

High Cognitive Ability is Associated with High Need for Cognition: Evidence for the Hungry-Mind Hypothesis from Five Independent Samples
Franzis Preckel | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Franzis Preckel | Germany
Carlotta Kauka | Germany

The Hungry-Mind Hypothesis suggests that people with high cognitive abilities (CA) have an active, exploring mind and a need for intellectual stimulation and challenge. This characteristic can be described as a high Need for Cognition (NFC), the tendency to seek out, engage in, and enjoy effortful cognitive activity. However, CA and NFC only show small meta-analytic correlations, but correlations do not inform us about individual combinations of CA and NFC within people, i.e. CA-NFC profiles. We investigated the Hungry-Mind Hypothesis, using latent class analysis on five independent samples of children, adolescents and adults, who were assessed using different CA tests (BIS-HB, BIS+, KFT 4-12+R, THINK 1-4) and NFC scales (NFC-Kids, NFC-Teens, short-form of the Petty-Cacioppo scale). Sample sizes varied from 422 to 2,380 participants (total N = 5,118); one sample provided data from two measurement points (nT1 = 1,035; nT2 = 937; 2-year time gap between assessments). In each sample, a model with three or four latent classes provided the best fit to the data. In all samples, the latent class with the highest CA also had a high NFC. No other latent class consistently emerged in all samples. In 50% of the samples, there were latent classes with average CA/NFC, low CA/NFC, low CA and average NFC, or average CA and low NFC. In support of the Hungry-Mind Hypothesis, these findings indicate systematic associations between high CA and high NFC.

New Perspectives on the Role of Social Identity in Coping with Stressful Events
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Nina M. Junker (University of Oslo, Psykologisk institutt (PSI))
Diana Usmanova (Goethe - Universität Frankfurt a. M.)
Room: AT
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Stressful events are a defining feature of contemporary life and pose major challenges for individuals, organizations, and societies. Although stress is often experienced and treated as an individual phenomenon, stressful events rarely unfold in isolation but are embedded in social contexts that fundamentally shape how stressors are perceived, understood, and managed. The Social Identity Approach to health and well-being is a well-established framework for understanding stress-related processes, and this symposium advances this tradition by offering new perspectives on the role of social identification in coping with stressful events. Building on and integrating various theories into the Social Identity Approach (e.g., the Transactional Model of Stress, Compensatory Control Theory, Group-Based Control Theory, the Dual Process Model of Bereavement Coping), this symposium integrates five complementary contributions that examine how social identities and identification shape coping at cognitive, motivational, and interpersonal levels and how social identification is shaped, in turn. Using various methodological approaches, including mixed-methods, experimental, cross-sectional and longitudinal data collections, and systematic reviews, the contributions demonstrate both beneficial and detrimental effects of social identity and clarify the conditions under which being part of a group facilitates or hinders coping with stressful events.
The symposium opens with research by Usmanova and colleagues, showing that stronger identification with one’s work group predicts more collective appraisals of stressful work events. Their longitudinal mixed-methods study demonstrates that collective appraisal complements individual appraisal by shaping threat perception and perceived group resources. The second talk by Häusser and colleagues shows that social support from ingroup members is perceived as warmer and attributed more altruistic motives than equivalent support from outgroup members. Their experimental studies help explain why identity-based support is a particularly effective buffer against stress. Building on that, a systematic review by Junker and colleagues on coping with child loss at work shows that social identities can both hinder and facilitate coping. While social norms and impression management may impede coping, shared identities can provide belonging and support, with important implications for organizational practice. Following this, the last two contributions focus on factors that contribute to increasing social identification. Lautenbach and colleagues address why individuals turn to groups when personal control is threatened. Their research shows that well-structured ingroups enhance perceptions of collective agency, which in turn restores personal control. At work, van Dick demonstrates how leaders who foster a shared sense of “us” enable collective coping processes that promote employee well-being. His contribution also highlights challenges related to dysfunctional support and individual differences in the need to belong.
Overall, this symposium contributes to applied social psychology by bringing together well-established perspectives on social identity, stress, and well-being across different theoretical traditions and methodological approaches. In doing so, the symposium weaves together a contemporary and nuanced portrait of research within the Social Identity Approach, providing a shared platform for future work and the refinement of identity-based interventions in organizational and applied settings.

This study examines how social identification shapes the way individuals appraise stressful situations. Drawing on the Social Identity Approach and the Transactional Model of Stress, we propose that individually perceived group identification predicts whether people frame stressors collectively (“we”) or individually (“I”). Using a longitudinal mixed-methods design with employees working in teams, we analyzed linguistic markers in stress-related narratives.
A total of 114 participants completed a survey assessing individually perceived group identification (Time 1) and, three to four weeks later, described a recent stressful work event in interviews (Time 2). Transcripts were coded for collective versus individual pronoun use. Stronger individually perceived group identification predicted greater collective (“we”) pronoun use in both primary and secondary appraisals but did not predict reduced individual pronoun use. These findings refine the transactional model of stress by suggesting that individually perceived group identification extends rather than replaces individual appraisal. The group becomes a salient psychological resource in evaluating threats and coping possibilities, indicating resource gain rather than cognitive replacement. This perspective broadens the Social Identity Approach to Stress by showing how group identification enriches individual stress appraisal.

Moreover, we predict that these effects are mediated by increased perception of warmth. In open answer formats and Likert scale ratings, participants were asked to indicate potential motives underlying the behavior of the support provider. In line with our predictions, we found that ingroup support was attributed to more altruistic and less egoistic motives as compared to outgroup support, and these effects were mediated by global perceptions of warmth. Because identification as a football fan might constitute a higher-order identity that transcends specific group memberships (football clubs), we exploratively examined participants’ identification strength as a football-fan as a moderator. A total of 51 studies from various disciplines and forms of child loss were included in this review. Besides consequences through role identities, we identified tensions and complementarities related to individuals’ social identities. Tensions add requirements that hamper employees’ coping, including impression-management and norm-conformity requirements. Conversely, complementarities provide resources that help in the coping process, including belongingness and social support. We develop recommendations for organizations, supervisors, and co-workers, as well as for future research considering these limitations.

Compensatory Control Theory posits that threats to personal control elicit a desire for structure and order, leading to greater endorsement of clear group structures. Prior research suggests that the (hierarchical) structuredness and stability of groups serve as heuristic cues for their agentic potential. Together, these findings support a novel integrative framework—the Utility Model of Certainty and Control—linking compensatory and group-based pathways of control restoration. We conclude by discussing how this model helps explain the motivational appeal of highly structured and action-oriented political groups, and how such dynamics may contribute to broader societal developments such as polarization and radicalization.

Identity leadership, which builds a shared sense of ‘us,’ helps employees identify more strongly with their teams, creating a powerful foundation for collective coping processes that drive health and well-being. This phenomenon is known as the "social cure" and this presentation advances our understanding of this process by investigating the specific mechanisms through which these benefits are transmitted. While prior work by Frenzel et al. (2023) established emotional and instrumental support as distinct mediators, we introduce dysfunctional support—unhelpful or negatively experienced team interactions—as a critical third facet that can undermine well-being. Furthermore, I examine the need to belong as a moderator, testing whether individuals with a stronger affiliative drive benefit more from identity-led teams. I present evidence from three studies (N=643), including one with flight attendants and two with working adults, mapping the relationships between identity leadership, team identification, the three forms of support, and various well-being parameters, including stress, burnout, and self-efficacy. A final confirmatory study (N=226) demonstrates that these relationships are stable and specific to identity leadership, persisting even when statistically controlling for other established leadership constructs, such as servant or inclusive leadership. Overall, this research program demonstrates that identity leadership is a crucial starting point for the social cure effect within teams. However, its ultimate impact on employee health is not uniform; the link to different well-being outcomes is uniquely mediated by distinct supportive and dysfunctional mechanisms within the team environment, with the individual’s need to belong shaping this dynamic.

DEVELOPMENTAL DYSLEXIA AND MULTILINGUALISM
Chair(s) Dr. Aliette Lochy (University of Luxembourg)
Co-chair(s) Prof. Dr. Christine Schiltz (University of Luxembourg)
Room: UK
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

This symposium brings together researchers focusing on cognitive and neural aspects of developmental dyslexia, with a particular focus on cross-linguistic perspectives, impact of orthographic transparency and bi/multilingualism. The symposium will be framed by a theoretical model of dyslexia that integrates orthographic and language-related factors, providing a conceptual backdrop for the discussion. It will then raise the practical challenge of diagnosing reading disorders in multilingual children, followed by the presentation of empirical evidence suggesting that dyslexia manifests differently depending on orthographic characteristics of the language. Finally, predictors of reading ability will be examined though two recent lines of research: first, findings from naturalistic paradigms to assess speech processing that enable cross- language comparison; and second, training paradigms demonstrating how learning trajectories can inform about later reading outcomes.

A multi-level model of dyslexia
Prof. Dr. Thomas Lachmann | University of Kaiserslautern-Landau (RPTU) | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Thomas Lachmann | University of Kaiserslautern-Landau (RPTU) | Germany

Developmental dyslexia is a neurodevelopmental disorder marked by unexpected difficulties in literacy acquisition, leading to poor academic achievement and possible secondary effects. A multi-level framework conceptualizes dyslexia across interconnected levels of a causal pathway, through which genetic influences are expressed and hierarchically transmitted under increasing modulation by individual learning-related traits, environmental factors, and cultural conditions. Risk factors may emerge at each level, increasing the likelihood of dyslexia, while transitions between levels are neither unidirectional nor inevitable, highlighting opportunities for prevention and intervention. We also consider the influence of different languages, writing systems and orthographies on skill development.

For regular words, however, no response was detectable in either dyslexic group while a lexical response was present in control participants. Culture and Psychology: How Cultural Differences Come About and Why They Matter
Chair(s) Dr. Ruben Laukenmann (University of St Gallen)
Co-chair(s) Prof. Dr. Tobias Ebert (University of St Gallen)
Room: FR
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Human life does not occur in a vacuum but is embedded within cultural contexts that shape how people think, feel, and behave. It is therefore essential to explain how cultural differences emerge and how they, in turn, shape psychological outcomes. This symposium brings together five talks that examine both the origins and consequences of cultural differences across a wide range of psychological domains. The first three talks focus on the causes of cultural differences, drawing on large-scale cross-sectional and longitudinal data. Talk 1 uses large-scale survey data (N = 4,268,616) on Big Five personality traits and residential biographies to study how personality traits shape relocation decisions. Results suggest that individuals selectively migrate to places that match their personality, thereby creating cultural differences in the prevalence of personality traits. Talk 2 examines the temporal development of cultural values and beliefs across 90 nations (N = 172,466) over the past two decades. The results indicate that cultures have not converged globally, suggesting that increasing globalization does not necessarily lead to cultural homogenization. Talk 3 draws on 13 years of longitudinal panel data (N = 42,362) linked to regional economic indicators. The results show that immigration concerns rise in regions experiencing poorer economic development, indicating that economic conditions play an important role in the emergence of cultural differences in immigration attitudes. The final two talks shift the focus to the consequences of cultural differences. Talk 4 surveys police officers (N = 648) in a northern German city about space-based stereotypes related to their patrol areas. Officers described areas with a higher proportion of residents with a migration background more negatively, illustrating how local cultural differences shape everyday policing. Talk 5 presents two large-scale cross-national experiments (N = 3,500) conducted in ten culturally diverse countries, in which participants interacted with AI systems. The studies find that the features that constitute perceived “human-likeness” vary systematically across cultural contexts, implying that design choices that foster trust in AI in one culture may undermine trust in another. In sum, by combining large-scale observational data with experimental approaches across diverse contexts, the symposium highlights the central role of culture in shaping human behavior.

Show details
Authors:

Previous research suggests that regions differ in personality and that these differences predict meaningful regional outcomes such as economic prosperity, health, and social cohesion. However, only little is known on how regional differences in personality emerge in the first place. Here, we combine concepts from sociology and personality psychology to suggest that selective residential choice drives the emergence and persistence of regional differences in the personality trait of Openness. Specifically, we argue that individuals show personality homophily in residential choice (i.e., they select themselves into areas with similar Openness to their own). We focus on Openness because compared to the other Big Five it is the most perceivable trait, shows the strongest geographic clustering, has the clearest associations with regional amenities, and drives residential mobility strongest. To test this argument, we use data from a large-scale online survey (GPIPP; N = 4,268,616 participants from the US). These data contain residential biographies, individual personality scores, and geographically aggregated personality estimates. We then use discrete choice models to analyze how the interaction of individual and geographical personality shapes residential choice. Aligning with our hypothesis, we find that individuals are drawn to areas with Openness levels similar to their own. Importantly, these effects hold beyond established effects of demographic and economic residential homophily, suggesting a unique effect of personality. In sum, our research (a) identifies personality homophily as a mechanism driving the emergence of geographic personality differences and (b) uncovers personality as a previously hidden, yet relevant factor in understanding residential choice.

Show details
Authors:
Anne Wendelken | University of St. Gallen | Switzerland
Dr. Jana Berkessel | University of Mannheim | Germany

Cultures are changing; a fact that today’s cross-cultural psychologists agree on, prompting various theoretical frameworks to explain why these changes occur. One common perspective focuses on globalization. Regarding culture, globalization is often linked to two key processes: homogenization, the increasing convergence of cultures, and hybridization, the emergence of new cultural forms through the blending of existing cultures. Against this background, we examine whether the world has become more culturally homogeneous. Using the newly developed Cultural Fixation Index and large-scale survey data on cultural values and beliefs, we analyze cultural distances among up to 90 nations (N = 172,466) across four waves spanning from 1999 to 2022. Additionally, we perform three robustness tests for a comprehensive answer to the research question. Our findings indicate that the world has not become more culturally homogeneous. However, the results are mixed and not consistent across robustness tests. To illustrate, under certain exclusion rules, such as only analyzing waves 4 to 6 or reducing the nation sample to only those nations surveyed in every wave, we observed a tendency toward homogenization, but not under all exclusion rules. While this study provides a starting point, further research is necessary to gain a more comprehensive understanding of global cultural change.

Prof. Dr. Tobias Ebert | University of St. Gallen | Switzerland

Attitudes toward immigration vary not only between individuals but also between regions, such that in some regions people tend to be more concerned about immigration than in others. But how do these regional cultural differences come about? Group threat theory identifies regional economic disparities as one likely cause. Specifically, it posits that in regions suffering from economic downturns, people perceive increased competition for scarce economic resources, leading immigrants to be seen as a threat to job security and financial well-being. As a result, concerns about immigration may increase in regions with poor economic development. This link is societally most important and has been widely studied. However, existing research relies primarily on cross-sectional or repeated cross-sectional designs, which cannot fully disentangle whether observed effects reflect true individual attitude change or shifts in underlying sample composition. What is therefore needed is evidence from longitudinal designs that track changes in immigration concerns within individuals over time. In this study, we provide such evidence by integrating historical regional economic data with longitudinal individual-level data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP; N = 42.362; 2007–2019). Using logistic two-way fixed-effects panel regressions, we show that rising unemployment at the federal-state level predicts increased concerns about immigration within individuals, even when controlling for individual unemployment experiences. In sum, our findings (1) suggest that economic disparities may indeed be a driver of regional differences in immigration attitudes and (2) highlight a core tenet of group threat theory: concerns about immigration are not confined to those directly affected by economic hardship but extend throughout the broader regional population.

How do police officers perceive the neighborhoods they patrol? Research on space-focused stereotypes suggests that urban spaces are perceived differently depending on the social groups ostensibly inhabiting those spaces. We surveyed 648 police officers in a Northern German city about the areas they primarily patrol. Responding to open-ended questions, police officers described each area and rated the valence of their own descriptors. Overall, patrol officers’ portrayals of areas were predominantly negative. Importantly, negativity of these space-focused stereotypes sharply increased with the share of residents with a migrant background (r = -.44). Moreover, analyses of open-ended descriptions revealed that areas with lower shares were often described as friendly, communal, affluent, and green; areas with medium shares as diverse, dirty, busy, disorder, and violence; in contrast, areas with high shares of residents with migrant background were described as diverse, dirty, crime-ridden, misery, and violence. These patterns mirror prior experimental findings among civilians, highlighting how demographic composition shapes police officers’ perceptions of place. Our findings underscore the real-world relevance of space-focused stereotypes and highlight how social environments may influence perceptions in everyday policing

Cultural Divergence in Human-AI Interaction: Anthropomorphism, Trust, and the Limits of Western-Centric AI Governance
Dr. Robin Schimmelpfennig | Max Planck Institute for Human Development | Germany
Show details
Authors:

Vinodkumar Prabhakaran | Google Research
Aida Davani | Google Research

Over a billion users worldwide interact with AI systems engineered to mimic human traits, triggering urgent debate about anthropomorphism and its potential to induce misplaced trust or emotional dependency. However, prevailing safety frameworks rely on theoretical assumptions derived from Western populations, overlooking the cultural dimensions that shape human-AI interaction globally. We address these gaps through two large-scale cross-national experiments (N=3,500) across 10 culturally diverse nations, involving real-time, open-ended interactions with a state-of-the-art AI system. We find that users' perceptions of AI human-likeness focus less on theoretical aspects often cited in policy (e.g., sentience) but more on experiential qualities (e.g., response speed, emoji use) but crucially, what constitutes "human-likeness" varies substantially across cultural contexts. We demonstrate that humanlike design causally increases anthropomorphism; however, downstream consequences for trust are culturally contingent: design choices that foster trust in some populations (e.g., Brazil) trigger opposite effects in others (e.g., Japan). This cultural variance challenges narratives of uniform risk in humanlike AI and reveals a culturally mediated landscape demanding adaptive approaches in AI governance rather than one-size-fits-all frameworks derived from WEIRD samples.

Das TriCORE-Modell der Radikalisierung
Dr. Mike Lüdmann | University of Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Mike Lüdmann | University of Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Lisa Schniesko | University of Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Annika Schillings | University of Duisburg-Essen | Germany

Im Vortrag wird das neu entwickelte und aktuell empirisch untersuchte TriCORE-Modell der Radikalisierung vorgestellt (Tri = Triple + CORE = Core Beliefs). Konträr zu monokausalen Prozessmodellen beschreibt das TriCORE-Modell die radikalisierungsdynamische Wechselwirkung eines Tripels aus Affekt, Kognition und Vertrauen in vier aufeinander folgenden Phasen. Gesteuert wird der Prozess maßgeblich durch zentrale Überzeugungssysteme als Mediatoren (beispielsweise Ungerechtigkeitsüberzeugungen), die sich von selbstbezogenen über generalisierte zu ideologisierten Core Beliefs entwickeln und die kognitive Verarbeitung prägen.
Ausgehend von begünstigenden Vorbedingungen in Phase 1 (bindungsbezogene Repräsentationen, geringes soziales Vertrauen, reduzierte kognitive Exploration) führen negative Erfahrungen (z.B. soziales Ausschlusserleben) zu einem allgemeinen Krisenmodus (Phase 2), gekennzeichnet durch ein Geflecht aus kognitiver Verengung, Unsicherheitsgefühlen und Vertrauensverlust. Extremistisches Denken (Ideologisierung) kann als vermeintlicher Ausweg aus der Krise fungieren und den Eintritt in Phase 3 (Radikalisierungsmodus I) markieren, gekennzeichnet durch kognitiv rigide Verarbeitungsmuster, die in Wechselwirkung mit ideologisierten Core Beliefs stehen, sowie Bedrohungsgefühle und ausgeprägtes Misstrauen. Bei unzureichender Selbstregulation folgt Phase 4 (Radikalisierungsmodus II), die durch Wut/Hass (bzgl. der abgewerteten Gruppen), kognitive Radikalität (z.B. Dehumanisierung) und einem ausschließlichen Ingroup-Vertrauen gekennzeichnet ist. Die phasenweise ansteigende Wahrscheinlichkeit des Anschlusses an extremistische Gruppe bzw. der Durchführung extremistischer Taten erreicht hiermit ihren Höhepunkt.
Aufgrund seiner Komplexität ermöglicht das Modell eine sehr differenzierte Beschreibung von Radikalisierungsprozessen und bietet zahlreiche Ansatzpunkte für Prävention und Intervention. Im Vortrag sollen erste empirische Ergebnisse zur Validität des Modells vorgestellt werden. Dabei sollen auch erste Ergebnisse zu den von uns eingesetzten indirekten bzw. impliziten Erfassungsmethoden von Radikalisierungstendenzen präsentiert und in ihrer Aussagekraft miteinander verglichen werden.

Evaluating Offender Treatment: Challenges and Outcomes
Dr. Martin Schmucker | FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Martin Schmucker | FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg | Germany

Offender treatment is often viewed ambivalently. On the one hand, it is considered essential and legally required in many jurisdictions. On the other hand, there is disagreement regarding its effectiveness. This is often fuelled by methodologically weak evaluations and ambiguous findings that come from these studies. Since studies take place in highly regulated field settings with many restrictions, the implementation of ideal research is limited. For example, it is difficult to form adequate control groups due to legal treatment obligations at least for certain offender groups. This talk will address the opportunities and limitations of study designs such as RCTs as well as quasi-experimental approaches such as regression-discontinuity or matching designs and why even the latter are often difficult to implement and what it would need to overcome these limitations. Alongside taking stock of the international research, the talk will draw on examples of recent primary studies conducted by our research team on the effects of treating sexual, violent and juvenile offenders in prison and in the community as well as a meta analysis of sexual offender treatment. Despite the difficulties, we cannot refrain from drawing conclusions. A pragmatic stance is promoted: While we need to remain cautious in interpreting results of studies with more or less serious limitations and acknowledge the lack of highest-quality research we still need to weigh the findings from less than ideal research to inform practitioners and policymakers. However, we also must inform them that we need their assistance to advance research in this area.

Human-centered implementation of AI in healthcare
