Wie die Gestaltung interner Kommunikation Mitarbeitendenloyalität beeinflusst: Eine Untersuchung anhand des Kommunikationsquadrats nach Schulz von Thun
Prof. Dr. Caroline Trautwein | IU Internationale Hochschule | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Caroline Trautwein | IU Internationale Hochschule | Germany
Sandrina Lorenz
Prof. Dr. Christoph Böhmert | Hochschule Aalen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Christine Flaßbeck | IU Internationale Hochschule

Fachkräftemangel, eine dynamische Umwelt sowie digitale Arbeitssettings fordern die interne Unternehmenskommunikation heraus, Bindung und Loyalität insbesondere bei jüngeren Mitarbeitenden gezielt zu fördern. Organisatorische Loyalität lässt sich als positive Bindung an die Organisation verstehen, die sich in der Bereitschaft ausdrückt, zusätzliche Anstrengungen bezüglich organisationaler Ziele zu unternehmen (Fettouh, 2022, S. 19). Bisher bleibt ungeklärt, wie interne Kommunikation gestaltet sein sollte, um Loyalität wirksam zu stärken. Aufbauend auf dem Kommunikationsquadrat (Sach-, Beziehungs-, Appell- und Selbstkundgabeseite) nach Schulz von Thun (1981) untersucht unsere Studie daher, ob die Betonung einzelner Seiten die vermittelte Mitarbeitendenloyalität erhöht.
In einem Online-Between-Subjects-Experiment wurden Erwerbstätige randomisiert einer von vier Seitenbetonungen zugewiesen. Als Stimuli dienten drei typische Inhalte interner Kommunikation (Benefits Kooperation, Schulung, Anerkennungsprogramm), jeweils in vier, den Seitenbetonungen entsprechenden, Varianten. Zwei Pretests (Stimuli Optimierung, Expertenvalidierung) stellten die intendierte Manipulation sicher. Die Hauptstichprobe umfasste N = 283 Erwerbstätige. Loyalität wurde mittels einer 3 Item Kurzskala erfasst (ω = 0,82; KFA stützt Eindimensionalität). Die Welch ANOVA zeigte einen signifikanten Haupteffekt der Seitenbetonung (F_{Welch} = 14,49, p < .001, η² = 0,132). Post-hoc Analysen (Tukey) ergaben, dass Beziehungs- und Selbstkundgabeseite zu höherer empfundener Loyalität führten als Sach- und Appellseite (alle p < .001), während sich zwischen Beziehungs- und Selbstkundgabeseite kein signifikanter Unterschied zeigte.
Wir schlussfolgern, dass loyalitätsförderliche interne Kommunikation wertschätzende Beziehungsbotschaften mit transparenter Selbstkundgabe (z. B. Werte, Motive) verbinden sollte. Dies gewinnt insbesondere in digitalen Arbeitsumgebungen an Bedeutung, in denen direkte und informeller Kommunikation seltener sind. Limitationen beziehen sich auf die Gelegenheitsstichprobe, das Online- Setting und potenziell intervenierende Variablen.

A Multi-Criteria Taxonomy of Measurement Noninvariance Effect Sizes: Guidance for Two-Group Comparisons in CFA and IRT Frameworks
Lisa Peuckmann | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Lisa Peuckmann | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany
Elisabeth Prestele | RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau
Dorota Reis | Universität des Saarlandes

Applied psychological research often relies on self-report instruments to measure latent constructs. Meaningfully comparing these constructs across groups requires assessing measurement (non)invariance or differential item functioning (DIF). Measurement noninvariance or DIF occurs when individuals with the same true construct value yield different observed scores. However, the binary classification of instruments as invariant or noninvariant offers little guidance on the practical impact of such measurement differences. To instead quantify the extent of measurement differences, numerous effect size measures have been proposed within confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and item response theory (IRT) frameworks. Using a human-guided approach with AI assistance during the search phase, we systematically reviewed the literature and identified 63 effect size measures for two-group comparisons. To assist applied researchers in selecting appropriate effect size measures to understand in how far measurement differences bias their observed results, we classified the effect size measures by multiple criteria, including but not limited to: framework (CFA vs. IRT), scope (item vs. scale), directionality (signed vs. unsigned), and whether they allow cancellation across levels of the latent construct or multiple items in a scale. Despite the abundance of measures, they are rarely reported in applied research. Our work aims to reduce barriers to their use by providing a comprehensive overview and practical guidance on incorporating effect size measures when evaluating measurement differences.

Effekte von Zielstrukturen im Arbeitskontext und sozialen Vergleichen auf emotionales Erleben und Erfolgserwartung von Wissenschaftler:innen
Ronja Steinhauser | University of Mannheim | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Ronja Steinhauser | University of Mannheim | Germany
Johanna Ott | University of Augsburg | Germany
Markus Dresel | University of Augsburg | Germany
Martin Daumiller | University of Freiburg | Germany
Oliver Dickhäuser | University of Mannheim | Germany
Stefan Janke | University of Mannheim | Germany

Wissenschaftler:innen stehen unter hohem Wettbewerbsdruck, und soziale Leistungsvergleiche spielen eine Rolle für Karrierechancen und Kompetenzerleben. Eine Lernzielstruktur, die den Fokus primär auf Kompetenzentwicklung legt, könnte helfen, gut mit dieser herausfordernden Karrieresituation umzugehen. Wir führten eine präregistrierte experimentelle Studie mit 327 Wissenschaftler:innen im Fachbereich Psychologie durch. Den Teilnehmenden wurde eine fiktive Arbeitsgruppe vorgestellt. In einem 2 (Zielstruktur) × 2 (Leistungsvergleich)-Design wurde ihnen ein Vorgesetzter zugeordnet, der entweder eine Lern- oder Leistungszielstruktur vermittelte, und sie lernten - über Profilseiten mit Informationen zu Publikationen, Promotionsdauer und Fördersummen - drei potenzielle Kolleg:innen kennen, die entweder alle sehr erfolgreich oder weniger erfolgreich waren. Anschließend schätzten die Teilnehmenden ihren erwarteten Erfolg in der Arbeitsgruppe ein und berichteten die beim Lesen der Vergleichsinformationen empfundenen Emotionen.
Die Konfrontation mit hoch erfolgreichen Kolleg:innen führte zu niedrigeren Erfolgserwartungen und zu einem stärkeren Erleben von Angst, Hoffnungslosigkeit und Neid, ging jedoch gleichzeitig mit stärker empfundener Inspiration und Stolz sowie geringerem Mitleid einher. Eine durch den Vorgesetzten vermittelte Lernzielstruktur führte im Vergleich zu einer Leistungszielstruktur zu geringer ausgeprägter Angst, Hoffnungslosigkeit und Mitleid.
Obwohl die Konfrontation mit einer erfolgreichen Vergleichsgruppe generell herausfordernd zu sein scheint, verursachte sie auch positive Emotionen (z. B. Inspiration). Eine Leistungszielstruktur scheint Vergleichssituationen generell herausfordernder zu machen – unabhängig vom Erfolg der Vergleichsgruppe. Dies könnte darauf hindeuten, dass Wissenschaftler:innen, die in einem Umfeld arbeiten, in dem leistungsbezogene Zielaspekte besonders salient sind, sich generell mit einer unsicheren Grundhaltung in Vergleichssituationen begeben. Eine stärkere Betonung einer Lernzielstruktur durch Vorgesetzte, könnte Wissenschaftler:innen dabei helfen, sozialen Vergleichen mit größerer Sicherheit zu begegnen.

What Ergodicity Means for Psychology
Prof. Dr. MANUEL VOELKLE | Universität Freiburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. MANUEL VOELKLE | Universität Freiburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Timo von Oertzen | Thomas Bayes Institut | Germany

Derived from ergodic theorems, it has been shown that in psychology results based on variation between individuals usually do not generalize to the individual level and vice versa (Molenaar, 2004). While the theoretical arguments remain undisputed, their implications for empirical research are subject of debate. Some researchers argue that unless ergodicity holds, between-person (BP) information cannot be used to infer within-person (WP) effects and vice versa. Other researchers try to establish conditions under which generalizations from one level to the other are possible. We demonstrate that a strict separation of the BP and WP level is almost never justified. Specifically, we show that ergodicity is not necessary to (1) improve parameter estimation of a WP model by considering BP information, (2) infer a causal effect at the WP level based on BP information, and (3) generalize results from a BP model to a WP model after conditioning. We conclude that in most psychological research we can neither expect BP results to perfectly generalize to WP results and vice versa, nor expect that BP and WP results are independent. Both are boundary conditions that are exceptions rather than the rule. We argue that most processes have an ergodic and a non-ergodic part, so that some information about the WP structure can be determined from the BP structure, and vice versa. Future research should focus on how to optimally leverage information from both levels to infer effects of theoretical interest at either level.

Arbeitszeugnisse und der g-Faktor der Arbeitsleistung
Prof. Dr. Klaus Moser | Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Klaus Moser | Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) | Germany
Prof. Dr. Cynthia Sende | Hof University of Applied Sciences

Auch wenn eine geringe Übereinstimmung zwischen Arbeitszeugnissen als Beleg für deren geringe Zuverlässigkeit kritisiert wird, werden sie bei der Personalauswahl intensiv genutzt. Wir zeigen, dass eine geringe Übereinstimmung zwischen Arbeitszeugnissen keine Überraschung ist, sondern aufgrund der Art des Verfassens von Arbeitszeugnissen zu erwarten ist. Allerdings ist sie ohnehin kein geeignetes Maß für die Reliabilität. Tatsächlich ist auch nach methodischen Verbesserungen nicht damit zu rechnen, dass die Übereinstimmung zwischen den Verfassern von Arbeitszeugnissen über .40 hinausgeht. Diese Annahme wurde exemplarisch anhand einer Stichprobe von 335 halbstrukturierten Arbeitszeugnissen von 120 Personen getestet. Mit einem Koeffizienten von 0,27 (0,31 nach Korrektur um die Unzuverlässigkeit des Lesens von Arbeitszeugnissen) ist die Korrelation zwischen Arbeitszeugnissen nur geringfügig höher als die Koeffizienten, die für unstrukturierte Empfehlungsschreiben berichtet wurden. Die Übereinstimmung zwischen Arbeitszeugnissen kann jedoch alternativ auch als Maß für die Arbeitsleistung an verschiedenen Arbeitsplätzen betrachtet werden und somit als Schätzwert für deren Stabilität, die bei > .40 liegt. Dies kann als Evidenz für die Existenz eines „g-Faktors der Arbeitsleistung“ interpretiert werden.

Position Paper: Theory /.Formal Modelling
Room: PL
Topic:
Form of presentation: Position Paper
Duration: 90 Minutes
Theory formalization in personality and social psychology: difficult, but worthwhile
Prof. Dr. Daniel Leising | TU Dresden | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Daniel Leising | TU Dresden | Germany

I will present an overview of a series of projects in which my collaborators and I attempted to translate key theoretical concepts from the personality and social psychology literature into a more formal language (i.e., math). Although often quite challenging, theory formalization bears many advantages over the mostly "narrative" theorizing that is still common in both fields. For example, formal theories are stricter in terms of the phenomena that they are supposed (not) to account for. Therefore, they afford more exact predictions. The use of formal theories also helps determine how different theories relate to one another, thus enabling more complex predictions and theory integration. Large quantities of narrative theory text may often be condensed to just a few mathematical expressions. Sometimes, the formal versions of seemingly different narrative theories (using different terminology) turn out to be highly similar or even redundant with one one. Identifying and eliminating such redundancies will help increase the efficiency of theorizing. All of these advantages are likely to help foster traceable scientific progress, which has often been bemoaned as lacking in these branches of psychology. I will also talk about some recent experiences I have had trying to teach theory formalization "hands on".

The Best of Two Worlds: Combining Formal Modelling and Empirical Data
Rahel Geppert | HMU Health and Medical University Erfurt | Germany
Show details
Author:
Rahel Geppert | HMU Health and Medical University Erfurt | Germany

It is well established that social psychology is facing a theory crisis, marked by fragmented explanations and limited cumulative progress. Formal modelling has been proposed as a possible route forward, yet it is often perceived as detached from empirical practice. In this Position Talk, I argue that formal modelling and empirical research should not be seen as competing approaches, but as mutually reinforcing components of a single scientific process.
The talk outlines how formal models can sharpen empirical data collection by making theoretical assumptions explicit, generating precise and testable predictions, and thus guiding data collection. Empirical data can then be used to constrain, calibrate, and refine formal models, increasing their ecological validity. When combined, these approaches form a recursive cycle in which theory and data continuously inform and improve one another.
I illustrate this recursive cycle using an agent-based model as a formal model of political polarization driven by justice-related personality traits. The example demonstrates how modelling can make the mechanisms linking individual differences to collective outcomes more precise, while empirical calibration enhances the model’s explanatory power and links it to more realistic outcomes. This example shows the benefits of closer integration of formal modelling and empirical research to help social psychology move beyond isolated findings toward more coherent, cumulative theory building.

Designing Work for Sustainability: Learning, Engagement, and Collective Action Across Levels
Chair(s) Dr. Marie Ritter (TU Braunschweig)
Dr. Hannes Schilling (TU Braunschweig)
Room: HR
Topic: Psychology of Sustainable Behavior
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

The socio-ecological transformation and the transition towards a circular economy (CE) are fundamentally reshaping work. While sustainability is often framed as an outcome of individual or organizational activity (e.g., energy and resource use, reduced emissions), it is equally a question of how work itself is designed, learned, enacted, and coordinated. Sustainable work design thus becomes a central psychological challenge: it requires simultaneous change at the individual, team, organizational, and societal levels, and it demands that ecological objectives be pursued without undermining social sustainability, employee well-being, or the quality and safety of work. This symposium brings together four empirical contributions that examine sustainable work design as a multi-level transformation task, spanning individual learning and proactive work design, team interaction processes, and broader organizational and value-chain contexts.
The first contribution, “How Work Design Enables Learning for Environmental Sustainability: A Systematic Review,” synthesizes evidence in a review on how employees develop sustainability-relevant knowledge and skills in everyday work settings. Moving beyond a focus on formal training programs and organizational learning structures, the review adopts a work design perspective and integrates motivational, social, cognitive, and physical job characteristics as antecedents of formal, informal, and self-regulated green learning. By structuring the field through the Work Design Growth Model, this contribution develops a framework that links work design to the development of “green skills,” thereby providing an evidence-based foundation for sustainable work redesign.
The second contribution, “Towards a Process Model of Playful Work Design in the Circular Economy: Insights from Blue-Collar E-Waste Recycling,” examines sustainability-relevant work in a context where ecological goals, efficiency demands, and safety requirements intersect. Drawing on qualitative case study data from e-waste recycling sites, the study conceptualizes Playful Work Design as a bottom-up form of proactive engagement in tightly scripted tasks. The findings highlight how material variability, temporal routines, and peer interactions can create opportunities for playfulness, while safety regimes and social tensions constrain it. Importantly, the paper illuminates potential risks—such as unsafe improvisation or exclusionary dynamics—thereby sharpening our understanding of sustainable work design as one that must balance engagement, safety, and social inclusion.
The third contribution, “From Individual Ideas to Collective Green Action: An Interaction Analysis of Sustainability Workshops in Organizations,” shifts the focus to the team level and asks how individual sustainability ideas become translated into collectively supported solutions. Based on video-based interaction analysis of organizational sustainability workshops, the study investigates micro-level communication processes through which teams construct shared understanding and develop actionable ecological measures. Results suggest that ideas gain implementation potential when they are actively taken up and elaborated by multiple team members, underscoring the role of interaction dynamics for collective sensemaking and solution quality in sustainability contexts. This paper advances sustainable work design by specifying the collaborative mechanisms that enable teams to turn individual intentions into collective action.
Finally, “Exploring the Twin Transformation in the Circular Value Chain: A Qualitative Study on Drivers and Barriers in Germany’s Circular Economy,” adopts a multi-level perspective on the interplay between digitalization and sustainability. Drawing on interviews across different positions within the circular value chain, the paper demonstrates how the same societal drivers (e.g., environmental regulation) may be experienced as enabling or constraining, depending on organizational context. Across the value chain, pro-environmental motivation emerges as a key driver. Yet particularly in end-of-life stages, employees are concerned about the accompanying digitization and possible job loss through automation—highlighting an important tension between ecological progress and social sustainability. This contribution thus deepens the symposium’s cross-level perspective by linking societal structures, organizational positions, and employee experiences within the circular transformation.
Together, these papers demonstrate that sustainable work design cannot be reduced to “green” outcomes alone: it requires psychologically informed approaches to learning, motivation, interaction, and multi-level coordination in circular work systems. The symposium concludes with an integrative discussion by Dr. Clara Kühner (University of Leipzig) who will synthesize the contributions and outline implications for theory and future research on sustainable work design.

How Work Design Enables Learning for Environmental Sustainability: A Systematic Review
Annelie Lorber | University of Bremen
Show details
Author:
Annelie Lorber | University of Bremen

The green transformation is rapidly changing job profiles and creating rising demand for “green skills” across sectors, driven by technological change and tightening environmental regulation, yet evidence points to substantial skill gaps ahead. Despite this relevance, research syntheses largely focus on organizational-level learning or the presence of green training programs, while systematic evidence on how employees actually learn for environmental sustainability at work remains fragmented. Much learning at work occurs outside formal programs, including informal and self-regulated learning processes. This systematic review examines how work design can promote learning for environmental sustainability. Specifically, it addresses (1) which work design characteristics foster formal, informal, and self-regulated green learning, and (2) what consequences such learning has. Guided by the Work Design Growth Model, the review links motivational, social, cognitive, and physical work characteristics to green learning processes and outcomes such as knowledge, skills, abilities and other characteristics.
A comprehensive search was conducted in Lens.org, SciTech Premium Collection, and Web of Science Core Collection, complemented by structured grey literature searches. Screening and extraction follow predefined SPIDER-based criteria, and evidence will be synthesized using a structured narrative approach. Data synthesis will be finished before the conference.
This review contributes to the literature by shifting the focus from institutional practices to individual learning processes. A rapid transition toward a Circular Economy (CE) depends on industries such as e-waste recycling. In these plants, dismantling work must meet strict quality and safety requirements while remaining engaging enough to sustain individual well-being, team productivity, and organisational retention. We conceptualise Playful Work Design (PWD) as a bottom-up phenomenon through which workers inject fun or challenge into tightly scripted tasks without altering formal workflows. While PWD has been studied mainly in white-collar settings, little is known about how it emerges or is constrained in blue-collar work.
Following an interpretivist epistemology and a theory-elaborating approach, we employed a case study design, treating e-waste recycling as a single case with two sites as embedded units of analysis. Guided by a proactive motivation perspective on PWD, the study draws on 20 interviews with workers and supervisors, 80 hours of shadowing, and organisational documents. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis within an abductive, process-oriented framework.
PWD emerged episodically and was context-sensitive. Material variability, routine rhythms, and peer interactions opened windows for playful engagement, whereas safety regimes, supervisory control, and social tensions constrained it. Under certain conditions, playful initiatives shifted into risky improvisation, problematic competition, or exclusionary humour. These dynamics informed a process model capturing how PWD is initiated, negotiated, amplified, and constrained or redirected in blue-collar CE work.
The study positions PWD as a contextually embedded process in the Circular Economy, highlighting both its potential to sustain engagement in monotonous work and its inherent risks in safety-critical environments.

We conduct workshops (N = 19) in which employees collaboratively develop and plan ecological solutions for their organizations. Using an extended version of the act4teams-short coding scheme, the study is designed to examine how teams iteratively construct solutions through interaction. Preliminary insights from written action plans suggest that sustainability ideas are more likely to be included in measure plans when they are collectively discussed by multiple team members, whereas ideas mentioned without further team engagement rarely progress into concrete measures. In addition, the data indicate variation in the environmental reach of proposed solutions, providing initial descriptive indicators of outcome quality prior to full video coding. These observations will be systematically examined and validated through subsequent video-based interaction analysis.
The study contributes a process-based perspective on the emergence of sustainability solutions in teams and advances methodological discussions by demonstrating how interaction analysis can illuminate key mechanisms of collective green action.

The Twin Transformation, understood as a symbiotic process of change between digitalization and sustainability, presents organizations with new opportunities and challenges, such as the creation of sustainable workplace designs. Particularly in the circular economy, this transformation can have long-term positive effects on ecological sustainability and support the holistic implementation of circular economy principles. This study therefore examines how employees’ experiences regarding the drivers and barriers of the Twin Transformation in circular economy organizations differ depending on the company’s position within the value chain. Thirty-nine interviews with employees and managers from various companies involved in the circular economy in Germany formed the data basis for the subsequent qualitative content analysis. The analysis suggests, for instance, that at the societal level, environmental regulations are perceived by employees in design and production companies as driving factors for change within the Twin Transformation. In contrast, employees in collection and recycling companies tend to associate these regulations with increased bureaucratic effort and therefore regard them as barriers to the Twin Transformation. In addition, the importance of the employee level and its influence on the Twin Transformation is emphasized. Across the value chain, the motivation to protect the environment is described as a strong driver. However, this motivation exists in a field of tension, especially among employees in collection and recycling companies, because of fears of job loss resulting from increasing automation. The implications of the study are discussed particularly with regard to its novel multi-level perspective on the Twin Transformation within the circular economy.

Climate change communication can be an effective way to support climate-friendly behaviour. However, being confronted with one’s own limits and shortcomings regarding climate-friendly behaviour can lead to defensive reactions, such as psychological reactance. These reactions can affect attitudes as well as (communicative) behaviour. We examine how climate messages affect psychological reactance and willingness to discuss climate change in two preregistered experiments. In both studies, participants were presented with a short video explaining the life cycle of a shirt. In Study 1 (N = 442), we varied whether the climate impact of clothing was framed as an individual (e.g., buying clothes) or a non-individual (e.g., selling clothes) issue. The manipulation successfully increased perceived personal targeting and perceived freedom threat in the individual condition; however, no direct significant effect of the manipulation on reactance or willingness to discuss climate change was found. Perceived threat to freedom mediated the effect of individual framing on reactance. Exploratory text analyses revealed higher word counts in the individual condition, which was associated with a higher willingness to discuss. Study 2 (2 x 2 design) replicated the framing effects while also varying material type (photorealistic vs. illustrative). The findings of the studies emphasise the importance of careful message framing to minimise threats to freedom and foster constructive climate change communication.

Although these strategies share the same goal, people differ in their willingness to engage in them – even when global climate change mitigation is important to them.

Overall, the study offers important insights into relevant determinants of people’s engagement in climate-protection strategies and how such engagement can be effectively promoted.

Climate change is considered one of the most existential threats humanity has faced throughout history. It evokes distributive justice dilemmas of global scale. Who has access to clean drinking water? How should aid goods be distributed in humanitarian crises? (How) Should novel technologies to fight climate change be shared internationally?

The global community is advised to answer these pressing questions quickly – and to learn from a recent other emergency: During the COVID-19 pandemic, global leaders did not succeed in establishing an effective health resource distribution regime. As we have recently shown, this did not only contravene ethical and epidemiological advice, but also public preference: Both in 2021 and 2024, large representative samples in the UK and Germany preferred distributing scarce resources equally, equitably and efficiently, rather than prioritising countries based on merit or financial capacities.

Can insights on pandemic public opinion be extrapolated onto climate change, or do justice contexts show individual preference patterns?

For the current study, we recontacted our 2024 German sample in 2025. We adapted our justice measure onto climate change and asked the N=727 responding participants to rate twelve distribution strategies. Structural equation modelling analyses revealed large cross-sectional consistency across contexts (.58≤Cons≤.91). Moreover, pandemic preferences measured in 2024 were able to predict climate change preferences one year later (.11≤R2≤.38). Taken together, our data show that citizens' global distribution preferences can be similar across very different justice contexts. However, results also suggest that this does not discharge the global community of consulting citizens again and again.

The present study aimed to investigate these divergent findings, examining (a) the relationship of climate anxiety and other predictors like self-efficacy and social norms with climate-related outcomes, and (b) potential moderating effects of environmental identity and future time perspective. Climate anxiety was positively associated with both career-related climate considerations and pro-environmental behavior, even when controlling for self-efficacy and social norms. Environmental identity moderated the association between climate anxiety and career-related climate considerations, such that this link was stronger in participants with a stronger environmental identity. Our findings suggest that climate anxiety is neither uniformly harmful nor sufficient for climate action on its own. Especially regarding long-term decisions such as considering climate in career decisions, the relationship between climate anxiety and climate-related outcomes may in part depend on identity as well.

The Extended Moral Foundations Vignettes (eMFV): Development and Validation of a Combinatorial Moral Scenario Database
Sarah M. Müller | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Sarah M. Müller | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID) | Germany
Jun.-Prof. Frederic R. Hopp | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID) | Germany

We present the Extended Moral Foundations Vignettes (eMFV), a standardized, validated stimulus database for moral judgment research. The eMFV expands the original Moral Foundations Vignettes (Clifford et al., 2015) in important ways by systematically adding and varying three theoretically central features: moral foundation, actor agency, and moral valence. Each of 400 concise scenarios depicts a moral or immoral action reflecting one – and only one – of nine moral foundations reflecting recent theoretical advancements of Moral Foundations Theory: physical care/harm, emotional care/harm, equality/inequality, proportionality/disproportionality, liberty/oppression, loyalty/betrayal, authority/subversion, purity/desecration, and ownership/theft. The eMFV also contain social norm scenarios serving as a “morally neutral” control. Actor agency was manipulated along five dimensions (direct/indirect, active/passive, voluntary/coerced, individual/group, intentional/accidental). The full set was developed in English and also translated into German to broaden the applicability of the eMFV and to enable future cross-cultural comparisons. In validation studies conducted online via Prolific Academic, English (N = 800, 30 scenarios/participant) and German (N = 540, 20 scenarios/participant) participants rated pseudorandom subsets of vignettes on moral rightness/wrongness, realism, and the extent to which different moral foundations were represented. Results show high perceived realism and clear differentiation across moral foundations. The eMFV provide an open-access, standardized, and cross-linguistically validated tool for advancing research on moral cognition and judgment.

Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) offers a framework for understanding and explaining moral judgements and concerns. Apart from contextual influences, ethically and socially aversive personality traits play a key role in shaping the endorsement of the five moral foundations. Bayesian multilevel structural equation modeling was used and country-level variables were considered as moderators. These associations were more pronounced in countries culturally closer to the US (i.e., more WEIRD). The three foundations of ingroup/loyalty, authority/respect, and purity/sanctity were also negatively associated with D on average, but showed substantial cross-cultural variation both in strength and direction. WEIRDness and individualism further moderated these relationships. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of considering cultural context when analyzing the relationship between personality and moral concerns.

Psychologists have long recognized that the average person sees themselves as better than average, particularly in the moral domain. Previous research on self-other comparisons has identified where judgments reveal normative violations, but so far left unanswered whether people see themselves and others in an absolute positive or negative light. The present research introduces a novel measure, moral thresholds, that reflects people's idiosyncratic beliefs about the behavioral tipping point that differentiates being good from being bad. We find that participants consistently view themselves as moral (performing moral behaviors more often than required and immoral behaviors less often than what is condemnable; Studies 1-3). However, judgments of others are more nuanced: Although collectives are judged to fall short of the moral threshold, randomly selected individuals in those collectives—whether or not individuating information is provided—are perceived to be moral (Studies 2-4). We use an experimental causal chain design (Studies 4a-4b) to identify one reason for which individuals are afforded (greater) positivity: People anticipate feeling worse were they to be cynical about individuals, compared to collectives. These heightened anticipated negative emotions, in turn, result in more positive behavioral forecasts. Our results help explain how people can sustain positive impressions of interaction partners (individuals), all while harboring cynicism towards others in general (collectives). Moreover, the introduction of subjective moral thresholds allows the moral perception literature to join other psychological domains (e.g., monetary outcomes, attitudes) in which identifying such neutral reference points has proven to be theoretically and empirically relevant.

Markus Germar | University of Hildesheim | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Markus Germar | University of Hildesheim | Germany
Alexa Weiss | University of Bonn | Germany

Moral decisions are often studied in social isolation, even though they are inherently embedded in social contexts shaped by peers, groups, and societies. While it is well established that individuals tend to align their decisions with social consensus, evidence for such effects in moral decision-making has been inconsistent. Some studies suggest an asymmetric pattern—stronger conformity to deontological than utilitarian majorities—whereas others do not. The present research resolves these discrepancies and identifies the conditions under which asymmetric moral consensus effects occur. Across six studies (total N = 2,638), we found several distinct asymmetric consensus effects in sacrificial moral dilemmas. Participants consistently conformed to deontological and omissive majorities, regardless of the dilemma’s realism, causal structure, or outcomes. When confronted with a split (50:50) consensus, individuals again preferred the deontological option. By contrast, conformity to utilitarian majorities emerged only when the utilitarian choice represented an omission rather than an action. These findings show that social influence on moral decision-making is systematic yet context-sensitive. Moral conformity reflects selective use of social information that favors harm avoidance, omission, and the moral status quo, revealing how individuals navigate moral uncertainty through socially “safe” coordination strategies.

To highlight characteristics of this group, the present study examined group differences between individuals identifying and not identifying as femcels in potentially relevant variables relating to mental-health outcomes and sexual behavior and explored potential heterogeneity within the femcel population through latent profile analysis. These findings suggest substantial intra-group heterogeneity among women who self-identify as femcels, indicating potential differences in causes, pointing to differences in negative effects for others, and highlighting the need for tailored interventions that address varying symptom profiles.

Over the past decade, there has been exponential growth in individual-centered interventions aiming to reduce misinformation susceptibility and political polarization. Despite their differentiation and efficacy in controlled settings, initial real-world applications have raised questions about their effectiveness and practicality. This symposium shifts the focus from average treatment effects to examine potential shortcomings and real-world viability. We bring together research addressing three critical challenges: identifying the vulnerable populations that would benefit most from these interventions, assessing whether these populations are successfully reached, and evaluating the field effectiveness and heterogeneity of intervention outcomes. Research in the behavioural and social sciences has introduced several interventions aimed at improving users' competencies and behaviours to curtail the spread of misinformation. While such digital literacy interventions generally improve accuracy discernment, critical gaps remain regarding their targeted effectiveness and real-world uptake. This study addresses three key questions: For whom are digital literacy and boosting interventions most effective? Who voluntarily engages with these tools when given a choice? And does the act of self-selecting an intervention enhance its efficacy (a "self-determination" effect)?
To answer these, we employ a large-scale, pre-post experiment utilizing a representative YouGov panel (N = 7,000) across Germany and the United States. The design crosses assignment mechanisms (randomized vs. self-selected) with three intervention types (Inoculation, Lateral Reading, Media Literacy Tips) to disentangle tool efficacy from user motivation. We estimate Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE) and model uptake preferences, combining standard Bayesian regression and propensity score matching. By isolating the self-determination effect and assessing preference-efficacy alignment, this research moves beyond average treatment effects to understand user engagement, offering insights for designing scalable misinformation interventions.

Many intervention scholars concur that media literacy is crucial for distinguishing misinformation from facts. Consequently, enhancing skills like lateral reading, source evaluation, and understanding journalistic practices has proven not only efficacious in laboratory settings but have been adapted by non-academic stakeholders. Our study explores media literacy's relationship to misinformation resilience from a different perspective: Do consumers of alternative media hold a different concept of truth and employ verification strategies distinct from those taught in textbooks? Using qualitative data from 50 semi-structured interviews and two focus groups with Germans, we investigate how these individuals differentiate between facts and opinions and scrutinize the strategies they use to evaluate truthfulness. Our findings reveal a mirrored reality: alternative media users show high awareness of information practices and manipulation tactics, while employing epistemic strategies similar to those taught by media literacy literature. However, the fundamentally different information environment they engage with leads them to draw conclusions that still diverge from a shared reality. This study evaluates two interventions: a lateral reading intervention that trains users to assess the trustworthiness of online news sources by consulting external sources and a claim-focused search strategy that encourages searching for evidence behind specific claims made in online news articles. The latter strategy was previously found to backfire in a US sample which could be attributed to a particularly polarized information environment with high levels of misinformation in the subgroup with the strongest backfire effects (Aslett et al., 2023). Conducted with a nationally representative German sample (N = 2,666), our randomized controlled experiment found that both interventions improve the ability to discern trustworthy sources and credible claims from untrustworthy sources and false claims without backfire effects in Germany. Lateral reading also proved effective for supporters of populist and far-right parties – those with highest levels of misinformation exposure; and both strategies were particularly beneficial for younger and less-educated individuals. Behavioral data revealed that lateral reading increased on-topic browsing as well as online searches to identify untrustworthy sources, whereas claim-based search boosted immediate search activity and trust in credible information, indicating complementary mechanisms. Our findings suggest that combining the strategies and targeting specific demographics can help to enhance media literacy without backfire effects in a context characterized by overall low exposure to misinformation according to web-tracking data. However, effect sizes were very small, suggesting that behavioral interventions can only be one piece of a complex puzzle to increase societal resilience against misinformation.

Show details
Author:
Philipp Schmid

Meta-analytic results reveal that debunking is an effective means to mitigate the impact of health misinformation. According to a recent review of empirical evidence, debunkers should mention the misinformation explicitly, include an alternative, detailed explanation, and make use of credible sources. However, even after receiving a sophisticated debunking message, misinformation often persists in influencing individuals’ judgements and decision-making. This so-called continued influence effect of misinformation is, inter alia, the result of a lack of integration of debunkings into individuals’ mental models. This shortcoming of debunkings might result from a feeling of discomfort of the receiver when being corrected. In this talk, I present the results of an expert review that identified three psychological processes that might increase discomfort, undermine debunking effectiveness, and provide a barrier to updating beliefs. I will then present the expert reviews' results on how empathy and empathetic language might contribute to mitigating the three barriers and ultimately reducing the continued influence of misinformation. Thus, in the first part of the talk, I will present how common debunkings can lead to unintended effects like (1) increased perceived threat to underlying attitude roots, (2) increased perceived threat to face and (3) decreased perceptions of trustworthiness and therefore fail to neutralize the continued influence effect of misinformation. In the second part I will introduce empathy as a potential remedy and will discuss potential backfire effects of empathy when debunking misinformation.

Psychological and behavioural interventions play a key role in addressing societal challenges, but their real-world impact is the subject of heavy debate. Intervention rejection (where a person sees an intervention, considers participation, and decides against it) is extremely common, but very little research examines why this happens, and how intervention uptake can be optimised. In the first part of this talk, we propose a simple model for intervention rejection based on people's prior beliefs about intervention relevance, its effectiveness, and source reliability (Roozenbeek et al., 2025, Current Opinion in Psychology). In the second part, we move beyond individual-level interventions and explore the feasibility of psychologists enacting system-level change. Rather than approaching societal problems through a dichotomous “i-frame versus s-frame” lens (Chater & Loewenstein, 2022, Behavioural Brain Sciences), we argue that psychologists and behavioural scientists can and should play a role in informing system-level changes. While we cannot reasonably address the roots of many societal issues (e.g., kindly asking Vladimir Putin to stop spreading disinformation), designing interventions that illuminate how systems and individuals interact is firmly within grasp. As a case study, we discuss the Cambridge Online Trust and Safety Index (cotsi.org; Dek et al., 2025, Science), a website which tracks the daily price of fake accounts across countries and digital platforms. Though it is impossible to change the motivations of those who produce and spread inauthentic content, we can shed light on the infrastructures they use to do so, and find innovative ways to render it more expensive.

Let’s leave the Lab: Insights into Everyday Memory
Chair(s) Dr. Johanna Hartung (Universität Bamberg)
Prof. Dr. Gizem Hülür
Room: LU
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

A well-functioning memory is essential for everyday life. Given this importance, research beyond laboratory settings is needed, assessing memory in real-word contexts. In this symposium, we present five empirical studies that explore the assessment, nature, correlates, consequences, interventions of everyday memory across the adult lifespan.
Hartung et al. investigate how assessment frequency influences reports of subjective memory lapses (ML) in two studies with young adults, demonstrating that assessments of ML in daily live are only moderately related to retrospective reports and more frequent assessments yield higher lapse reports. Ballhausen & Brehmer asked younger and older adults to report ML seven times per day over six days. Younger adults reported more ML and prospective ML were more common and more consequential in everyday life. Von Glahn et al. study everyday correlates of ML and memory performance in a sample of healthy older adults with data collected three times daily over a 14-day period. Polk et al. present data from remote, unsupervised digital assessments in cognitively unimpaired and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) groups, showing that frequent testing captures short-term episodic memory decline in MCI patients and correlates with multi-year change on in-person assessments. Finally, Altgassen et al. explore interventions, showing a reduced intention execution in ADHD and beneficial effects of episodic future thinking on intention execution in everyday life.
Together, these studies highlight the value of ecologically valid methods in uncovering dynamic memory processes, individual differences, and potential intervention strategies in daily life.

Measurement Matters: Interval-Contingent, End-of-Day, and Retrospective Assessments of Subjective Memory Lapses in Two Experience Sampling Studies
Prof. Dr. Gizem Hülür
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Gizem Hülür
Johanna Hartung

This presentation synthesizes findings from two studies on subjective memory lapses. Study 1 used experience sampling to capture intraindividual variations in working memory performance and memory lapses over ten days with 325 university students. Using three daily assessments, we found a positive correlation of about .50 between retrospective and momentary reports of memory lapses. While retrospective evaluations were associated with lower working memory performance, interval-contingent reports of lapse occurrences showed no relation. Additionally, participants with higher average working memory performance perceived lapses as less interfering. Study 2 examines the effect of assessment frequency on reported memory problems with a final sample of 60 participants. They engaged in one week of end-of-day assessments and one week of three assessments per day, with the order of assessment frequency being randomly assigned. Findings revealed that participants reported more memory lapses on average during the week with the interval-contingent assessment compared with the week with end-of-day assessments. This was the case for the sum of all types of lapses as well as for all three types of lapses (retrospective, prospective, attentional) separately. Notably, average lapse frequencies between the two conditions were highly correlated (about .70) and both correlated with a retrospectively assessed memory lapse frequency at the end of the study period at about .50. Together, these studies highlight the complexity of measuring subjective memory, emphasizing the need for nuanced approaches. They reveal critical interactions between assessment methods, cognitive performance, and individual differences, paving the way for future investigations into everyday cognitive functioning.

Using ecological momentary assessments, naturally occurring memory lapses, their predictors and consequences, can be studies using shorter delays, improving ecological validity. 160 younger and older adults were asked 7 times/day over 6 days whether they forgot anything since the last assessment, how busy and social they were in the moment they forgot, how irritated, stressed and worried they were because of the lapse, along with other contextual information. At baseline, participants completed various cognitive tasks and filled in questionnaires on meta-cognition, personality, busyness, routine, and depression. The reported memory lapses were classified into prospective (PM) and retrospective memory lapses (RM).
Younger adults reported more memory lapses than older adults, and both age groups reported more PM than RM lapses. Preliminary analyses showed that PM lapses were overall linked to more negative consequences, while RM lapses were experienced as particularly negative in older adults. Analyses of interindividual and intraindividual predictors of memory lapses are currently ongoing and will be presented.
Using ecological momentary assessment, our results demonstrated more memory lapses in younger than older adults and more PM than RM. PM lapses seem to have strongest consequences in everyday life overall, yet RM lapses show a particularly negative impact in aging. Lastly, a better understanding of interindividual and intraindividual predictors of memory lapses, differing for memory types and age groups, will enable the development of targeted interventions.

Population aging is leading to a growing proportion of older adults in our society. Since old age is an important risk factor for cognitive impairment and neurodegenerative disease, the number of individuals at risk of cognitive decline is increasing rapidly. In contrast, knowledge regarding fluctuations of memory performance and memory complaints in the daily lives of older adults remains limited. In our current study, we investigate daily fluctuations in objective cognitive performance and subjective memory lapses among adults aged 60 and over. Using the experience sampling method, we are currently collecting data over a 14-day period, three times daily, from three groups: healthy older adults, older adults with subjective cognitive decline (SCD), and older adults with depression. Furthermore, we investigate the everyday correlates of memory lapses and memory performance as they relate to older adults´ daily experiences, such as physical and cognitive activity, social interactions and wellbeing. In this presentation, we will present preliminary results based on the group of healthy older adults (N ≈ 90).

Traditional pen-and-paper neuropsychological assessments are not sensitive to short-term cognitive changes in the earliest stages of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), limiting their utility for monitoring subtle disease progression. Here, we show that frequently administered remote unsupervised digital cognitive assessments may be better suited to capture short-term cognitive decline in early AD. We investigated episodic memory trajectories using self-administered remote digital testing in 202 participants (52–85 years, 58% female) who completed unsupervised tests for at least 30 weeks. We looked at feasibility of longitudinal remote data acquisition based on adherence. Linear mixed modeling was used to investigate main effects of cognitive status (n = 152 cognitively unimpaired [CU], n = 50 with mild cognitive impairment [MCI]), as well as interaction effects of cognitive status by time, that is, group differences in change. Analyses were repeated, stratifying the MCI group by amyloid-β (Aβ) status (nAβ− = 21, nAβ+ = 24). Change-change associations with in-person neuropsychological assessments were examined using Pearson correlations. A short-term decline in the familiarity-dependent recognition memory task was observed in all patients with an MCI diagnosis, while both the familiarity-dependent task and memory precision for objects task were sensitive to decline in the MCI Aβ+ group specifically. Change in remotely assessed familiarity-dependent memory was correlated with multi-year change on annual in-person neuropsychological assessments. Finally, in-person tests were not sensitive to short-term cognitive changes in MCI in a limited sub-sample. Altogether, these findings show that frequent remote cognitive testing is a promising tool to feasibly capture subtle, short-term cognitive decline.

Effects of Episodic Future Thinking on the execution of everyday intentions in ADHD

Authors:

Studies consistently report reduced prospective memory performance in adults with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), both in lab-based tasks as well as in everyday life. First empirical evidence shows that engaging in episodic future thinking (EFT; i.e., imagining executing the planned activity) during intention formation increases the execution of everyday intentions in adults with ADHD. Typically, studies that investigated the impact of EFT on intention implementation focused on envisioning the process of initiating and executing the intended actions; though, particularly for aversive tasks, focusing on the to be reached outcome may be more effective. This study aimed to investigate the impact of process- versus outcome-focused EFT on the execution of everyday intentions in participants with and without ADHD. Using a 2x3 between-subjects design, a total of 196 adults with ADHD and neurotypical controls were allocated to a process-, outcome-focused EFT condition or a standard encoding condition. The execution of everyday intentions was assessed with the diary task. Analyses of variance indicated significant differences between groups, with the ADHD group realizing less everyday intentions than the control group. Overall, both EFT conditions improved the execution of intentions relative to the standard encoding condition; performance was best in the outcome-focused EFT condition, followed by the process-focused EFT condition and last the standard encoding condition. There was no significant interaction effect. The study confirms previous findings of reduced intention execution in ADHD and of beneficial effects of EFT on intention execution in everyday life.

Theories and empirical findings suggest that interindividual differences such as personality traits predict the acquisition of social status. Furthermore, studies on hormonal mechanisms show that individuals with higher testosterone levels are more motivated to achieve higher status and exhibit more status-related behaviours. However, the relationships between personality traits and testosterone levels in relation to status acquisition are unclear. In a pre-registered experimental laboratory study, we investigated the effects of transdermal testosterone administration (versus placebo gel) on (interaction partner-reported subjective) social status in a competitive group interaction in men (n = 243) and women (n = 272) in same-sex groups (4-6 participants each). In addition, moderating effects of self-reported dominance, extraversion, and narcissism were examined. We predicted higher social status after testosterone versus placebo gel administration, as well as positive moderating effects of the three personality traits dominance, extraversion, and narcissism. Hence, this experimental study provides new insights into causal effects of testosterone on the acquisition of social status in face-to-face groups, as well as moderating influences of personality.

The Impact of Personality Traits on Sexual Satisfaction and Frequency of Sex: Does It Differ between Single and Partnered Individuals?
Dr. Martha Ottenbacher | University Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Uwe Jirjahn | University of Trier, Germany
Dr. Martha Ottenbacher | University Luxembourg | Luxembourg

Previous research on personality and sexual well-being has focused on individuals who are in a romantic relationship. Our study advances the literature by comparing the role of the Big Five personality traits in the sex life of partnered individuals and singles. Expanding the analysis to singles is timely as singlehood has increased around the world. Being a single does not equate to sexual abstinence. The sex life of singles is characterized by casual sex and, hence, by a shorter time horizon of sexual relationships. Thus, we hypothesize that personality traits should play different roles in the sex life of singles and partnered individuals. Using representative panel data, our study shows that the sex life of singles suffers from lower satisfaction and frequency of intercourse than the one of partnered individuals. Most importantly, our empirical analysis confirms that the role of the Big Five indeed depends on relationship status. While extraversion has a positive influence on the sex life of both single and partnered individuals, the influence is much stronger for singles. By contrast, the positive role of conscientiousness in sexual fulfillment is stronger for partnered individuals. Openness to experience and agreeableness play a positive role only in the sex life of partnered individuals. Neuroticism has a detrimental impact on people’s sex life with the impact being stronger for singles. Our findings fit theoretical considerations. Personality traits play different roles in the sex life of single and partnered individuals as sexual relationships of these individuals are characterized by different time horizons.

The Self as a Target of Positivity: Affective Foundations of Self-Esteem
Dr. Melanie Schliebener | Witten/Herdecke University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Melanie Schliebener | Witten/Herdecke University | Germany
Dr. Sascha Krause | Leipzig University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Michael Dufner | Witten/Herdecke University | Germany

Prominent theoretical accounts suggest that spontaneous self-related affective positivity is a key emotional building block of self-esteem. Previous research indicates that such self-related affectivity can manifest in pronounced physiological and experimental reactions to self-relevant stimuli. Building on this work, our study sought to further clarify how such affective measures relate to self-rated self-esteem as well as to personality and social outcomes more generally. In a sample of 236 participants, we used facial electromyography (EMG) and an affective priming task (APT) to measure spontaneous positive responses to pictures of the self, in comparison to reactions to pictures of unfamiliar others. We also collected self- and peer-reports of self-esteem and personality, as well as observer-ratings of self-secure behavior. The results indicate that even though the EMG and APT were uncorrelated, each of them was positively related to self-rated self-esteem. Both measures also showed links to personality and social outcomes. However, on most cases, these relations were mediated by self-rated self-esteem. Overall, the findings support the view that self-esteem is linked to spontaneous self-related affective positivity, even though its broader social consequences are primarily reflected in self-reports.

Keywords: self-esteem, affect, electromyography, priming

From daily dynamics to long-term development: Need satisfaction and Big Five personality across major life transitions
Paula Bange | Tilburg University | Netherlands
Show details
Authors:
Paula Bange | Tilburg University | Netherlands
Dr. Eeske van Roekel | Tilburg University
Dr. Manon van Scheppingen | Tilburg University
Prof. Anne Reitz | Greifswald University

Life transitions are pivotal periods for socioemotional and personality development, yet the mechanisms linking daily experiences to longer-term change remain poorly understood. This talk presents two complementary studies examining the interplay between basic psychological need satisfaction (autonomy, competence, relatedness) and Big Five personality during major life transitions at both daily and developmental timescales. Study 1 uses intensive experience-sampling data from two longitudinal cohorts undergoing the education-to-work transition (total N = 571). Using dynamic structural equation modeling, we test the bidirectional interplay between daily need satisfaction and Big Five personality states. Preliminary results show robust same-day associations: On days with higher need satisfaction, individuals reported more positive personality states. Ongoing analyses examine temporal dynamics and whether individual differences in these micro-level processes predict longer-term personality development. Study 2 uses propensity score-matched trait-level samples (N = 1,324) to compare individuals experiencing major life transitions (entering the workforce, becoming a parent, beginning cohabitation) with matched controls. We examine how need satisfaction and Big Five traits co-develop across these transitions. Together, these studies illuminate how need satisfaction may serve as a key mechanism through which major life transitions shape both daily personality expression and longer-term socioemotional and personality development.

In the Words of a Narcissist - Narcissistic Verbal Expressions in Everyday Life
Dr. Tobias Altmann | Universität Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Tobias Altmann | Universität Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Marcus Roth

Narcissism is typically studied as a dispositional trait, assessed through more or less abstract self-descriptions. Yet narcissistic tendencies are not only descriptions of oneself — they are enacted in social interaction and mostly realized in spoken language. The way individuals talk about themselves and others provides a direct window into how narcissism is experienced and expressed in real-life contexts. Focusing on naturally occurring verbal expressions may therefore reveal structural and relational aspects of narcissism that remain less visible in traditional approaches.
Using a new approach toward studying narcissism based on real-life verbal narcissistic expressions, we conducted three studies. First, we collected quotes uttered by individuals high in narcissism in real-life contexts. These expressions were systematically categorized into 29 content categories based on recurring themes of how narcissism is verbally enacted (Study 1). Based on these categories, we formulated 101 questionnaire items that closely preserved the tone and meaning of the original statements. Subsequent factor analyses identified four coherent components underlying these verbal expressions — experienced disadvantage, charisma, devaluation of others’ abilities, and devaluation of others’ morality — suggesting a multidimensional structure that complements existing models of narcissism (Study 2). Finally, we examined the relational relevance of these expressive components in a dyadic sample of couples. Specifically, we investigated how the four dimensions were associated with relationship satisfaction and contrasted their patterns with those obtained from an established narcissism measure (Study 3). The opportunities and limitations of using naturally occurring trait expressions as a basis for construct operationalization are discussed.

What makes a house feel inviting? Investigating human evaluations of facades using GANs

Kira Pohlmann | Max Planck Institute for Human Development | Germany
Dr. Nour Tawil | Max Planck Institute for Human Development
Prof. Dr. Timothy Brick | Pennsylvania State University
Dr. Ehsan Yaghoubi | Universität Hamburg
Prof. Dr. Simone Kühn | Max Planck Institute for Human Development

The built environment plays a central role in shaping psychological well-being, yet there is limited understanding of the visual features that underlie these effects. In two consecutive studies, we investigated how generative adversarial networks (GANs) can be used to model, analyse, and systematically manipulate the psychological impressions evoked by house facades, focusing on the evaluation dimensions of invitingness, hominess, relaxation, and safety. In the first study, we trained StyleGAN2-ADA on a dataset of 2000 house facades annotated with ratings from 204 participants. A separate group of 204 participants then evaluated the GAN-generated facades, indicating that human ratings aligned with the intended psychological attributes encoded in the model. Facades rated as, e.g., more inviting consistently exhibited specific architectural characteristics, including larger building size, more windows, and increased presence of greenery.
To further understand the influence of architectural structure and low-level image properties, we next employed StyleGAN2-ADA’s style-mixing function to generate 900 images combining fixed architectural features with systematic variation in visual style, such as brightness, colour, and contrast. These images were rated by 303 participants, and analysed using linear mixed-effects models. Results identified both architectural and style features to predict positive evaluations: two-storey houses were rated more favourably, as were images with higher proportions of green pixels, greater variability in brightness and saturation, and lower contrast. Together, these findings demonstrate that GANs provide a powerful framework for isolating and modifying visual features that shape psychological responses to architecture.

Antecedents and Carbon Impact of Climate-Protective Behavior: Contradictory Roles of Political-Economic Ideology and Environmental Consciousness
Severin Hornung | Universität Innsbruck | Austria
Show details
Authors:
Severin Hornung | Universität Innsbruck | Austria
Christine Unterrainer | Universität Innsbruck | Austria
Thomas Höge | Universität Innsbruck | Austria

Average greenhouse gas emissions in Germany and Austria by far exceed the estimated carbon budget to limit global warming to non-catastrophic levels. This study examined the psychological roles of system justification, the political-economic ideology of neoliberalism, and environmental consciousness in influencing climate-protective behavior and its resulting impact on the personal carbon footprint. An online survey (N=344) was conducted among students and employed persons (mean age 28 years; two thirds female). Established self-report scales measured general system justification (7 items), neoliberal ideological beliefs (22 items; subdimensions: individualism, competition, instrumentality), and climate-protective behavior (20 items; subdimensions: housing, energy, mobility, consumption, nutrition, activism). Environmental consciousness comprised three scales, specifically, attitudes towards environmental protection (15 items), ecological knowledge (8 questions), and felt connection with nature (5 items). Carbon footprint was calculated based on 14 questions according to a model by the German Federal Environment Agency. Control variables were age, gender, education, income, and social status. Statistical analyses included scale metrics, multiple regression, mediation bootstrapping, and structural equation modeling. Confirmed was a chain of serial mediation effects, connecting system justification, neoliberal ideology, climate-protective behavior, and estimated carbon footprint. Environmental attitudes, ecological knowledge, and connection with nature showed largely expected and partly differential effects on these constructs. Income level was a substantial predictor of carbon emissions. In conclusion, market-based consumer societies confront individuals with contradictory messages regarding climate-protection. While individual behavior change can impact the personal carbon footprint, counter-directed systemic forces, reflected in internalized political-economic ideologies, are bound to undermine efforts directed at ecological sustainability.

A systematic review of workplace aggression diary studies
Dr. Philipp Sischka | University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Philipp Sischka | University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Hannah Streubert | Fernuni Hagen
Prof. Karen Niven | University of Sheffield
Prof Sarah-Geneviève Trépanier | Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières

Background. Workplace aggression is among the most harmful work-related stressors, with detrimental effects well established in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Although most primary studies rely on cross-sectional designs, diary studies have become increasingly common in recent years. These designs allow researchers to examine short-term dynamics of workplace aggression and better disentangle cause–effect relationships. However, existing diary studies vary widely in methodological (e.g., sample size, measurement frequency) and substantive characteristics (e.g., type, source, and perspective of aggression). To date, no systematic review has synthesized this growing body of diary research.

Method. Following PRISMA guidelines, this study systematically reviews diary studies on workplace aggression. Searches in Web of Science, Scopus, and Ovid identified 3,321 records. After screening, 167 studies from 162 articles were included.

Results. The reviewed studies consistently document short-term negative effects of workplace aggression, including increased negative affect, reduced well-being, and impaired performance. Incivility was the most frequently examined construct, followed by abusive supervision, mistreatment, bullying, and deviance. Most studies adopted the target’s perspective, with client/customer aggression investigated most often, followed by supervisor aggression. Face-to-face aggression predominated over digital forms. Typical studies involved slightly more than 100 participants, used interval-contingent sampling, and collected data multiple times per day across 10–15 waves. Open science practices were rare: few studies shared data or syntax, and none were preregistered.

Conclusion. Diary research on workplace aggression has neglected perpetrator and bystander perspectives as well as online aggression. Substantial improvements are also needed regarding open science practices.

Information Type and Policy Acceptance: Evidence from Two Food Tax Experiments in Germany
Hellen Temme | Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Hellen Temme | Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine | Germany
Dr. Philipp Sprengholz | University of Bamberg
Dr. Mattis Geiger | Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine
Prof. Dr. Cornelia Betsch | Institute for Planetary Health Behaviour (University of Erfurt)

Changes in food taxes can facilitate sustainable food choices and reduce CO₂ from food production. Models of policy acceptance (e.g., Public Policy Acceptance Framework) identify perceived costs and perceived environmental impact as relevant factors. Two experimental studies examined whether personal financial costs (i.e., monetary price changes) (Study 1) and understanding the policy's environmental rationale (CO₂ emissions from food production) (Study 2) positively affect acceptance of a VAT change in Germany.
In Study 1 (N = 299), participants received monetary information about how a VAT increase for animal-based and a decrease for plant-based foods would affect the price of a typical grocery receipt. Concrete price information increased VAT acceptance compared to basic VAT information (d = .33).
In Study 2 (N = 974), participants learnt about the carbon footprint of foods by undergoing a seeding procedure where they estimated the carbon footprint of food items with corrective feedback on a subset, followed by re-estimation. While seeding improved the estimation (ηp² = .54), it neither increased policy acceptance nor perceived policy effectiveness (p > .05). Unlike the direct link between VAT and prices, the causal chain from VAT change to consumption change to CO₂ reduction is too complex for consumers and needs further explanation.
These findings suggest that tax changes aiming at reducing CO₂ emissions should be communicated with proximal rather than distal outcomes. Therefore, a preregistered follow-up experiment will test whether explaining the policy's steering mechanism while making CO₂ reduction tangible via seeding can increase policy acceptance and sustainable food choices.

Tiergestützte Interventionen in Psychiatrie und Psychotherapie: wie Tiere helfen können
Chair(s) Dr. Petra Schmid (University Ulm: Clinic for Psychiatry and Psychotherapy I)
Co-chair(s) Prof. Dr. Elisabeth Schramm (Universitätsklinikum Freiburg)
Room: BG
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Dass Tiere einen positiven Effekt auf die Gesundheit und das Wohlbefinden von Menschen haben können, ist hinlänglich bekannt. Auch in der Psychiatrie und Psychotherapie können Tiere bei unterschiedlichen Störungsbildern die Behandlung unterstützen. Tiergestützte Interventionen haben sich daher mittlerweile in der Psychiatrie und in der Psychotherapie etabliert. Die Wirksamkeit und die Wirkmechanismen tiergestützter Interventionen werden in empirischen Studien mit zunehmend besserer methodischer Qualität untersucht. In unserem Symposium werden neben einem Überblick über den aktuellen Stand der Thematik Ergebnisse einzelner Studien zu diesem Themenkomplex aus Deutschland und der Schweiz vorgestellt. Insbesondere interessiert dabei die Wirkung von Tieren auf Symptomreduktion, Achtsamkeit, Emotionalität, Funktionsfähigkeit, Lebensqualität und Selbstwirksamkeit bei unterschiedlichen Störungsbildern (Suchterkrankungen, Persönlichkeitsstörungen, Depressionen, Trauma).

Vortrag 1:
Ob Hund, Pferd oder Kaninchen – Tiere können Türen öffnen, wenn es in der Therapie schwierig wird. Doch was sagt die Forschung dazu? In diesem Vortrag werden die Grundlagen der Mensch-Tier-Beziehung anhand von Forschungsergebnissen beleuchtet und aktuelle Studien zur Wirksamkeit tiergestützter Interventionen bei unterschiedlichen Störungen vorgestellt. Darüber hinaus werden allgemeine und spezifische Wirkfaktoren diskutiert und anhand von aktuellen Beispielen aus der Praxis veranschaulicht. Zudem werden zentrale Aspekte der Qualitätssicherung sowie die notwendigen Voraussetzungen für professionelles Arbeiten mit Tieren beleuchtet.

Vortrag 2:
Tiergestützte Interventionen sind auch in der stationären psychiatrischen Behandlung zunehmend beliebt. In der vorliegenden Studie wurden die Auswirkungen der An-/Abwesenheit eines Stationshundes auf Emotionalität und soziale Interaktion bei komorbid und chronisch erkrankten Patient:innen einer psychiatrischen Suchtstation untersucht. Hierfür wurden in einem prospektiven Prä-Post-Design im naturalistischen Setting 50 Patient:inen ohne Einsatz des Therapiehundes und 52 Patient:innen mit Erfahrung mit dem Therapiehund, mittels Fragebogen zu den Themenfeldern soziale Interaktion/Stationserleben, Emotionalität und suchtpathologisches Verhalten befragt. Die Ergebnisse werden vorgestellt.

Vortrag 3:
Emotionsregulation ist die Fähigkeit, mit affektiven Erfahrungen umzugehen und sie zu modulieren. Defizite in der Emotionsregulation stehen im Zusammenhang mit der Entwicklung und Aufrechterhaltung von psychischen Störungen. Störungsmodelle zu Suchterkrankungen und zur Borderline-Persönlichkeitsstörung berücksichtigen defizitäre bzw. dysfunktionale Emotionsregulationsstrategien, welche zu Problemverhalten wie Substanzkonsum bzw. selbstverletzendem Verhalten und Suizidalität führen können. Ziel therapeutischer Interventionen ist es somit unter anderem, zu erleben und zu lernen, dass aktivierte unerwünschte Emotionen reguliert und positive Emotionen aktiv gestärkt werden können. Der Erfolg hängt hierbei maßgeblich von der eigenen Achtsamkeit, als einer wahrnehmenden, nicht-bewertenden, akzeptierenden Grundhaltung gegenüber dem aktuellen Erleben ab. Dies könnte durch eine zielgerichtete, manualisierte tiergestützte Therapie erreicht werden. Die Frage ist: gelingt es bei stationär-behandelten psychiatrischen Patient:innen mit Emotionsregulationsstörungen durch eine tiergestützte Intervention mit Schafen positive Emotionen, Achtsamkeit und Selbstwirksamkeit zu aktivieren und negative Emotionen zu reduzieren. Dies wurde in einem RCT mit 29 Suchterkrankten und 31 Patient:innen mit Borderline-Persönlichkeitsstörung im Vergleich zu treatment as usual untersucht.

Vortrag 4:
Tier- und naturgestützte Interventionen stellen vor allem in der Depressionsbehandlung einen Indikationsbereich dar. Dies gilt besonders bei Patienten, die im Rahmen früher zwischenmenschlicher Traumatisierungen (z.B. emotionaler Missbrauch) Schwierigkeiten haben, sich auf Psychotherapie einzulassen. Denn der Einsatz von Tieren wirkt vertrauensfördernd, angstreduzierend, motivierend und stimmungsaufhellend.
Zur Verhinderung von Wiederauftreten häufig rezidivierender Depressionen erwies sich ein tier- und naturgestütztes Achtsamkeitsprogramm bei 67 Patienten mit einer Vorgeschichte von Depressionen und frühen Traumatisierungen als gut durchführbar und im Langzeitverlauf wirksamer als eine herkömmliche Behandlung. Die Teilnehmer fühlten sich bei den Achtsamkeitsgruppenübungen durch die Naturumgebung sicherer und geerdeter als in einem geschlossenen Raum. Der Kontakt zu den Schafen wurde als äußerst hilfreich empfunden.
Aber genügt auch die Naturumgebung alleine, um zu positiven Effekten zu kommen? Im Rahmen eines Dismanteling-Designs vergleichen wir bei 24 Patienten die Wirksamkeit des Achtsamkeitsprogramms in der Natur mit versus ohne Begleitung durch die Schafe. Erste Ergebnisse werden vorgestellt.
