Hierfür wurden in einem prospektiven Prä-Post-Design im naturalistischen Setting 50 Patient:inen ohne Einsatz des Therapiehundes und 52 Patient:innen mit Erfahrung mit dem Therapiehund, mittels Fragebogen zu den Themenfeldern soziale Interaktion/Stationserleben, Emotionalität und suchtpathologisches Verhalten befragt. Die Ergebnisse werden vorgestellt.

Tiergestützte Intervention mit Schafen bei Emotionsregulationsstörungen
Dr. Petra Schmid | University Ulm: Clinic for Psychiatry and Psychotherapy I | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Petra Schmid | University Ulm: Clinic for Psychiatry and Psychotherapy I | Germany

Emotionsregulation ist die Fähigkeit, mit affektiven Erfahrungen umzugehen und sie zu modulieren. Defizite in der Emotionsregulation stehen im Zusammenhang mit der Entwicklung und Aufrechterhaltung von psychischen Störungen. Störungsmodelle zu Suchterkrankungen und zur Borderline-Persönlichkeitsstörung berücksichtigen defizitäre bzw. dysfunktionale Emotionsregulationsstrategien, welche zu Problemverhalten wie Substanzkonsum bzw. selbstverletzendem Verhalten und Suizidalität führen können. Ziel therapeutischer Interventionen ist es somit unter anderem, zu erleben und zu lernen, dass aktivierte unerwünschte Emotionen reguliert und positive Emotionen aktiv gestärkt werden können. Der Erfolg hängt hierbei maßgeblich von der eigenen Achtsamkeit, als einer wahrnehmenden, nicht-bewertenden, akzeptierenden Grundhaltung gegenüber dem aktuellen Erleben ab. Dies könnte durch eine zielgerichtete, manualisierte tiergestützte Therapie erreicht werden. Die Frage ist: gelingt es bei stationär-behandelten psychiatrischen Patient:innen mit Emotionsregulationsstörungen durch eine tiergestützte Intervention mit Schafen positive Emotionen, Achtsamkeit und Selbstwirksamkeit zu aktivieren und negative Emotionen zu reduzieren. Dies wurde in einem RCT mit 29 Suchterkrankten und 31 Patient:innen mit Borderline-Persönlichkeitsstörung im Vergleich zu treatment as usual untersucht.

Tiergestützte versus naturgestützte Intervention bei früh traumatisierten, depressiven Patienten
Prof. Dr. Elisabeth Schramm | Universitätsklinikum Freiburg | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Elisabeth Schramm | Universitätsklinikum Freiburg | Germany

Tier- und naturgestützte Interventionen stellen vor allem in der Depressionsbehandlung einen Indikationsbereich dar. Dies gilt besonders bei Patienten, die im Rahmen früher zwischenmenschlicher Traumatisierungen (z.B. emotionaler Missbrauch) Schwierigkeiten haben, sich auf Psychotherapie einzulassen. Denn der Einsatz von Tieren wirkt vertrauensfördernd, angstreduzierend, motivierend und stimmungsaufhellend.
Zur Verhinderung von Wiederauftreten häufig rezidivierender Depressionen erwies sich ein tier- und naturgestütztes Achtsamkeitsprogramm bei 67 Patienten mit einer Vorgeschichte von Depressionen und frühen Traumatisierungen als gut durchführbar und im Langzeitverlauf wirksamer als eine herkömmliche Behandlung. Die Teilnehmer fühlten sich bei den Achtsamkeitsgruppenübungen durch die Naturumgebung sicherer und geerdeter als in einem geschlossenen Raum. Der Kontakt zu den Schafen wurde als äußerst hilfreich empfunden.
Aber genügt auch die Naturumgebung alleine, um zu positiven Effekten zu kommen? Im Rahmen eines Dismanteling-Designs vergleichen wir bei 24 Patienten die Wirksamkeit des Achtsamkeitsprogramms in der Natur mit versus ohne Begleitung durch die Schafe. Erste Ergebnisse werden vorgestellt.

Technology-assisted Supplementary Work: Exploring the Antecedents and Well-being Outcomes in Nigerian Bank Workers
Prof. Anthony Ejike Okonkwo | Enugu State University of Science and Technology | Nigeria
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Anthony Ejike Okonkwo | Enugu State University of Science and Technology | Nigeria
Prof. Sandra Ohly | University of Kassel | Germany
Prof. Kathrin Reinke | Fresenius Hochschule | Germany

Research indicates that the association between technology-assisted supplemental work and well-being has continued to gain traction. Despite this growing relevance, and remarkable amount of research conducted on a widespread; there have, ironically, been few studies of these concerns in diverse national contexts, specifically in non-Western contexts. Most studies have concentrated majorly on American and European populations, few on Asian populations and relatively little in developing countries. Hence, the empirical evidence is still sparse. This research gap is particularly problematic and calls for research involving African populations, thus, this present study in a non-Western context of Nigeria. While the antecedents and well-being outcomes of technology-assisted supplemental work may vary across occupations and culture, the experience of bank workers in Nigeria makes them an ideal population for this study. We argue that the high levels of family motivation and collectivism in Nigeria might be connected to technology-assisted supplemental work. In response, relying on the Theory of Planned Action, we examined the antecedents and well-being outcomes of technology-assisted supplemental work in a sample of 195 bank workers in Nigeria. Results of correlation analysis and structural equation modelling revealed that technology-assisted supplemental work related to higher collectivism, injunctive norm, task interdependence, job demands and perceived job control; not family motivation as antecedents. Technology-assisted supplemental work related to none of the well-being outcomes (need for recovery, work-family balance and life satisfaction). Moderation effects were not observed. Our study suggests the value of examining a non-Western and developing country, and exploring boundary conditions of previous findings.

Leisure Sickness – exhausted instead of relaxed: A representative cross-sectional study on relaxation, constant activation, and mental health
Prof. Dr. Stefanie André | IU International University | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Stefanie André | IU International University | Germany

Background:
While classic stress models assume that stress arises during working hours and decreases during leisure time, many people report the opposite: physical and psychological complaints occur particularly during periods of relaxation. This phenomenon, known as leisure sickness, describes the occurrence of exhaustion and malaise precisely when recovery would be possible. From an occupational and health psychology perspective, leisure sickness reflects disruptions in central recovery processes, especially impaired psychological detachment from work. This study examines leisure sickness as a pattern of limited regeneration and its relation to work-related activation and mental health.
Method:
In a representative cross-sectional study, N = 2,004 working individuals aged 16–65 were surveyed. Leisure sickness was operationalized via the self-reported frequency of physical and psychological symptoms during leisure time. Psychological recovery was measured using indicators of mental distancing, recovery effectiveness, and ability to switch off. Work-related activation was assessed through overtime, digital availability outside working hours, and perceived impairment of recovery due to work-related contact.
Results:
71.9% reported having experienced leisure sickness at least once; 19.3% indicated frequent or almost constant symptoms during leisure periods. The phenomenon was particularly pronounced among participants under 25, who showed higher digital availability, greater difficulties switching off, and lower perceived recovery. High work-related activation, low psychological detachment, and limited regeneration skills were consistently associated with stronger leisure sickness.
Conclusion:
Leisure sickness is a widespread stress–recovery phenomenon. The findings highlight the need to strengthen psychological detachment, regeneration skills, and organizational recovery cultures in occupational health and prevention.

Cross-Cultural Differences in Proactivity’s Effect on Emotional Experiences
Jako Roder | Potsdam Universität | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jako Roder | Potsdam Universität | Germany
Prof. Dr. Doris Fay | Potsdam Universität | Germany
Dr. Ruta Pingel | Potsdam Universität | Germany
Dr. Tina Urbach | Potsdam Universität | Germany

Recent research has focused on the individual-level consequences of proactive work behaviors. There is accumulating evidence that performing proactive behaviors at work is associated with positive emotional experiences. The present research explores this finding adopting a cross-cultural lens. We propose that the positive effect of proactivity on emotions differs by culture. Specifically, cultural differences in performance-orientation should influence the strength of emotional responses to proactivity. We conducted two studies, each using a scenario-based within-person experimental design. We compared the level of discrete emotional reactions (pride, happiness, and relief) in response to scenarios depicting a proactive or non-proactive way to dealing with a work-related problem. Study 1 (N=1,222) compares the experimental effect between samples from countries with a comparatively higher level (Germanic European; Germany & Austria) with lower level (Latin European; France & Spain) of performance orientation. Results showed positive effects of proactivity on emotional responses across the full sample. Multi-level group analyses indicated stronger effects for the Germanic European samples (performance orientation: high) than for the Latin European samples (low). Study 2 tests the psychological process that may underly this effect. We replicated Study 1 in the United Kingdom (N=318), including work accomplishment as the mediator. In line with our hypotheses, work accomplishment mediated the effect of proactivity on all discrete emotions. Overall, these findings underscore the importance of cultural context when anticipating consequences of proactivity at work.

Towards Accessible Assessment: Cultural Adaptation and Psychometric Evaluation of the RESTQ for D/deaf individuals
Dr. Alon Markov-Glazer | Friedrich Schiller University Jena | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Alon Markov-Glazer | Friedrich Schiller University Jena | Germany
Prof. Rainer Schliermann | OTH Regensburg, Technical University of Applied Sciences | Germany

Introduction: Deaf and hard-of-hearing individuals (DHH) represent a heterogeneous population, differing in communication modalities. Yet research addressing standardized diagnostic tools suitable for this population remains limited. As written questionnaires often lack accessibility for DHH individuals, the development of appropriate assessment tools is essential. This study addresses this need by adapting the Recovery–Stress Questionnaire (RESTQ; Kellmann & Kallus, 2025) into German Sign Language (DGS) and examining its psychometric properties.
Methods: The RESTQ was culturally adapted into DGS following established protocols. Using a cross-sectional design, we recruited 101 DHH participants (35% female). The questionnaire was presented in a bimodal format, allowing participants to both read the items and view corresponding DGS videos. Reliability analyses and construct validity were examined.
Results: The adapted RESTQ demonstrated overall acceptable internal consistencies. Only two subscales yielded Cronbach’s alpha values below 0.70, comparable to the original RESTQ validated in hearing individuals. Construct validity was examined using exploratory factor analyses with principal axis factoring and varimax rotation. The data were suitable for factor analysis (Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin values ≥ .80; Bartlett’s tests of sphericity p < .001). The extracted factor solutions consistently reflected the two theoretically expected higher-order dimensions of stress and recovery.
Conclusions: This study responds to a gap in accessible psychological assessment for D/deaf individuals. By validating an adapted version of a recovery-stress measure, the study contributes to Deaf Studies research and supports improved applied practice with D/deaf clients. The findings underscore the importance of tailored diagnostic tools to support the psychological well-being of DHH individuals.

Human or Chatbot Lover? Implicit and Explicit Partner Choices in Human–Chatbot Relationships Across Cultures
Paula Ebner | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Paula Ebner | Germany
Dr. Jessica M. Szczuka | Universität Duisburg-Essen | Germany

Romantic partnerships have existed almost exclusively between humans throughout history, serving as the relational standard. However, recent advances in generative AI have introduced companions offering constant availability, acceptance, and sustained emotional engagement, enabling relational experiences that differ substantially from human partnerships, where conflicts and fluctuating emotional availability are common challenges. Whether these AI qualities translate into genuine partner preference may depend on cultural context, as societies differ fundamentally in their acceptance of technology in intimate domains and in philosophical frameworks for attributing consciousness to non-human entities. Given these developments, critical questions emerge: Do individuals with chatbot partners actually view AI companions as their preferred choice over human partners, and do these evaluations vary across cultural contexts? This cross-cultural study addresses these questions by examining partner preferences among individuals with chatbot partners across two culturally distinct samples (N = 102 Western participants; N = 102 Japanese participants) recruited through online communities with detailed verification procedures. We employed complementary methodological approaches: the Implicit Association Test to measure subconscious biases, and explicit forced-choice questions and qualitative open-ended measures to assess deliberate partner choice. This represents the first cross-cultural empirical investigation of partner preferences among individuals actively engaged in AI romantic relationships, offering insight into whether AI companions have the potential to transform human intimacy or whether human partnerships remain the psychological ideal despite technological advances.

1. Persönlichkeitsdiagnostik im Kindesalter: Die Entwicklung eines bildbasierten Persönlichkeits-Inventars für Kinder des Grundschulalter (6-10 Jahre) und der Zusammenhang mit psychischer Gesundheit und schulischem Leistungsverhalten
Dr. Nancy Tandler | Martin-Luther-Universität Halle-Wittenberg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Nancy Tandler | Martin-Luther-Universität Halle-Wittenberg | Germany
Prof. Dr. René T. Proyer
Prof. Dr. Dr. Uwe Wolfradt

Im Vortrag wird ein neu entwickeltes bildbasiertes Persönlichkeits-Inventar für Kinder des Grundschulalters (6-10 Jahre; Tandler, Wolfradt & Proyer, in prep.) zur Erfassung der Big-Five Persönlichkeitsfaktoren (PF) vorgestellt. Für diese Altersgruppe gibt es im deutschsprachigen Raum kaum Testverfahren zur Persönlichkeitsdiagnostik. Zudem können bei jüngeren Kindern noch keine Fragebögen eingesetzt werden und Ratings durch Bezugspersonen sind zeitintensiv und entsprechen nicht unbedingt den Einschätzungen der Kinder. Wir haben ein Set aus 25 Bilderkarten entwickelt, mithilfe dessen sich Kinder selbst beschreiben sollen. Das Ziel war, ein psychometrisches Verfahren zur Bestimmung entwicklungsrelevanter Persönlichkeitsmerkmale für die klinische und pädagogische Praxis zu erstellen. Im Vortrag wird zunächst der mehrstufige Entstehungsprozess der Bilderkarten beschrieben, der insgesamt N = 1600 Kinder einbezog. Dieser umfasste umfangreiche qualitative Vorstudien zur Erstellung des diagnostischen Bildmaterials sowie quantitative faktorenanalytische Schritte zur Prüfung der zugrunde liegenden Struktur. Anschließend präsentieren wir die Ergebnisse der externalen Validierung, bei der die Zusammenhänge der Selbstauskünfte der Kinder zu den bildbasierten Big-Five PF mit deren Schulleistungen, selbstberichtetem Wohlbefinden (KIDSCREEN-10) und den Fremdauskünften der Eltern zu klinischen Symptomen (DISYPS-III - Diagnostik-System für psychische Störungen) betrachtet werden. Insgesamt zeigen die bisherigen Befunde des Projekts, dass ein kindgerechter Zugang mittels Bildmaterials zu einer angemessenen und akkuraten Persönlichkeitserfassung im Kindesalter nicht nur geboten, sondern auch möglich ist.

3. Adaptive Motion Localization: How Context Shapes the Speed Prior
Dr. Simon Merz | University Trier | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Simon Merz | University Trier | Germany
Charles Spence
Christian Frings

How does the brain perceive a moving object? Recent models, specifically the "Speed Prior Account," suggest we rely on an internal speed expectation to resolve sensory uncertainty. But is this expectation fixed or flexible?
In this series of experiments, we investigated the influence of short-term speed statistics on the perception of movement onset and offset. By manipulating angular velocity profiles (slow vs. fast contexts; congruent vs. incongruent trials), we demonstrate that motion localization is highly context-dependent.
The results reveal a systematic "shift" in localization errors: the range of accurate perception moves dynamically toward the statistically most probable speed of the current context. This provides strong evidence that the "Speed Prior" is continuously updated by sensory input. This poster outlines the core mechanisms of the Speed Prior Account and illustrates how flexible priors optimize our interaction with dynamic objects.

4. If Job Autonomy were a Supervillain, it Would be Two-Face: Parallel Positive and Negative Effects on Well-Being
Franziska Julia Till | Justus Liebig University Giessen, Giessen, Germany | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Franziska Julia Till | Justus Liebig University Giessen, Giessen, Germany | Germany
Jan A. Häusser | Justus Liebig University Giessen, Giessen, Germany
Stacey L. Parker | University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia | Australia
Sascha Etgen | Justus Liebig University Giessen, Giessen, Germany

In flexible work environments, employees experience the opportunity but also the necessity to make work-related decisions. Although job autonomy is typically conceptualized as a crucial job resource for enhancing well-being and motivation, empirical findings on its effects are not that uniform (Häusser et al., 2010). This experimental study examines simultaneous positive versus negative effects by proposing two parallel mechanisms through which job autonomy influences well-being: a positive indirect pathway via self-determination and a negative indirect pathway via uncertainty. We conducted an experimental between-person work simulation with an employee sample (N = 203) randomly assigned to either a low-autonomy (n = 105) or high-autonomy (n = 98) condition. Participants took the role of an HR manager performing email processing and personnel decision-making tasks. In the high-autonomy condition, participants defined their own evaluation criteria and chose the order of email processing, while in the low-autonomy condition, they followed predefined criteria and a fixed sequence. Parallel mediation analyses supported the hypothesized dual-pathway model. Job autonomy showed a positive indirect effect on well-being through self-determination: higher autonomy increased self-determination, which was associated with higher well-being. Simultaneously, job autonomy showed a negative indirect effect through uncertainty: higher autonomy increased uncertainty, which was associated with lower well-being. This study reveals hidden costs of autonomy that may explain why job autonomy is not always beneficial for well-being. These findings highlight that organizations should maximize autonomy's benefits while minimizing its downsides to enhance employee well-being.

5.The Crossover of Life Satisfaction: How Entrepreneurs Affect Their Close Social Network
Maximilian Weldert | University of Münster | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Maximilian Weldert | University of Münster | Germany
Philipp Schäpers
Henrik Heinemann

Over the past decade, entrepreneurship research has increasingly paid attention to well-being. Entrepreneurs do not operate in a vacuum, but are embedded in far-reaching social networks, yet research still largely overlooks how entrepreneurial well-being affects close others. Building on the spillover–crossover model, this paper examines whether entrepreneurs’ life satisfaction is associated with the life satisfaction of close standing persons (friends, colleagues, partners, or family members), and whether this association differs from non-entrepreneurs.
We draw on survey data from 150 entrepreneurs and 135 non-entrepreneurs, complemented by 193 peer ratings of life satisfaction. Using both self-reports and peer reports allows us to test crossover effects while reducing concerns about common method bias. Consistent with prior research, entrepreneurs report higher life satisfaction than non-entrepreneurs. Across all matched data, participants’ life satisfaction is positively associated with peers’ life satisfaction, indicating a robust crossover effect. This association emerges for both entrepreneurs and non-entrepreneurs and remains stable when controlling for peers’ occupational status. In addition, peers of entrepreneurs report higher life satisfaction than peers of non-entrepreneurs.
Exploratory analyses suggest that spillover-related indicators, such as income satisfaction and time spent with family and friends, are positively associated with entrepreneurs’ life satisfaction, which in turn relates to peers’ life satisfaction in a spillover–crossover model.
Overall, the findings show that entrepreneurs’ life satisfaction extends beyond the individual and affects close others. Therefore, more attention should be drawn to the social context when studying entrepreneurial well-being.

6. Blood, Sweat and Blinks: The Effects of Task and Team Mental Workload on Cardiovascular, Electrodermal and Ocular Activity.
Joshua Braun | Technical University of Applied Sciences Augsburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Joshua Braun | Technical University of Applied Sciences Augsburg | Germany
Natalie Hogh | Technical University of Applied Sciences Augsburg
Prof. Dr. Simone Kubowitsch | Technical University of Applied Sciences Augsburg

Understanding mental workload is central to ergonomics, as it affects performance and well-being. Eye-based and physiological measures offer promising workload indicators, yet their validity in collaborative contexts, where task and teamwork demands interact, remains underexplored.

This experimental study examined the effects of two components of workload during team tasks, team mental workload (teamMWL) and task mental workload (taskMWL), on ocular, electrodermal, and cardiovascular activity. Thirty participants completed a dual-task paradigm involving verbal interaction with a simulated team alongside a reaction-time task using stimuli from a cooperative video game. Within a 2 × 3 repeated-measures design, teamMWL and taskMWL were manipulated, and multilevel mixed-effects models were used to analyze their effects on physiological markers. Related variables were grouped using exploratory factor analysis, yielding latent factors representing underlying physiological phenomena. These factor-derived variables were entered into the models to analyze workload-related physiological responses. Analyses included control variables to account for confounds (e.g., gaming experience), and manipulation checks verified the effectiveness of the workload manipulations.

While electrodermal activity was not sensitive to changes in teamMWL or taskMWL, the two workload components exerted distinct, sometimes opposing, effects on ocular and cardiovascular metrics. For instance, a factor representing fixation behavior decreased with higher teamMWL (standardized β = -0.33, FDR-corrected p = .001) but increased with taskMWL (standardized β = 1.03, FDR-corrected p < .001). These patterns likely reflect different coping strategies or by-products of task and teamwork demands, indicating differential impacts of task- and teamwork-related workload on visual attention and autonomic activity.

7. The dark side of social support: How social identification shapes its effects on depression
Louisa Theisges | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Louisa Theisges | Germany
Tegan Cruwys
Antonia J. Kaluza
Prof. Dr. Rolf van Dick

Depression is a prevalent mental health disorder influenced by social determinants, including social support and social identification. While social support is typically protective, recent research highlights its potential "dark side", particularly when perceived as dysfunctional. This study examined whether social identification with family and friends reduces depressive symptoms in part via reducing dysfunctional social support. Drawing on the social identity approach, we hypothesized that stronger social identification would predict lower depression severity both directly and indirectly via decreased dysfunctional social support, even when controlling for functional social support. Using a time-lagged design, 222 individuals with diagnosed affective disorders completed measures of social identification, social support (functional and dysfunctional), and depression severity at two timepoints. Mediation analyses supported our hypotheses. Clinically, these findings suggest that interventions targeting maladaptive support or fostering positive group identification may benefit individuals with affective disorders. This study advances the social cure literature both by illustrating the mental health benefits of social identification among people with diagnosed clinical disorders, and by delineating a potential mechanism: the potential detrimental effects of dysfunctional social support in depression.

8. Hyperarousal – a bridge symptom linking posttraumatic stress disorder and chronic pain? - A multilevel ecological momentary assessment study
Helena Rinberger | Paris Lodron University Salzburg | Austria
Show details

Sabrina Hettegger | Paris Lodron University Salzburg | Austria

Dr. Stephan Miedl | Paris Lodron University Salzburg | Austria
Dr. Michael Liedlgruber | Paris Lodron University Salzburg | Austria
Prof. Dr. Frank Wilhelm | Paris Lodron University Salzburg | Austria

The Mutual Maintenance Model proposes multiple cognitive, affective, and physiological processes maintaining the high comorbidity between posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and chronic pain (CP). However, recent evidence within the framework indicates that hyperarousal (HA) shows the strongest associations to pain severity and interference. Converging findings further identify HA as a central symptom in both PTSD and CP, connected to symptom persistence and prospective symptom change.
With most existing research relying on cross-sectional designs, inferences are limited to between-person associations, excluding conclusions about within-person symptom dynamics. This study therefore aims to examine the temporal interplay of HA, PTSD and CP using a multilevel network approach. Participants with symptoms of PTSD and CP fill out a 7-day Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) measuring HA, pain intensity & interference and the general PTSD symptoms intrusions, avoidance, and dissociation five times a day. Additionally, pain and PTSD symptoms are assessed via online questionnaires before and three months after the EMA period. Firstly, it will be tested whether momentary increases in hyperarousal (t-1) predict subsequent increases in pain (intensity & interference) and PTSD symptoms (t). Secondly, analyzing network connectivity, we hypothesize that higher connectivity and stronger temporal persistence of hyperarousal during EMA will predict smaller reduction in overall pain severity and PTSD symptoms at 3-month follow up.
The data collection has just been completed, and results will be presented at the conference.

Keywords: PTSD, chronic pain, hyperarousal, ecological momentary assessment (EMA), network-analysis

9. Promoting Mental Health in Youth Elite Sport: A Participatory, School-Based Approach
Nadine Vietmeier | Humboldt Universität zu Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Nadine Vietmeier | Humboldt Universität zu Berlin | Germany
Prof. Dr. Valerie Kastrup | Bielefeld University | Germany

Background:
Youth elite athletes face high sport-related, academic, and psychosocial demands and show an increased risk for mental health problems. However, structured and low-threshold support services within school-based elite sport settings remain scarce. Existing services are often fragmented and underutilized due to stigma and access barriers.

Aim:
MENTALiS aims to develop a participatory, stepped, school-based concept to promote mental health in youth elite sport by integrating sport psychological, psychotherapeutic, psychiatric, and sport pedagogical perspectives.

Methods:
A pilot project is conducted at a German elite sports school. Quantitative questionnaires and qualitative interviews are carried out with youth elite athletes as well as with parents, teachers, and coaches to assess mental health indicators, perceived stressors, resources, and support needs across stakeholder groups. Low-threshold workshops serve as an introduction to sport psychology and as participatory feedback formats. Based on the mixed-methods data, a context-sensitive multiprofessional support concept is developed, combining preventive measures, school-based counselling formats, and clearly defined referral pathways to specialized mental health services.

Outlook:
By embedding mental health support within the school context, MENTALiS aims to reduce stigma and barriers to help-seeking. The project provides a foundation for sustainable support structures and future evaluation and funding initiatives.

10. Beyond Diagnosis: Paternal Overprotection as a Predictor of Parasympathetic Regulation
Dr. Raphaela J. Gärtner | University of Konstanz | Germany
Show details
Authors:

Dr. Annika B.E. Benz | University of Konstanz | Germany

Dr. Maria Meier | University of Konstanz | Germany
Dr. Bernadette Denk | University of Konstanz | Germany
Stella Wienholdt | University of Konstanz | Germany
Nina Volkmer | University of Konstanz | Germany
Prof. Dr. Jens C. Pruessner | University of Konstanz | Germany


The interplay between childhood maltreatment (CM) and the development of mental disorders, like borderline personality disorders, is complex, with changes in the autonomic nervous system (ANS) proposed as one underlying mechanism. Specifically, CM has been associated with blunted baseline parasympathetic activity. To further examine this relationship, we investigated the relaxation response to nature videos, defined as an increase in cardiac parasympathetic activity indexed by heart rate variability (HRV), in a clinical sample with emotion regulation difficulties at the beginning and end of an inpatient Dialectical Behavior Therapy program (CS; n=32). Healthy controls (HC; n=61) were assessed once for comparison. Additionally, CM (operationalized using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire and the Parental Bonding Instrument) and therapeutic outcomes were assessed and analyzed.
The CS reported significantly higher levels of CM than the HC. Psychometric results demonstrated significant improvements in borderline personality disorder–specific symptoms, depressive symptoms, and anxiety. Nature video exposure did not induce acute changes in HRV. Overall, HRV was higher in HC, compared to both CS assessments. Among CM-related factors, paternal overprotection was the only variable significantly associated with lower HRV. These findings indicate a symptomatic improvement without changes in ANS functioning following treatment. Overall, the results suggest that paternal overprotection as a form of CM may contribute to ANS dysregulation independent of the development of mental disorders. Future studies should place greater emphasis on paternal overprotection as a critical variable, particularly with respect to its effects on parasympathetic activity.

11. Rethinking theoretical approaches for kinesiophobia in patients with cardiovascular disease: A scoping review
Leanne Torgersen | Trier University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Leanne Torgersen | Trier University | Germany
Sebastian Mertes-Spoo | Trier University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Heike Spaderna | Trier University | Germany

Introduction: Kinesiophobia is considered a possible barrier to physical activity in patients with cardiovascular diseases (CVDs). Despite kinesiophobia being well-researched on chronic pain, terminology and theoretical foundations for measuring kinesiophobia in CVD patients appear unclear.

Objective: This scoping review aimed to assess which definitions and theoretical reasonings were applied to the fear measurements collected on CVD patients.

Methods: Following the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology, articles from 7 databases were gathered. Articles were reviewed for kinesiophobia terminology and definitions, the theories applied for assessing kinesiophobia, and the methodological approaches adopted for measuring kinesiophobia.

Results: From the 65 articles assessed, 51 used kinesiophobia as either the primary term (40 articles) or the umbrella term (11 articles). Fourteen articles did not state kinesiophobia. Five additional terms were proposed in 9 articles with 4 terms cited as unique from kinesiophobia (fear of physical activity, fear of activity, fear of exercise, and exercise sensitivity). The pain fear avoidance model was cited as the theoretical construct in 25 articles (27%). Thirteen articles (14%) did not reference any theoretical basis, and 42 articles (46%) provided other theoretical reasonings. Twenty-three cross-sectional studies described correlates of kinesiophobia, 17 studies focused on questionnaire development, and 11 studies quantified associations with physical activity indicators.

Conclusion: Lack of standardized terminology and theoretical basis for outlining kinesiophobia in CVD patients remain. Theoretical assumptions of kinesiophobia in CVD have not been tested systematically. Further research is needed to establish a coherent framework for identifying fear levels and for developing adequate interventions for CVD populations.

12. Defining and Separating Information and Communication Overload – Theory-Based Derivation and Scale Development
Dr. Benedikt Graf | Vienna University | Austria
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Benedikt Graf | Vienna University | Austria
Dr. Rebecca Beinig | TU Eindhoven
Sophia Schwickert | Trier University
David Schischke | Trier University | Germany

Information and communication overload can be found in numerous publications and are considered central stressors in view of the rapid development and increasing use of information and communication technology and AI at the workplace. Both concepts are often used interchangeably and show an insufficient construct conceptualization. In many studies, this leads to a misspecification of measurement. We argue that information and communication overload can occur independently and require different organizational measures to counteract, necessitating a valid scale of measurement. Therefore, this preregistered study had the goal of delineating both constructs across a) theories such as cognitive load theory, four contents of communication, and media naturalness theory, and b) empirical evidence, making them more accessible and precise for further research. We present a theory-based differentiation and precise definition of the constructs, and both theoretical measurement models were transferred to an integrative scale development (N1=46) and tested within two distinct samples (N2=105, N3=288) from the professional context. For this, existing scales were adapted and new items created. Results support the theoretical assumptions that information and communication overload are two separate constructs that share common variance but may be determined by distinct processes. This study contributes to a uniform definition and clarification of the concepts of information and communication overload and offers two derived scales. This clear differentiation of the concepts helps to reduce measurement misspecification that has accompanied previous research. In addition, this study helps to derive more targeted and effective measures for organizations and stress prevention.

Lea Penning | Helmut Schmidt Universität Hamburg; Universität Münster; IDeA Research Center for Individual Development and Adaptive Education of Children at Risk | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Lea Penning | Helmut Schmidt Universität Hamburg; Universität Münster; IDeA Research Center for Individual Development and Adaptive Education of Children at Risk | Germany
Prof. Dr. Monika Daseking | Helmut Schmidt Universität Hamburg; IDeA Research Center for Individual Development and Adaptive Education of Children at Risk | Germany
JProf. Dr. Julia Kerner auch Koerner | Universität Münster; IDeA Research Center for Individual Development and Adaptive Education of Children at Risk

Theoretischer Hintergrund: Aufmerksamkeitsdefizit-/Hyperaktivitätssymptome (ADHS) von Jungen werden in Elternurteilen höher als von Mädchen eingeschätzt (Mowlem et al., 2019). Späte Diagnosen bei Mädchen gehen mit langfristigen psychosozialen Folgen einher (Gershon & Gershon, 2002). Es wird diskutiert, ob Eltern im Vergleich zu ErzieherInnen ADHS-Symptome von Jungen über- und die von Mädchen unterschätzen (Korsch & Petermann, 2014; Kuschel et al., 2007; Young et al., 2020).

Folgende Forschungsfragen sind zu beantworten:
1. Gibt es Geschlechtsunterschiede in Fremdbeurteilungen und variiert die Übereinstimmung je nach Geschlecht?
2. Gibt es Geschlechtsunterschiede in den Testleistungen?
3. Besteht ein Zusammenhang zwischen ADHS-Symptomen und Testleistungen?

Methode: Die Studie untersucht in einer nicht-klinischen Stichprobe (N = 159; 72 Mädchen, M-Alter = 3.44, SD = 0.32) Geschlechtsunterschiede in ADHS-Symptomen im Eltern- und ErzieherInnenurteil (DISYPS-III FBB ADHS-V; Döpfner & Görtz-Dorten, 2017), sowie deren Zusammenhang mit Inhibitionsfähigkeit (EF Touch; Ulitzka et al., 2023) und Belohnungsaufschub (Delay task, Murray & Kochanska, 2002). Es wird erwartet, dass Jungen höhere Symptomausprägungen zeigen (Gaub & Carlson, 1997), Eltern Kinder auffälliger bewerten und Mädchen eine bessere Testleistung erbringen (Brocki & Bohlin, 2004; Ulitzka et al., 2023). Geplant sind t-Tests für unabhängige Stichproben, Mixed-ANOVA und Regressionsanalysen.

Ergebnisse: Die Datenerhebung und -aufbereitung des Projektes (https://osf.io/jp97t ) laufen (N ≥ 180 bis 04/2026).Die Hypothesenprüfung erfolgt bis zum Konferenzbeitrag.

Implikationen: In der frühen Kindheit ist bislang wenig über Geschlechtsunterschiede in ADHS-Symptomen und miteinhergehenden Verhaltensweisen bekannt. Diese Studie kann einen ersten Beitrag dazu leisten, zu verstehen, ob Eltern die ADHS-Symptome von Mädchen schon bei sehr jungen Kindern anders als die Symptome von Jungen einschätzen.

14. Translation, Adaptation and Validation of the Sensory Processing Sensitivity Questionnaire (SPSQ) for German-Speaking Adults (G-SPSQ), Children and Adolescents (G-SPSQ 9 - 15)

Show details
Authors:
Stefanie Heßels | Witten/Herdecke University, Germany | Germany
Professor Susanne Buecker | Witten/Herdecke University, Germany | Germany

Sensory Processing Sensitivity (SPS) is described as a personality trait, characterized by an increased affective and physical reactivity, deeper processing of sensory information, greater attention for social and environmental stimuli as well as ease of excitation. In recent years, SPS has attracted growing public and scientific interest due to its associations with various life domains, including physical and mental health, interpersonal relationships, and academic functioning.
In adults, SPS can be assessed using the Sensory Processing Sensitivity Questionnaire (SPSQ; De Gucht et al., 2022)—a 43-item tool, developed to compensate for inconsistencies of earlier SPS measurement instruments. Since there is no German version, this study aims to translate the English version of the SPSQ for N = 645 German-speaking adults and further adapt and validate its short form for N = 390 children and adolescents. Following a pilot study as part of the adaptation process, data will be collected during two measurement periods respectively. Confirmatory factor analyses will be conducted to examine the multidimensional structure, proposed by De Gucht et al. (2022). In addition, correlational analyses will be performed to examine bivariate associations of SPS and related constructs, including loneliness, the Big Five, and indicators of mental and physical health.
By providing a psychometrically sound German assessment of SPS across different age groups, the study aims to advance the conceptual clarity of SPS and contribute to a more nuanced, multidimensional understanding of social-emotional well-being in highly sensitive individuals across the lifespan.
Keywords: Sensory Processing Sensitivity, SPSQ, Loneliness, Children, Adolescents.

15. Prädiktoren des Muskulositätsstrebens: Implikationen für die Prävention von Körperunzufriedenheit
Katharina Hommes | Universitätsmedizin Mainz | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Katharina Hommes | Universitätsmedizin Mainz | Germany
Florian Hammerle | Universitätsmedizin Mainz

Theoretischer Hintergrund: Ein zentraler Aspekt der Prävention von Essstörungen ist die Verringerung von Risikofaktoren und der Aufbau von Resilienzfaktoren: Unzufriedenheit mit bzw. Wertschätzung des eigenen Körpers sind hierbei von zentraler Bedeutung. In bisherigen Ansätzen steht vor allem das Schlankheitsstreben im Vordergrund (z.B. Bürger, Ernst, Wolter, Huss, Kaess & Hammerle, 2019). In Anbetracht eines sich wandelnden Schönheitsideals nimmt jedoch die Relevanz von Muskulositätsstreben für Männer und Frauen zu. Um relevante Prädiktoren des Muskulositätsstrebens zu untersuchen, wurde die Online-Studie „Einflüsse auf das Muskulositätsstreben“ durchgeführt.

Fragestellung: Welche Prädiktoren sagen das Muskulositätsstreben bei erwachsenen Personen im deutschsprachigen Raum signifikant vorher und ergeben sich hieraus Risikogruppen?

Methode: In einer querschnittlichen Online-Erhebung (Ethikvotum, präregistriert in DRKS mit ID: DRKS00035241) wurden im Zeitraum von Dezember 2024 bis Januar 2025 Daten von 266 deutschsprachigen Teilnehmenden im Alter von 18 bis 67 Jahren mit REDCap erhoben. Erfragt wurden nach informed consent soziodemographische Daten, sportbezogene Merkmale wie die Sportmenge und der Trainingsmodus (Solo- vs. Gemeinschaftstraining), Körperdysmorphe Symptome (FKS), die wahrgenommene psychische Belastung (PHQ-4) und das Muskulositätsstreben (DMS). Die Auswertung erfolgte mit Hilfe multipler linearer Regression und Welch-t-Tests, sowie Effektstärken (Cohen‘s d) in RStudio.

Ergebnis: Das Gesamtmodell war signifikant und die Prädiktoren Alter, Sportmenge, Trainingsmodus und Körperdysmorphe Symptome konnten das Muskulositätsstreben signifikant vorhersagen. In Welch-t-Tests zeigte sich, dass Männer signifikant höhere Ausprägungen aufwiesen als Frauen.

Schlussfolgerung: Junge Erwachsene, die sportlich sehr aktiv sind und Sport vorwiegend allein betreiben könnten eine Risikogruppe für erhöhtes Muskulositätsstreben sein. Präventions- und Interventionsprogramme für Körperunzufriedenheit sollten auch das Muskulositätsstreben thematisieren.

Dr. Evelyn Steinberg | Veterinärmedizinische Universität Wien | Austria
Prof. Dr. Franziska Perels | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany

Veterinary students (VT) are at higher risk for mental health problems compared to the general population (Humer et al., 2023). Similar risks have been reported for students in other care-oriented professions, such as primary school teacher training students (Mašková et al., 2025). In this context, self-compassion, a caring, mindful, and action-oriented attitude toward oneself in the face of adversity, represents a promising protective resource associated with resilience and adaptive coping (Neff, 2022).

The present study provides a comparison of self-compassion between VT and teacher training students. In an exploratory design, VT (n=102, 88% female) were compared with a teacher training student sample (primary: n=69, 96% female; secondary: n=169, 73% female) using established self-compassion measures. It was hypothesised that VT would differ from secondary school teacher training students (STT) in terms of self-compassion, but not from primary school teacher training students (PTT).

A multivariate analysis of variance revealed a significant group effect (Wilks’ Λ=.94, F(8, 636)=2.36, p=.017, partial η²=.03) for the three student groups in the Self-Compassion Scale. Univariate analyses revealed significant group differences in self-judgment, over-identification, and self-kindness (p≤.031, partial η²=.02–.03) insofar as VT reported higher self-judgment, higher over-identification, and lower self-kindness compared to STT. No differences emerged between VT and PTT and between PTT and STT.

The absence of differences between veterinary and primary school teacher training students may reflect shared emotional-motivational demands, underscoring the relevance of self-compassion in care-oriented study programs.

The specific results of these analyses are discussed in more detail on the poster.

17. How Work Characteristics Shape Absence Rate, Frequency, and Duration
Dr. Yannick Metzler | Leibniz-Institut für Arbeitsforschung an der TU Dortmund (IfADo) | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Yannick Metzler | Leibniz-Institut für Arbeitsforschung an der TU Dortmund (IfADo) | Germany

Purpose: This study examines how a wide range of work characteristics, grounded in multiple theories of work stress and design, predict sickness absence over a 12-month period. Distinct absence metrics - rate, frequency, and duration - are analyzed.

Design: Data were collected from 1,935 employees in the construction materials sector, nested in 63 shifts. Work characteristics were measured using the Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire, and unit-level sickness absence was obtained from organizational records. LASSO regression identified key predictors from 19 COPSOQ scales plus demographic factors.

Findings: Gender significantly predicted all three absence metrics in varying directions. Work–privacy conflict, social support, role clarity, leadership quality, and trust and justice emerged as additional predictors of absence frequency and duration, suggesting a multifaceted influence of psychosocial work characteristics across employee absence metrics.

Originality: By integrating multiple theoretical models and disaggregating different types of absence metrics, this study clarifies how a diverse set of work characteristics shape employee absences, offering a more comprehensive framework than single-model approaches and a more nuanced perspective for workplace health management.

Practical implications: Organizations should tailor interventions to address the unique predictors underlying each metric. Strategies focusing on leadership support, fair treatment, and mitigating work–privacy conflict may be particularly effective in reducing frequent or lengthy absences.

Dr. Jan Engelmann | University Medical Center, Mainz, Germany

Major depressive disorder (MDD) represents a major public health burden, with antidepressants being the most established and effective pharmacological treatment. However, therapeutic response varies considerably, highlighting the need for molecular markers that can predict treatment outcome and provide insights into the biological mechanisms underlying antidepressant efficacy. While cross-sectional epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have identified DNA methylation signatures associated with antidepressant response, findings remain inconsistent and longitudinal analyses examining DNA methylation trajectories across multiple timepoints during pharmacological treatment are lacking.
Within the Early Medication Change trial, we generated DNA methylation data for 162 patients with MDD (81 responders, 81 non-responders) and 48 healthy controls. Patients were assessed at four timepoints across eight weeks of antidepressant treatment, while controls were assessed twice. We identified differentially methylated positions (DMPs) and regions (DMRs) using longitudinal EWAS models and the comb-p algorithm.
Baseline DNA methylation levels were associated with depressive symptom severity after eight weeks of treatment through six DMRs, including genes such as TNRC6C and CAT, whereas no single DMP reached significance. Longitudinal analyses identified one DMP associated with symptom improvement across treatment (YLPM1) and three DMRs showing DNA methylation changes over time, including GPR126 and PM20D1. The identified genes are involved in neuroplasticity and inflammatory processes.
This study provides the first longitudinal evidence of DNA methylation changes during antidepressant pharmacotherapy that are associated with clinical response. These findings underscore the potential of epigenetic markers for personalized treatment approaches in MDD, though replication and functional validation remain essential next steps.

Arieja Farugie | Goethe - Universität Frankfurt am Main

As more people live in cities than rural areas and at least one quarter of health issues are mental, interest in environmental influences on mental health has increased. Regional Deprivation, the disadvantage of a group living in a specific area, consistently showed a negative influence on one’s mental health. Guided by the Person-in-Environment-Framework, this study aimed at investigating the spatial distribution and influence of regional deprivation, combining socioeconomic (mGISD) and additional dimensions, on psychological distress (PD) being a marker of a discomforting, emotional state. Objective regional deprivation data were combined with subjective data from an online survey conducted in Frankfurt am Main. As predicting spatial influence, spatial methods (LISA-Cluster and SLX-Model) and were used. N = 446 inhabitants of Frankfurt participated in the study and were aggregated into n = 37 districts, whereby some districts of Frankfurt had to be combined. The analyses revealed clear spatial clusters for PD and regional deprivation factors. Socioeconomic regional deprivation showed a spatial correlation with PD at the global level (Global Moran's I = .15, p = .048) and predicted symptoms of PD in the SLX model (βtotal = 4.73, p = .019), with this effect largely attributable to neighbourhood (“indirect”) effects. Evidence of further, non-significant correlations with other deprivation factors can be seen in the form of spatial clusters. In summary, the study strengthens the evidence for spatial influence and provides indications for future research and health policies on a on a way from a health city to healthy one.

20. The Interplay between Minority Stresses and Loneliness among Turkish-Origin Adults in Germany
Dr. Laura Scholaske | MSB Medical School Berlin | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Laura Scholaske | MSB Medical School Berlin | Germany

Background. Loneliness is a major public health concern, particularly among ethnic minority groups exposed to chronic stressors. While minority stress has been linked to adverse mental health outcomes, less is known about its association with loneliness and the role of coping strategies. This study examined associations between minority stress and loneliness among Turkish-origin adults in Germany and tested adaptive and maladaptive coping as moderators.

Methods. A total of 133 Turkish-origin adults (90% born in Germany) completed an online survey. The questionnaire included the Ethnic-Racial Discrimination Stress Inventory, Multidimensional Acculturative Stress Inventory, Socioeconomic Stress Inventory, short version of the UCLA Loneliness Scale, and Brief COPE. Adaptive coping included active coping, planning, positive reframing, acceptance, use of emotional support, and use of instrumental support; maladaptive coping included denial, behavioral disengagement, self-blame, and substance use.

Results. Minority stress was positively associated with loneliness. Three moderation patterns emerged: (1) buffering — adaptive coping was linked to lower loneliness under high stress; (2) exacerbating — maladaptive coping predicted higher loneliness under low stress; (3) crossover — maladaptive coping predicted higher loneliness at low stress but lower loneliness at high stress. Several stress–loneliness associations were not moderated by coping.

Conclusions. Coping strategies operate in a context-dependent manner. Adaptive coping may buffer the impact of high stress, whereas maladaptive strategies can exacerbate loneliness under low stress but be protective under high stress. Given the cross-sectional design, causal inferences cannot be drawn. Longitudinal research is needed to clarify how minority stress and coping jointly influence loneliness over time.

21. Validation of the German Cognitive Emotion Regulation Questionnaire–Kids (CERQ-k): Factor Structure and Associations with Mental Health in Late Childhood

Authors:
Steven Stelz | Johannes Gutenberg Universität Mainz | Germany
Prof. Dr. Anne Mareike Altgassen | Johannes Gutenberg Universität Mainz | Germany

The Cognitive Emotion Regulation Questionnaire–Kids (CERQ-k) is a self-report measure designed to assess the cognitive strategies children use to regulate emotions following negative or stressful events. Although the CERQ-K has been validated in several languages, a German version has not been available to date. Therefore, the aim of the present study was to develop a German translation of the CERQ-K, to examine its factor structure and psychometric properties in a community sample of children.
The sample comprised 390 children aged 8–12 years (M = 9.55, SD = 1.11). Participants completed the German CERQ-k along with other measures of emotion regulation (FEEL-KJ) and clinical symptoms, including depression, anxiety and attention difficulties (DIKJ; KAT-II; PSC-D). The factor structure was examined using exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses.
Results supported the intended nine-factor correlated model. A parsimonious short version with three items per factor showed the best model fit and is therefore recommended for future use. Internal consistencies were acceptable to good for most subscales, with the exception of Reappraisal, which showed lower reliability. Maladaptive cognitive strategies - particularly Self-blame, Rumination, and Catastrophizing - were positively associated with internalizing symptoms such as depression, anxiety, but not with externalizing symptoms, providing evidence for criterion validity. Associations with the FEEL-KJ supported convergent and divergent validity.
Overall, the German CERQ-Kids proved to be a psychometrically adequate and efficient measure of cognitive emotion regulation strategies in late childhood. It offers a valuable tool for research and applied contexts, including clinical and psychotherapeutic settings.

Maureen Schitter | Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Maureen Schitter | Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule | Germany
Prof. Dr. Tina Braun | Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule | Germany

Humor is a multifaceted construct associated with a range of well-being-related outcomes. People differ substantially in how they use and endorse different styles of humor. Because humor styles tend to co-occur in meaningful patterns, this study applied a typological approach to examine individual differences in humor profiles with respect to coping humor and perceived stress. Based on eight comic styles (fun, humor, nonsense, wit, irony, satire, sarcasm, and cynicism), a k-means cluster analysis was conducted in a sample of N = 240 participants, which yielded balanced clusters corresponding to four known humor profiles: general humor endorsers, positive humor endorsers, negative humor endorsers, and humor deniers.

Differences between the humor profiles were examined using one-way analyses of variances with coping humor and perceived stress as outcome variables. Significant cluster differences emerged for both coping humor and perceived stress. Post-hoc analyses indicated that general and positive humor endorsers reported higher levels of coping humor compared to negative humor endorsers and humor deniers, whereas humor deniers reported the lowest levels of coping humor. Furthermore, humor deniers experienced higher perceived stress than positive humor endorsers, while no additional pairwise comparisons reached statistical significance.

The present findings support the usefulness of person-centered approaches for understanding humor-related individual differences and their relevance for psychological well-being.

23. Einsamkeit, interpersonelles Vertrauen und die Lebenswelt Studierender: Eine quantitative Untersuchung im Hochschulkontext
Levi Moritz Schöberl | Hochschule Düsseldorf (HSD) – University of Applied Sciences | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Levi Moritz Schöberl | Hochschule Düsseldorf (HSD) – University of Applied Sciences | Germany
Prof. Dr. Antje Hunger | Hochschule Düsseldorf (HSD) – University of Applied Sciences | Germany

Einsamkeit wird empfunden, wenn eine quantitative oder qualitative Diskrepanz zwischen den eigenen Wünschen an das Beziehungsnetzwerk und dessen tatsächlicher Ausprägung besteht (Perlman & Peplau, 1981). Sie ist – spätestens seit den Kontaktbeschränkungen im Rahmen der Covid-19-Pandemie – ein Thema von zunehmendem Interesse. Dies liegt unter anderem an den gefundenen Zusammenhängen zwischen Einsamkeit und psychischer Gesundheit (Berger et al., 2021; Cacioppo & Cacioppo, 2018; Entringer & Kröger, 2021; Jensen-Campbell et al., 2023; Strauß, Berger & Rosendahl, 2021). Junge Menschen wurden wiederholt als Risikogruppe für Einsamkeit identifiziert (Berger et al., 2021; Bücker et al., 2021). Dies könnte unter anderem daran liegen, dass jüngere Menschen häufiger strukturell bedingte Übergänge erleben, bei denen bestehende Netzwerke verloren gehen können. Misslingt die Anbindung an die neue Peer-Gruppe, könnte dies zu einer erhöhten, ortsabhängigen Einsamkeit führen. Unter dieser Prämisse wurde eine quantitative Fragebogenstudie entworfen, die Einsamkeit vor dem Hintergrund der Lebenswelt von Studierenden untersuchen soll. Im Rahmen der Studie sollen zusätzlich lebensweltliche Aspekte wie das Kontakt- und Medienverhalten Studierender, das interpersonelle Vertrauen, die allgemeine Lebenszufriedenheit sowie psychosoziale Beratungsangebote untersucht werden. Erste quantitative Daten und Ergebnisse zu psychosozialer Beratung im Kontext von (campusbezogener) Einsamkeit unter Studierenden sowie Korrelationen und Risikofaktoren sollen auf dem Kongress vorgestellt werden.

Early childhood is a pivotal window for development; untreated mental health problems (MHP) during this period can have lasting consequences. Early regulation disorders are a risk factor for later MHP. Interventions that lower caregiver stress and enhance caregiver child interaction quality are essential for reducing children’s regulation disorders and promoting healthy development. Because evidence-based group programs targeting this need are lacking, we developed “PROmini”, that aims to improve early regulation disorders by promoting caregiver-child interaction and lowering caregiver stress and MHP. This presentation will introduce PROmini and present results and experiences from the feasibility study. To prepare a multicentre, randomised, wait list-controlled trial (N = 104 caregiver-child dyads), we are currently conducting a feasibility study to evaluate feasibility and preliminary uncontrolled efficacy of PROmini. The feasibility study enrols mothers and their children aged 0-5 years who meet DC: 0-5 criteria for regulation disorders (crying, sleeping, feeding, aggression or anxiety). The intervention comprises 12 weekly 90-minute group sessions and two individual sessions. Feasibility outcomes include e.g. session attendance and participant satisfaction. Changes in efficacy outcomes - child regulation disorders, maternal stress and MHP, and quality of mother-child interaction - will be assessed over three time points (baseline, post, 12-week follow up) using Repeated Measures ANCOVAs. If effective, PROmini could be a cost effective approach for addressing early childhood MHP and may serve both therapeutic and preventive functions across the lifespan. Findings from the feasibility study will guide revision of the manual and provide practical insights for the subsequent trial and implementation.

Over the past two decades, research on interindividual differences in decision-making has often focused on the distinction between maximizers, who (over)invest effort to find the best possible option, and satisficers, who select an option they consider good enough (Cheek & Schwartz, 2016). However, there has been little consensus on the conceptualization and measurement of these personality constructs, leading to inconsistencies in their assessments and outcomes (Cheek & Schwartz, 2016; Misuraca et al., 2018). To address this, we took a systematic approach to construct validation, clarifying the position of maximizing in a nomological network with other personality and decision-making constructs. After developing a new scale using exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, we analysed the costs of being a maximizer in daily life decisions as well as its ultimate effect on people’s mental health, including depression, anankastia, and anxiety.

26. Developing the Social Relationship Expectations Scale: a multi-country study to help tailor loneliness interventions
Rodrigo Huerta-Gutierrez | Medizinische Hochschule Brandenburg (MHB)
Dr. Samia Akhter-Khan | Medizinische Hochschule Brandenburg (MHB) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Rodrigo Huerta-Gutierrez | Medizinische Hochschule Brandenburg (MHB)
Dr. Samia Akhter-Khan | Medizinische Hochschule Brandenburg (MHB) | Germany

People experiencing loneliness are at increased risk of adverse health outcomes, including stroke, dementia, and mortality. However, interventions targeting loneliness remain largely ineffective. One major gap in loneliness research is that interventions are rarely tailored to individuals and their contexts. Moreover, our knowledge is mainly based on studies from high-income countries. Built on lifespan developmental theories and experiences of people from lower- and middle-income countries (LMICs), the Social Relationship Expectations (SRE) framework offers a new theoretical approach to tailor loneliness interventions in context. The SRE framework proposes six expectations, that can result in loneliness if unmet: proximity, support, intimacy, fun, generativity, and respect. Although the first four expectations have been captured in existing loneliness scales, generativity and respect are less addressed in loneliness scales and interventions and may become more important in later life. In this talk, we present results from the Social Relationship Expectations Scale development in Hong Kong, Germany, and the US. The published protocol is divided into three phases: (i) comprehensive item generation and prioritization of items with a three-round Delphi process with global experts, (ii) cognitive interviews and (iii) online assessment and analysis. In addition to the items generated in the Delphi Study, experiences of people from LMICs from published qualitative loneliness research are included. To ensure a robust analytical approach and compare diverse cultural contexts, data will be analyzed using both classical test theory and network analysis. Understanding an individual’s unfulfilled relationship expectations–the core mechanism of loneliness–can move the field towards tailoring effective interventions globally.

Forensisch-psychiatrische Einrichtungen sind in vielerlei Hinsicht restriktiv. Neben objektiven Einschränkungen gibt es auch eine subjektive Komponente. Forschungsergebnisse zeigen, dass ein starkes subjektives Erleben von Einschränkung unerwünschte Effekten haben kann. Um das Erleben von Einschränkung im deutschen Maßregelvollzug zu erfassen, wurde der britische Forensic Restrictiveness Questionnaire (FRQ) übersetzt und validiert. 175 Patient*innen nahmen an der Validierung teil. Die interne Konsistenz wurde mittels Cronbachs α bestimmt. Um die Konstruktvalidität zu prüfen, wurden explorative Faktorenanalysen durchgeführt und Korrelationen zwischen FRQ und dem Essen Climate Evaluation Scheme (EssenCES), des Fragebogens zur Messung der Lebensqualität im Strafvollzug (MQPLa) und des Fragebogens zur Gesundheitswahrnehmung (Kurzform, SF-12) bestimmt. Die Kriteriumsvalidität wurde anhand von Korrelationen zwischen FRQ und Lockerungsstufen bzw. dem Auftreten kritischer Vorfälle in einer Teilstichprobe (n = 87) ermittelt. Die interne Konsistenz ist als gut zu bewerten (α = 0,88). Faktorenanalytisch scheint ein Drei-Faktoren-Modell am naheliegendsten zu sein. Die konvergente Validität zeigt signifikante Korrelationen mit dem EssenCES (r = -.625, p < .001), dem MQPLa (r = -.721, p < .001) und der SF-12-Subskala für psychische Gesundheit (r = -.226, p = .005). Die geringe Korrelation mit der SF-12-Subskala für körperliche Gesundheit (r = -.163, p = .044) deutet darauf hin, dass die diskriminante Validität gegeben ist. Die Ergebnisse für die Korrelationen des FRQ mit Lockerungen und kritischen Vorfällen sind gemischt.

Die vorliegenden Ergebnisse deuten darauf hin, dass die deutsche Version des FRQ in deutschen forensisch-psychiatrischen Einrichtungen valide sein könnte. Um robustere Ergebnisse zu erzielen, sind eine klarere theoretische Grundlage und größere Stichproben nötig.

Anna Fichtenkamm | German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) | Germany
Show details
Author:
Anna Fichtenkamm | German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) | Germany

Background: Cancer survivors frequently experience major distress that can substantially affect their mental health. While trajectory research on reactions following exposure to adversity describes that most individuals stay resilient (i.e., maintain or quickly regain mental health), evidence on mental health trajectories among cancer survivors remains limited. Furthermore, the influence of resilience factors has not been systematically examined in this context.
Method: This systematic review, conducted in collaboration with the ResiMETA database, aims to synthesize longitudinal studies investigating trajectories of resilience and associated resilience factors in cancer survivors.
Results: Data analysis hast not started yet, and will be finished until September 2026. The review will (1) identify common trajectories of resilience outcomes and related factors through descriptive synthesis, (2) analyze their prevalence estimates via meta-analysis, and (3) examine the predictive value of individual, social, and societal resilience factors for trajectory membership.
Implications: Findings will provide a comprehensive overview of resilience outcomes and factors, identify resilience trajectories and insights into their heterogeneity among cancer survivors, and inform the development of resilience-enhancing interventions to improve long-term mental health and quality of life.

Prof. Dr. Stephan Getzmann | Leibniz Research Center for Working Environment and Human Factors at the TU-Dortmund | Germany

Early childhood stress can have significant long-term effects on mood, stress reactivity, depression, personality, quality of life or occupational performance in adulthood. However, there is only limited research on the role of childhood trauma or early life stress on cognitive functions. Thus, it is unclear which of the crucial cognitive functions are mostly affected. This study examines the relationship between severity of early childhood stress and series of cognitive functions, such as speed of processing, verbal fluency, short-term and working memory, selective attention and executive functions as well as the g-factor reflecting fluid intelligence and cognitive failures in daily life. Data from up to 570 healthy adults aged 20 to 70 who completed questionnaires and cognitive tests as part of the Dortmund Vital Study (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05155397) were evaluated. The results show that early childhood stress has a significant long-lasting impact on speed of processing, attentional control, verbal learning and recall, Stroop interference, the g-factor, and cognitive failures in daily life. The higher the level of early childhood stress, the lower the cognitive performance. Some of the effect persists even after dividing the sample into two age groups using median split. No effects were found on crystallized intelligence, logical reasoning, spatial rotation, trail making test and word fluency. The results emphasize the long-lasting consequences of early childhood stress on specific attentional and memory functions in late adulthood. Future research should use longitudinal designs to analyze temporal and causal relationships between early childhood stress and cognitive functions in a more differentiated manner.

30. Motivational biases in feedback-based learning are unaltered in obsessive-compulsive disorder
Prof. Dr. Jutta Peterburs | MSH Medical School Hamburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Julian F. Vahedi | Heinrich Heine Universität Düsseldorf | Germany
Dr. Armin Bahic | LVR Klinikum Düsseldorf | Germany

Prof. Dr. Reinhard Pietrowsky | Heinrich Heine Universität Düsseldorf | Germany
Prof. Dr. Jutta Peterburs | MSH Medical School Hamburg | Germany

Humans tend toward action execution in the promise of reward and action suppression when anticipating punishment. However, whether these motivational biases reflect biased action selection or biased learning and outcome processing is still debated. Reward-related striatal dopamine has been suggested as the neural origin for these biases, which may thus be reflected in the feedback-related negativity (FRN). Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is characterized by dysregulated fronto-striatal circuits with deficits in action control and goal-directed behavior. However, no previous studies tested whether motivational biases are altered in OCD. The present study compared OCD patients (n=28) with healthy controls (HCs; n=27) and patients with social anxiety (SAD; n=29) who completed an active and observational variant of an orthogonalized go/nogo task. Behavioral results revealed a robust motivational bias both in active and observational learning, but no differences between groups. In active and observational learning, the FRN was biased by cue valence, with more negative amplitudes for unfavorable versus favorable feedback in win conditions but the reverse pattern for avoid-losing conditions, again with no significant group differences. Interestingly, OCD patients showed generally larger P3 amplitudes compared to HCs, and reduced P3 valence coding relative to SAD in observational learning only. Unaltered motivational biases and FRN amplitudes in OCD therefore challenge views assuming striatal origin for these biases, although OCD may be associated with differences in self-other monitoring.

Carina Galler | Universität der Bundeswehr München, Neubiberg | Germany
