Virtual reality (VR) provides access to scientific environments and can enhance motivational engagement in STEM learning. Immersive characteristics such as representational fidelity, presence and cybersickness are central to learners’ experiences in VR, yet little is known about how these factors jointly predict distinct motivational components in virtual field trips (VFTs). This study examined the extent to which they predict the motivational components of the ARCS framework during a VFT to a wastewater treatment plant to examine their combined motivational predictive effects in detail.
The sample comprised N=126 10th grade students who participated in a pre–post design. Following the 35-minute VR session, the post-test assessed fidelity, presence, cybersickness and ARCS-based motivation (attention, relevance, confidence and satisfaction).
Regression analyses showed that immersive quality was the dominant predictor of motivation. For attention R²=.458, fidelity b=.350 and presence b=.283 predicted higher scores, whereas cybersickness b=−.168 reduced attention. Relevance R²=.271 was predicted by presence b=.325. Confidence R²=.275 increased with fidelity b=.282 and presence b=.199. Satisfaction R²=.488 was predicted by fidelity b=.461 and presence b=.281, and decreased with cybersickness b=−.149. Instructional factors showed no meaningful contribution.
These findings highlight immersive quality as a key determinant of motivational processes in VR-based STEM learning, indicating that strengthening fidelity and presence while minimising cybersickness is essential for effective VFT design. They also contribute to current discussions on digital transformation in education by showing that the motivational impact of VR depends primarily on immersive quality, highlighting that learners’ motivation is largely driven by how they experience the VR environment.

32. Potenziale dynamischer Achtsamkeit - Eine randomisierte kontrollierte Studie
Prof. Dr. Anna Mikhof | Hochschule Bochum (ehemals HS für Gesundheit) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Anna Mikhof | Hochschule Bochum (ehemals HS für Gesundheit) | Germany
Leonie Wieners | Hochschule Bochum (ehemals HS für Gesundheit)

Achtsamkeit und achtsamkeitsbasierten Ansätzen wird mit Blick auf ihre vielfältigen positiven Effekte in den Bereichen der Psychologie und Medizin sowie ihre Beliebtheit in populärwissenschaftlichen Kreisen die Bedeutung eines Megatrends konzediert. Dynamische Ansätze mit dem primären Fokus auf eine bestimmte Form körperlicher Aktivität als Teil der Achtsamkeitspraxis sind bisher jedoch unzureichend erforscht. Unter Berücksichtigung von Herausforderungen, die im Rahmen klassischer achtsamkeitsbasierter Ansätze entstehen können, sowie von sich bei benachteiligten Gruppen abzeichnenden Barrieren ist ein dynamischer Achtsamkeitsansatz konzipiert worden. Besonders die Kohorte der jungen Erwachsenen, die oftmals stärkeren psychischen Belastungen ausgesetzt ist, könnte von der Evaluierung solcher Ansätze profitieren.
In Rahmen einer randomisierten kontrollierten Studie (N = 74) wurden junge Erwachsene drei Gruppen zugewiesen: (1) einer dynamischen Achtsamkeitsübung, (2) einer klassischen Achtsamkeitsübung oder (3) einer Kontrollgruppe mit einer Placebo-Intervention.
Im Prä-Post-Vergleich zeigten sich signifikante Verbesserungen hinsichtlich verschiedener psychischer Variablen: Die Teilnehmenden gaben nach der Intervention an, geringere Ausprägungen von Angst, Stress, negativem Affekt und depressiven Tendenzen zu erleben. Darüber hinaus berichteten sie über gesteigertes psychisches Wohlbefinden, ausgeprägtere Achtsamkeit und höhere Lebenszufriedenheit. Ein signifikanter Gruppenunterschied erwies sich allerdings ausschließlich in Bezug auf die Achtsamkeit: Nach der Durchführung der dynamischen Achtsamkeitsübung zeigte sich eine signifikant stärkere Zunahme der eigenen Achtsamkeitseinschätzung als nach der klassischen Achtsamkeitsübung.
Mit Blick auf die Befunde lässt sich schlussfolgern, dass dynamische Achtsamkeitsansätze ein vielversprechendes Potenzial hinsichtlich der psychischen Gesundheit vulnerabler Gruppen entfalten können, besonders unter der Berücksichtigung von zielgruppenspezifischen Herausforderungen. Zukünftige Implikationen für die Forschung und Praxis werden thematisiert.

33. Health-related Impairments in Leadership Positions: Organizational Conditions of Disclosure, Participation, and Leadership Culture
Irina Volvakov | University Cologne | Germany
Irina Volvakov | University Cologne | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Irina Volvakov | University Cologne | Germany
Irina Volvakov | University Cologne | Germany

Work and organizations are central areas of social participation in which inequalities are both reproduced and transformed. While health-related impairments in employment have received increasing attention, the perspective of leaders with health-related impairments remains largely unexplored. This contribution examines organizational conditions shaping participation in leadership positions, focusing on the relationship between disclosure of health-related impairments, perceived belonging, and organizational culture.

The empirical basis is a secondary analysis of a cross-sectional survey conducted at a German university (N = 849). The analysis focuses on leaders (n = 185), of whom 36% report health-related impairments. Results show that a substantial part of impairments remains invisible in the workplace, next to a high demand for accommodations, particularly regarding working time and work location. Disclosure is less associated with the severity of impairment or the availability of formal support measures than with social and cultural working conditions. Perceived belonging, authenticity, and an employee-centered leadership culture emerge as key influencing factors.

Compared to leaders without impairments, affected leaders report lower levels of psychological safety, weaker feelings of belonging, and more critical perception of supervisors’ ethical and employee-oriented behavior, indicating reduced trust in the social work environment. Overall, the findings highlight the central role of organizational culture for participation in leadership. From a practical perspective, they underscore the need to systematically integrate health-related diversity into leadership development, organizational design, and workplace policies, with a particular focus on psychological safety, flexible work arrangements, and inclusive leadership cultures.

34. Täglicher Need-Supply-Fit zeitlicher und räumlicher Flexibilität: Eine Tagebuchstudie zu Erholung und Wohlbefinden
Johanna Krandick | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Johanna Krandick | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany
Jenna Amaya Louise Baldy | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg
Anne Marit Wöhrmann | Bundesanstalt für Arbeitsschutz und Arbeitsmedizin Berlin, Leuphana Universität Lüneburg
Prof. Dr. Laura Venz | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg

Flexible Arbeitsarrangements (FAAs), wie Autonomie bezüglich Arbeitszeit und -ort, gelten als Ressourcen zur Förderung von Erholung und Wohlbefinden von Beschäftigten. Bisherige Forschung lässt jedoch offen, inwieweit die Passung zwischen Flexibilitätsangeboten (supply) und individuellen Flexibilitätsbedürfnissen (need) mit Outcomes zusammenhängt. Auf Basis der Need-Supply-Fit-Theorie, wonach Passung (Fit) Wohlbefinden und Erholung fördert, Misfit hingegen Beanspruchung erhöht, untersuchen wir, wie Need-Supply-Fit von zeitlicher und räumlicher Flexibilität mit Arbeitsengagement, Erschöpfung und mentalem Abschalten zusammenhängt. Dabei berücksichtigen wir, dass Need-Supply-Fit nicht statisch ist, sondern von Tag zu Tag schwanken kann, da sowohl der Flexibilitätsbedarf als auch die Angebote täglich variieren können. Wir nehmen an, dass eine tagesspezifische Passung zwischen Bedürfnis und Angebot bezüglich (a) zeitlicher und (b) räumlicher Flexibilität auf hohem Level mit höherem Arbeitsengagement, niedrigerer Erschöpfung und höherem mentalem Abschalten einhergeht als Passung auf niedrigem Level und dass tägliche Unterversorgung (Flexibilitätsbedürfnisse überstiegen das wahrgenommene Angebot) mit niedrigerem Arbeitsengagement, höherer Erschöpfung und schlechterem mentalen Abschalten zusammenhängt.

Um unsere Hypothesen zu testen, führen wir eine präregistrierte zweiwöchige Tagebuchstudie durch. Die Datenanalyse erfolgt mittels (Mehrebenen-)Polynomregressionen in Kombination mit Response-Surface-Analysen. Die Datenerhebung wird im Februar 2026 abgeschlossen, sodass beim DGPs-Kongress die vollständigen Ergebnisse präsentiert werden können.

Die Studie trägt zu einem differenzierteren Verständnis von FAAs bei, indem sie adressiert, dass das strukturelle Vorhandensein von FAAs allein möglicherweise nicht für Erholung und Wohlbefinden genügt, sondern die Passung zu den tagesspezifischen individuellen Flexibilitätsbedürfnissen relevant ist. Damit erweitern wir bestehende Forschung zu FAAs um eine Need-Supply-Fit Perspektive und berücksichtigen, dass Flexibilitätsbedürfnisse und -angebote von Tag zu Tag variieren können.

35. Investigating the trade-off between spending cognitive effort and accepting negative environmental impacts of generative AI
Sarah Kusch | UGent | Belgium
Show details
Authors:
Sarah Kusch | UGent | Belgium
Prof. Ruth Kreb | UGent | Belgium

Every day, students have to decide whether to use generative artificial intelligence (genAI) models for their course work. This decision involves a trade-off between incurring direct personal costs (i.e., cognitive effort and time) and accepting hidden environmental consequences of using genAI.
This preregistered study (n = 163) systematically tested this trade-off. Students made nine choices on whether to use a genAI model to write an essay. On each trial, we varied the required essay length and the environmental impact of the genAI model. Afterwards, participants wrote an essay with or without genAI, depending on their choices. We then asked them about the meaningfulness and effortfulness of the task, and the subjective value of their essay. We also collected qualitative data on their choice reasoning.
We found that the shorter the essay length and the higher the environmental impact, the less likely participants were to use genAI. The qualitative responses confirmed that these two factors determined their decisions. We also found that that perceived meaningfulness and effortfulness were significantly higher in the group that did not use genAI while there was no difference in the subjective value of the essay. Factors such as confidence in writing skills mediated the observed effects.
The environmental impact of a genAI model is a determining factor in students’ decisions on their use, when this information is available. Our findings support the call for more transparency of genAI models regarding their environmental impact to enable students to make informed decisions that align with their preferences.

This research explores how the presence of comparison groups shapes societal stereotypes of criminal offenders, drawing on the Stereotype Content Model and theories of social comparison. Across three studies which were conducted via online questionnaires, we demonstrate that perceptions of offenders are shaped not only by type of crime but also by comparative context. Using k-means cluster analysis, we found that in Study 1 (N= 68, German university students) crimes causing direct harm were perceived colder and less competent. Study 2 (N = 5,174, representative for German adult population) revealed that offenders were rated significantly lower in warmth and competence when compared to non-offending groups, underscoring the impact of social context. Study 3 (N = 595, adult Prolific sample) experimentally confirmed these findings by manipulating the presence (or absence) of non-offending reference groups, demonstrating that their inclusion amplifies negative perceptions of offenders. These results highlight the importance of context in shaping societal judgments and offer implications for criminal justice policy and offender reintegration.

Environmental effectiveness knowledge (EEK)—knowing about the mitigation impact of behaviors on climate change—helps people make choices that have the greatest positive impact on the environment. However, research on EEK and its behavioral relevance across sociocultural contexts is limited. This study investigated EEK in adults from Bolivia (N = 365) and Germany (N = 456). EEK was operationalized by participants' ability to correctly rate the climate mitigation impact of various behaviors. We examined (1) predictors of EEK and then (2) the relationship between EEK and self-reported pro-environmental behavior (PEB), including potential moderators. Results revealed a general lack of EEK in both subsamples. Greater involvement in climate-related activities predicted higher EEK in both countries. However, EEK was only associated with PEB in the German subsample. These findings highlight a lack in EEK as a global problem and emphasize the need for targeted educational interventions—both formal and informal. Additionally, our results point to a need for methodological refinement in the Bolivian context, suggesting that commonly used psychological constructs may not transfer directly across cultural settings.

Plastic is one of the most critically discussed materials in environmental discourse. Importantly, the same material can be described using different labels—plastic, synthetic material, or polymer.
The present study examined whether labeling an identical, environmentally contested material affects attitudes toward its use and whether such effects depend on individual differences in environmental identity, critical thinking disposition, and affinity for science and technology.
In an online experiment, 303 participants were randomly assigned to evaluate a material labeled as either plastic, synthetic material, or polymer.
Results showed that attitudes toward material use were shaped by both labeling (H1) and individual differences (H2). Consistent with H1, attitudes toward material use differed significantly by label, F(2, 300) = 6.18, p = .002, with plastic evaluated more negatively than synthetic material and polymer. Furthermore (H2), significant main effects of individual difference variables and interaction effects indicated that environmental identity amplified negative attitudes—particularly toward plastic—whereas higher critical thinking disposition attenuated negative responses to plastic. Affinity for science and technology predicted more positive attitudes toward polymer. After accounting for these dispositional factors, the main effect of labeling was no longer significant.
Additional analyses of semantic evaluations revealed systematic differences across multiple semantic dimensions; for example, plastic evoked more negative eco-moral associations, whereas polymer was perceived as more environmentally positive but less familiar, aiding interpretation of the attitude effects.
Overall, the findings highlight the importance of audience-specific language choices in environmental and materials-related communication.

Prof. Kathrin Ackermann | University of Siegen | Germany
Prof. Jan Rummel | Heidelberg University | Germany

Floods and other climate change induced disasters are becoming increasingly common, threatening the livelihood of many individuals across the world. Intuitively, experiencing such events first-hand can have wide-reaching impacts and may foster pro-environmental responses of individual citizens, including cognitions, such as belief in and the perceived risks of climate change, as well as behaviors, such as personal mitigation efforts. However, the empirical evidence on how first-hand experience influences such pro-environmental responses seems to be mixed. Arguably, a key contributing factor to inconclusive results lies in the methodological limitations of most studies which largely prevented them to identify causal effects of natural disaster experience to begin with. To address this, we conducted a quasi-experimental study comparing a total of N = 398 individuals affected with those unaffected by the 2021 floods in Germany on different pro-environmental responses before and after the event. To identify causal effects of the event, we conducted propensity score matching of individuals affected by the floods with those unaffected and employed Bayesian mixed models to analyze the data. Our findings suggest flooding experience to only have marginal effects on pro-environmental responses. Although we observed small effects on some outcomes, such as personal norms to act against climate change or political participation, affected individuals did not differ from those unaffected on most other outcomes. We discuss our results in the context of factors shaping individual-level pro-environmental responses and derive practical implications for climate change mitigation strategies.

Life in rural eastern Germany is shaped by limited regional opportunities (Bernard et al., 2023) including low density of adult education facilities, cultural offerings, and suppliers of high-quality food. Participatory approaches to food production such as community-supported agriculture (CSA) could improve access to sustainable, healthy food while providing spaces for exchange, learning, and negotiation in rural regions (Spanier, 2025). In CSA, members pay a fixed membership fee to support a farm and receive a weekly harvest share in return. They may also participate in horticultural activities, community management, or decision making. Given this level of involvement in production, consumers potentially become prosumers. However, research identified several barriers for engaging in CSA such as high costs, low accessibility, or social exclusion (e.g., Hennchen & Schäfer, 2022). These barriers may be particularly prevalent in rural, economically disadvantaged areas. In the current study, we investigate the psychological processes underlying CSA member involvement. Following a mixed-methods approach, we conducted four focus groups that served as the basis for a structured survey with n = 270 members of 15 CSA initiatives in rural eastern Germany. Using quantitative models, we intend to specify relationships between a) the perceived conditions for member involvement on the organizational level of the CSA initiative, b) the felt attachment to the initiative, and c) the willingness to participate in CSA member activities. Our findings provide insights into the psychological determinants of collective sustainable behavior (cf. Fritsche et al., 2018) and offer guidance to practitioners from participatory food production in rural regions.

Digital information (DI) literacy is essential for social participation and professional integration in our digital society. Even though DI skills are part of school curricula in Germany, their development still depends heavily on socio-economic factors as adolescents who are disadvantaged due to their living conditions or international family history are at particularly high risk of being excluded from educational processes. Consequently, this group usually faces challenges in developing DI literacy which makes it hard for them to use digital information self-determined, critical, and responsible in order to achieve their goals.

Our interdisciplinary project aims at developing and evaluating an integrated training app for promoting DI literacy among disadvantaged young people in the vocational transition system. In this regard, we aim at promoting seven key socio-emotional and cognitive DI skills such as identifying false information or protecting self-concept and well-being in a digital context. The training app will comprise a total of seven 30-minute modules (one for each DI skill), which are intended to be used independently and as supplement in classroom teaching.

In focus groups, we evaluated learning goals and design elements of the training app with our target group and their educators (n = 22). Next, comprehensibility and acceptance of the training app will be evaluated (n = 40 per module). Afterwards, the effectiveness of the training app in fostering DI literacy will be tested in randomized pre-post studies with a waiting control group design (n = 140 per module). Results of these studies will be presented.

The global decline of pollinators is a critical concern for ecosystem stability and global food security. Pollinator-dependent crops account for 35% of the world's food production by volume and about 40% of global nutritional supply for humans. Additionally, it is estimated that 87% of all flowering plants are pollinated by animals. Home gardens are increasingly recognized as valuable natural habitats that provide food, water, and shelter for wild pollinators. This is especially important in urban areas with limited natural environments and in regions with large-scale intensive agricultural landscapes. However, many households are unaware of pollinator-friendly gardening practices, despite positive attitude towards pollinator conservation. Our study will test whether implementation intention and knowledge interventions can increase the likelihood that gardeners will purchase pollinator-friendly plants. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of three groups: 1) the treatment group will be tasked with implementation intentions planning and provided with pollinator-friendly information, 2) the control group will be provided with pollinator-friendly information only, and 3) the baseline group will receive neither. We hypothesize that forming implementation intentions will increase participants' willingness to pay for pollinator-friendly plants when tasked with creating a shopping list for garden plants. Including an information-only group will allow us to assess the effectiveness of an intervention that is based on actionable knowledge. The findings of this study will provide insights into the use of implementation intentions to encourage environmentally conscious behaviors in general and assess the potential of promoting pollinator-friendly gardening as a viable intervention to foster pollinator stewardship.

Prof. Dr. Florian Klapproth | Medical School Berlin (MSB) | Germany
Show details
Authors:

Carolin Beyte | Medical School Berlin (MSB)

This experimental vignette study investigates how academic performance, subject domain, student gender, and teachers’ attitudes toward grade retention jointly shape promotion decisions. A sample of N = 146 pre-service and in-service teachers evaluated 12 systematically varied student profiles differing in grade point average (poor vs. very poor), failing subject (language vs. mathematics/science), and gender. In addition, participants completed a 16-item scale assessing attitudes toward grade retention. Using generalized estimating equation models to account for the clustered data structure, we found that lower academic performance markedly increased the likelihood of recommending grade retention. Moreover, failure in language subjects was evaluated more critically than failure in mathematics/science. Beyond these main effects, a significant Gender × Subject interaction emerged: female students were more likely to be recommended for retention when failing in mathematics, indicating the presence of subject-specific gender stereotypes. Teachers’ pro-retention attitudes independently predicted a higher propensity to recommend retention, whereas professional status (pre-service vs. in-service) was unrelated to decision-making. Overall, the findings suggest that although teachers’ promotion decisions are primarily guided by academic criteria, they are also subtly influenced by gendered expectations linked to subject domains and by individual belief systems. Implications for teacher education, bias-sensitive assessment practices, and educational policy are discussed.

45. Between Environmental Values and Organizational Constraints: Making Sense of Sustainability at Work
Sabrina Schopf | Johannes Kepler Universitaet Linz | Austria
Show details
Authors:
Sabrina Schopf | Johannes Kepler Universitaet Linz | Austria
Prof. Dr. Barbara Stiglbauer | Johannes Kepler Universitaet Linz

As sustainability-related demands and expectations become increasingly present in professional contexts, tensions can emerge between personal environmental values and work-related actions shaped by organizational roles and conditions. These tensions reflect a value-action gap and are particularly pronounced in contexts where opportunities for sustainable action are perceived as limited. Understanding how employees navigate these tensions in everyday work is therefore crucial for practice-oriented sustainability transformations. Accordingly, the present study addresses the research question of how employees experience, interpret, and cope with sustainability-related value-action conflicts in their everyday work.
This qualitative study draws on 15 semi-structured interviews with employees from organizations involved in plastic manufacturing and processing. We used thematic analysis to explore how employees negotiate and integrate value-action conflicts into everyday work practices under conditions of limited agency.
Preliminary findings indicate that employees often experience ambivalence when personal environmental concerns conflict with perceived organizational demands. Participants used the following coping strategies: shifting responsibility to organizational structures and external constraints, legitimizing plastic-related practices through necessity and trade-off reasoning, and reframing sustainability tensions as technical or managerial challenges. These patterns align with theoretical concepts of moral disengagement and cognitive dissonance.
This study contributes to existing research by extending the analysis of sustainability behavior beyond voluntary or leisure contexts to organizational settings characterized by limited individual agency. Drawing on the plastics sector as a sustainability-challenged context, this analysis highlights how organizational conditions shape attitudes, responsibility, and action, thereby offering insights into the psychological processes underlying value-action conflicts at work.

Neurowissenschaftliche interindividuelle Unterschiede werden im Kontext von „Personality Neuroscience“ experimentell untersucht. Basierend auf den Ergebnissen einer publizierten Meta-Analyse (Leue & Wichert, 2024) werden in diesem Beitrag die wichtigsten Ergebnisse vorgestellt. Für k = 66 Primärstudien (N > 9000) konnte gezeigt werden, dass bimodale Stimuli zu einer substanziell besseren Performanz von Mock-Ohrenzeugen*innen führen im Vergleich zu unimodalen Stimuli. Desweiteren zeigte sich für die Stimulusdauer bei auditiven target-present Line-ups ein substanzieller Populationseffekt. Längere Stimuli führten dabei im Vergleich zu kürzeren Stimuli zu einer substanziell besseren Performanz von Mock-Ohrenzeugen*innen. Darüber hinaus zeigten weibliche verglichen mit männlichen Mock-Ohrenzeugen*innen eine substanziell bessere Performanz. Zur Beschreibung der meta-analytischen Performanzergebnisse sollen aufbauend auf dem Value of Computation Modell (Shenhav et al., 2017) Annahmen zum neurowissenschaftlichen Mechanismus Mental Effort hergeleitet werden. Dazu wird mit Bezug zu vier Benchmarks des Arbeitsgedächtnisses (Oberauer et al., 2018) vor allem die experimentelle und trait-bezogene Modulation des Mental Effort für die Verarbeitung auditiver Stimuli herausgestellt. Der Beitrag beschreibt hypothesenbezogen zwei experimentelle Bedingungen und zwei Trait-Arten aus dem Kontext des „Rationalen Meta-Reasoning“ sowie die P3-Komponente des ereigniskorrelierten Potenzials als physiologischen Parameter zur mentalen Ressourcenallokation des Arbeitsgedächtnisses. Schließlich werden Annahmen zum Aufbau hierarchischer und non-hierarchischer Netzwerkmodelle des Arbeitsgedächtnisses von Baddeley und Vandierendonck vorgestellt. Die neurowissenschaftliche experimentelle Konzeption soll mit dem Vortrag vorgestellt werden. Die Studie soll untersuchen, ob und wie Menschen mit unterschiedlichen Ausprägungen des „Meta-Reasoning“ nach dem Value of Computation Modell mentale Ressourcen des Arbeitsgedächtnisses allozieren. Damit sollen für den Bereich „Personality Neuroscience“ möglichst neue Erkenntnisse zu trait- und arbeitsgedächtnisbezogenem Mental Effort gewonnen werden.

Ecological sustainability is increasingly important in competitive sports, as athletes’ activities can contribute to environmental harm (e.g., by traveling and using resources), and they themselves and their activities are vulnerable to climate change impact (e.g. extreme heat, lack of snow). For athletes, sustainability is not only a contextual, but also a psychological challenge. Sustainability-related cognitions and affects can shape attention, stress regulation, motivation, and decision making, which may have direct influence on their performance. Moreover, athletes may experience cognitive dissonance when pro-environmental attitudes conflict with sport-specific constraints, potentially triggering rumination and negative affect. However, instruments to measure these effects are currently lacking in the research field, as global scales do not capture the ecological and sports-related content nor differentiate between cognitions and affects.
Therefore, the aim of this study is to develop a questionnaire for assessing sustainability-related cognition and affect in competitive sports. To this end, three steps are used to generate a sufficient item pool. In doing so, we are carrying out a) a systematic review of respective psychometric measures, b) conducting 10 semi-structured interviews with athletes from different disciplines, and c) generating items with AI-support to broaden content coverage. In a second step, we are developing a questionnaire on sustainability-related cognitions and affects in competitive sports by reducing the generated item pool, using prototype ratings. The completion of this questionnaire is expected by July 2026, followed by a subsequent study to validate the scale.

Today, children encounter digital media at an increasingly early age. However, studies show that they struggle to recognize fake news reliably. Their judgments often remain at chance level and are strongly influenced by surface cues such as layout or language (Xu et al., 2022; Shtulman, 2024). Recent research also indicates that targeted media literacy programs can strengthen both recognition skills and confidence in personal judgment (Allaire-Duquette et al., 2025). This highlights the need for age-appropriate approaches that foster critical awareness and informed participation in digital environments.
To address this, we developed Escape the Fake, a gamified training program for lower secondary students. The concept builds on Potter’s (2004) and Baacke’s (2007) media literacy models and combines narrative scenarios, escape-room logic, and teamwork to promote analytical and reflective skills. Gamification elements, based on Deterding et al. (2011), are used to increase engagement and motivation. The training focuses on three key topics: fake news, data privacy, and cyberbullying.
We evaluated the program using a pre-post design (see Kirkpatrick’s model Levels 1 and 2; Kirkpatrick, 1996) with N = 159 students from fifth and sixth grade. Data were analyzed using paired-sample t-tests and qualitative feedback analysis. Results show clear improvements across all three key topics, particularly in identifying fake news (p < .001, d = 1.13), along with high engagement and positive feedback.
Our findings suggest that game-based, narrative learning formats can effectively build media literacy and digital resilience at an early age, translating theory into practice in an engaging and sustainable way.

50. A user-centered approach to LLM-supported HCI in Controlled Agricultural Environments
Dr Vivien Lungwitz | TU Chemnitz, Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr Vivien Lungwitz | TU Chemnitz, Institut für Psychologie | Germany

Controlled Agricultural Environments (CAE), such as indoor farms and aquaponic systems, have advanced rapidly in recent years and are increasingly deployed across economic sectors. Indoor farming offers high yield stability, consistent product quality, and improved resource efficiency, but simultaneously introduces complex, highly automated systems. This increasing system complexity challenges day-to-day operators, scientists, and managers in understanding system behavior and in developing trust in automated control strategies, not only in fault situations.
This contribution presents a user-centered design approach for developing human computer interaction (HCI) interfaces supported by LLMs in Controlled Agricultural Environments. Following DIN EN ISO 9241-210, a requirements analysis was conducted using interviews and shadowing with heterogeneous stakeholder groups. Based on these empirical data, personas were developed to represent distinct user groups with differing goals, levels of expertise, and mental models. These personas serve as a foundational design artifact to tailor LLM-based feedback and explanations of complex dynamic processes within CAE systems in a comprehensible, trustworthy, and role-appropriate manner.
Planned user studies will investigate how persona-driven, LLM-mediated interaction influences system understanding, acceptance of automation, and willingness to adopt novel CAE technologies in the future. This work contributes to human-centered AI design in sustainability-critical production environments.

51. Measuring a Summative and Abstract Attitude of Technology Usage: A Scale Development of Usage Perception
Marvin Schittko | Technische Universität Berlin | Germany
Show details
Author:
Marvin Schittko | Technische Universität Berlin | Germany

Attitudes play a central role in technology evaluation by integrating emotional and cognitive judgments that shape acceptance and behavior. As technologies increase in complexity, these attitudes emerge layered, encompassing evaluations of system design and broader perceptions of a technology’s usage and impact. Existing Human–Computer Interaction measurements predominantly capture system-related attitudes, leaving higher-level, usage-oriented evaluations underrepresented. To account for these, this paper validates the measurement of Usage Perception (UP), a summative and abstract attitudinal construct reflecting users’ cognitively weighted evaluations of a technology’s overall usage and impact beyond the direct interaction with the system.

The UP scale was developed following a best-practice, tripartite validation strategy. First, the construct was theoretically specified to ensure conceptual clarity and construct purity. Second, its measurement structure was empirically validated using confirmatory factor analysis. Third, nomological validity was established by embedding UP within a broader theoretical framework. The resulting scale consists of a stable core of seven semantic differential items, with optional context-sensitive extensions that allow flexible application while preserving comparability.

Empirical validation was conducted across three complementary studies: an online experiment, a controlled laboratory human–robot interaction, and a longitudinal in-field driving study involving an SAE Level 2+ advanced driver assistance system. Together, this paper tests a comprehensive and diverse dataset across different technologies and interactions within more than N = 1300 samples in total. It provides convergent evidence for the reliability, validity, and applicability of UP.

52. LLM Hallucinations from a Human-Centred Perspective - A Scoping Review
Leon Hannig | Universität Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Leon Hannig | Universität Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Dr. Greta Ontrup | Universität Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Paul-Vincent Heisenberg | Technische Universität München (TUM)

Hallucinations, defined as incorrect, irrelevant, or incongruent outputs generated by large language models (LLMs), are among the most critical challenges in their application. While prior research has focused on technical mitigation strategies, far less attention has been paid to the role of humans in preventing, detecting, and responding to hallucinations. This scoping review synthesizes existing research on LLM hallucinations from a human-centred perspective.

The review addresses four research questions: (1) how user-centred research on LLM hallucinations is conducted across disciplines, application contexts, and methodological approaches; (2) which user behaviours and user-related consequences are observed in relation to hallucinations; (3) which interventions and influencing factors have been examined with regard to users’ prevention, detection, and responses to hallucinations; and (4) which recommendations for practice, policy, and future research are reported.

A systematic literature search was conducted in October 2025 across six scientific databases, yielding 1,902 records. Eligible studies had to centrally address how real human users prevent, detect, or respond to LLM hallucinations. Following abstract screening, 38 studies are currently included in full-text screening and data extraction (to be completed before March 2026). The included literature spans multiple disciplines, including psychology, education, and computer science , and comprises studies with participants from North America, Europe, and Asia.

Taken together, the study will identify patterns in user-centred hallucination research, highlight key gaps, and summarize strategies that support appropriate responses to unreliable outputs. The findings aim to inform the responsible design and deployment of LLM-based systems in contexts where factual accuracy is essential.

Emotional processes play an important role in situations of peer exclusion (Arsenio & Lemerise, 2004). Understanding and recognizing one’s own and others’ emotions is crucial for children to act prosocially (Ettekal et al., 2015). With Virtual Reality (VR) becoming more accessible, the question arises whether VR can be an additional tool to study and foster children’s emotional competencies in such situations beyond existing methods. VR offers a realistic, real-time simulation of the situation from multiple perspectives in a first-person point of view (Tan et al, 2022). Children can experience emotions as the situations unfold from different perspectives, which can be targeted by educators to increase emotional competencies in children. However, research on VR in this context is rare (Boboc & Damaševičius, 2024), and the question remains, how children experience virtual situations.
In this study we investigated children’s sense of being there (adapted measure by Verhoef et al., 2022 and Herrera et al., 2018) and emotional experience (derived from Ongley & Malti, 2014) when witnessing peer exclusion in different VR and non-VR modes from the perspectives of a bystander and the victimized child.
Preliminary results (n=124 children, mage=10.86 years, 41.9% female) revealed no difference in presence for modes and perspectives. For emotions, preliminary analysis showed a significant main effect of perspective (F(1,110) =11.51, p < .001). Future analysis will further explore the results.
We will discuss the potentials and limitations of different VR and non-VR modes and contribute to a better understanding of the role of new technology in developmental research.

Sarah Zabel | University of Hohenheim | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Sarah Zabel | University of Hohenheim | Germany
Nicolas Neef
Prof. Dr. Siegmar Otto

When working with conversational agents (CAs), people can reduce interaction to a minimum or engage in close collaboration—much like in human–human settings. This variability raises the question of which individual factors shape how people collaborate with such systems. One relevant factor is social camouflaging, a social coping strategy that entails adapting one’s behaviour to meet social expectations, often at considerable cognitive and emotional cost. Across three preregistered studies (N = 950), we examined how camouflaging relates to collaboration intensity with text- and voice-based CAs. Consistently, individuals reporting stronger camouflaging tendencies —particularly those high in compensation—showed higher collaboration intensity with conversational agents. These associations did not extend to human–human collaboration or to general attitudes toward AI. Thus, despite the interaction via natural language, individuals who find social interaction demanding may perceive collaboration with conversational agents as a more predictable and less judgmental space for social interaction.

Ida Schulze Tast | Universität Münster

The potential of artificial intelligence to support and improve the empirical research process has become a topic of intense discussion. We think that methodologically grounded AI agents, that are deliberately designed, quality-controlled, and validated by methodological experts, may pose a better framework than universal AI chatbots for supporting human researchers throughout all stages of the scientific process.
In my poster presentation, I will present a prototype of an “AI mentor” that guides users step by step through the full analytical process: from the translation of a verbal theoretical idea to a statistically testable hypothesis, the selection and execution of suitable statistical analyses, to the result interpretation and verbalization of a substantive conclusion. The AI mentor shall promote methodologically sound research by guiding users through the whole process with directive questions, systematically aligning later analytical steps with earlier theoretical and methodological decisions. All the while, human oversight is embedded as an essential mechanism for validating and, where necessary, correcting AI output. The AI mentor will be illustratively tailored to multiple linear regression and may serve as a blueprint for subsequent AI mentors dedicated to other statistical methods.
The poster presents the current state of the prototype and illustrates its application with an exemplary research plan that was designed in collaboration with the AI mentor. Moreover, I will discuss the potential benefits and the challenges that may be associated with integrating AI agents into research practice.

Der Einsatz von KI-Systemen in gesundheitskritischen Kontexten erfordert nicht nur ein hohes initiales Vertrauen, sondern insbesondere wirksame Mechanismen zur Wiederherstellung von Vertrauen nach Vertrauensverletzungen. Dies ist im medizinischen Bereich von besonderer Bedeutung, da Fehler hier potenziell schwerwiegende gesundheitliche Konsequenzen für Patient:innen haben können. Aufbauend auf dem Vertrauensmodell von Mayer und Kollegen sowie aktuellen Arbeiten zur Kalibrierung von Vertrauen in KI und Strategien zur Vertrauenswiederherstellung untersucht die vorliegende Studie, wie unterschiedliche Reparaturstrategien nach einem KI-Fehler die Vertrauensrekonstruktion beeinflussen.
In einem Szenario-basierten Online-Experiment mit medizinischem Anwendungskontext wird zunächst Baseline-Vertrauen in eine KI erfasst. Anschließend erleben die Teilnehmenden entweder einen Vertrauensbruch durch eine fehlerhafte Empfehlung oder eine fehlerfreie Kontrollsituation. Nach dem Vertrauensbruch erhalten sie eine von drei Interventionen zur Vertrauenswiederherstellung: (a) eine Erklärung der Fehlerursache mit handlungsbezogenen Anweisungen zur zukünftigen Fehlervermeidung, (b) eine reine kausale Fehlererklärung oder (c) eine bloße Entschuldigung ohne inhaltliche Aufklärung. Eine vierte Gruppe dient als fehlerfreie Kontrollbedingung. Das Design kombiniert Within- und Between-Subject-Faktoren und erfasst Vertrauen sowie die zugrunde liegenden Dimensionen Kompetenz, Integrität und Wohlwollen zu mehreren Messzeitpunkten.
Theoretisch wird erwartet, dass beobachtete KI-Fehler als negativer Hinweis die wahrgenommene Vertrauenswürdigkeit reduzieren und dass Reparaturstrategien, die kausale Attributionen und Kontrollierbarkeit adressieren, Vertrauen stärker wiederherstellen als rein affektive Strategien. Insbesondere sollten erklärende und handlungsorientierte Interventionen die Kompetenzzuschreibung und damit kalibriertes Vertrauen fördern.
Die Datenerhebung befindet sich aktuell in Durchführung. Die Ergebnisse werden zur Konferenz vollständig vorliegen und dort berichtet. Die Studie leistet einen Beitrag zum Verständnis funktionaler Mechanismen zur Vertrauenswiederherstellung in alltagsnahen, sicherheitskritischen KI-Anwendungen.

57. Re-Learning Morality? A Framework on the Effects of Technology-Mediated Moral Outrage on Individuals, Groups, and Networks

Show details

Prof. Dr. German Neubaum | University of Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Hannah T. Logemann | University of Duisburg-Essen

Moral outrage, which refers to anger or disgust in response to moral violations, is recognized as a strong catalyst for social change. Recent academic opinions suggest that this influence has been amplified by emerging network technologies, but unfortunately not for the better. It is expected that moralized messages in social media desensitize our sense of morality and cultivate a desire to publicly punish others which, in turn, may foster societal divides. This work presents a theoretical framework on the diverse effects of technology-mediated moral outrage on an intrapersonal, intergroup, and network level. A newly introduced model of morality disruption and disconnection offers psychological explanations for the immediate and long-term effects of technology-mediated moral outrage on human beings’ inner morality and social conduct.
By integrating different strands of moral, social, and media psychological as well as communication research, this model specifies how moral outrage, distributed through network technologies, can a) affect expressors’ and recipients’ moral cognitions (i.e., shaping their moral convictions and moral identity), b) create intergroup animosities based on moral divergences, and c) lead to a moral fragmentation within a network.
The presentation will cover the theoretical underpinnings of these hypotheses as well as suggestions for an empirical research agenda and will hopefully provoke a scholarly debate to systematically uncover the efficacy of network technologies to shape human beings’ morality.

This study investigates how AI-generated art is perceived based on labeling practices while
analyzing the impact of threat framing and occupational status. We employed a mixed
experimental design to assess six AI-generated paintings through 186 participants comprising
64 professional artists and 122 non-artists. The participants assessed the paintings through
three framing conditions (disruptive threat, collaborative opportunity, control group), while the
authorship labels were presented as either AI-generated or human-made in a fully randomized
manner. The analysis revealed that human-authorship labels increased creativity ratings.
Contrary to expectations, threat framing did not moderate this effect. Occupational status,
however, proved decisive: lay participants relied strongly on authorship labels, whereas
professional artists did not show significant differences in their evaluations of AI- and human-
labelled works. This study demonstrates that symbolic cues, expertise, and identity shape the
reception of AI art, with authorship labels playing a central role in evaluative judgments. We
therefore introduce the concept of a Creativity Attribution Bias, defined as the tendency to
ascribe higher creativity to human-labelled works—a pattern that is substantially attenuated
among professional artists.

Seit der breiten Verfügbarkeit generativer Sprachmodelle ist der Einsatz künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) im Arbeitskontext ein intensiv beforschtes Thema. Empirische Studien zeigen ein gemischtes Bild: KI-Nutzung kann sowohl positive Effekte auf Motivation und Wohlbefinden haben als auch mit Belastung einhergehen, während die Ursachen dieser Ambivalenz bislang unzureichend bekannt sind. Frühere Arbeiten betrachteten die Auswirkungen von KI auf Ebene ganzer Berufe, jüngere Beiträge legen hingegen nahe, dass relevante Effekte primär auf Aufgabenebene entstehen und stark von Tätigkeitskontext und Nutzungsverhalten abhängen. Dennoch fehlen bislang Taxonomien und Messinstrumente, die systematisch KI-Nutzungsverhalten erfassen. Dies erschwert Forschung dazu, welche Aufgabenmerkmale den Einsatz von KI begünstigen oder hemmen und wie das Nutzungsverhalten subjektiv erlebt wird. Ziel dieses Forschungsprojektes ist daher die Entwicklung einer empirisch fundierten Taxonomie von (gelingendem und hinderlichem) KI-Nutzungsverhalten.
Wir adressieren diese Forschungslücke durch eine qualitativ-explorative Untersuchung der KI-Nutzung im Arbeitsalltag. In einer Online-Befragung beschrieben N = 30 berufstätige Personen aus unterschiedlichen Tätigkeitsfeldern ihre Arbeitsaufgaben, ihren KI-Einsatz sowie die Bedingungen, unter denen sie KI als hilfreich, belastend oder verzichtbar wahrnahmen. Die Fragen wurden deduktiv aus Forschungssträngen der AOW- und der Ingenieurspsychologie abgeleitet (Arbeitsgestaltung, Job Characteristics Modell, Job Demands–Resources Theorie, Meaningful Work, Technologieakzeptanzmodelle). Die Daten werden aktuell mittels qualitativer Inhaltsanalyse und computergestützter Textanalyse ausgewertet, um inhaltlich-thematische Kategorien sowie Muster subjektiver Bewertungen zu identifizieren. Die Ergebnisse werden auf dem Kongress präsentiert.
Indem sie die Mensch-KI-Interaktion im Arbeitskontext in etablierte Konzepte einbettet, leistet die Studie einen Beitrag zur menschenzentrierten KI-Forschung und -Implementierung und bildet die Basis für ein Messinstrument zur systematischen Operationalisierung des KI-Nutzungsverhaltens bei der Arbeit.

Show details

Artifical Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in higher education, yet adoption differs across academic roles. Existing research has focused primarily on system-level characteristics, while organizational and psychological conditions shaping trust in AI remain understudied. This study conceptualizes trust in AI as a multidimensional construct comprising cognitive trust (evaluations of reliability and competence) and emotional trust (feelings of comfort and safety), and examines how these dimensions relate to AI use in academic contexts.
This study contributes to the literature by integrating organizational trust, psychological safety, and the Theory of Planned Behavior into a configurational model of AI trust that distinguishes between emotional and cognitive pathways across academic roles. Survey data were collected within a university context from students (N = 565) and professors (N~183, data collection ongoing). Emotional trust showed consistently stronger associations with AI use intentions than cognitive trust, with effects of small-to-moderate magnitude, whereas cognitive trust was primarily related to attitudes toward AI and perceived behavioral control. Group comparisons suggest differences between students and professors not only in trust levels, but also in the configuration linking emotional and cognitive trust to AI use.
Overall, the findings indicate that AI adoption in higher education is shaped less by isolated trust levels than by the alignment of emotional and cognitive trust within specific academic roles and organizational contexts. This highlights intentional AI use—balancing emotional confidence with cognitive caution—as a relevant future competence, while acknowledging the substantial potential of AI to support and enhance academic work when embedded in supportive organizational environments.

Dr. Astrid Carolus | University of Würzburg | Germany

As AI-based recommender systems increasingly shape media usage, e.g., conversational agents become a common interface for guiding content choices on streaming platforms. Beyond algorithmic accuracy, user acceptance depends on psychological factors such as trust, perceived competence, communication style, and users’ domain expertise.
Drawing on the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) framework, this study investigates how a film recommendation chatbot’s competence (high vs. low) and its communication style (anthropomorphic vs. neutral) influence users’ trust, performance expectancy, and behavioral intention, while examining the mediating role of film expertise.
The chatbot is based on API-accessed, GDPR-compliant Large Language Models (Mistral), with a Python-based application orchestrating prompt-driven response generation and the controlled implementation of different experimental conditions.
Using a 2 × 2 between-subjects experimental design, participants were randomly assigned to one out of four chatbot versions that asked for users’ movie preferences to provide personalized recommendations. Results show a main effect of competence: high-competence chatbots significantly outperformed others across all outcome measures. Anthropomorphic language, however, showed no consistent main effect and interaction effects were weak or non-significant.
By disentangling social cues from recommendation quality, this study confirms that functional performance outweighs anthropomorphic design in film selection. Future research should examine if this functional primacy persists in high-stakes domains like finance or medicine.

62. Akademische Zugehörigkeit im Wandel: Eine Untersuchung des Zugehörigkeitserlebens von Studierenden und der Einflussfaktoren darauf im Hinblick auf generative künstliche Intelligenz
Ekaterina Saveleva | Universität Hamburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Ekaterina Saveleva | Universität Hamburg | Germany
Dr. Jonas Breetzke | Universität Hamburg | Germany
Dr. Alexa Brase | Universität Hamburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Carla Bohndick | Universität Hamburg

Zugehörigkeit ist ein grundlegendes menschliches Bedürfnis (Baumeister & Leary, 1995) und Prädiktor für Wohlbefinden und Studienerfolg (van Kessel et al., 2025). Dabei werden in den letzten Jahren Lehre, Lernen und soziale Beziehungen an Hochschulen durch generative künstliche Intelligenz (GenKI) beeinflusst (Crawford et al., 2024). Dennoch liegen bislang nur wenige empirische Erkenntnisse zur Wirkung der GenKI-Nutzung auf das Zugehörigkeitsgefühl der Studierenden vor (Al-Zahrani, 2025; Crawford et al., 2024).
Ziel dieser Studie ist es, anhand leitfadengestützter Interviews mit Studierenden (N = 21) zu untersuchen, (1) wie sie Zugehörigkeit an der Hochschule erleben, (2) welche Faktoren das Zugehörigkeitserleben fördern oder beeinträchtigen und (3) welche Rolle GenKI dabei spielt. Die Auswertung transkribierter Interviews erfolgt mittels thematischer Analyse (Braun & Clarke, 2006).
Die Ergebnisse zeigen, (1) dass Zugehörigkeit primär über soziale Beziehungen zu Mitstudierenden sowie wertschätzende Interaktionen mit Lehrenden erlebt wird. Die Rolle der Hochschule besteht dabei darin, Rahmenbedingungen für ein positives Umfeld zu schaffen. (2) Förderlich sind insbesondere konstante Lerngruppen, persönlicher Bezug und Augenhöhe mit dem (Lehr-)Personal, organisatorische Klarheit und Transparenz sowie informelle soziale Räume am Campus. Nicht-Zugehörigkeit ist hingegen geprägt von Unpersönlichkeit, Intransparenz und Unsicherheit. (3) GenKI wird als funktionales Werkzeug wahrgenommen und nicht als soziales Gegenüber. Ihr Einfluss auf Zugehörigkeit ist indirekt: Eine offene, hochschulweite Kommunikation sowie ein souveräner Umgang mit GenKI sind förderlich, während Intransparenz zu Unsicherheit und wahrgenommener Ungerechtigkeit führen kann.
Die Studie bildet eine Grundlage für weiterführende Forschung und für eine informierte Hochschulpraxis, indem sie erste Ansatzpunkte für eine zugehörigkeitsfördernde Lehrarchitektur im GenKI-Zeitalter liefert.

63. Kritische Online-Informationsbewertung bei Studierenden: Fähigkeitsprofile und epistemologische Überzeugungen
Paul Frederik Hodes | JGU Mainz | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Paul Frederik Hodes | JGU Mainz | Germany
Dr. Marie-Theres Nagel | JGU Mainz
Prof. Dr. Zlatkin-Troitschanskaia Olga | JGU Mainz | Germany

Studierende nutzen in ihren Lernprozessen zunehmend digitale Informationsquellen, wodurch die Fähigkeit zur kritischen Bewertung online verfügbarer Informationen zentrale Bedeutung für akademisches Lernen gewinnt. In diesem Kontext fokussiert diese Studie das Konzept des Critical Online Reasoning (COR), das die kompetente Nutzung offener Internetumgebungen beschreibt. Die Facette der Critical Information Evaluation (CIE) adressiert dabei die Beurteilung der Glaubwürdigkeit und Qualität digitaler Informationen. Ergänzend werden epistemologische Überzeugungen berücksichtigt (Klopp et al., 2023), da sie als zentrale Voraussetzungen selbstregulierten Lernens gelten und die Auswahl sowie Bewertung von Informationen steuern.

Aufbauend auf dem Web-Credibility-Modell von Wathen & Burkell (2002) werden vier Subfacetten der CIE unterschieden: Message Credibility, Source Credibility, Surface Credibility und Presumed Credibility. Ziel der Studie ist es, Fähigkeitsprofile Studierender in diesen CIE-Subfacetten zu analysieren und Zusammenhänge mit epistemologischen Überzeugungen zu untersuchen.

Die Studie basiert auf einer performance-basierten COR-Erhebung in einer offenen Internetumgebung mit 309 Bachelorstudierenden. Schriftliche Begründungen zur Auswahl glaubwürdiger Online-Quellen wurden mittels eines kriterien-basierten Scorings mit 20 Indikatoren den 4 CIE-Subfacetten zugeordnet und von vier geschulten Rater:innen kodiert.

Die Ergebnisse zeigen ein differenziertes Fähigkeitsprofil der kritischen Online-Informationsbewertung. Studierende vermeiden ungünstige Bewertungsstrategien, insbesondere im Bereich Presumed und Surface Credibility, während inhalts- und quellenbasierter Kriterien deutlicher seltener genutzt werden. Zudem zeigen sich erwartungskonforme Zusammenhänge mit epistemologischen Überzeugungen: Die Überzeugung, dass Wissen durch den Vergleich mehrerer Quellen geprüft werden sollte, geht mit einer geringeren Nutzung von Presumed Credibility einher, während die Auffassung von Wissen als veränderbar mit einer stärkeren Nutzung inhaltsbezogener Bewertungsstrategien einhergeht. Die Befunde verdeutlichen die Bedeutung epistemologischer Überzeugungen für eine differenzierte kritische Online-Informationsbewertung.

Lisa Löffler | University of Vienna, Faculty of Psychology | Austria

Arnd Florack | University of Vienna, Faculty of Psychology
Show details
Authors:
Lisa Löffler | University of Vienna, Faculty of Psychology | Austria
Teresa Koch | University of Vienna, Faculty of Psychology
Arnd Florack | University of Vienna, Faculty of Psychology

Studies in social psychology have repeatedly demonstrated naïve realism, whereas individuals fail to recognize the subjectivity of their own perspective, thereby overestimating the commonness of their own views. Building on this research, we hypothesized that this naïve realism bias leads to an overestimation of others’ ability to identify fake news. To test this hypothesis, we conducted an experiment with two phases. In Phase 1, participants (N = 100) reported their spontaneous impressions of real and fake news items while being unaware of their veracity. In Phase 2, a separate group (N = 247) who were informed which news items were fake or real, estimated how many uninformed Phase 1 participants expressed skepticism when exposed to fake news. Further, we hypothesized that this overestimation would be reduced by increased awareness of naïve realism and higher digital maturity, defined as competence for self-determination in digital environments. We manipulated the awareness of naive realism through an intervention and measured digital maturity. The results revealed a strong tendency to overestimate others’ ability to detect fake news. Contrary to our hypotheses, neither awareness of naive realism nor digital maturity reduced the overestimation. We argue that this overestimation bias may undermine awareness of the societal threat posed by misinformation. Future research could further investigate how such biases can be reduced.

Prof. Dr. Siegmar Otto | University of Hohenheim
Prof. Dr.-Ing. Matthias Wölfel | Karlsruhe University of Applied Sciences
Sarah Zabel | University of Hohenheim

The growing pervasiveness of artificial intelligence (AI) raises fundamental questions about how human decision-making is influenced by AI. First empirical findings suggest that individuals are vulnerable to AI recommendations when making ethical decisions. In this context, we investigate whether participants’ choices in a social dilemma game are influenced by AI advice. To examine this effect comprehensively, we account for individual differences in Honesty-Humility (Ashton & Lee, 2007), a well-established predictor of prosocial behavior in social dilemma games. We conducted an online experiment (N = 348) in which two experimental groups interacted with differently primed AI chatbots before making their decisions. Participants in the control group made decisions without AI advice. We examined the varying orientation of the AI advice as a predictor of participants’ choices. Logistic regression analysis showed that participants exposed predominantly to collective-benefit-oriented AI advice were significantly more likely to make prosocial choices than participants who did not receive any AI advice. In contrast, participants exposed to predominantly individual-benefit-oriented AI advice showed choice behavior similar to the control group. These patterns remained when controlling for individuals’ dispositional Honesty-Humility (Ashton & Lee, 2007). Taken together, the results suggest that the influence of AI advice on human decision-making in social dilemmas is content-dependent: advice emphasizing collective benefit can shape behavior, whereas advice emphasizing individual benefit does not exert influence beyond baseline decision-making.

66. AI and Me - Tool, Servant, or Partner?
Dr. Tom Schiebler | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Tom Schiebler | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany
Prof. Dr. Julia A. M. Reif | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany
Dr. Johannes F. W. Arendt | MCI Innsbruck | Austria
Prof. Dr. Ellen A. Schmid | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany

Do humans form relationships with computer programs? Until recently, this question was largely confined to speculative future scenarios and science fiction. However, with the emergence of increasingly sophisticated generative AI capable of human-like interaction, how people relate to AI agents has become a highly relevant real-world issue. This question becomes even more pressing as AI systems are assigned roles traditionally fulfilled by humans, such as tutors, leadership-related functions, or even romantic partners. To address this issue, we integrate empirical findings and theoretical models from research on human-human interaction and human-machine interaction. Drawing on Relational Models Theory (RMT), social relationships are regulated through four fundamental relational models and associated moral motives: Communal Sharing, Authority Ranking, Equality Matching, and Market Pricing. Emerging evidence suggests that these relational models are, at least partially, applied to interactions with AI systems, even when users are aware of layered relationships in which direct interaction with an AI mediates the actions of a human agent deploying the system. At the same time, research highlights potential risks of human-AI relationships, including the misallocation of human resources through the application of social norms to non-human agents, as well as shifts in social norms and expectations toward humans following interaction with inhumanly capable AI systems. Looking ahead, we argue for the continuous testing and refinement of existing models of social relationships in order to adequately address the social and societal challenges associated with the growing ubiquity of AI.

67. Maschinelle Übersetzung und Glaubwürdigkeitsurteile in der mehrsprachigen Lügendetektion
Hannah Strerath | Hochschule für Technik Stuttgart | Germany
Prof. Dr. Patrick Müller | Hochschule für Technik Stuttgart | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Hannah Strerath | Hochschule für Technik Stuttgart | Germany
Prof. Dr. Patrick Müller | Hochschule für Technik Stuttgart | Germany

Die Nutzung maschineller Übersetzungstools wie DeepL oder Google Translate verändert, wie sprachliche Inhalte wahrgenommen und bewertet werden. Aufbauend auf Befunden zum Language Proficiency Credibility Attribution Bias untersucht die vorliegende Studie, wie automatisierte Übersetzungen die Wahrnehmung der Glaubwürdigkeit schriftlicher Aussagen beeinflussen. Im Fokus steht die Frage, ob maschinelle Übersetzung bestehende Verzerrungen gegenüber Nicht-Muttersprachlern reduzieren oder verstärken kann.
In einer quantitativen Online-Studie bewerteten n = 335 Deutsch-Muttersprachler schriftliche Aussagen, deren Wahrheitsgehalt (Lüge vs. Wahrheit), Sprachhintergrund des Senders (Englisch-Muttersprachler vs. Nicht-Englisch-Muttersprachler) sowie Textversion (Englisch vs. maschinell ins Deutsche übersetzt) systematisch variiert wurden. Erfasst wurden Glaubwürdigkeitsurteile sowie die Genauigkeit der Bewertungen. Die Daten wurden mithilfe logistischer Mehrebenenmodelle analysiert.
Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass maschinell übersetzte Aussagen insgesamt als weniger glaubwürdig eingeschätzt wurden als Originaltexte. Entgegen der Annahme, dass Übersetzung den bekannten Glaubwürdigkeitsbias gegenüber Nicht-Muttersprachlern beeinflusst, zeigte sich kein moderierender Effekt der Textversion auf den Bias. Maschinelle Übersetzung erwies sich somit nicht als geeignetes Mittel zur Reduktion bestehender Verzerrungen. Darüber hinaus bestätigte sich der Glaubwürdigkeitsbias im schriftlichen Kontext auch bei nicht-muttersprachlichen Personen als Bewertende.
Die Befunde verdeutlichen, dass maschinelle Übersetzung zwar die sprachliche Form von Aussagen und damit auch deren Wahrnehmung verändert, strukturelle Verzerrungen in der Glaubwürdigkeitsbewertung jedoch nicht auflöst. Die Ergebnisse leisten einen Beitrag zum Verständnis der Wirkung künstlicher Intelligenz in mehrsprachigen Kommunikationssituationen und unterstreichen die Notwendigkeit einer kritisch-reflektierten Nutzung digitaler Übersetzungstechnologien.

The present study aimed to adapt and validate the Brief Solastalgia Scale (BSS) for use in German-speaking populations, referred to as the BSS-D. Solastalgia is a type of melancholia or grief in the face of a change or assault on a place one feels attached to. It is used mainly in the context of climate change and environmental degradation. Our study examined whether the BSS-D demonstrates a unidimensional factor structure, meets established psychometric quality criteria, and is associated with constructs from climate psychology. Data was collected via an online survey with a representative sample of 530 adults from Germany. The results confirmed a one-factor structure characterized by a good internal consistency and acceptable model fit when applying model specifications using k-fold cross-validation. The BSS-D showed significant correlations with multiple climate-related constructs, particularly climate anxiety (r = .46) and climate sorrow (r = .47), with pro-environmental social identity (r = .38), and pro-environmental policy support (r = .35) as well as depression and anxiety ( r =.28). These findings indicate that the BSS-D is a reliable and valid measure of solastalgia and offers practical applications for research and interventions. Further studies should examine its applicability across diverse cultural and contextual settings.

69. PSYNDEX Tests: Improving the Discoverability and Interoperability of Psychological Measures
Dr. Martin Kerwer | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Martin Kerwer | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID) | Germany
Eva Zender | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID) | Germany

Psychometric tests are an essential part of psychological research and practice. However, finding suitable measures for a particular research question can be a burdensome and challenging task for researchers. This is especially true since new measures are proliferating in psychological science, and the psychological measures landscape has therefore been described as fragmented. The PSYNDEX Tests database of the Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID) assists researchers and practitioners in navigating this landscape. It provides curated metadata on over 9,200 measures that are used in the German-speaking countries. These metadata include information such as publications containing the items of a measure, its psychometric properties, and its license. These metadata are complemented by more than 4,000 comprehensive test reviews that are freely available via the disciplinary repository PsychArchives.
In this presentation, we illustrate how we are currently transforming the PSYNDEX Tests database into a Linked Open Data format to enhance the discoverability of psychometric measures. As a part of this process, we developed a psychology-specific metadata schema for describing psychological measures. This metadata schema enables users to describe tests with interoperable information that goes beyond the basic information contained in codebooks. Furthermore, it was designed to be flexibly extensible and freely reusable both within psychology and across disciplinary boundaries. We will outline how PSYNDEX Tests may, thus, support researchers in making their measures interoperable, machine-readable and human-readable, and how it can support linking the currently fragmented landscape of psychological measures in the long term.

70. Private IKT-Nutzung während der Arbeitszeit – Kann die eigene Bewertung bereichernde und konfligierende Prozesse zwischen Privat- und Arbeitsleben erklären?
Ann-Katrin Wolf | University of Münster | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Ann-Katrin Wolf | University of Münster | Germany
Prof. Dr. Carmen Binnewies | University of Münster | Germany

Informations- und Kommunikationstechnologien (IKT) sind im digitalen Zeitalter ständig verfügbar. Daher ist es nahezu unvermeidbar und oftmals akzeptiert, dass Arbeitnehmende ihre IKT für private Zwecke während der Arbeitszeit nutzen (z.B. für private Absprachen oder Social Media). Für arbeitsbezogene Outcomes (z.B. Leistung) zeigten sich diesbezüglich bisher gemischte Ergebnisse. In dieser Studie konzentrieren wir uns auf den Beitrag der eigenen Bewertung der privaten IKT-Nutzung zur Erklärung von bereichernden und konfligierenden Spillover-Prozessen zwischen dem Privat- und Arbeitsleben. Basierend auf dem work-home resources model von ten Brummelhuis und Bakker sowie Erkenntnissen aus der appraisal-Forschung postulieren wir einen affektiven sowie einen selbstregulatorischen Pfad (über positive und negative affektive Zustände sowie selbstregulatorische Ressourcen). Konkret nehmen wir an, dass eine indirekte Beziehung zwischen der täglichen positiven und negativen Bewertung der privaten IKT-Nutzung mit täglichen arbeitsbezogenen Outcomes (d.h., Aufgabenleistung, Eigeninitiative und Arbeitszufriedenheit) besteht. Die positive Bewertung der IKT-Nutzung sollte dabei indirekt und positiv mit den genannten Outcomes zusammenhängen und über niedrigere negative sowie höhere positive affektive Zustände und selbstregulatorische Ressourcen vermittelt werden. Im Gegensatz dazu sollte die negative Bewertung indirekt negativ mit den Arbeitsoutcomes assoziiert sein und über höhere negative sowie niedrigere positive affektive Zustände und selbstregulatorische Ressourcen erklärt werden. Um diese Annahmen zu testen, führen wir derzeit eine präregistrierte fünf-tägige Tagebuchstudie mit Arbeitnehmenden durch (bisher 86 Teilnehmende). Während der Mittagspause werden die positive und negative Bewertung, die affektiven Zustände sowie die selbstregulatorischen Ressourcen erhoben. Die Arbeitsoutcomes werden am Feierabend erfasst. Wir streben an mindestens 100 Teilnehmende zu erreichen, die in die geplanten Multilevel-Analysen einbezogen werden können.

71. Does sleep loss impair perspective-taking?
Dr. Emma Halfmann | Justus Liebig Universiät Gießen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Emma Halfmann | Justus Liebig Universiät Gießen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Jan A. Häusser | Justus Liebig Universiät Gießen

Sleep loss impairs cognitive capacities, increases self-focus, and thereby alters social interaction. Perspective-taking constitutes an effortful social-cognitive mechanism for understanding another person’s viewpoint (Theory of mind), which should be vulnerable to sleep loss. To date, however, only sarcasm detection as a specific facet of perspective-taking has been found to deteriorate under sleep loss. This experimental study (N = 176) systematically tests whether three nights of 50% sleep restriction impair perspective-taking performance across three established tasks (Strange Stories Task, Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test, and the Faux-pas Recognition Test) and whether trait perspective-taking moderates these associations. Initial analyses indicate that while sleep loss enhances subjective tiredness, it does not impair performance on the Strange Stories Task, and trait perspective-taking does not moderate this association. Further results from the remaining tasks will be presented to provide a more comprehensive assessment of whether—and under which conditions—sleep loss affects perspective-taking.

Hendrik Isenbart | Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule - University of Psychology | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Hendrik Isenbart | Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule - University of Psychology | Germany
Prof. Dr. Lena Nadarevic | Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule - University of Psychology | Germany

The truth effect is the stable tendency to rate repeated statements as being more truthful than novel ones. However, when participants rate statements for truth instead of interest (or other shallow processing instructions) at their initial presentation, the effect seems to disappear. One possible explanation is that, when rating statements for interest at encoding, participants rely on their subjective feelings of familiarity or fluency to judge the truth of these statements in a later test phase. However, when rating the statements for truth at encoding, participants primarily rely on other cues (e.g., knowledge) in the test phase. In this study, we tested how cognitive load influences the use of different cues when rating repeated statements, as this has not yet been systematically considered. In two conditions statements were either rated for interest or truth at encoding. Moreover, as a within manipulation, statements were presented with or without a cognitive load task in the test phase. The results show no differences between encoding conditions or between statements presented with or without cognitive load. Repeated statements were rated as being more truthful in all conditions. However, since we did not expect a truth effect for statements rated for truth at encoding, these findings suggest that cognitive load promotes the use of fluency over knowledge, but has no influence when people already rely on fluency. In upcoming research, a between-subject manipulation of cognitive load will be tested to rule out that sample or material effects account for the lack of differences between conditions.

73. Struktur- und Prozessqualität der dezentralen Präventionsberatung als Capacity Building Maßnahme
Prof. Dr. Melanie Jagla-Franke | Hochschule Neubrandenburg University of Applied Sciences | Germany
Show details

Tessa Marie Mey | Hochschule Magdeburg - Stendal
