Hannah Pongratz | University of Mannheim | Germany
Dr. Martin Schoemann | Technische Universität Dresden (TU Dresden) | Germany
Henrike Willrich | TU Dresden | Germany

Research on decision making under risk and over time has largely developed along separate lines, focusing either on probabilistic monetary outcomes or on certain outcomes delivered after a delay. Even when uncertainty and time are studied jointly, both dimensions usually apply to the outcome itself, such that delayed outcomes are also probabilistic. Time lotteries offer an alternative paradigm in which the outcome is guaranteed and uncertainty instead applies to the delay until receipt. The present study uses this approach to examine how probabilistic delays are evaluated and whether probability discounting of time shows sensitivity to delay magnitude and framing, as observed in standard probability discounting.
Participants repeatedly chose between two options yielding the same monetary amount: one with a smaller, certain delay and one with a larger, probabilistic delay. The risky option varied in delay probability and delay length, resulting in a fully within-subject design with seven probability levels and four delay magnitudes. Indifference points were elicited using an adaptive titration procedure. Additionally, a between-subjects manipulation contrasted a standard framing with an explicit-zero frame stating the complementary probability of immediate receipt.
The primary dependent measure is the indifference delay, analyzed descriptively and using factorial analyses to assess effects of probability and delay magnitude. Individual-level model fitting will compare alternative functional forms of probability discounting for delays.
By extending probability discounting to time lotteries, this study tests whether established regularities, such as magnitude and framing effects, generalize from traditional risky choice to delays, informing unified theories of intertemporal and risky choice.

113. How time pressure shapes online impulsive buying: Evidence from eye tracking, emotion analysis, and behavioral data
Celine Blettner | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Celine Blettner | Germany
Marc Ritter
Prof. Dr. Gerhard Raab | Germany

Impulsive buying in digital shopping environments is strongly influenced by situational marketing elements such as scarcity, specifically time pressure (Wu et al., 2021). While prior research has primarily focused on self-reported outcomes, the underlying cognitive–affective processes have received limited empirical attention (Redine et al., 2023). Building on the Stimulus–Organism–Response model (Mehrabian & Russell, 1974), this pilot study examines how time pressure affects visual processing, emotional activation, and impulsive purchasing responses in a simulated online shopping environment.
Using an experimental multimethod design implemented in iMotions (2022), participants completed a fictional shopping task under time pressure or neutral conditions. Eye-tracking metrics, facial expression indicators (engagement and neutrality), self-reported urge to buy impulsively, and actual impulsive purchases were assessed.
Results indicate that time pressure alters visual decision strategies, reflected in larger saccade amplitudes suggesting more global and heuristic scanning. Affectively, time pressure reduced emotional neutrality and elicited heightened activation among a subset of participants, although effects did not consistently reach conventional levels of statistical significance. Effects on the urge to buy impulsively were moderate but strongly associated with actual purchasing behavior. Moderation analyses further suggest that buying impulsivity amplifies the impact of time pressure on both the urge to buy impulsively and purchasing behavior.
Overall, the findings support conceptualizations of buying behavior as a psychologically multifaceted process involving emotional regulation and spontaneous behavioral responses (Raab et al., 2011), highlight the value of biobehavioral process measures for understanding impulsive online buying and providing important methodological implications for a subsequent main study.

114. Gesendet und angekommen: Die Dynamik von Wertschätzung in interkulturellen Arbeitsbeziehungen an Universitäten
Ria Grimmelsmann | IHF Bayern | Germany
Show details
Author:
Ria Grimmelsmann | IHF Bayern | Germany

In der heutigen Arbeitswelt zeigt sich, dass ein scheinbar einfacher Faktor eine erhebliche Wirkung hat: das Gefühl, wertgeschätzt zu werden. Wertschätzung bedeutet die Anerkennung der Person, ihrer Leistung und ihres Engagements am Arbeitsplatz. Die positive Bewertung führt zu höherer Arbeitszufriedenheit, größerer Motivation und geringerer Fluktuation.
Während bestehende Forschungsarbeiten die Bedeutung von Wertschätzung hervorheben, ist über die zwischenmenschlichen Prozesse, durch die Wertschätzung kommuniziert und wahrgenommen wird, weniger bekannt. Unsere Studie schließt diese Lücke, indem sie die bidirektionale Dynamik zwischen der von einer Partei zum Ausdruck gebrachten Wertschätzung und der von einer anderen Partei wahrgenommenen Wertschätzung im abteilungsübergreifenden Kontext der Universitäten untersucht.
Universitäten bieten aufgrund ihrer dualen Struktur aus akademischer und administrativer Kultur eine besonders interessante Arbeitsumgebung für die Betrachtung der Fragestellung, da sie sich in ihren Werten, Kommunikationsstilen und Arbeitspraktiken unterscheiden. Diese heterogenen Umgebungen erfordern eine abteilungsübergreifende Zusammenarbeit, in der Kollegen auch als interne Kunden agieren.
Unsere Forschung zielt darauf ab, zentrale Dimensionen, Determinanten und Vermittlungsprozesse von Wertschätzung zwischen Wissenschaftler*innen und Verwaltungsmitarbeitenden zu identifizieren, indem wir (1) die Kongruenz zwischen ausgedrückter und wahrgenommener Wertschätzung untersuchen, (2) individuelle und organisationale Einflussfaktoren analysieren und (3) potenzielle vermittelnde Mechanismen zwischen beiden Systemen identifizieren.
Die deutschlandweite Datenerhebung im universitären Kontext beginnt zum Zeitpunkt der Einreichung. Auf der Konferenz werden erste Befunde zur Wertschätzung am Arbeitsplatz und Implikationen für die Zusammenarbeit von Wissenschaftler*innen und Verwaltungsmitarbeitenden dargelegt und diskutiert.

Social media environments expose users to moral outrage far more frequently than face-to-face contexts. Previous research suggests that the repeated exposure to moral transgressions leads to an affective desensitization and a reduced moral condemnation of the transgression. However, it remains unclear how these processes operate in social media settings, where users are exposed not only to moral transgressions but also to others’ moral outrage.
We hypothesize that frequent exposure will reduce judgments of moral reprehensibility and weaken affective reactions such as anger, disgust and contempt. We further expect these effects to be attenuated among individuals with a stronger moral identity. Moreover, we investigate whether greater exposure to moral outrage broadly diminishes evaluations of the reprehensibility of other moral transgressions and reduces the variance in judgement. Lastly, we test whether outrage originating from multiple sources increases perceived public condemnation and individuals’ motivation to publicly express moral outrage.
We will conduct an online experiment with a German sample (approximately N = 1,100) using a 2 × 2 between-subjects design manipulating the frequency of outrage posts (many vs. few) and the variance of their sources (high vs. low). A pre-post design will assess changes in moral judgments and affective responses before and after exposure. Data will be collected in February 2026 and analyzed subsequently.
By clarifying how repeated and socially distributed moral outrage shapes moral judgments and emotions, this study advances understanding of moralized communication in digital environments.

About 40% of the German population speak a dialect that differs from standard German. Consequently, many children grow up hearing a dialect at home that is different from the language they encounter in school. So far, however, very few studies have investigated how this may impact children around the start of formal schooling. How do parental use of Bavarian dialect and parental quality of language affect children’s standard German spoken language and literacy just before school entry (age 6) and after two years of schooling (age 8)? To answer this, data was analyzed from the Bavarian Longitudinal Study (N = 1,395, 49.2% girls), which follows children that were born in Bavaria in the mid-1980s. Structural equation modelling revealed that parental dialect use had small but significant negative effects on children’s spoken language skills at age 6 (articulation: β = −.096, SE = .038, p = .003, language: β = −.108, SE = .028, p = .001), whereas parental language quality had small-to-moderate and significant positive effects on both children’s spoken language (β = .279, SE = .024, p < .001) and pre-literacy skills (β = .260, SE = .105, p < .001) at the same age. However, these effects disappeared after two years of formal schooling. All effects were controlled for SES and sex. These findings suggest that although children who are exposed to dialect at home begin school with weaker standard German spoken language skills, these early differences do not lead to lasting disadvantages in language or literacy development.

Given the many conflicts around the world, the opinions of young people are particularly relevant in contemporary society and for research, as they are easily affected by radicalization processes and polarization (Oden & Porter, 2023; Schröder et al., 2022). We highlight the importance of language-poor methods such as interactive tasks, pictograms or scales in simple language (Bauer et al., 2025; Sauer, 2021) to enable a young audience to participate in research and uphold their motivation during survey-based assessments (Yan & Williams, 2022). The fact that more than 40% of students in general and vocational schools in Germany have a migrant background (Statistisches Bundesamt, 2025) underlines the importance of simple measures.
By drawing attention to the Middle East conflict and its consequences for the German society, we address the coexistence of different religious groups and their relations in Germany. We adapted established scales to measure constructs like othering, aversion, homogeneity or competitive victimhood, and converted them into simple language. Additionally, we created language-poor tasks to measure stereotypes and ingroup favoritism to offer participants interactive breaks during item-based measurements.
To test the internal and external validity of our measures, we conduct a cross-sectional laboratory-based survey study with German university students (N ~ 250). We look at scale properties and perform exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. Beyond this methodological evaluation, we examine how German university students as largely uninvolved third-party observers evaluate religious outgroups for example in terms of homogeneity, and how these perceptions relate to intergroup relations like prejudice, solidarity or punishment.

The self-prioritization effect (SPE) describes the tendency to preferentially process self-related versus third-person-related information. Using shape-label associations of self-/third-person-related information, SPE was only found when person-related-information was task-relevant, but not when it was irrelevant (i.e. shape-location; Caughey et al., 2021). Here we asked, if SPE might endure task-irrelevance when using personal pronouns in combination with affective content as affective primes, thus avoiding learned associations. In an EEG-study, task-irrelevant sentences of either self- vs. third-person reference combined with positive or negative content served as primes. These were followed by two simultaneously left and right sided presented emojis; one happy or angry emoji (target) and a neutral (distractor). The 41 participants had to immerse themselves into the sentences’ meaning, but to respond only for the target emotion. As a control, ERP data time-locked to the sentences revealed an enhanced occipital P1-activity for self- vs. third-person sentences confirming increased attentional engagement for self-related information when presented. Importantly, behavioral data indicated faster response times to target emojis after self- vs. third-person referential sentences. Correspondingly, ERP results indicated an increased P1 lateralized over parietal-occipital areas for targets after self- vs. third-person referential sentences. Thus, the persistence of an SPE even during emotional target presentation indicates that self-reference can implicitly enhance task performance even when it is not task-relevant. We propose that self-referential stimuli, as objects of high salience, cause a nonspecific and sustained increase in responsiveness even when task-irrelevant, that facilitates the processing of upcoming targets.

As we navigate daily life, our emotions fluctuate over time. In these dynamics, theory and preliminary empirical evidence suggest that emotions may display properties of nonlinear complex systems. However, emotion research to date has relied predominantly on standard linear models. Without a comprehensive investigation of the extent to which emotion time series display nonlinear complex-systems properties, it remains unclear how much linear models fail to capture. In the current study, we address this gap by assessing nonlinear complex-systems properties of 18 publicly available experience sampling method (ESM) datasets from the EMOTE database. In total, this analysis comprises data from N = 2,429 participants assessed at approximately 170,000 measurement occasions, and covers 30 different emotions. We will first identify suitable tests for detecting complex-systems properties (e.g., nonlinearity and state-dependence) using simulations, and then apply these tests to the empirical time series. As an initial proof-of-concept, preliminary analyses of two ESM datasets revealed that approximately 25-40% of tests applied to individual participants’ emotion time series detected complex-systems properties. By examining such properties across individuals and emotions in a massive corpus of ESM data, this project aims to comprehensively evaluate the support for a complex-systems perspective on emotions. This perspective would motivate further theoretical advancement and the application of methods from complexity science to emotion time series.

Prospective memory (PM) is the ability to remember to execute an intended action at a specific moment in the future which is especially crucial for older adults to maintain an independent life. In laboratory settings older adults usually perform worse than younger adults. Cognitive load has been shown to negatively influence PM performance in the lab especially in older adults, but these effects are less clear in everyday life.
We conducted an in-depth assessment of cognitive load on PM performance in the laboratory using a combined task-switching and PM task design varying ongoing task load. In everyday life we used a smartphone app in young (20-35 years) and old (60-75 years) adults assessing PM performance, busyness and concentration. This study is pre-registered, data collection is still ongoing.
In the lab-based setting, preliminary data (n = 59 older, n = 51 younger participants) showed noticeable differences in PM performance between age groups - older participants performing at a lower level. Furthermore, older participants’ performance was lower under conditions of high compared to low cognitive load whereas the performance among younger adults was not affected by higher cognitive load. In an everyday life setting, cognitive load predicted intention execution (n = 49 older, n = 51 younger participants). In both age groups, busyness affected intention execution positively.
After completing data collection, we expect that analyses including further variables, e.g. concentration and stress, will contribute to our understanding of the effects of cognitive load and age-related differences in PM performance across settings.

Not executing a prepared motor activity is supposed to be a matter of inhibition. Here we suggest that action inhibition can be construed as reversed action planning (e.g. Mocke et al., 2024). While action planning rests on the activation and binding of perceptual action features, action inhibition might be the opposite, feature deactivation and unbinding. Participants had to stop, briefly before execution, one of two highly prepared motor activities. Executing the not stopped action was delayed as compared to executing both actions, a stopping interference effect. The stopping interference effect, as well as other measures of stopping performance, depended on the degree and level of feature overlap between stopped and unstopped action. These observations support the idea that feature-based representations of the stopped action become downregulated and partly dismantled during stopping.

Mocke, V., Beste, C., Pastötter, B., & Kunde, W. (2024). Action plan discarding leads to unbinding of action features. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 50(9), 903–917.

Workplace populism refers to employees’ populist attitudes directed toward top-management, conceptually related to but distinct from political populism directed toward political elites. The present study aimed to advance the understanding of workplace populism and political populism by examining their associations with political orientation and attitudes toward labor unions. Using a cross-sectional, correlational design, data were collected from 193 German employees. Multiple regression analyses were conducted to test direct and moderation effects. Results indicated that higher levels of political populism were associated with higher levels of workplace populism. Furthermore, workplace populism was significantly associated with attitudes towards labor unions, such that higher workplace populism was linked to higher union attitudes. A quadratic analysis indicated that high levels of populism were associated with less support for unions than moderate expressions of populist attitudes. In addition, the association between workplace populism and union attitudes was stronger than the association between political populism and union attitudes. Political orientation did not significantly moderate the relationship between political populism and workplace populism, nor did it moderate the relationship between workplace populism and union attitudes. Overall, these findings support the conceptual distinction between political populism and workplace populism and highlight the relevance of labor-related attitudes for understanding populist dynamics within organizations.

Organizations often aim to optimize several performance outcomes simultaneously, which poses a persistent challenge for practitioners in personnel selection and development. We compared eight cognitive ability measures and found that seven significantly predicted overall performance, operationalized via a supervisor rating. Among the Big
Five personality traits, only Agreeableness showed a significant positive relationship with overall performance. Authors:
Marieke Klöppel | Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg | Germany
Dr. Lena Wimmer | Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg
Prof. Dr. Markus Appel | Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg
Prof. Dr. Tobias Richter | Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg

Das Lesen narrativer Texte kann kurzfristig Empathie erhöhen. Theoretische Ansätze postulieren, dass hochnarrative Geschichten mit ausgeprägtem Spannungsbogen stärkere Effekte entfalten, da sie Leser*innen intensiver in die narrative Welt transportieren (Green & Brock, 2000). Ob Effekte der Narrativität über Leseprozesse wie Transportation vermittelt werden und ob sich daraus stabile Veränderungen in Empathie und Altruismus ergeben, wurde in einem präregistrierten Experiment (N = 162) untersucht.
Eine Woche vor dem Laborexperiment wurden Empathie, Altruismus und Need for Cognition (NFC) erhoben. Im Labor wurden die Teilnehmenden randomisiert einer von drei Bedingungen zugeteilt: Geschichte mit hoher Narrativität vs. niedriger Narrativität vs. keine Geschichte. Zusätzlich wurden Leseverständnis, Lesevolumen, Lesezeit und Transportation erfasst. Zwei Wochen später erfolgte ein Online-Follow-up.
Die hochnarrative Version führte zu längeren Lesezeiten und höherer Transportation als die niedrig-narrative Version. Kurzfristig zeigte sich nach dem Lesen einer Geschichte (unabhängig von der Narrativität) eine höhere Empathie im Vergleich zur Kontrollgruppe. Langfristig ergaben sich keine Unterschiede in der Empathie zwischen den Bedingungen. Die Empathie nahm insbesondere in der Kontrollgruppe sowie in der niedrig-narrativen Bedingung zum Follow-up ab. Für Altruismus zeigten sich weder kurzfristig noch langfristig Effekte der verschiedenen Bedingungen. Mediationsanalysen deuteten auf indirekte Effekte der Narrativität über Transportation auf Empathie und Altruismus hin. NFC moderierte den Zusammenhang zwischen Geschichtendarbietung und Empathie, für Leseverständnis und Lesevolumen ergaben sich keine Moderationseffekte.
Die Befunde zeigen kurzfristige empathische Reaktionen auf Geschichten, Altruismus kann durch eine Kurzgeschichte nicht verändert werden, möglicherweise da eine Erhöhung von Altruismus eine nachgelagerte Konsequenz von Empathie darstellen könnte. Narrative Effekte werden durch Leseprozesse beeinflusst.

The open science movement emphasizes transparent scientific reporting, including visualizations that accurately reflect underlying data. Traditional bar graphs of continuous data have been widely criticized for obscuring distributional properties such as skewness and outliers, leading to the recommendation to replace them with distribution-revealing visualizations (e.g., dot plots, boxplots, violin plots). Although such recommendations have been incorporated into some journal guidelines, the extent to which they have been adopted remains unclear. We report a preregistered large-scale analysis of visualizations in empirical open-access articles from 2018 to 2025 retrieved from the psychology literature database PSYNDEX. Visualization types were identified automatically from article PDFs using a machine-learning approach previously validated in the biomedical literature (Riedel et al., 2022). Preliminary descriptive results are based on N = 12,994 articles. Each article was assigned to one of four categories: bar-only, distribution-only, both, or neither. Over time, the share of bar-only articles decreased substantially (23% in 2018 to 9% in 2025), whereas distribution-only articles increased (11% to 19%), indicating a shift toward more transparent visualizations. Articles containing both plot types were uncommon and stable (3%). In articles with open-science indicators (preregistration and/or open data), distribution-only plots were more common than bar-only plots (54% vs. 36%), whereas in non–open science articles bar-only plots exceeded distribution-only plots (49% vs. 42%). These findings suggest that plotting practices in psychology are changing over time and that open science indicators are associated with greater adoption of transparent plotting practices.

Ein positiver Zusammenhang von Lehrkräfteeinschätzungen der Leistungsfähigkeit von Lernenden mit deren zukünftigen Leistungen (z.B. Gentrup et al., 2020; Upadyaya & Eccles, 2015) und Selbstkonzept (z.B. Bergold & Steinmayr, 2023; Hollenstein et al., 2024) ist, als Spezialfall des psychologischen Phänomens der selbsterfüllenden Prophezeiung (z.B. Madon et al., 1997), gut belegt. Lehrkräfteeinschätzungen sind allerdings nicht allein von tatsächlichen Leistungen der Lernenden abhängig, sondern können auch, wie im sozialpsychologischen Kontinuum-Modell beschrieben (Fiske & Neuberg, 1990), von der Kategorisierung nach soziodemografischen Merkmalen wie dem Geschlecht, sozioökonomischem Status und Zugehörigkeit zu ethnisch-sprachlichen Minderheiten beeinflusst werden (z.B. Brandmiller et al., 2024; Timmermans & Rubie-Davies, 2023). Da diese soziodemografischen Merkmalen, insbesondere im sprachlichen Kontext, ebenfalls mit Leistung und Selbstkonzept zusammenhängen können (z.B. McElvany et al., 2023) wird das Forschungsdesiderat untersucht, inwiefern die Lehrkräfteeinschätzungen als Mediator dieser Zusammenhänge wirken. Analysegrundlage stellen Angaben und Testwerte von N = 1113 Lernenden und ihren Lehrkräften (N=74 Klassen) zu zwei Messzeitpunkten (MZP1: 2./3. Klasse; MZP2: 3./4. Klasse) dar. Die Lehrkräfteeinschätzungen (MZP1) wurden in Bezug auf Lesen und Schreiben erhoben, die sprachlichen Kompetenzen und das Selbstkonzept (MZP1/2) mittels etablierter Tests und Skalen. Das Strukturgleichungsmodell ergab im Mittel höhere Lehrkräfteeinschätzungen bei besseren sprachlichen Kompetenzen, höherem Leseselbstkonzept, weiblichem Geschlecht, höherem sozioökonomischem Status, aber niedrigere Lehrkräfteeinschätzungen für multilinguale Schüler:innen. Sowohl die Lesekompetenz als auch das Leseselbstkonzept zum zweiten Messzeitpunkt wurden positiv durch die Lehrkräfteeinschätzungen vorhergesagt, welche die Effekte der soziodemografischen Variablen sowie Kompetenzen und Selbstkonzept zum ersten Messzeitpunkt (teilweise) mediierten (βind = -.03 – .12). Die Relevanz der Ergebnisse für Forschung und Praxis wird diskutiert.

Intelligence or general cognitive ability (GCA) is fundamental to human behaviour and cognition. It impacts important life outcomes like educational success and even health and longevity have been related to differences in GCA. Understanding the biological basis of such individual variations presents a crucial goal of neuroscience. The mismatch negativity (MMN) is an event-related brain potential that can be measured when within a series of frequent standard stimuli rare deviants are presented and is suggested to reflect conscious (active) or unconscious (passive) detection processes of the brain. Importantly, variations in MMN amplitude and latency have been linked to differences in GCA. Yet, findings in this field vary considerably. This preregistered meta-analysis provides a comprehensive and structured overview of the current state of research. Following the study selection process in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines, and the rating of study design quality with the Study Design and Implementation Assessment Device for Individual Difference research (DIAD-ID), the association between GCA and MMN amplitude and latency was examined in 695 healthy adults across 13 included studies. The estimated across-sample associations between MMN and GCA were small, but significant (MMN amplitude–GCA: r = -0.08, MMN latency–GCA: r = -0.13; p < 0.05) and moderators were identified. Between-sample heterogeneity was moderate, with no evidence of publication bias. Our findings suggest that higher intelligence is associated with slightly stronger and faster MMN responses. However, the low estimated across-sample effect sizes and the small number of included studies also highlight the need for more research.

Lisa Langhammer | Ulm University | Germany

Open Science (OS) comprises a broad repertoire of practices (e.g., preregistration, sharing datasets, and replication studies) intended to foster transparency and robustness of research activities. To date, however, no standardized instrument is available that enables efficient assessment of OS knowledge or rigorous evaluation of knowledge gains following educational interventions (e.g., whether students who complete an OS-focused course demonstrate increased OS knowledge). To address this gap, we are developing an OS knowledge test with three parallel versions (25 items per version) that is designed to cover the seven knowledge clusters proposed by the Framework for Open and Reproducible Research Training (FORRT): reproducibility and replicability knowledge; conceptual and statistical knowledge; reproducible analyses; preregistration; academic life, ethics and culture; replication research; and FAIR data and materials. We created 180 multiple-choice items (one attractor, three distractors each) intended to cover these clusters, assessing declarative, conceptual, and procedural OS knowledge across a broad difficulty range. Across two studies (total N = 129 Psychology undergraduates), we demonstrate that (a) the item pool spans the intended difficulty spectrum; (b) revision of items of unsatisfactory difficulty and/or distractor attractiveness proved to be effective; (c) grades in research methods and statistics courses are plausibly associated with OS test performance; (d) OS test performance is unrelated to general crystallized intelligence; and (e) item difficulty is unrelated to question length. We present detailed information on the item generation, revision, and selection procedures. Overall, the resulting test provides an efficient tool for assessing OS knowledge (gains) in educational and training contexts.

As discussed in the context of instructional explanations and tutoring, explainers and explainees must consider each other’s characteristics and needs and adapt to them to achieve satisfactory explanations (Chi et al., 2004; Kulgemeyer, 2024). This requires mental representations, so-called partner models, which include assumptions about the conversation partner relating to different dimensions (e.g., knowledge, interest) relevant for explanations (Dillenbourg et al., 2016). It is assumed that partner models change over the course of explanations (Buhl et al., 2024). However, little is known about how these processes occur on the level of the partner model dimensions. To address this gap, an observational study was conducted with N = 118 adults, randomly combined to dyads and to the roles of explainer and explainee. We investigated changes of six partner model dimensions – knowledge, co-construction, interest, joy, extrinsic motivation, and cooperation – during naturalistic board game explanations. Partner models of both were assessed at five time points: prior to the initial encounter, at the beginning and end of a first explanation without the game present, and at the beginning and end of a second explanation with game play. rmANOVA revealed significant differences between measurement points for the explainer’s partner model of the explainee regarding knowledge, interest, joy, co‑construction, extrinsic motivation, and cooperation. In contrast, for the explainee’s partner model of the explainer, the analyses of variance indicated significant differences only on the dimensions of knowledge and co‑construction. Results are discussed in relation to ongoing research on the perceptions of interlocutors in explanations.

Can Large Language Models (LLMs) support text-based science communication? In the project “KLARpsyLLM”, psychologists and computational linguists develop an LLM-based tool that generates plain language summaries of psychological meta-analyses.
The summarization process is guided by 37 criteria that are defined in the KLARpsy guideline for writing plain language summaries. The system employs a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system, using engineered prompts within GPT-4, to produce the pilot tool. Its evaluation was two-fold: The automatic evaluation was based on 99 texts. With text-based measures, 99 tool-written texts were compared with expert-written texts and with texts written by FlexRAG, an out-of-the-box RAG system. The human evaluation was based on ten texts. Experts rated 16 text sections for ten tool-written texts on six dimensions.
The tool replicates expert-written summaries better than FlexRAG, as indicated by BLEU, a score used to evaluate machine-translated text, and by semantic similarity to expert-written summaries. Further, the tool is able to generate plain language summaries on high school to early college reading level, similar to expert-written plain language summaries. However, expert raters reported the tool hallucinates and generates over-assertive statements in some cases.
Based on the results of the first evaluation, the interdisciplinary team discussed further improvements and implementation strategies. The development of an automatic confidence rating system for tool-written texts is currently underway, with the objective of enabling experts to more accurately assess the residual workload required for processing the texts. Next steps are to evaluate the improved tool and to plan and prepare the application in practice.

Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging (DEIB) is increasingly discussed as an integral part of organizational sustainability strategies. However, DEIB measures often face limited visibility, acceptance, and utilization. Therefore, understanding the psychological factors that influence both endorsement and support-seeking behavior is crucial for an effective, health-promoting implementation. The present study examined attitudes towards DEIB measures targeting ableism and sexism in higher education, as well as their self-reported use. In a quantitative online survey of N=70 master's students, key constructs, including ambivalent sexism, essentialist beliefs, belief in a just world, self-stigmatization, and self-esteem, were assessed. Correlational analyses were used to investigate associations between these constructs, approval of institutional DEIB measures, and utilization of available support services. Results showed that stronger endorsement of DEIB measures was negatively associated with ambivalent sexist attitudes and belief in a just world. Contrary to the initial hypotheses, higher levels of self-stigmatization were associated with greater use of support services, whereas higher self-esteem was linked to lower utilization. This may be explained by theoretical concepts such as the threat to self-esteem model, which assumes that offers of help can be perceived as a potential threat to self-image or autonomy. The overall results demonstrate that not only objective experiences of discrimination but also subjective beliefs influence whether DEIB measures are advocated and utilized. The present study provides psychological insights for the further development of more effective DEIB measures in higher education and related organizational contexts, thereby contributing to the achievement of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

The rising incidence of skin cancer, particularly melanoma, highlights the importance of early detection. A preregistered 3×2 between-subjects experiment (N = 824) manipulated provider type (dermatologist, AI, personalized AI) and rating valence (positive vs. negative) using a realistic app interface. Participants evaluated behavioral intention to use (BI), perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEOU), trust, and willingness to pay (WTP).
MANCOVA analyses showed no significant main effect of provider type (p = .057), whereas rating valence had strong effects on PU, PEOU, trust, and BI (all p < .001). No interaction effects emerged (p = .41). Mediation analyses indicated that the effect of rating valence on BI was fully mediated by PU and trust, and partially mediated by PEOU (all p < .001). The effect of provider type on BI was fully mediated by trust (p = .05). Moderation analyses revealed that AI attitude, AI knowledge, and age were associated with BI (all p ≤ .004) but did not moderate the experimental effects. Lasso regression identified trust as the strongest predictor of BI.
The findings highlight trust as a key precursor to the acceptance of AI-based health apps and demonstrate that positive user reviews represent an effective mechanism for fostering trust. Future research should develop and evaluate targeted interventions to strengthen trust-related components of the TAM.

Figurative language is something fundamentally human: from classic poetry to its use as a therapeutic tool in clinical psychology, metaphors convey creative imagery, evoke emotional responses, and frame information by mapping abstract concepts onto literal expressions. With the increasing use of large language models (LLMs) in education, scientific writing, and AI-based mental health support, an important question emerges: How well can models like ChatGPT, which generate language by predicting the most likely next word based on large-scale text data, approximate the human ability to comprehend expressions whose meanings extend beyond literal interpretation? The proposed work summarizes existing findings on LLMs’ ability to interpret and generate figurative language in comparison to humans. It further assesses the performance of different generations of OpenAI’s GPT models (e.g., GPT-3.5, GPT-4.1) on the German Proverb–Metaphor Test (PMT). In humans, figurative language comprehension is positively associated with Openness to Experience, reflecting creative imagination and engagement with abstract ideas. To extend this perspective to LLMs, it is examined whether a similar relationship can be approximated by systematically manipulating model personas. Using system prompts, the models are instructed to perform the figurative language task in accordance with predefined Openness profiles based on the BFI-2. The findings may show implications for possible uses of LLMs as “digital test subjects” or digital tutors with tailored personas, especially in contexts where non-literal interpretation of language is needed.

Prompted journal-writing is a powerful tool to support self-regulated learning (Berthold et al., 2007; Nückles et al., 2009). Typically, students produce an initial journal draft from memory (closed-book phase), and subsequently revise it using a lecture script (open-book phase). The initial closed-book phase (a retrieval affordance) serves a consolidation function, and learners’ metastrategic knowledge is critical for effectively enacting strategies during journal-writing. To this end, we investigated the individual and combined effects of memory-retrieval affordance (closed-then-open book vs. pure-open book) and metastrategic-knowledge instruction on how to write and revise a learning journal (with vs. without instruction) on the coverage of idea units, the use of learning strategies in the journals, and learning outcomes. In this study, 272 undergraduate teacher students (54% female, 46% male) watched a video lecture on Piaget’s theory of cognitive development and subsequently wrote and revised their learning journals. In the metastrategic-knowledge condition, participants received instructional videos prior to both the lecture and the revision. In the closed-then-open-book condition, they wrote journals in a closed-book format and revised them in an open-book format; in the pure open-book condition, materials were available throughout. A posttest assessing retention and comprehension was administered after 1 week. The results showed that an initial retrieval affordance during closed-then-open-book journal-writing did not benefit retention and was even detrimental for comprehension after 1 week. However, metastrategic-knowledge instruction increased the quality of elaboration strategies and enhanced comprehension, but only when journal-writing afforded initial memory retrieval. Thus, metastrategic knowledge compensates for comprehension disadvantages in retrieval-based journal-writing.

It is well documented that parents significantly influence their children's development during childhood and adolescence. However, very few studies examine how parenting impacts adult outcomes. We use prospective data to conduct a conceptual replication of a previous study that found mothers who recalled their parents being supportive to have lower levels of depressive symptoms and higher marital relationship quality, show more sensitive parenting, and have children with higher social and emotional skills (Huffhines et al., 2024). Our use of prospective instead of retrospective data will ensure that the measures are less likely to be impacted by memory biases or current relationship dynamics and emotional states. In contrast to Huffhines et al. (2024), we will also include fathers to capture potential differences or similarities between maternal and paternal pathways. Using data from the TRAILS (TRacking Adolescents’ Individual Lives Survey) and TRAILS NEXT sample, we will apply latent profile analysis to create groups based on participants’ rearing experiences during adolescence. Next, profile membership will be tested as a predictor of the four outcomes (adult depressive symptoms, marital relationship satisfaction, parenting practices, and social and emotional skills of the infant) three and 30 months after birth of the participants first child. This will provide insight into whether the associations observed by Huffhines et al. (2024) remain consistent in a longitudinal study design, and whether these associations differ between mothers and fathers. The results will be available at the time of the conference.

138. Die Rolle persönlicher und beruflicher Ressourcen bei der Entstehung von Arbeitsplatzunsicherheit nach Karriereschocks – Eine Vignettenstudie
Josephine Debus | University of Bremen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Josephine Debus | University of Bremen | Germany
Lily Kollender | University of Bremen
Dr. Katharina Klug | University of Bremen

Vor dem Hintergrund globaler Veränderungen, dem Aufstieg künstlicher Intelligenz und anhaltendem organisatorischen Wandel, gewinnt qualitative Arbeitsplatzunsicherheit – die wahrgenommene Bedrohung wichtiger Arbeitsmerkmale – zunehmend an Bedeutung. Unerwartete Ereignisse wie beispielsweise Umstrukturierungen, die als Karriereschocks wirken können, können diese Wahrnehmung von Unsicherheit weiter verstärken, indem sie das subjektive Stabilitätsgefühl der Mitarbeitenden beeinträchtigen. Basierend auf dem Transaktionalen Stressmodell kann die Reaktion der Mitarbeitenden auf solche Ereignisse davon abhängen, wie stark sie jene als Bedrohung wahrnehmen und über welche Ressourcen sie verfügen. Die Studie zielt darauf ab, tiefere Einblicke in die Wahrnehmung qualitativer Arbeitsplatzunsicherheit nach einer Umstrukturierung als potenzieller Karriereschock zu gewinnen. Konkret untersucht sie mittels Vignetten-Designs, die vermittelnde Rolle der qualitativen Arbeitsplatzunsicherheit im Zusammenhang zwischen Karriereschocks und der allgemeinen Arbeitszufriedenheit sowie persönliche Kontrollüberzeugung und Aufgabenvielfalt als arbeitsbezogene Ressource. Die Vignetten variieren im Vorhandensein einer Ankündigung organisationaler Veränderung sowie dem Grad der Aufgabenvielfalt (2x2 between-subject design). Die Teilnehmenden (derzeit N=199) wurden randomisiert einer der vier Bedingungen zugeordnet. Mittels multipler Regressionsanalysen werden die direkten, vermittelnden und moderierenden Effekte innerhalb des vorgeschlagenen Modells bewertet. Es wird erwartet, dass Umstrukturierungen als Karriereschocks die qualitative Arbeitsplatzunsicherheit erhöhen und dadurch die Arbeitszufriedenheit mindern. Gleichzeitig wird angenommen, dass eine hohe interne Kontrollüberzeugung und größere Aufgabenvielfalt diese Effekte abschwächen, da sie das Gefühl von Kontrolle und Kompetenz stärken. Die Datenerhebung wird bis zum Zeitpunkt der Einreichung abgeschlossen sein, sodass die Ergebnisse zur Konferenz vorliegen werden. Die Studie leistet einen Beitrag zum Verständnis der Entstehung qualitativer Arbeitsplatzunsicherheit nach arbeitsbezogenen Veränderungen und identifiziert relevante Ressourcen zu deren Minderung.

139. AI influence on credibility perception of misinformation on social media
Inga Nießen
Anna Maria Abrams | RWTH Aachen University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Inga Nießen
Anna Maria Abrams | RWTH Aachen University | Germany

The spread of misinformation is worsened by generative artificial intelligence (AI), which can rapidly create and share content across platforms, posing a significant global risk (World Economic Forum, 2024). Previous research has examined AI-driven credibility indicators and fact-checking tools, but their effectiveness in improving news accuracy and influencing sharing intentions remains mixed (Lu et al., 2025; Danry et al., 2024). Social media dynamics further complicate credibility assessments, as information from trusted contacts is often seen as more credible than that from other sources (Metzger et al., 2010; Osatuyi & Dennis, 2024). However, there is limited understanding of how AI-generated content or an AI publisher influences perceived credibility and sharing intentions compared to humans.
This ongoing study aims to investigate how the credibility of misinformation is assessed on social media by varying both the source of content (AI vs. scientist vs. unknown) and the publisher (AI vs. scientist vs. friend). 170 participants in an online study will view a pre-tested social media post featuring a climate-change statement identified as misinformation by the United Nations (2025). We hypothesize that message credibility, source credibility, sharing intentions, and emotional reactions will vary based on these factors and their interaction. The nine experimental conditions will be analyzed using multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) and multiple linear regression.
This research aims to shed light on the complex interaction between AI and human influences on perceived credibility in social media misinformation.

140. Leadership Reloaded: Generational Differences in Attitudes toward women in leadership positions
Jennifer Zwetzich
Hannah Hirzel
Anna Kämmerer | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jennifer Zwetzich
Hannah Hirzel
Anna Kämmerer | Germany
Prof. Dr. Friedrich Meixner

Despite ongoing societal progress toward gender equality, women remain structurally underrepresented in leadership positions. Guided by Role Congruity Theory (Eagly & Karau, 2002), this study examined perceptions of female leadership as a function of participant gender, generation, educational background, and occupational status.
In a cross-sectional online experiment, N = 188 participants (124 women, 64 men; M_age = 33.1, SD = 12.3) were randomly assigned to one of two leadership vignettes depicting either a female (“Anna Müller”) or male (“Maximilian Schneider”) leader. Leadership perceptions were assessed using validated instruments: the Attitudes Toward Women as Managers Scale (Peters et al., 1974) and the Gender Stereotype Scale (Sekhar & Parameswari, 2020).
Women evaluated female leaders significantly more positively than men did (p < .05, d = 0.27). Generation Z demonstrated the most favorable attitudes toward women in leadership compared to older cohorts (p < .05, η² = 0.83). Across the full sample, the female leader vignette received more positive evaluations than the male version (p < .05, d = 0.17), contradicting classical predictions of Role Congruity Theory. Educational level and occupational status showed only small effects (p < .05, η² = 0.19), with participants holding vocational qualifications rating female leadership slightly more positively than those with academic degrees (p < .05, d = 0.42).
Although the overrepresentation of women and students limits generalizability, the findings suggest a partial weakening of traditional gender stereotypes, particularly among younger and vocationally trained individuals. Overall, the results indicate generational shifts in leadership perceptions and provide relevant implications.

141. Effects of Exercise on Depression in Adolescent Patients with Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes
Prof. Michael Yafi | University Of Texas Health Science Center At Houston | United States
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Michael Yafi | University Of Texas Health Science Center At Houston | United States
Prof. Mona Eissa | United States

Background
Exercise is recognized to reduce depression in adults. This study aims to examine the relationship between exercise and depression symptoms in adolescents with obesity and Type 2 Diabetes.
Methods
A retrospective chart review was conducted of patients with obesity who were seen at a university pediatric weight management clinic between 2018 and 2021. Demographic, anthropometric, clinical, physical activity, and laboratory data, psychiatric history, and depression status using the PHQ-9 score were analyzed. Selection criteria were: age 12-18 years, BMI 95th percentile. Charts included data on: BMI; PHQ9 scores, physical activity in minutes/week; and T2DM diagnosis. R 4.1.2, packages: ggplot2, epitools, and ggpubr were used for data analysis.
Results
Charts of 178 subjects were identified. Female adolescents had significantly higher PHQ9 scores compared to males. There was no significant difference in PHQ9 scores when patients were compared based on T2DM status. In a regression model that included T2DM status and psychiatric diagnoses, every minute added of exercise decreases the total PHQ9 score by 0.006 "P< 0.05". For a group that included only patients who have T2DM and reported physical activity at least 3 hrs/ week, there was a moderate negative correlation between PHQ9 scores and min/ week of exercise with r = - 0.54 (p=0.057).
Conclusions
In adolescents who have both obesity and T2DM, and who exercised at least 3 hrs/week, increased exercise was associated with lower total PHQ 9 scores. Promoting physical exercise in depressed adolescents with obesity and T2DM can improve symptoms of depression.

142. When Do Decision-Makers Listen to AI? Human-Likeness Cues and Perceived AI–Task Fit
Nicolas Tamm | Technical University of Munich (TUM) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Nicolas Tamm | Technical University of Munich (TUM) | Germany
Dr. Anely Bekbergenova
Prof. Dr. Claudia Peus

Despite recent advances in AI and their objective predictive superiority to humans, decision-makers systematically discount advice from algorithmic sources, thus exhibiting algorithmic aversion bias. Research points out that factors such as algorithm design characteristics, user attitudes, and task attributes are key contributors to this bias; however, there is a lack of coherent predictors with consistent outcomes to predict what contributes to this bias. The current research leverages person–job fit theory, which conceptualizes fit as a perception-based judgment and has been shown to reliably predict downstream attitudes and behavior. Extending this logic, we define AI–Task Fit as users’ perceived alignment between an AI system’s inferred capabilities and the requirements they attribute to a decision task. Furthermore, research shows that individuals respond to displays of human-like cues (i.e., appearance, vocal features) by artificial intelligence. We thus investigate the impact of anthropomorphism and the display of human-like cues on perceived AI-Task fit and AI-advice utilization in a series of three studies. Study 1 is a vignette-based evaluation to establish baseline perceptions of AI–Task Fit. Study 2 extends this approach to an incentivized decision-making task in which the advisor is either human or algorithmic, and Study 3 repeats this while introducing 3 levels of human likeness for the AI advisor. Together, this research provides a novel analytical framework for AI-human interaction and contributes to a better understanding of decision-making with AI advice.

143. Autoimmunität und hormonelle Stressregulation in der adoleszenten Depression: Eine psychoneuroimmunologische Analyse
Leonie Lisette Kühner | Universität Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Leonie Lisette Kühner | Universität Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Reinhild Klein | Universität Tübingen
Lars Libuda | Universität Paderborn
Manuel Föcker | Universität Bochum
Anke Hinney | Universität Duisburg-Essen
Johannes Hebebrand | Universität Duisburg-Essen
Alexandra Kulle | Universitätsklinikum Schleswig Holstein
Paul-Martin Holterhus | Universitätsklinikum Schleswig Holstein
Corinna Grasemann | Universitätsmedizin Mainz
Raphael Hirtz | Helios Universitätsklinikum Wuppertal

Zielsetzung:
Eine Vielzahl an Befunden deuten darauf hin, dass Immun- und Stresssysteme an der Pathophysiologie depressiver Störungen beteiligt sind. Unklar ist jedoch, inwieweit autoimmunologische Prozesse, insbesondere Autoantikörper gegen zentrale Nervensystemstrukturen, mit depressiven Symptomen im Jugendalter assoziiert sind. Diese Studie prüfte (1) Zusammenhänge zwischen Autoantikörpern gegen Schilddrüsenstrukturen (TPO-AK) und zentralnervösen Autoantikörpern sowie (2) Beziehungen zwischen der Aktivität der Hypothalamus-Hypophysen-Nebennierenrinden-(HPA-)Achse, Autoimmunität und Depressionsschwere.
Methoden:
Analysiert wurden Daten aus zwei klinischen Querschnittsstudien mit insgesamt 360 Jugendlichen (11–19 Jahre) mit mindestens leichten depressiven Symptomen (BDI-II > 13), erhoben an der Klinik für Kinder- und Jugendpsychiatrie des LVR-Klinikums Essen. Verglichen wurden (a) depressive Jugendliche mit (N=18) vs. ohne (N=18) erhöhte TPO-AK sowie (b) depressive Jugendliche mit nach Alter, Geschlecht und Reifestadium gematchten gesunden Kontrollen (N=38) hinsichtlich IgM- und IgG-Antikörper gegen zentrale Nervensystemstrukturen (alpha-Tubulin) und Serotonin. Mittels multipler Regressionsanalysen wurden Zusammenhänge der Autoantikörper mit Cortisol und Depressionsschwere geprüft.
Ergebnisse:
Depressive Jugendliche zeigten signifikant höhere Titer aller Autoantikörper im Vergleich zu Kontrollen (p < .005), insbesondere erhöhte ZNS-IgM-Antikörper (p = .003). Es bestanden allerdings keine Unterschiede zwischen Jugendlichen mit und ohne TPO-AK (p = .053–.91) sowie keine signifikanten Zusammenhänge zwischen Antikörpertitern, Cortisol und Depressionsschwere.
Schlussfolgerung:
Die Ergebnisse sprechen für eine immunologische Beteiligung an depressiven Störungen im Jugendalter, insbesondere durch erhöhte ZNS-IgM-Antikörper. Eine Verbindung zu Schilddrüsenautoimmunität oder endokriner Dysregulation zeigte sich nicht. Die Ergebnisse unterstreichen die Bedeutung, biologische Stress- und Immunparameter in psychologischen Modellen der Depressionsentstehung stärker zu berücksichtigen. Weitere Studien sind erforderlich, um die funktionelle Relevanz dieser Antikörper mit verlässlicher Fallzahl und zusätzlicher in-vivo-Analysen zu untersuchen.

144. Der Start in den Arbeitstag: Routinen und Reattachment am Morgen
Dr. Elisa Lopper | Humboldt- Universität zu Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Elisa Lopper | Humboldt- Universität zu Berlin | Germany
Sophie Pöhler
Alexandra Haas
Marilu Tripler-Hornbach

Bevor die erste E-Mail versendet wird oder das erste Meeting stattfindet, hat der (Arbeits)Tag bereit begonnen. Der Übergang zwischen privaten und beruflichen Lebensbereichen am Morgen stellt eine psychologisch bedeutsame Zeit dar, die die Motivation, das Wohlbefinden und die Leistungsfähigkeit von Beschäftigten über den Arbeitstag hinweg prägt. Studien zeigen, dass das sogenannte Reattachment – das mentale Wiederanknüpfen an die Arbeit zu Beginn des Arbeitstages – einen zentralen Prozess für den Übergang zur Arbeit darstellt. Die vorliegende Studie untersucht die Zeit vor dem Reattachment. Ausgehend von der Annahme, dass Routinen den Übergang zwischen Lebensbereichen strukturieren und erleichtern, fokussiert die Studie Morgenroutinen und deren Einfluss auf Reattachment. Wir nehmen an, dass Morgenroutinen Mechanismen darstellen, durch die Beschäftigte die während der arbeitsfreien Zeit gesammelten Ressourcen in arbeitsorientierte kognitive und motivationale Ressourcen umwandeln. Diese helfen wiederum, sich mental auf die Arbeit einzustellen. Insbesondere interessiert uns, welche Morgenroutinen – oder mögliche Störungen – Reattachment fördern oder hemmen. Gleichzeitig werden kontextuelle Bedingungen sowie (berufliche) Ressourcen und Anforderungen hinsichtlich ihres Einflusses auf den täglichen Ressourcentransfer berücksichtigt. Die explorative Studie basiert auf semi-strukturierten Interviews mit 34 Beschäftigten in Deutschland. Die Datenauswertung erfolgt mittels Thematischer Analyse (Braun & Clarke, 2006) unter Kombination deduktiver und induktiver Ansätze. Zur Sicherstellung der Reliabilität und Interpretationstiefe werden vier unabhängige Kodierende am Kodierprozess beteiligt sein. Die bis zum Kongress vorliegenden Ergebnisse sollen Kategorien und Muster von Morgenroutinen identifizieren, die den Beginn des Arbeitsalltags erleichtern. Die Befunde dienen als Grundlage für zukünftige quantitative Studien sowie der Entwicklung von Interventionsansätzen.

145. Mechanisms of Dynamic Belief Updating in Children and Adolescents with Anxiety Disorders
Johannes M. Lehnen | Friedrich Schiller University Jena | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Johannes M. Lehnen | Friedrich Schiller University Jena | Germany
Prof. Dr. Julia Asbrand | Friedrich Schiller University Jena

Making inferences and predictions in uncertain, dynamically changing environments is a core aspect of human learning, particularly in threatening contexts. This requires forming internal beliefs about environmental states and updating them when systematic changes occur, a process known as dynamic belief updating (DynBU). Patients with mental disorders often show dysfunctional or negatively biased learning. Anxiety disorders (ADs), for example, are characterized by aberrant emotional-associative learning and heightened fear generalization. As childhood and adolescence are critical periods for the development of ADs, understanding DynBU in both typical development and the emergence of these disorders is essential. Consequently, this project investigates alterations in DynBU in ADs with a developmental focus, studying children and adolescents aged 10–17 years, as well as a community pilot sample of children aged 8–9 years. Based on prior literature, we hypothesize excessive learning rates in ADs, particularly during stable task phases.
To ensure valid classification into anxiety and control groups, participants undergo a structured clinical interview and a comprehensive assessment battery. The main sample is aimed at a total of 64 participants. DynBU is assessed using two gamified predictive inference tasks, the “confetti-cannon task” and the “predator task”, which measure belief formation and updating in volatile environments. In addition, heart-rate variability and pupillometry are recorded as physiological indices of DynBU.
First, very preliminary results suggest no differences in dynamic learning rate adjustment between participants with ADs and healthy controls. This is in line with recent evidence from sub-clinical samples.

146. Tool or Teammate? The Role of Anthropomorphic Framing in Shaping Trust in AI
Philip Porwol | Paderborn University | Germany
Dr. Tobias Peters | Paderborn University
Show details
Authors:
Philip Porwol | Paderborn University | Germany
Dr. Tobias Peters | Paderborn University
Prof. Dr. Ingrid Scharlau | Paderborn University

Within the domain of artificial intelligence (AI), it is common to anthropomorphize AI applications, i.e., to attribute human characteristics to them. Using human-like voices or appearances are prominent examples. Similarly, the language employed to explain and describe AI applications is anthropomorphized. AI is fed with data and trains on it; it learns, acts, and decides. While anthropomorphic features are well researched, less is known about the effects of using such anthropomorphizing metaphors when describing AI. Previous research identified that anthropomorphic appearance increases the trust of people interacting with AI applications.

To test whether this translates to anthropomorphizing metaphors used in descriptions of AI, we conducted a pre-registered online experiment (N = 1083) comparing two conditions in which an AI application is either linguistically anthropomorphized or not. Participants read a fictitious newspaper article about the usage of an AI application in radiology that was either introduced as a new teammate or as a tool for clinicians. In this metaphor framing experiment, participants had to judge their trust and distrust towards the AI application.

Contrary to our expectations, the reported trust and distrust did not differ significantly between conditions. Further subgroup analyses considering domain expertise also did not indicate a difference in the reported (dis)trust.

These results suggest that metaphorical language alone may be insufficient to shift (dis)trust in a high-stakes context, like healthcare. Further, the absence of significant results indicates boundaries for metaphorical framing effects in general, and specifically on trust.

147. Predictors of Enjoyment of Sexual Self-Expression in Women: The Role of Ideological and Psychological Factors
Prof. Dr. Sandra Schladitz | Hochschule Fresenius Heidelberg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Sandra Schladitz | Hochschule Fresenius Heidelberg | Germany
Lena Franziska Roesler
Dr. Marie Drüge

Enjoyment of Sexual Self-Expression is considered an important component of sexual well-being and sexual agency. Feminist psychology emphasizes the role of gender ideology and feminist identification in promoting sexual autonomy. At the same time, embodiment-based approaches highlight the importance of body-related self-evaluations for positive sexual experiences. This study tries to determine which of these factors are more strongly associated with enjoyment of sexual self-expression.

It was assumed that
a) as positive ideological factors, feminist identity and feminist attitudes correlate positively with Enjoyment of Sexual Self-Expression,
b) as positive psychological factors, self-esteem and body image correlate positively with Enjoyment of Sexual Self-Expression, and
c) as a negative psychological factor, body-dysmorphic disorder correlates negatively with Enjoyment of Sexual Self-Expression.

A sample of 152 young women (M = 22.00, SD = 2.36, range: 18 to 31 years) completed an online survey including established questionnaires on the ideological and psychological factors, as well as a newly developed measure for Enjoyment of Sexual Self-Expression.

Multiple regression analyses revealed no significant effects of ideological factors: neither feminist identity nor feminist attitudes predicted Enjoyment of Sexual Self-Expression. In contrast, psychological factors showed effects in the expected directions, with higher self-esteem and more positive body image predicting greater enjoyment, and body-dysmorphic symptoms predicting lower enjoyment.

These findings suggest that Enjoyment of Sexual Self-Expression is more closely linked to micro-level variables based on self-experience than to macro-level variables like ideology. Feminist beliefs may serve as a societal backdrop for female self-expression, but prove insufficient to explain personal behavior.

148. Too Good to Be True? A Simulation Study Illustrating the Risks of Feature Selection Leakage in Cross-Validation.
Vivienne Désirée Walser | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Vivienne Désirée Walser | Switzerland
Dr. Caren Hasler

Psychological research is often faced with data sets of limited size and the need to specify which potential predictor variables should be included in an analysis model. Cross-validation is a widely used tool in this context, for estimating predictive performance and carrying out model selection without the need for new data. However, for cross-validation to work properly, all steps, including feature selection, need to be applied to the training data within each resampling fold. In practice, this requirement is often violated, leading to what is commonly called data leakage. For instance, feature selection is sometimes performed on the full dataset prior to cross-validation, allowing information from the test data to influence the choice of the final analysis model. This has been shown to lead to overly optimistic results. Using a controlled simulation framework, we study the impact of data leakage induced by feature selection on cross-validation-based estimates of misclassification error. We compare two pipelines: a correct pipeline in which stepwise feature selection is repeated independently within each training fold and an incorrect pipeline in which stepwise feature selection precedes cross-validation. By contrasting these correct and incorrect pipelines across different scenarios, the study illustrates how and under which conditions feature selection leakage leads to over-optimistic results, which can affect the substantive interpretation of the research findings. The study's findings therefore can serve as an orientation for researchers in psychology on how to perform feature selection via cross-validation in a valid and safe manner.

149. Emotional Intelligence in Leadership: A Qualitative Comparison of Theory and Leadership Practice
Lea Cäsar | Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt (THI) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Lea Cäsar | Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt (THI) | Germany
Dr. Huong Pham | Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt (THI) | Germany

In increasingly dynamic and complex organizational environments, emotional intelligence is widely regarded as a crucial leadership competence. Although numerous studies have shown links between emotional intelligence and effective leadership (Kerr et al., 2006; Kour & Ansari, 2024; Miao et al., 2018), we still know little about how these theoretical dimensions translate into everyday leadership behavior. It also remains unclear which aspects leaders actually rely on when navigating real organizational challenges.
This study draws on the model by Mayer and Salovey (1997) and Goleman’s (1995) model, both of which provide distinct conceptualizations of emotional intelligence. To explore their practical relevance, qualitative semi-structured interviews were conducted with experienced leaders from several industries (N = 5) and analyzed using structured content analysis.
The findings reveal that emotional intelligence is recognized as a meaningful resource in challenging leadership situations, particularly in conflict management, the communication of organizational change, and relationship-building. At the same time, the analysis shows that many emotional processes are guided by intuition rather than a conscious application of the theoretical dimensions. Leaders rely predominantly on tacit, experience-based knowledge, which only partially aligns with established models.
By contrasting theoretical constructs with everyday leadership behavior, this study contributes to a more practice-oriented understanding of emotional intelligence. It highlights which facets are genuinely impactful in organizational contexts and identifies blind spots that may hinder its systematic development.

150. Die OGRS 3 im Jugendstrafvollzug: Eine empirische Untersuchung zur Prognose von Rückfälligkeit und intramuralem Fehlverhalten
Richard Beyer | Technische Universität Braunschweig - Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Show details
Author:
Richard Beyer | Technische Universität Braunschweig - Institut für Psychologie | Germany

Ziel der Untersuchung war die Überprüfung der prognostischen Validität der Offender Group Reconviction Scale 3 (OGRS 3) im Jugendstrafvollzug hinsichtlich krimineller Rückfälle sowie erstmals auch intramuralen Fehlverhaltens (IMF). Grundlage bildete die retrospektive Analyse von N = 592 inhaftierten Jugendstraftätern, für die OGRS 3-Werte berechnet und mittels Receiver-Operating-Characteristic- sowie Kalibrierungsanalysen hinsichtlich ihrer prognostischen Güte überprüft wurden. Die OGRS 3 sagte sowohl allgemeine kriminelle Rückfälle (AKR) als auch gewalttätige Rückfälle (GR) signifikant vorher. Für die Beobachtungszeiträume von einem Jahr (AKR: AUC = 0,611; GR: AUC = 0,610), zwei Jahren (AKR: AUC = 0,604; GR: AUC = 0,614) und fünf Jahren nach Haftentlassung (AKR: AUC = 0,613; GR: AUC = 0,618) fanden sich kleine Effekte. Die Kalibrierungsanalysen zeigten systematische Abweichungen zwischen den von der OGRS 3 vorhergesagten und den tatsächlich beobachteten Rückfallraten. Bei der Analyse von IMF zeigte sich eine moderate Diskriminationsfähigkeit für sämtliche Fehlverhaltensweisen (AUC = 0,668). Für schwerwiegende (AUC = 0,582) und gewalttätige intramurale Fehlverhaltensweisen (AUC = 0,570) zeigten sich kleine Effekte. Insgesamt belegt die Untersuchung eine stabile, aber begrenzte prognostische Validität der OGRS 3. Für eine verlässliche Anwendung im Jugendstrafvollzug ist eine spezifische Neukalibrierung des Instruments sowie dessen Einbettung in ein multimodales Diagnostikkonzept unerlässlich.

151. Developmental change through different eyes: Parental and child perceptions of sibling relationships
Dr. Tina Schiele | University of Munich (LMU) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Tina Schiele | University of Munich (LMU) | Germany
María Valcárcel Jiménez | Germany
Öykü Camligüney | Germany
Frank Niklas | Germany

Sibling relationships are central for young children’s socioemotional development, with sibling gender constellation potentially influencing relationship quality. Prior research showed that sister pairs typically exhibit warmer interactions, whereas brother pairs and mixed-gender dyads tend to display more conflict (Buist et al., 2013). Additionally, perceptions of sibling relationships differ by informant: parents and children generally align in evaluating harmonious relationships but diverge in assessing conflict, with parents often underestimating conflictual dynamics (Howe et al., 2011). The present study investigated whether (1) parents and children differ in their assessments of warmth and conflict across sibling constellations, (2) perceived warmth and conflict vary by sibling constellation, and (3) the size of discrepancies between parent and child assessments change over a one-year interval. N=271 children (MAge_T1=94.95/SD=4.49) and their parents (86.5% mothers) rated sibling warmth and conflict at the end of first and second grade. Linear mixed effect models included informant, sibling constellation, and time as fixed effects with dyad as random effect. Parents and children differed significantly in their ratings, with parents perceiving sibling relationships as both warmer and more conflictual than children, regardless of gender constellations. Discrepancies in warmth were largest in mixed-gender dyads, while differences in conflict were strongest in sister pairs. Across one year, parent-child differences in warmth increased, whereas differences in conflict decreased. These findings show that parents and children perceive sibling relationships differently, with parents reporting more nuances. The results highlight the importance of collecting assessments from multiple informants to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of sibling relationship dynamics.

Prosocial and Antisocial Behavior in Multiple Social Categorization Settings: Evidence from the US and Brazil
Bernhard Schubach | FernUniversitaet in Hagen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Bernhard Schubach | FernUniversitaet in Hagen | Germany
Pinar Uğurlar | Özyeğin University, Istanbul
Marc Jekel | University of Cologne
Angela R. Dorrough | FernUniversitaet in Hagen

Intergroup bias, the tendency to favor ingroup over outgroup members, is pervasive. Research shows that increasing the number of shared group memberships mitigates this effect when two groups are salient. We extend previous findings by testing the effects of multiple categorizations of three groups. We tested in three high-powered, preregistered, and incentivized experiments whether people are more prosocial and less antisocial as the number of shared group memberships increases. In Studies 1a and 1b (n = 191 and 231), U.S. participants transferred more money to others as the number of shared group memberships increased. Study 2 (n = 314) replicated this effect in a culturally different sample (i.e., Brazilian). Additionally, participants took less money from others as the number of group memberships increased. The effect on prosocial behavior was quadratic, whereas the effect on antisocial behavior was linear. Overall, multiple categorizations mitigated intergroup bias across two national contexts and two interpersonal behaviors.

Sharing and Memory: Remembering What We Share on Social Media
Luise Metzger | Universität Mannheim | Germany
