Jaskirat Bajwa | Kwantlen Polytechnic University
Gordon Pennycook | Cornell University
Daniel Bernstein | Kwantlen Polytechnic University
Edgar Erdfelder | Universität Mannheim

Our sharing behavior shapes our collective memory. We wondered what people remember about their sharing behavior. In three online experiments (total N = 695), we explored recognition and source memory effects of sharing news headlines on social media. Unbeknownst to participants, half the headlines were real and half were fake. Participants first chose which headlines to share. After a retention interval (10 minutes in Experiments 1 and 2; 1 week in Experiment 3), participants completed an unexpected old-new recognition test and indicated whether they initially shared each recognized headline. Multinomial processing tree analyses revealed no impact of headline truth on memory parameters, while true headlines were shared more often than fake headlines. In Experiments 1 and 2, while recognition was significantly better for shared headlines, source memory for shared vs. not shared was high for all recognized headlines. In Experiment 3, as expected, recognition memory declined for the longer retention interval but preserved better recognition of shared headlines. Interestingly, source memory declined more for shared compared to not shared headlines. These results are in line with the idea that shared headlines are tagged in memory, thereby increasing distinctiveness which boosts recognition memory and additionally provides memory cues indicating whether a recognized headline was shared vs. not shared (tag retrieved vs. not retrieved). Retrievability of such tags decreases across time, explaining poor source memory for shared headlines after one week. Hierarchical MPT analyses additionally suggest that analytic cognitive styles moderate these effects by improving memory and diminishing sharing of fake headlines.

Emotional (In)Congruency in Source Memory: When Negative Words Come From Happy People
Dr. Nikoletta Symeonidou | University of Mannheim | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Nikoletta Symeonidou | University of Mannheim | Germany
Dr. Meike Kroneisen | RPTU University Kaiserslautern-Landau
Anna W. Tieftrunk | RWTH Aachen University

Previous research has shown that source memory is enhanced for sources that are incongruent with schematic expectations. Across three online experiments, we investigated whether such incongruency effects also occur when an emotional schema is violated, that is, when items and sources mismatch in their valence. In Experiment 1 (N = 97), normed positive and negative words (items) were paired with normed happy, neutral, or sad faces (sources), and participants incidentally encoded the material by rating word pleasantness. Experiment 2 (N = 108) replicated Experiment 1 to evaluate robustness. Experiment 3 employed the same procedure with two modifications: the neutral source was removed to amplify expectancy violation, and encoding was manipulated such that one group (n = 108) rated word pleasantness (as in Experiments 1 and 2), while another group (n = 108) rated item-source-fit. Across experiments, multinomial analysis revealed that source memory was highest for happy faces paired with positive words, indicating a congruency – rather than incongruency – effect for positive valence. When source memory failed, participants preferably guessed the neutral face. When the neutral option was not chosen (or unavailable, cf. Experiment 3) they preferentially selected the valence-congruent face, suggesting that a valence schema was activated during retrieval. Furthermore, in Experiment 3, item-source-fit ratings showed that positive–happy pairs were judged as more fitting than negative–sad pairs, whereas no differences emerged between incongruent pairs. Thus, we propose that the congruency effect for positive item-source pairs might rely on the higher associative potential of positive material.

Wording of Questions Influences Eyewitness Reports Only in the Absence of Event Memory
Lars Köchling | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Lars Köchling | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany
Dr. Danna Oomen | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg
Teresa Nguyen | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg
Valerie Ferrari | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg
Prof. Dr. Oliver Genschow | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg

It is widely accepted that subtle differences in the wording of questions can influence eyewitness reports. One of the most influential studies supporting this claim was conducted by Loftus and Palmer in 1974. The authors showed that simply replacing a single word in a question about a car accident that participants witnessed changes how fast they remembered the cars to be. Despite its widespread impact for different research disciplines, close replication attempts of this misinformation effect have been sparse and evidence for it inconclusive. We conducted five high-powered and preregistered experiments (total N = 5,779) to closely replicate and extend the original research. Overall, we did not find support for the idea that the wording of questions asked about a witnessed car accident influence estimates of vehicular speed (Hedges’ g = 0.08) or related impressions. Only in cases where participants had no active memory of the accident, we found that more drastic words describing the accident were related to higher speed estimates and accident severity. These findings indicate that although slight variations in questions’ wordings influence reports about accidents, mere changes in wording cannot overwrite the memory representation of an actually witnessed accident.

Evaluative Conditioning with Multiple Unconditioned Stimuli – The Presentation Format Matters
Florian Weber | Ruhr University Bochum | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Florian Weber | Ruhr University Bochum | Germany
Hans Alves | Ruhr University Bochum | Germany
Tobias Vogel | Darmstadt University of Applied Sciences | Germany
Moritz Ingendahl | Ruhr University Bochum | Germany

Evaluative Conditioning (EC) – making a neutral conditioned stimulus (CS) more/less likable by pairing it with a positive/negative unconditioned stimulus (US) – is a well-established and widely researched effect in attitude research. While most studies on EC have focused on pairing a CS with a single US, some have examined pairings with multiple different USs. These studies differ in how a CS is paired with multiple USs: simultaneously (all USs are paired with the CS at the same time) or sequentially (each US is paired individually with the CS). Across two preregistered online experiments (N = 600), we investigated whether these two presentation formats cause different integration rules governing the CS attitudes. In both experiments, CSs appeared with either one extremely positive (negative) US, one mildly positive (negative) US, or multiple USs, specifically one extremely positive (negative) US and three additional mildly positive (negative) USs. Importantly, these multiple USs either appeared simultaneously or sequentially with the corresponding CS. We found that presentation format indeed led to different integration rules: When multiple USs appeared simultaneously with a CS, conditioned attitudes followed the average valence of all paired USs, whereas a sequential presentation resulted in a peak effect, where CS attitudes followed the valence of the most extreme paired US. Memory data further suggests that the presentation format induces different memory representations of CS-US pairs. These results imply that practical applications of EC (e.g., advertising) differ in their effectiveness depending on the number, affective quality, and presentation format of stimulus pairings.

Current challenges and future directions of AI from a human-centered and interdisciplinary perspective
Chair(s) PD Dr. Magnus Liebherr (University of Duisburg-Essen)
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Annette Kluge (Ruhr-Universität Bochum)
Verena Nitsch (RWTH Aachen)
Prof. Dr. Janet Wessler (Fresenius University of Applied Sciences)
Prof. Dr. Tobias Bruckmann (University of Duisburg-Essen)
Dr. Katharina Weitz (Fraunhofer Heinnrich Hertz Institute)
Prof. Dr.-Ing. Andreas Scholz (Otto-von-Guericke-Universität Magdeburg, IEPS-MTK)
Room: Room C
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Panel discussion
Duration: 60 Minutes

Automation and artificial intelligence are fundamentally transforming how humans interact with technology across work and everyday life. Addressing these challenges requires dialogue across disciplinary boundaries, not because our fields differ, but because we share fundamental values that can only be realized through collaborative effort. This panel brings together representatives from psychology (DGPs), work science (GfA), engineering (VDI), AI research (DFKI), computer science (GI), and industry, united by common commitments to human-centered technology development. Across our disciplines, we share the conviction that technology must serve human capabilities and dignity, that ethical considerations are foundational to good design, and that those affected by technological systems deserve meaningful participation in their development. These values, which are rooted in the German and European approach to technology, provide the foundation for our dialogue. The panel explores how these shared commitments take shape across different perspectives: How do these shared commitments guide our work across psychology, ergonomics, engineering, and computer science? What insights, methods, and criteria does each field bring to ensuring safe, transparent, and participatory AI systems? We discuss concrete cases where interdisciplinary collaboration has succeeded in creating solutions that honor our shared values in ways unattainable within single disciplines. The intended outcome is to establish actionable pathways for collaborative research and practice, grounded in our common commitment to human dignity, self-determination, and the public good, that address the technical, human, organizational, and societal dimensions of automation and AI more effectively than isolated disciplinary approaches.

Produktivität, Qualität, Pluralität: Was zählt in der Psychologie als wissenschaftliche Exzellenz?
Chair(s) Dr. Gordon Feld (Zentralinstitut für Seelische Gesundheit)
Maximilian Frank (Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München (LMU))
Prof. Dr. Sebastian Ocklenburg (MSH Medical School Hamburg)
Chair(s) Anne Gärtner (TU Dresden)
Prof. Dr. Birgit Spinath (Psychologisches Institut)
Dr. Tanja Kollei (German Research Foundation / Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG))
Prof. Dr. Cornelius J. König (Universität des Saarlandes)
Dr. Matthias F.J. Sperl (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Psychologie (DGPs))
Prof. Dr. Paul Pauli (Julius-Maximilians-University Würzburg)
Room: Workshop 0
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Panel discussion
Duration: 75 Minutes

Exzellenz ist zu einer zentralen Leitkategorie des Wissenschaftssystems geworden – nicht zuletzt im Kontext der Exzellenzstrategie in Deutschland. Doch was genau gilt in der Psychologie als exzellente Wissenschaft? Wird Exzellenz primär über quantifizierbare Produktivität – Publikationen, Drittmittel, Sichtbarkeit – definiert, oder müssen auch andere Dimensionen wissenschaftlicher Qualität stärker berücksichtigt werden, etwa epistemische Sorgfalt und Reproduzierbarkeit, Offenheit und Transparenz, Kooperation und Forschungsinfrastrukturen, Lehre und Nachwuchsentwicklung sowie institutionelle Arbeitsbedingungen?
Wir diskutieren, welche Exzellenzkriterien in der Praxis tatsächlich wirksam sind, welche Anreize sie erzeugen und welche Folgen sie für Wissenserzeugung, Karriereverläufe und die Entwicklung der Psychologie haben. Vertreten sind die DFG, Expert:innen zur Evaluation wissenschaftlicher Leistung, Mitglieder der Hochschulleitungen, Nachwuchswissenschaftler:innen sowie Akteur:innen aus Wissenschaftsrat und Fachgesellschaften.
Ziel ist es, konkurrierende Verständnisse von Exzellenz sichtbar zu machen und Optionen für eine pluralere und zukunftsfähige Bestimmung wissenschaftlicher Exzellenz aufzuzeigen.
